# MyPortfolio

[![CI](https://github.com/SebastianLopezO/MyPortfolio-SOLID/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/SebastianLopezO/MyPortfolio-SOLID/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![Publish Docker Image](https://github.com/SebastianLopezO/MyPortfolio-SOLID/actions/workflows/packaging.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/SebastianLopezO/MyPortfolio-SOLID/actions/workflows/packaging.yml)
[![Production Checks](https://github.com/SebastianLopezO/MyPortfolio-SOLID/actions/workflows/production.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/SebastianLopezO/MyPortfolio-SOLID/actions/workflows/production.yml)
[![PageSpeed Insights](https://img.shields.io/badge/PageSpeed-check-36BFB1)](https://pagespeed.web.dev/analysis?url=https://sebastianlopezo.page/en)

Bilingual portfolio of **Sebastián López Osorno**, backend and integration developer, live at
[sebastianlopezo.page](https://sebastianlopezo.page). This repository is its Astro and SolidJS edition, migrated from
the React one with the same pages, content, design, tests and deployment (
see [Migration from React](#migration-from-react)).

- Pages generated by Astro in English and Spanish (`/en`, `/es`), whose interactive parts are SolidJS islands.
- One general profile plus five role views that reorder and emphasize the same content, each reached by its own
  address (there is no switcher on the page).
- Thirty-two project pages: five full case studies (integration platform, SmartPot, GoPoli, MarTech, email
  signatures) and twenty-seven lighter pages for the other work, product and education projects, each with its
  achievements, architecture, figures and repositories, its decisions shown whole as a flow from the problem to the
  solution and its cost, and links to the job, program, organization and certifications behind it; a projects index by
  category and a
  filterable archive of public repositories.
- A page for every job, program, certification and GitHub organization (4, 5, 29 and 10, each collection with its
  index): titles and role changes, a timeline built from the facts that filters by kind and groups by year, projects,
  recommendations, courses, each certificate as its issuer publishes it and where it shows in the work, and the
  commits in each organization.
- Shareable role links; a locked one keeps its view on every link the visitor follows.
- Complete SEO per page: titles and descriptions that fit a search result (a build test checks them), canonical and
  `hreflang` links, an Open Graph image for every project, job, program, certification and organization, JSON-LD with
  each project's screens and each certificate, a sitemap with image entries that dates each page by the day its
  text last changed, robots, and an `llms.txt` that maps the English pages, the resumes and the contact for language
  models from the titles and descriptions the pages already carry.
- An interactive journey: a transit-style SVG map of education and work from 2019 to the 2030 goals, a capability
  heatmap per year, a focus radar of what is core, growing, exploring or paused, and the next steps (data science
  specialization, cybersecurity master's) tied to the UN 2030 Agenda goals.
- A client-side profile assistant that answers from the portfolio content, with no AI service: about thirty kinds of
  question (each job, program and project by name, certifications by topic, services, reasons to hire, GitHub
  activity, availability), each answer linking to the page that tells more, with follow-up questions and a catalog of
  the 42 questions it was built for.
- Dark design system with WCAG AA contrast checked in CI.
- Motion the browser draws from CSS: parts that rise as they enter the screen, a reading progress bar on the header,
  pages that fade into each other and figures that count up once, all of it off for a reader who asks for less motion.
- Shipped as a ~30 MB unprivileged nginx image on GHCR and deployed with Docker Compose.

Lighthouse CI holds every build to 100 in accessibility and SEO, 95 or more in best practices and warns under 90 in
performance (`lighthouserc.json`); the **Production Checks** workflow runs it again against production after every
deploy. Performance varies with the runner.

`?locked=true` and every internal link keeps that view as well.

## Getting started

Requirements: Node.js 22.18 or newer and pnpm 10 (`corepack enable`).

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm dev        # http://localhost:8080
pnpm build      # prerendered site in dist/
pnpm preview    # serves dist/ with the same rules as production on http://127.0.0.1:4173
```

| Script                         | Purpose                                                                                                                                              |
|--------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `pnpm lint` / `pnpm typecheck` | ESLint and TypeScript checks                                                                                                                         |
| `pnpm test`                    | Unit tests (content parity, paths, role views, SEO, assistant)                                                                                       |
| `pnpm test:dist`               | Checks the built pages, crawler files and size budgets                                                                                               |
| `pnpm test:e2e`                | Playwright tests on desktop and mobile against `dist/`                                                                                               |
| `pnpm check:contrast`          | Verifies WCAG contrast of the design tokens, in the light and the dark theme                                                                         |
| `pnpm check:links`             | Requests every external link in the content and reports broken ones (run before a release)                                                           |
| `pnpm illustrations`           | Redraws the project, hero, skill and page illustrations into `public/illustrations` from `scripts/illustrations` (`--sheet` writes a contact sheet)  |
| `pnpm images`                  | Regenerates AVIF/WebP variants from `assets-src/`                                                                                                    |
| `pnpm metrics`                 | Copies the latest GitHub and WakaTime figures from the profile repository into `src/content/shared/github-stats.json` (CI builds do it on their own) |
| `pnpm og`                      | Regenerates the Open Graph images and the Apple touch icon                                                                                           |
| `pnpm resumes`                 | Renders the resume PDFs and their previews from the OhMyCV sources in the `SebastianLopezO` repository; previews need poppler, or Docker to run it   |

## How it works

```
src/
  pages/                [...path].astro generates every page from lib/paths; 404.astro
  layouts/Page.astro    the document: head, theme script, inlined styles
  islands/              PageIsland (one part of a page), the parts each island loads, the client renderer, the
                        build-time registry of every part and the head of each page
  views/                project, detail and 404 page bodies
  components/
    layout/             header, footer, sections, language switcher
    sections/           one component per page section; below the hero each loads in its own chunk
    assistant/          launcher (an island) and lazy panel
    journey/            journey map, capability heatmap, focus radar and horizon (lazy chunk)
    case-study/         layered architecture diagram, figures and screenshots (lazy chunk)
    projects/           project card shared by the home section and the projects index
    page/               article parts shared by the project and detail pages: sections, page index, breadcrumb
    ui/                 form controls, carousel, toggle and the Lucide icons as static templates
  content/
    shared/             language-neutral facts: dates, tech, links, counts, role tags, projects, archive
    case-studies/       case study text in both languages (lazy chunk)
    project-pages/      text of the other project pages in both languages (lazy chunk)
    detail-pages/       text of the job, program, certification and organization pages (lazy chunk)
    en/, es/            localized text, checked against the Content type; startup.ts is what hydrates first
    roles.ts            section order, stack and priorities of each role view
  context/              language and role providers (accessors, so a role change updates in place)
  lib/                  paths, SEO head, sitemap, role ordering, formatting, assistant engine
  routes/               the location of a page and its links
  styles/               design tokens and global styles
scripts/                build and post-build, image, OG and resume generators, static server
nginx/                  production server config
e2e/, tests/            browser and build output tests
```

**Rendering.** `pnpm build` (`scripts/build.ts`) runs Astro, which renders the 182 pages (12 profile views, 2 project
indexes, 64 project pages, 8 detail indexes and 96 detail pages) and `404.html` with the CSS inlined, then
`scripts/postbuild.ts`, which writes `sitemap.xml`, `robots.txt`, `llms.txt` and the root's language redirect, hashes
each page's text into `page-dates.json` (a page keeps the `lastmod` the live site gave it until its text changes), and
pre-compresses everything with Brotli and gzip. Every page is one catch-all route, `src/pages/[...path].astro`, built
from the same parts: a part without a client directive is plain HTML that ships no JavaScript (the skip link, the
highlights, the footer, the WhatsApp button, the 404), and a part with one is a Solid island (`islands/PageIsland.tsx`)
that hydrates on its own. Like the earlier editions, nothing loads before the page has settled: the header, the hero,
the assistant's launcher, the body of a project or detail page and the part that loads the web fonts hydrate in the
first idle period after both the `load` event and the first paint (`client:settled`, `islands/settled.ts`), and each
home section then waits until it comes within 600 px of the screen. The pages are complete without JavaScript, and the
first paint uses fallback faces with matching metrics, so the web fonts' swap does not move the layout.

**Content.** Facts live once in `content/shared`; text lives in `content/en` and `content/es`. Collections are keyed
by id, so a missing translation is a type error, and a unit test fails if both languages drift apart. The years of
experience are computed from the first job (August 2022) at build time.

**Islands.** Each island wraps its part in what the single-page app gave the whole page once: the location, the
language with `content/{en,es}/startup.ts` (head, header, hero and figures) and the role view (`islands/shell.tsx`).
Its props are only the part's name, the language, the path and the view, so the page carries no serialized state. In
the browser an island's component and copy load in chunks of their own (`islands/parts.ts`, `content/sections.ts`)
before Solid hydrates it (`islands/client.ts` wraps Astro's Solid renderer for that), so every island hydrates in one
synchronous pass over its prerendered HTML. A section's chunk resolves only with the copy it reads
(`components/sections/section-loaders.ts`), so its components read the copy synchronously.
`<html data-hydrated="true">` appears once the islands of the first screen have hydrated, and each home section marks
itself the same way (`lib/ready.ts`).

**Projects.** Every project has its facts in `content/shared/projects.ts` (category, dates, stack, links, figures,
diagram and the archive organization that holds its repositories) and its card text in `content/{en,es}/projects.ts`.
Five of them are full case studies, with facts in `content/shared/case-studies.ts` and text in
`content/case-studies/{en,es}.ts`; the other twenty-seven pages take their text from `content/project-pages/{en,es}.ts`.
The slugs, and the projects each job links to, live in `content/shared/project-links.ts`. The project pages are
generated like the profile pages; their body is an island whose code and text load in chunks of their own
(`content/project-copy.ts`), with the head builders in `lib/seo-projects.ts`. Each page has its
own Open Graph image, generated by `pnpm og` (`case-*.jpg` for the case studies, `project-*.jpg` for the rest).

**Detail pages.** The jobs, programs, certifications and organizations reuse their facts in `content/shared` and the
home sections' text; what only their pages tell (positions, intros, areas, courses, issuers) lives in
`content/detail-pages/{en,es}.ts`, and the commits per organization in `content/shared/organization-activity.ts`.
`lib/details.ts` relates them (the projects of a job, the recommendations from it, the certifications earned while it
lasted, the jobs and programs going on when a certification was earned), so a page never states a link the facts do
not hold, and the timelines are built from the same facts. The slugs live in `content/shared/detail-links.ts`; the
pages render like the project pages (`views/DetailPages.tsx`, `islands/parts/detail-body.tsx`), with
their heads in `lib/seo-details.ts`. Every job, program, certification and organization has an Open
Graph image of its own (`experience-*.jpg`, `education-*.jpg`, `certifications-*.jpg`, `organizations-*.jpg`); a
certification's image shows the certificate when the page has a copy of it.

**Journey.** Milestones, capability levels, the radar and the GitHub activity per year live in
`content/shared/journey.ts`; planned dates and future levels are targets and are drawn dashed. The section is
prerendered with the page, and like every section its code and its text (`content/journey-copy.ts`) load in their own
chunk, so they do not count against the startup budget.

**Role lock.** The role comes from the URL path and the lock from `?locked=true`. Every internal link keeps the lock,
also the links of a section followed before it hydrates (`lib/lock.ts`). Nothing is stored in the browser.

## Migration from React

The edition came in two steps, each checked against the React build: SolidJS on the same Vite pipeline first, then Astro
with SolidJS islands. It keeps the React edition's markup, classes, content, routes and tests; the components were
ported one by one. Comparing the HTML of all 182 pages and the 404 element by element against the React build (ignoring
only Solid's `data-hk` keys, Astro's `<astro-island>` wrappers and scripts, generated ids and hashed asset names) finds
no difference in the head, the structured data, the text, the links or the attributes, and `page-dates.json` hashes
every page as before, so the sitemap keeps its dates. The unit, build and end-to-end suites pass in what they check; the
end-to-end tests scroll to a home section before using it, as a reader does, since it hydrates as it comes near. What
changed:

- **Rendering.** Astro generates the pages with Solid's server renderer, and only the islands hydrate. Solid's
  hydration is written for one root, so two steps before each island make it work island by island
  (`islands/client.ts`): its code and copy load first, because Solid keeps the nodes left to hydrate in one registry
  per page that each island's hydration starts afresh; and its hydration starts again, because Solid takes the first
  event it handles as the end of hydration and would otherwise render the islands that come later afresh. Astro's own
  `client:idle` starts loading while the page is still parsing; `client:settled` keeps the earlier editions' timing,
  after the `load` event and the first paint, so Lighthouse does not count the islands' scripts against the first paint.
- **Navigation.** Every page is its own document, so a role change, like any other link, loads the page of that view
  instead of re-rendering the open one. The
  locked view travels on every internal link, also before a section hydrates (`lib/lock.ts`), and the role view rides
  on the click that opens a project or detail page (`lib/role-links.ts`).
- **Reactivity.** Components run once and the providers hand out accessors, so the `?from=` view a project or detail
  page learns after hydration reaches every part that reads it, such as the way back, because they read it inside JSX.
- **Dependencies.** `react`, `react-dom`, `lucide-react` and `clsx` are gone: the 31 icons are static templates in
  `components/ui/icons.tsx` and `cn()` is a local helper. The runtime dependencies are `astro`, `@astrojs/solid-js`,
  `solid-js` and the three font packages; `eslint-plugin-solid` replaces the React hooks rules and Vitest runs a jsdom
  project and a Node project for the server render.
- **CSP.** Astro's island runtime, the `client:settled` directive and Solid's `HydrationScript` are inline scripts, each
  allowed by its hash (`nginx/security-headers.conf`).

Measured on the same content (`pnpm build`, gzip level 9; SolidJS + Vite is the first step, kept for reference):

| Measure                                              | React 19 | SolidJS + Vite | Astro + SolidJS |
|------------------------------------------------------|---------:|---------------:|----------------:|
| JavaScript before the first screen responds on `/en` |  91.3 KB |        39.8 KB |         36.7 KB |
| Every JavaScript chunk                               | 359.2 KB |       326.6 KB |        327.0 KB |
| First paint on `/en` (HTML up to the first section)  |  17.0 KB |        17.2 KB |         19.7 KB |
| Whole `/en` page                                     |  59.7 KB |        67.4 KB |         70.9 KB |
| Project page (`/en/projects/smartpot`)               |  23.2 KB |        24.6 KB |         27.2 KB |
| `node_modules`                                       |   523 MB |          56 MB |          320 MB |

On `/en` the islands of the first screen need 36.7 KB; each home section adds its own chunk only as the reader nears
it, where the earlier editions loaded and hydrated every section once the page had settled. The pages
grow because Solid marks every hydratable element with a `data-hk` key and Astro adds its island runtime (about 2 KB)
before the first island; the JavaScript that has to download, parse and run before the page responds is less than half
of what it was. `node_modules` grows again with Astro's compiler and its toolchain, which only the build uses. Part of
the saving is outside Solid: the hero's figures count the certifications and recommendations from
`content/shared/counts.ts` instead of importing both lists, which a test keeps in step.

The three production images were also compared side by side in Docker, each with the limits of `compose.yaml` (half a
CPU for nginx): Chromium on a phone screen with a 4× slower CPU, median of four alternating rounds of three loads, and
Lighthouse (mobile, median of five runs per page). Transfer sizes are Brotli.

| Measure                                                   |     React 19 | SolidJS + Vite | Astro + SolidJS |
|-----------------------------------------------------------|-------------:|---------------:|----------------:|
| Lighthouse performance (`/en` · `/es/backend` · SmartPot) | 92 · 92 · 93 |   88 · 93 · 95 |    99 · 98 · 96 |
| Lighthouse total blocking time on `/en`                   |       337 ms |         466 ms |          133 ms |
| First contentful paint on `/en`                           |       832 ms |         632 ms |          474 ms |
| JavaScript on `/en` before scrolling                      |     196.1 KB |       151.4 KB |         42.1 KB |
| JavaScript on `/en` after scrolling to the end            |     196.1 KB |       151.4 KB |        152.6 KB |
| Script time on `/en` before scrolling                     |      1002 ms |         174 ms |           40 ms |
| JavaScript heap on `/en`                                  |       6.1 MB |        6.24 MB |         2.59 MB |
| Site build inside the image (two builds)                  |  16.5–18.0 s |    19.9–30.2 s |     21.3–35.4 s |

Lighthouse scores accessibility, best practices and SEO at 100 on every page of the three. A project or detail page
loads its whole body as one island, so there Astro weighs what SolidJS + Vite did; the gain is on the home pages,
where the sections below the first screen load only as the reader reaches them.

## Documentation

- [Design system](docs/design-system.md): palette, tokens, contrast ratios and usage rules.
- [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md): the same system described for screen generators such as Google Stitch.
- [Profile assistant](docs/assistant.md): architecture and how to extend it.
- [Deployment](docs/deployment.md): image, nginx rules, server setup, secrets and rollback.
- [Maintenance](docs/maintenance.md): the checklist before each release and the monthly pass over figures and text.

import {defineConfig} from "astro/config";
import solid from "@astrojs/solid-js";
import tailwindcss from "@tailwindcss/vite";
import path from "node:path";

const buildDate = process.env.BUILD_DATE ?? new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10);
const siteUrl = process.env.SITE_URL ?? "https://sebastianlopezo.page";
// The path the site is served from: "/" on the main domain (the nginx image), or the repository's path on GitHub
// Pages (BASE_PATH=/MyPortfolio-SOLID). It prefixes the bundled asset URLs; src/lib/base.ts carries it into the
// app's own links and the references to files in public/.
const base = process.env.BASE_PATH ?? "/";

// Astro's Solid integration, with its browser renderer wrapped by one that loads an island's part before hydrating it
// (src/islands/client.ts).
const solidIslands = () => {
    const integration = solid();
    const setup = integration.hooks["astro:config:setup"];
    integration.hooks["astro:config:setup"] = (options) => setup({
        ...options,
        addRenderer: (renderer) => options.addRenderer({
            ...renderer,
            clientEntrypoint: path.resolve(import.meta.dirname, "src/islands/client.ts").replaceAll("\\", "/")
        }),
    });
    return integration;
};

// The client:settled directive, which hydrates an island once the page has loaded and painted (src/islands/settled.ts).
const settledDirective = {
    name: "settled-directive",
    hooks: {
        "astro:config:setup": ({addClientDirective}) => addClientDirective({
            name: "settled",
            entrypoint: path.resolve(import.meta.dirname, "src/islands/settled.ts").replaceAll("\\", "/"),
        }),
    },
};

// Every page is generated at build time. The interactive parts are Solid islands that hydrate on their own, and the
// rest of each page is plain HTML that ships no JavaScript (src/islands).
export default defineConfig({
    site: siteUrl,
    base,
    output: "static",
    trailingSlash: "never",
    integrations: [solidIslands(), settledDirective],
    build: {
        format: "directory",
        // nginx serves /assets/ as immutable (nginx/default.conf), and the end-to-end tests block it to check the
        // pages without JavaScript.
        assets: "assets",
        // The stylesheet is small and every page needs it before the first paint, so it travels inside each page.
        inlineStylesheets: "always",
    },
    server: {host: true, port: 8080},
    devToolbar: {enabled: false},
    vite: {
        cacheDir: ".vite",
        define: {
            __BUILD_DATE__: JSON.stringify(buildDate),
            __SITE_URL__: JSON.stringify(siteUrl),
        },
        css: {transformer: "lightningcss"},
        plugins: [tailwindcss()],
        resolve: {alias: {"@": path.resolve(import.meta.dirname, "./src")}},
        build: {target: "es2022", cssMinify: "lightningcss"},
    },
});

FILE: DESIGN.md

# Design System: Sebastián López Osorno, portfolio

This file describes the look of the site in the words a screen generator such as Google Stitch reads (it follows the
`stitch-design-taste` format). The values come from [`src/styles/tokens.css`](src/styles/tokens.css), which stays the
source of truth, and [`docs/design-system.md`](docs/design-system.md) keeps the contrast table and the rules for
components. When the two disagree, the code wins and this file gets fixed.

## 0. Where it comes from

The redesign of November 2026 answers one problem: the site said everything in words, so cards grew long, the dark
teal theme tired the eye and a project read as a wall of text before anyone saw what it was. Two portfolios set the
direction.

- **[gabrielvaldivia.com](https://www.gabrielvaldivia.com/work).** A work index of square tiles, each an image on its
  own field, a name and three or four words; the whole tile is the link, and it grows 2.5% under the pointer. Filters
  are pills. Inner pages open with the name set very large, a paragraph beside a small table of facts (team, services,
  date), then large media panels separated by short sections whose title sits in a left column. Long lists (talks,
  clients, notes) are quiet rows: a title and a muted descriptor. The header folds into one round button once the page
  scrolls, and its menu is a floating panel that marks the current page with a dot.
- **[blunar.cz](https://www.blunar.cz/).** White and very light grey layers over a fine technical grid, a grotesk in
  several weights, eyebrows written as paths (`/about`, `/experiments`), an indexed list whose items carry small
  colored squares for their category, skills drawn as the dials of a device, and the `/experiments` board: objects
  lying on a grid, a little turned, that the reader drags around. On a phone the board becomes a row seen one object at
  a time.

What the site takes is the method, not the look of either: images say what a project is before words do, a tile
carries a name and a few words, and the details live one click away. Since there are few photographs of the work, the
images are illustrations drawn for the site (section 4, Illustrations).

## 1. Visual Theme & Atmosphere

A bench of small devices on clean paper. The interface is monochrome, ink on paper in the light theme and paper on ink
in the dark one; color appears only in layers: the soft field behind each illustration, the objects themselves, the
charts. Pages read like a product designer's case files: a large name, a sentence, a table of facts, a picture.

- **Density 3, Gallery Airy.** The first glance carries a name and a few words per item; everything else opens in
  place or lives on its own page.
- **Variance 5, controlled asymmetry.** The hero splits text and board; the reasons to hire me are a slide beside a
  list; lists are strict index rows.
- **Motion 6, Fluid CSS.** Illustrations rise onto their tiles as they come up, the page settles at the start of each
  screen, the skills turn on a ring one card at a time and the reasons slide in beside their slide. The browser
  draws nearly all of it from CSS; the one thing that moves on its own for more than five seconds, the skills ring,
  has a pause button, and `prefers-reduced-motion` turns the rest off and leaves the ring paused.

## 2. Color Palette & Roles

Every token is `light-dark(light, dark)` in OKLCH; the page follows the system and the header's button pins a theme
(`<html data-theme>`, remembered in `localStorage`). Hex values below are the sRGB conversions, light / dark.

- **Paper / Night** (#FBFCFD / #0D0D0D, `bg`): page background and `theme-color`. Never pure white or pure black.
- **Mist / Graphite** (#F2F4F5 / #161616, `surface`): panels, the skill cards, raised sections.
- **Fog / Smoke** (#E7EAEC / #202020, `surface-raised`): chips, quiet buttons, the menu's hover.
- **Hairline** (#DCDEE0 / #2E2E2E, `border`): dividers between index rows. Decoration only.
- **Control Edge** (#7D8185 / #747474, `border-strong`): borders that must be seen: inputs, outline buttons (3:1+).
- **Ink / Paper** (#141619 / #F5F5F5, `fg`): headings and body text (17.6:1 / 17.8:1).
- **Graphite text / Silver** (#3D4044 / #CACACA, `fg-muted`): summaries, briefs, descriptions (AAA on every surface
  and tile).
- **Slate / Ash** (#484A4F / #B4B4B4, `fg-subtle`): captions, dates, eyebrows (at least 7:1 everywhere).
- **Primary = Ink** (`primary`): the action color is the text color. A primary button is an ink pill with paper text;
  a link darkens to ink.
- **Cobalt** (#1745C2 / #9DBDFF, `accent`): one small highlight: the dot of the current menu entry, focus rings
  (`ring`), the first chart series.
- **Status Green** (`success`): the present, as a dot.
- **Tiles** (`tile-sky`, `tile-mint`, `tile-peach`, `tile-lilac`, `tile-butter`, `tile-rose`, `tile-sage`,
  `tile-stone`): the layers behind illustrations. Pastel paper in light (L 0.93), the same hue sunk to L 0.27 in dark.
  Ink and muted text keep AAA on every tile in both themes.

Chart colors (`viz-*`, `level-*`, `chart-*`, `sdg-*`) live in their own validated block. `pnpm check:contrast` checks
every pair in both themes.

## 3. Typography Rules

- **Three voices:** DM Serif Text (400) for display headings, IBM Plex Sans (400 and 600) for body text and UI, and
  Source Code Pro (400) for tools, dates, eyebrows and figures. Metric-matched local fallbacks keep the layout still
  while the faces load.
- **Headings:** `text-display` clamp(2.125rem → 4.25rem), leading 1.05, for the name and each project's title;
  `text-heading` clamp(1.75rem → 2.5rem), leading 1.15, for section titles; `text-title` 1.25rem, leading 1.3, for
  rows and tiles. Weight stays 400: hierarchy comes from size and tone, never from bold.
- **Two tones in a heading:** the hero writes the name in ink and the role under it in `fg-subtle`, the way a title
  card does.
- **Banned:** Inter, gradient text, all-caps beyond the smallest labels, faux bold.

## 4. Component Stylings

- **Project tiles** (`ProjectTile`): one layer of color with the project's illustration on a 4:3 field, then its name
  and a brief of two to five words, all inside the same rounded tile (1.25rem on phones, 1.75rem from 48rem). The whole
  tile is the link; under a pointer it grows 1.5%, lifts its illustration 8px and leans its arrow (always pinned to the
  tile's bottom-right corner). Two across on a phone, three at 64rem, four from 80rem. A featured project spans the row
  with its illustration beside its name, brief and one sentence.
- **Illustrations:** soft hardware seen from above, slightly tilted toward the reader: rounded plates with a darker
  side for thickness, a sheen and a bevel, lenses, lights, keys, screens and cables, over a blurred contact shadow.
  Each one hints at a project without picturing its screens: a hub with three cables for the integrations, a camera
  beside a database for the CRM snapshots, a planter with a probe for SmartPot. They are static SVG files drawn by
  `scripts/render-illustrations.mjs` from `scripts/illustrations`, with transparent backgrounds so the tile gives them
  their color; a light may pulse three times, a dial sweeps once, and nothing loops. The pages beyond the projects
  have objects of the same family (`scripts/illustrations/pages.mjs`): a job is a badge on its lanyard with a button of
  what it was about, a program is a book with what it led to on top (a mortarboard, a shield, a laptop), a GitHub
  organization is a cabinet of drawers with its sticker and a padlock when its code is private, and each service and
  each reason to hire me is one object that says it (a hub of cables, a stopwatch, a spirit level, one ball thrown in
  and three coming back). A flat glyph pressed into a face, the way a logo is, tells the objects of one kind apart.
- **The hero:** the name, the role, a sentence, a summary and two buttons beside the board; nothing that reads as a
  plea (no availability pill), no stack chips (the skills section has the tools) and no role switcher (a role view is
  reached by its address).
- **The hero board:** the portrait sits whole in a square socket at the middle of a board, as large as the room
  between the devices allows, and cables run from the socket's sides to six devices of the work. It says "I connect
  systems" before a word is read. The portrait is the largest paint and is drawn at
  once. Each device is a link to the project it stands for: with a pointer on the board a dashed outline marks every
  device, and the one under the pointer, or reached with the keyboard, shows a label with the project's name and a
  line about it, opening toward the middle of the board. Escape puts the label away.
- **Skills gallery** (`SkillsSection`): every group of tools is a Mist card on a 3D ring, with its object on a layer
  of color, how many tools it holds, its name and a short line. The ring turns one card at a time while it is in
  view and stops under a pointer, on focus, off screen or with its pause button; the cards at the sides fade and turn
  away. Each card leads to the group's page (`/skills/{slug}`), which tells its focus, what it is, what it is good for,
  all its tools and the projects, jobs, studies and services where it shows.
- **Services** (`ServicesSection`): no cards and no lists of points on the home. Each service is its object on a
  rounded layer, its name with an arrow and a few words, and the whole of it leads to the service's page, which tells
  what it covers, the projects that prove it, the jobs it was done in and the reasons that go with it.
- **The reasons to hire me** (`ReasonsSection`): a presentation. A slide holds the reason's object on a tile, its
  number (`03 de 11`) and the words of the recommendation behind it; beside it, the list of every reason, one bordered
  card each (object, number, title, sentence), sliding in from the side as it comes up. From 64rem the slide stays in
  view (`aspect-[16/10]`, capped at `40svh` so it never clips on 768px laptops) and turns to the reason whose card
  crosses the middle of the screen, which takes an ink border; below 64rem the active reason renders as a compact
  horizontal highlight card above the list instead of taking a full screen. Every reason has a page with the whole
  recommendation, the quoted words marked on the reason's color, where it shows in the work, and the projects, jobs,
  programs and services it links.
- **Header:** at the top of a page a strictly single-line quiet frosted bar: the whole name in ink, six primary
  sections (`about`, `experience`, `projects`, `skills`, `services`, `contact`) with the one being read underlined,
  and the controls capsule (language, theme and the round ink menu button that always opens the full twelve-section
  floating panel). Once the reader scrolls it folds into two high-contrast frosted floating pieces (94% opacity): the
  name pill at the left and the controls capsule at the right. The floating panel lists all twelve sections and marks
  the active one with a cobalt dot; below 80rem the navigation lives entirely inside that panel. A 2px line along the
  top edge draws the reading progress.
- **Section rhythm:** from 64rem wide and 40rem tall, the hero opens as a calm centered frame capped at
  `min(100dvh, 54rem)` so tall monitors never stretch empty space. Every section below flows naturally with fluid
  vertical rhythm (`clamp(3.5rem, 2.5rem + 3.2vw, 6rem)`) and `overflow-x: clip`, avoiding forced `100dvh` traps per
  card or empty vertical voids. Clicking any `#section` link smoothly aligns the target right beneath the fixed header
  (`scroll-padding-top: var(--header-height)`).
- **Buttons:** pills. Primary: ink fill, paper text, 48px in the hero, 44px elsewhere. Secondary: a Control Edge
  outline or a Fog fill. Pressing moves them down 1px. At most one primary button per view.
- **Chips:** pills in Source Code Pro, never below 13px, on Fog; outside the role view's focus they turn into a hairline
  outline.
- **Index rows:** jobs, certifications, skill groups, repositories. A row is a date column in mono, a title, its place
  and one sentence, separated by hairlines; its details open in place (`More`) and its page tells the rest.
- **Project pages:** the crumbs, the title at display size, then the tagline and summary beside a table of facts (role,
  place, period, team, status) with mono labels, then the illustration on its tile across the page (21:9 on a desktop),
  then screens, figures and sections.
- **Decisions** (`Decisions`): every decision of a project shown whole, never behind a tab. A row is a number in mono
  and a title, then a short flow: the problem on a Mist panel, a round joint with an arrow laid over the edges of both,
  and the solution on the project's own tile color, wider (2:3) since it says more, with its cost below a dashed line
  like the stub of a receipt. Side by side from 48rem, stacked on a phone with the arrow pointing down. As a row comes
  up the problem rises, the joint grows, the solution follows from the problem's side and the cost prints from left to
  right; under a pointer the joint fills with ink.
- **Disclosures:** a native `details` whose summary says what it opens ("Show more (9)"), with a chevron that turns;
  its text stays in the prerendered page.
- **Inputs:** label above, paper fill, Control Edge border, 0.75rem corners, cobalt ring on focus.
- **Open Graph cards** (`scripts/generate-og.mjs`, `scripts/og/template.html`): 1200 × 630 cards on Paper (`#FBFCFD`)
  with the hero's fine technical grid, an eyebrow in Source Code Pro with a status or cobalt dot, a two-tone heading in
  DM Serif Text 400 (title in ink, subtitle in slate), an ink pill for `sebastianlopezo.page` beside a Fog pill for the
  context, and a 460 × 460 rounded square tile on the right holding the page's illustration on its `tile-*` color (or
  the hero board with the portrait in its socket on the home card). Certifications link out to their credentials on
  Google Drive and issuer verification pages rather than embedding scanned documents on the site or in social cards.

## 5. Layout Principles

- **The home is the first glance, not the archive.** Each section keeps its claim and its best proof; the rest opens in
  place or lives on its own page. Every job, project, certification and organization has a page, and so do the
  services, the reasons to hire me and the GitHub metrics.
- **Three section layouts:** `wide`, the heading above content that needs the whole row (the projects, the skills, the
  journey); `split`, the heading in a left column that stays in view beside a list; `pair`, the heading and what it
  carries in the left half and the content in the right half, its top level with the title (the contact: the ways to
  reach me under the title, the form beside it). All stack below 64rem.
- CSS Grid for every multi-column layout; nothing scrolls sideways except the sliders.
- `container-page` is 72rem up to a 1440px viewport, then 82% of it up to 96rem. Full-height blocks use `100dvh`.

## 6. Motion & Interaction

- Durations of 120, 200 and 400ms on `ease-standard`, `ease-emphasized` and `ease-spring` (a settle with a touch of
  spring for what lands: a tile, a lifted object, the header). Transitions list their properties.
- **Scroll-driven:** section headings, rows and tiles rise into place as they enter; a tile's illustration rises onto
  its layer; screens paint in from their top edge; a decision flows from its problem to its solution; the journey map
  rises in as one piece; a reason's card slides in from the side of
  its slide; bars grow; figures count up once. Browsers without scroll-driven animations get the page at rest.
- **On load:** the illustrations' own lights pulse three times. Under five seconds in all.
- **Hover:** a tile grows and lifts its illustration; a service's object lifts; an arrow leans the way it leads. Only
  for pointers that hover.
- Following a link cross-fades between pages with the header held in place; a link to a part of the page scrolls
  there smoothly, so the sections on the way play their entrances.
- `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` turns every animation and transition off.

## 7. Anti-Patterns (Banned)

- No emoji in the interface, no Inter, no serif display, no faux bold, no gradient text.
- No accent color on text blocks: color lives in the layers and the illustrations.
- No pure black (#000000) or pure white (#FFFFFF) surfaces, no neon glow.
- No long cards: a tile is an illustration, a name and a few words; a row is a date, a title and a sentence.
- No stock photographs or AI renders standing in for the work: the illustrations are drawn for the site, one family.
- No endless loops: nothing moves on its own for more than five seconds (WCAG 2.2.2), and no spinners.
- No invented figures: every number has a source and a date (`docs/content.md`).
- No stock phrases ("elevate", "seamless", "next-gen", "passionate").
- No client names of TIVENOS or ADCOM anywhere (enforced by `src/content/content.test.ts`).

FILE: Dockerfile

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# Three stages: dependencies, build and runtime. Only the prerendered site and the nginx configuration reach the
# final image; Node, pnpm, the sources and node_modules stay behind. Base images are pinned by digest so a rebuild
# uses the same bytes; Dependabot moves the digests.

FROM node:24-alpine@sha256:116b800c3754b440ee0aa3ed2f20f5bf3d99a554bfd9adeea09ea8017f6e85f5 AS deps

ENV COREPACK_ENABLE_DOWNLOAD_PROMPT=0 \
    CI=true \
    PNPM_HOME=/home/node/.local/share/pnpm

RUN corepack enable

# Dependencies install and the build run as the image's unprivileged node user, so a package script cannot
# write outside /app or the pnpm store.
USER node
WORKDIR /app

COPY --chown=node:node package.json pnpm-lock.yaml ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,id=pnpm-store,target=/home/node/.local/share/pnpm/store,uid=1000,gid=1000 \
    pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

FROM deps AS build

COPY --chown=node:node . .

ARG SITE_URL=https://sebastianlopezo.page
# The build precompresses every text asset (.gz next to the file) for nginx's gzip_static.
RUN SITE_URL=$SITE_URL pnpm build

# nginx serves the .br files the build writes next to each text file once it has ngx_brotli's static module. The module
# is built here against the source of the very nginx the runtime runs: this stage starts from the same image, so the
# versions match even when Dependabot moves it, and with nginx's own configure arguments, which a module must share to
# load. Only the static module is built; it serves files and needs no Brotli library. The nginx source must carry a
# signature from one of the nginx developers' keys (nginx.org/en/pgp_keys.html), and git checks ngx_brotli against its
# commit hash.
FROM nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.31.7-alpine-slim@sha256:a8cb0f33d51fa107c96fd2bd3a71aaf564ec131e9d2bdf8700944f0ed8b170d7 AS brotli

USER root
ARG NGX_BROTLI_COMMIT=a71f9312c2deb28875acc7bacfdd5695a111aa53
ARG NGINX_SIGNERS="43387825DDB1BB97EC36BA5D007C8D7C15D87369 D6786CE303D9A9022998DC6CC8464D549AF75C0A 13C82A63B603576156E30A4EA0EA981B66B0D967 7338973069ED3F443F4D37DFA64FD5B17ADB39A8"
WORKDIR /build
RUN apk add --no-cache curl gcc git gnupg libc-dev linux-headers make openssl-dev pcre2-dev zlib-dev \
    && version="$(nginx -v 2>&1 | sed 's#^.*/##')" \
    && curl -fsSLO "https://nginx.org/download/nginx-$version.tar.gz" \
    && curl -fsSLO "https://nginx.org/download/nginx-$version.tar.gz.asc" \
    && for key in arut pluknet thresh sb; do curl -fsSL "https://nginx.org/keys/$key.key" | gpg --batch --quiet --import; done \
    && signer="$(gpg --batch --status-fd 1 --verify "nginx-$version.tar.gz.asc" "nginx-$version.tar.gz" 2>/dev/null | awk '$2 == "VALIDSIG" {print $NF}')" \
    && case " $NGINX_SIGNERS " in *" ${signer:-none} "*) ;; *) echo "nginx-$version is not signed by a known nginx key" >&2; exit 1 ;; esac \
    && git init -q ngx_brotli \
    && git -C ngx_brotli fetch -q --depth 1 https://github.com/google/ngx_brotli.git "$NGX_BROTLI_COMMIT" \
    && git -C ngx_brotli checkout -q FETCH_HEAD \
    && tar xzf "nginx-$version.tar.gz" \
    && cd "nginx-$version" \
    && eval "./configure $(nginx -V 2>&1 | sed -n 's/^configure arguments: //p') --add-dynamic-module=../ngx_brotli/static" \
    && make -j"$(nproc)" modules \
    && cp objs/ngx_http_brotli_static_module.so /build/

FROM nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.31.7-alpine-slim@sha256:a8cb0f33d51fa107c96fd2bd3a71aaf564ec131e9d2bdf8700944f0ed8b170d7 AS runtime

LABEL org.opencontainers.image.title="MyPortfolio" \
      org.opencontainers.image.description="Bilingual prerendered portfolio of Sebastián López Osorno served by unprivileged nginx" \
      org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/SebastianLopezO/MyPortfolio" \
      org.opencontainers.image.url="https://sebastianlopezo.page"

# Alpine publishes security fixes faster than the base image is rebuilt (pcre2, which nginx's regex locations use,
# was one of them), and CI fails on fixable HIGH or CRITICAL findings, so the runtime takes them at build time.
USER root
RUN apk upgrade --no-cache

COPY --chown=0:0 --from=brotli /build/ngx_http_brotli_static_module.so /usr/lib/nginx/modules/
RUN sed -i '1i load_module modules/ngx_http_brotli_static_module.so;' /etc/nginx/nginx.conf

# Files are owned by root and only readable by the nginx user (uid 101), so the server cannot change what it serves.
COPY --chown=0:0 nginx/default.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY --chown=0:0 nginx/security-headers.conf /etc/nginx/snippets/security-headers.conf
COPY --chown=0:0 --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html

USER 101:101
EXPOSE 8080
STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=5s --retries=3 \
    CMD wget -q -O /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8080/health || exit 1

                    argsIgnorePattern: "^_",
                    varsIgnorePattern: "^_",
                    destructuredArrayIgnorePattern: "^_",
                    ignoreRestSiblings: true
                },
            ],
        },
    },
    {
        files: ["src/**/*.{ts,tsx}"],
        ...solid,
    },
    {
        // A Solid ref is declared unassigned (let el!: HTMLElement) and assigned by ref={el} in JSX, which this rule cannot see.
        files: ["src/**/*.tsx"],
        rules: {"no-unassigned-vars": "off"},
    },
    {
        files: ["src/**/*.test.{ts,tsx}", "scripts/**/*.ts", "e2e/**/*.ts", "tests/**/*.ts", "*.config.ts"],
        languageOptions: {globals: {...globals.browser, ...globals.node}},
    },
);

# Memoria de la migración React → SolidJS (local, NO se comitea)

Excluido vía `.git/info/exclude`. Sesión privada: no guardar nada en la memoria global de Claude.

## Reglas del usuario

- Commits en inglés, título que empieza con verbo, sin `Co-Authored-By`; solo la autoría de git configurada
  (Sebastián López O). No hacer push.
- Migrar de a poco, commits pequeños y coherentes, hasta culminar.
- Objetivo: rendimiento, peso y seguridad (mejora continua).

- RESTRICCIÓN FUERTE (usuario): migración transparente; NO perder ni modificar funcionalidad ni contenido.
  Mejoras pequeñas permitidas solo si funcional/visualmente no son drásticas (el portfolio debe seguir reconocible).
  → Revertido el commit que describía el portfolio como SolidJS (textos/decisión nueva). Proponer al final, como
  opción, el ajuste mínimo factual ("Built with React" → SolidJS) sin aplicarlo.
- Despliegue: no preocuparse; dejar los .yml tal cual.

## Fase 2 (pedido 2): Docker + Astro

- Comparar en Docker React vs Solid+Vite (tiempos, peso, rendimiento). Luego migrar Vite→Astro (islas, el usuario
  escribió "astra") y comparar MyPortfolio(React) vs Astro, citando Solid+Vite solo como dato; conclusiones en chat.
- Commit de referencia Solid+Vite: 807ba1c (antes de Astro). Imagen local `myportfolio-cmp:solid-vite`.
- Docker Desktop: DNS intermitente → `docker build`/`pull` fuera del sandbox con reintentos (scratchpad/cmp/*.sh).
  Etapa brotli cacheada compartida entre imágenes. Bench: scratchpad/cmp/bench-all.sh <tag> → results-<tag>.json.
- Build en Docker (paso pnpm build): React 34,0 s; Solid+Vite 61,3 s (cliente Babel 6,5 s vs SWC 1,2 s).
- Astro: usar 7.3.8 (7.4 exige Node ≥22.22; host 22.18). Probe en scratchpad/astro-probe: con pnpm 10.33 global falló
  `#shiki-engine` (Node resolve); con npm funcionó. Verificar con pnpm 10.32.1 del repo.
- Astro emite inline: style astro-island, script idle, script astro-island runtime, HydrationScript de Solid, script
  visible → hashes CSP. Islas Solid: server renderToStringAsync+Suspense; estáticos con NoHydration (sin data-hk).
- Diseño: página catch-all `[...path].astro` (getStaticPaths de prerenderRoutes); islas `PageIsland` genéricas
  (part, lang, role, path) con lazy por parte + registro síncrono en server; estáticos (Highlights, Footer, SkipLink,
  WhatsApp, 404) sin directiva; secciones `client:visible` con rootMargin; header/hero/assistant/body/boot
  `client:idle`.

### Resultados Docker React vs Solid+Vite (scratchpad/cmp, report.mjs react solid-vite)

- Imagen 44,1 vs 44,7 MB; sitio 56,8 vs 59,6 MB; listo /health 3,1 s vs 1,2 s; RAM ~7,5→9,5 MiB ambos.
- HTML br /en 44,2→49,3 KB; JS+CSS+fuentes estáticos /en 86,2 KB·25 → 34,2 KB·19 (br).
- Throughput /en 1434 vs 1372 req/s (0,5 CPU nginx, igual). TTFB ~1 ms ambos.
- Lighthouse mediana 5 (contenedor): /en 91→92, /es/backend 88→92, smartpot 88→95; TBT 391→358, 449→342, 465→247;
  boot-up JS 719→509, 810→489, 355→230 ms; bytes 428→375, 431→377, 380→318 KB. a11y/bp/seo 100.
- Navegador (CPU 4x real, Playwright): script JS 3-6x menor en Solid; TBT/task variables entre rondas (ruido),
  en reposo /en TBT 513→314, task 2326→2025; layout ~740 ms ambos (dominante, del DOM/CSS).
- Build en Docker: React 34 s vs Solid+Vite 61 s.

## Origen

- `C:\Users\Sebastian-EDU\Documents\GitHub\MyPortfolio` (React 19 + Vite 8 + TS + Tailwind 4, pnpm 10, Node 22.18).
- 182 páginas prerenderizadas (es/en), hidratación tras `load` + idle, secciones en chunks perezosos.
- CSP con hashes de scripts inline (nginx/security-headers.conf) — cualquier script inline nuevo exige hash.
- Baseline build original: entry `index-*.js` 208 KB raw / 64,8 KB gzip; presupuesto test: startup JS ≤ 110 KB gzip,
  chunk perezoso ≤ 32 KB gzip, CSS ≤ 12,5 KB gzip, HTML ≤ 96 KB gzip, primer pintado ≤ 24 KB gzip antes de la 1ª
  sección.

## Decisiones

- Iconos lucide: ~30 iconos inline generados localmente (sin dependencia runtime).
- `_$HY` de Solid se inicializa en el entry del cliente (no `HydrationScript` inline) para no tocar la CSP.

## Técnica de port

- Copiado el original a `src/` sin comitear; codemod en scratchpad (`codemod.py`: className→class, atributos SVG
  kebab, quita `key`, iconos lucide → `@/components/ui/icons`, `aria-hidden` desnudo → `"true"`). Luego lógica a mano.
- Solo se hace `git add` de archivos ya portados. Archivos aún React = sin trackear.
- Hidratación: `lazy` de Solid mantiene el HTML del server y difiere los efectos hasta que cargan todos los chunks.
  `useHydrated()` = señal por componente (false en server/hidratando, true en render cliente).
- `useSectionCopy` es síncrono; `section-loaders.ts` declara qué copias necesita cada sección (COPIES).
- Carousel: props renombradas `slideClass`, `trackClass`, `controlsClass`, item `class`.
- `expectSections` se llama en `createRenderEffect` (antes que los onMount) para no marcar hidratado antes de tiempo.

### Astro (estado 2026-10-21)

- El usuario hizo 2 commits propios durante la pausa: 3960179 "Migrate portfolio to Astro islands" (estado intermedio,
  con clientEntrypoint como URL → el build lo descartaba) y 420ec7b "Update Router.tsx" (formato). Además pusheó hasta
  807ba1c (origin/main). Yo NO pusheo nunca.
- Bugs resueltos encima (commits a905f93..752ba91, 10 commits):
    1. Carrera de hidratación: Solid usa UN registry global por página y cada hydrate() lo reinicia; con `lazy` dentro
       de
       la isla, una isla que esperaba un chunk perdía sus nodos (error "t is not a function"/Hydration Mismatch en
       /en/projects). Fix: renderer cliente propio `src/islands/client.ts` que llama `PageIsland.preload(props)` (carga
       parte+copy y registra en `islands/registry.ts`) antes de `hydrate` → hidratación síncrona. astro.config envuelve
       solid() y cambia clientEntrypoint a string (path absoluto con /), Astro build ignora URL.
    2. Solid marca `sharedConfig.done=_$HY.done=true` en el primer evento delegado → islas posteriores hacen render (DOM
       nuevo, se pierde tamaño recordado de content-visibility y el ancla). Fix: reset done=false antes de cada hydrate.
       (Replay de eventos de Solid NO funciona: composedPath() vacío tras dispatch; no intentar restaurar events.)
    3. Links de secciones no hidratadas sin ?locked → `src/lib/lock.ts` carryLock() en Boot (capture click).

FILE: vitest.config.ts
================================================
import {defineConfig} from "vitest/config";
import solid from "vite-plugin-solid";
import {resolve} from "node:path";

const SERVER_TESTS = "src/**/*.server.test.{ts,tsx}";

export default defineConfig({
    define: {
        __BUILD_DATE__: JSON.stringify("2026-10-03"),
        __SITE_URL__: JSON.stringify("https://sebastianlopezo.page"),
    },
    test: {
        globals: true,
        setupFiles: ["./src/test/setup.ts"],
        coverage: {
            provider: 'v8',
            reporter: ['text', 'json', 'html'],
            exclude: ['node_modules/', 'src/test/setup.ts'],
        },
        // Solid ships a browser build and a server build: components render in jsdom with the first, and the
        // *.server.test files render to strings in Node with the second, as the prerender does. Tests render once,
        // so neither needs hot reload.
        projects: [
            {
                extends: true,
                plugins: [solid({hot: false})],
                test: {
                    name: "browser",
                    environment: "jsdom",
                    include: ["src/**/*.{test,spec}.{ts,tsx}", "scripts/**/*.test.ts"],
                    exclude: [SERVER_TESTS],
                },
            },
            {
                extends: true,
                plugins: [solid({ssr: true, hot: false})],
                test: {
                    name: "server",
                    environment: "node",
                    include: [SERVER_TESTS],
                },
            },
        ],
    },
    resolve: {
        alias: {
            "@": resolve(import.meta.dirname, "./src"),
        },
    },
});

# Profile assistant

A small question-answering panel that runs entirely in the browser. It does not call any AI or third-party
service: every answer is assembled from the same typed content modules that render the page, so it can never
contradict the portfolio.

## Loading

| Piece                                                                             | Where                                                             | Size (gzip) |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------|
| `AssistantLauncher`                                                               | an island that hydrates once the page settles                     | ~1.3 KB     |
| `AssistantPanel` + engine (`lib/assistant/*`)                                     | lazy chunk                                                        | ~12 KB      |
| `content/{en,es}/assistant.ts` copy, with the suggestions, follow-ups and catalog | lazy chunk per language                                           | ~5 KB       |
| Section copy (`content/{en,es}/*.ts`)                                             | the chunks the home sections already load (`content/sections.ts`) | shared      |
| `content/case-studies/{en,es}.ts` copy                                            | lazy chunk per language, shared with the project pages            | ~8.5 KB     |
| `content/detail-pages/{en,es}.ts` copy                                            | lazy chunk per language, shared with the detail pages             | ~9 KB       |

The launcher prefetches the lazy chunks on hover or focus, so the panel usually opens instantly. A click requests
whatever is still missing in one batch and opens the panel once its code and every copy it answers from have arrived;
if a download fails, the next click tries again.
The panel is a native `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()`: it traps focus, closes with Esc or a backdrop click,
makes the page inert and returns focus to the launcher.

## Pipeline

```
question ─► normalize ─► detect intents ─► compose answer
                 │                │
                 └─► terms ──► BM25 search over facts (details, examples, fallback)
```

1. **`normalize.ts`** lowercases, strips accents and joins compound terms (`C#`, `CI/CD`, `Node.js`, `Power BI`,
   `hoja de vida`, `full stack`). Whole phrases that carry an intent become one token first, in both languages ("who
   is", "por qué", "cómo trabaja", "this site", "MUV-U"), so the stopwords cannot erase them. `tokenize` keeps every
   word for intent rules; `terms` drops stopwords for retrieval.
   Words are stemmed lightly (plurals) and mapped through **`synonyms.ts`**, so Spanish and English land on the same
   canonical token (`certificaciones` and `certifications` → `certification`).
2. **`intents.ts`** matches token patterns in priority order and returns at most two of about thirty intents: who he
   is, years and current jobs, each job by name, each program by name, education and plans, security, languages,
   projects (and ten of them by name), certifications, recommendations, the resume, GitHub figures and organizations,
   coding time, AI, clients, industries, services, reasons to hire, how he works, his trajectory, leadership, this
   site and the role fit. Salary questions always win and are redirected to a direct conversation. Role keywords from
   `content/roles.ts` detect the role a question is about, with ties going to the role currently on screen; the role
   fit answer only comes when the question asks for nothing more specific.
3. **`knowledge.ts`** turns the content into 331 facts: experience summaries, bullets and titles, projects, skills,
   certifications, programs with their areas and courses, organizations, about, services and testimonials, each
   tagged with roles, plus the summary and approach of every case study. 276 of them link to a page of their own (a
   project, job, program, certification or organization) instead of a section of the profile.
4. **`retrieval.ts`** ranks facts with BM25 (`k1 = 1.2`, `b = 0.75`) and boosts facts tagged with the active or
   detected role by 25 %. Hits below half of the best score are discarded.
5. **`answer.ts`** fills the localized templates from `content/{en,es}/assistant.ts` with live facts (years of
   experience, current jobs, counts, the GitHub and WakaTime snapshot, the organizations' commits, the page count),
   quotes a real experience bullet for role questions and the recommendations behind each reason to hire, matches
   certifications by the title first and by what they covered second, and adds links to the pages that tell more,
   the page sections, the role view, the ATS PDF, WhatsApp or email. Text Sebastián wrote in the first person (a
   project's summary, how he works) is quoted as his own words.
6. Every answer brings **follow-up questions** about its topic. The panel shows four of them, without the questions
   already asked, and a **catalog** behind "More questions" lists every question the assistant was built for, by
   topic. A unit test asks all of them, in both languages, and fails if any falls back to "I don't have that".

When the page is opened with `?locked=true`, answers never link to another role view, and the links to project and
detail pages carry the lock (`/en/projects/gopoli?locked=true`); following one adds the role
(`?from=backend&locked=true`, `lib/role-links.ts`), so the way back returns to the same view. On a project or detail
page, links to a section open the profile at that section.

## Extending

- **New question type:** add the id to `IntentId` (`types/assistant.ts`), a rule in `intents.ts`, a template in both
  copy files, its follow-ups, a catalog entry and a fixture in `assistant.test.ts`. The content test fails if the two
  copies drift apart, and the catalog test fails if the new question is not understood.
- **New vocabulary:** add variants to a group in `synonyms.ts`; both questions and facts use it.
- **New facts:** add them to the content modules. `buildKnowledgeBase` indexes them automatically.

## Possible next step

If free-form answers are ever needed, the same `buildKnowledgeBase` output can feed a serverless endpoint as
retrieval context for an LLM. The current panel would keep its UI and only swap `createAssistant` for a fetch call,
keeping the local engine as the offline fallback.

# Content rules and sources

Every fact on the site has to be traceable to a source someone can open. This file lists those sources, the rules for
writing new text, and the figures that change over time with the date they were read.

## Writing rules

Every new or rewritten public text (site copy in `src/content/{en,es}`, case studies, the OhMyCV resumes and the READMEs
of the showcased repositories) goes through three passes before it is merged:

1. **Humanizer** (`~/.claude-personal/plugins/marketplaces/humanizer/SKILL.md`, v3.1.0). It removes the patterns of
   machine-written prose without adding or dropping facts. It never touches recommendation quotes or their
   translations, proper names, certificate titles, code identifiers or date ranges.
2. **HumanScope, the rules that fit factual text** (`anthropic-skills:humanscope`). The skill is written for fiction,
   and most of it (non-linear time, subplots, holding the key fact back) would hide or invent facts here. What applies:
    - No sentence states a lesson or a moral ("I learned that…"), and the narrator does not generalize.
    - Name the system, tool, team or institution instead of "several teams" or "organizations". Clients stay anonymous.
    - No stock phrases ("learning that never stops"), no sentence that repeats what the one before showed, and no em
      dash as punctuation.
    - Case studies keep what came from outside (a vendor change, a client decision), what each decision cost and what
      is still open, as long as it really happened.
3. **Fact-check at the Deep tier.** Claims the web can verify (institutions, issuers, course names, technology
   versions, live demos) are checked against at least two sources. Claims the web cannot see (private repositories, job
   titles) are checked against the primary source listed below. Every ❌ or ⚠️ is fixed before merging.

On top of that:

- No invented metrics. A figure appears only with a source and a date; otherwise the sentence ends at the action.
- First person, active voice, plain words. Colombian Spanish with *tú*; US English.
- Spanish headings capitalize only the first word and proper names ("Experiencia profesional"). Job titles and the names
  of degrees and courses keep the form used in the resume.
- Clients of TIVENOS and ADCOM are never named; `src/content/content.test.ts` fails if one appears.
- Quotes from recommendations are verbatim. Cut text is marked with `[…]`.

the rest together: the commit areas in `src/content/shared/github.ts` and the figures in

# Deployment

The site ships as a static, prerendered build inside an unprivileged nginx image published to GHCR.
The production server only pulls images; it never builds.

```
push to main ─► CI (lint, tests, build, e2e, Lighthouse, Docker smoke test)
            └─► Publish Docker Image ─► ghcr.io/sebastianlopezo/myportfolio:{latest, sha-xxxxxxx, x.y.z}
                                    └─► Deploy to Production (SSH + docker compose)
```

## Image

| Item         | Value                                                                                                                                                        |
|--------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Stages       | `deps` installs with pnpm, `build` prerenders and precompresses, `runtime` copies only `dist` and the nginx configuration                                    |
| Build user   | `node` (uid 1000): package scripts cannot write outside `/app` and the pnpm store                                                                            |
| Base         | `node:24-alpine` for the first two stages, `nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.31.7-alpine-slim` for the runtime, both pinned by digest (Dependabot updates them) |
| Runtime user | uid 101; the served files belong to root, so nginx can read them and not change them                                                                         |
| Size         | ~30 MB                                                                                                                                                       |
| Port         | `8080`                                                                                                                                                       |
| Health       | `GET /health` → `{"status":"UP"}` (also used by the Docker `HEALTHCHECK`)                                                                                    |
| Tags         | `latest` (main), `sha-<7 chars>` (every build), `x.y.z` and `x.y` (tags `vX.Y.Z`)                                                                            |
| Supply chain | SBOM and maximum provenance attestations on every push, and a keyless cosign signature of the digest in each registry                                        |
| Scanning     | CI runs Trivy on the image and fails on fixable HIGH or CRITICAL vulnerabilities                                                                             |

`nginx/default.conf` serves the prerendered pages and mirrors the routing rules of `scripts/serve-dist.mjs`:

| Request                               | Response                                                                             |
|---------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `/`                                   | `302` to `/es` when `Accept-Language` starts with `es`, otherwise `/en` (query kept) |
| `/en`, `/es/backend`, …               | `200` from `<path>/index.html`, `Cache-Control: no-cache`, `No-Vary-Search`          |
| `/path/`                              | `301` to `/path` (query kept)                                                        |
| `/path/index.html`, `/index.html`     | `301` to `/path` and `/` (query kept): one address per page                          |
| unknown path, `/404.html`             | `404` with the bilingual `404.html`                                                  |
| any method other than `GET` or `HEAD` | `405`; request bodies are capped at 1 KB and slow clients time out after 10 s        |
| `/assets/*`                           | `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`                                 |
| images, PDFs                          | `Cache-Control: public, max-age=604800`                                              |
| `robots.txt`, `sitemap.xml`           | `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600`                                                |

Pre-compressed `.br` and `.gz` files are served with `brotli_static` and `gzip_static`, also to a reverse proxy
that asks over HTTP/1.0 (`gzip_http_version 1.0`, `gzip_proxied any`): Brotli to the browsers that accept it, about
a quarter smaller than gzip on the pages, and gzip to the rest. `brotli_static` comes from ngx_brotli's static
module, which the Dockerfile builds against the source of the image's own nginx (signed by an nginx developer's
key) and loads in `nginx.conf`; the host needs nothing for it. Every response carries the headers in
`nginx/security-headers.conf` (CSP, HSTS, `nosniff`, `SAMEORIGIN`, `Referrer-Policy`, `Permissions-Policy`, COOP).

> The CSP runs no inline script it does not name by its SHA-256 hash, and no `eval`. The pages carry six inline
> scripts: the role lock and the speculation rules that prefetch the page a link is about to open
> (`src/layouts/Page.astro`), Astro's island runtime, the `client:settled` directive (`src/islands/settled.ts`),
> Solid's `HydrationScript`, which Astro writes before the first island, and the root's language redirect
> (`scripts/postbuild.ts`). Each has the same text on every page, so one hash covers it; the build
> tests fail with the hash to add if one of them changes, as an Astro or Solid update or a reformat of the lock can
> do. The GTM container holds only the
> Google tag. A Custom HTML tag or a Custom JavaScript variable added to it would need `'unsafe-inline'` or
> `'unsafe-eval'` back, so check its browser console after publishing a container version.

## Server setup (once)

1. Install Docker Engine with the Compose plugin.
2. Create a deploy user that can run Docker (member of the `docker` group, or with passwordless `sudo`) and add
   the public half of the deploy key to its `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`.
3. Point the host reverse proxy to the container. The previous image listened on port 80; this one is published on
   `127.0.0.1` at `PORTFOLIO_PORT` from the server's `.env` (8080 unless it says otherwise, so check it first):

   ```nginx
   upstream portfolio {
       server 127.0.0.1:8080;
       keepalive 16;
       # Under the container's keepalive_timeout (15s), so nginx never reuses a connection the container closed.
       keepalive_timeout 10s;
   }

   server {
       # The site asks nothing more of the host: compression and security headers come from the container. HTTP/2
       # stays the host's call, since before nginx 1.25.1 it switches every site on the address and port at once.
       listen 443 ssl;
       server_name sebastianlopezo.page;
       server_tokens off;

       ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/sebastianlopezo.page/fullchain.pem;
       ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/sebastianlopezo.page/privkey.pem;

       location / {
           proxy_pass http://portfolio;
           # nginx proxies with HTTP/1.0 and closes the connection after each request unless told otherwise.
           proxy_http_version 1.1;
           proxy_set_header Connection "";
           proxy_set_header Host $host;
           proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
           proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
       }
   }
   ```

   Then check and reload it with `sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx`. `server_tokens off` keeps the
   nginx version out of the `Server` header and the error pages.

4. Add the repository secrets below. Without the required ones the deploy job is skipped with a notice.

| Secret                                                  | Required                     | Purpose                                                                                                 |
|---------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `SERVER_HOST`                                           | yes                          | Server address                                                                                          |
| `SERVER_PORT`                                           | yes                          | SSH port                                                                                                |
| `SERVER_USER`                                           | yes                          | Deploy user                                                                                             |
| `SERVER_KEY`                                            | yes                          | Private SSH key of the deploy user                                                                      |
| `DEPLOY_PATH`                                           | yes                          | Folder that holds `compose.yaml` and `.env`, e.g. `/opt/myportfolio`                                    |
| `SERVER_KNOWN_HOSTS`                                    | recommended                  | Output of `ssh-keyscan -p <port> <host>`; without it the key is trusted on first use                    |
| `GHCR_READ_TOKEN`                                       | while the package is private | Token with `read:packages`, used for `docker login ghcr.io` during the deploy and logged out afterwards |
| `GHCR_USER`                                             | no                           | Owner of that token (defaults to the repository owner)                                                  |
| `ENV_FILE`                                              | no                           | Extra lines for `.env`, e.g. `PORTFOLIO_PORT=8080` (see `.env.example`)                                 |
| `DOCKER_USERNAME`, `DOCKER_PASSWORD`, `DOCKER_APP_NAME` | no                           | Also publish the image to Docker Hub                                                                    |

The optional repository variable `SITE_URL` changes the URL checked after each deploy (default
`https://sebastianlopezo.page`).

## How a deploy runs

1. `compose.yaml` and a temporary `.env` with `PORTFOLIO_TAG=sha-<commit>` are copied to a private staging folder.
2. A lock file prevents overlapping deploys.
3. `docker compose pull` and `docker compose up -d --remove-orphans --wait` replace the container once the new one
   is healthy; old images are pruned.
4. The staging folder and the registry login are removed, and the workflow checks that `/en` answers with `200`.

The container runs as uid 101 with a read-only root filesystem, `no-new-privileges`, all capabilities dropped, a
16 MB `tmpfs` for `/tmp` mounted `noexec,nosuid,nodev`, 0.5 CPU, 128 MB of memory and 64 processes. It listens only on
`127.0.0.1`; the host's reverse proxy terminates TLS, and the site sends HSTS with `preload`.

To check that an image was built and signed by this repository's workflow:

```bash
cosign verify ghcr.io/sebastianlopezo/myportfolio:latest \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/SebastianLopezO/MyPortfolio/' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
```

## Production checks

**Production Checks** (`.github/workflows/production.yml`) runs after every deploy, every Monday and on demand, against
`SITE_URL`:

| Job                | What it verifies                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|--------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Routes and Headers | The 12 pages answer `200`, `/health`, the language redirect with its query, the trailing-slash `301`, the `404`, sitemap, robots, the resume PDF, the security headers, gzip and Brotli on the HTML, and compression on the first script            |
| Browser Tests      | The whole Playwright suite with `BASE_URL` set to production: hydration without console errors, role switching and lock, the assistant, and the layout checks (no horizontal overflow, complete ASCII art and loaded photo at 360, 768 and 1440 px) |
| Lighthouse         | Mobile Lighthouse (median of three runs) on the 12 pages and a locked link. Accessibility, best practices and SEO must be 100; performance warns below 95. The scores are written to the job summary                                                |

## Rollback

Run **Deploy to Production** manually and set `tag` to a previous `sha-xxxxxxx` tag (or a version). Leaving it empty
deploys `latest`.

## Running it locally

```bash
docker build -t myportfolio .
docker run --rm --read-only --user 101:101 --tmpfs /tmp:uid=101,gid=101,mode=0700,size=16m,noexec,nosuid,nodev \
  --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges:true -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 myportfolio
```

Or pull the published image with the same compose file used in production:

```bash
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d --wait
```
