## 1. Content Navigability and Structure

### Landmarks

- **Place all content within landmarks:** Wrap each relevant part of the page in `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`,
  `<aside>`, and `<footer>` elements so assistive-tech users can jump between regions. (1.3.6 Identify Purpose (Level
  AAA))
- **Use the correct landmark:** Use the `<header>` element as a container for introductory content, the `<nav>` element
  as a container for site-wide or in-page navigation links, the `<main>` element as a container for the main content of
  the page, the `<aside>` element as a container for content that is tangentially related to the main content, and the
  `<footer>` element as a container for information about the related content, such as the author, copyright
  information, and links to related documents. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A))
- **Use one `<main>` landmark per page:** Avoid using multiple `<main>` elements on a single page. (1.3.1 Info and
  Relationships (Level A))
- **Provide distinguishable accessible names for navigation regions:** If a page contains multiple `<nav>` elements,
  apply the `aria-label` attribute to each element and set its value to a distinguishable accessible name for the
  region. For example: `<nav aria-label="Primary">`, `<nav aria-label="Secondary">`, and so on. (Best practice)
- **Don't overuse landmarks:** Too many landmarks dilute their value. In particular, avoid labeling a `<section>` (which
  turns it into a `region` landmark) — `region` should be a last resort when no other landmark fits. (Best practice)

### Headings

- **Structure main content with headings:** Use `<h1>`–`<h6>` elements sequentially so screen reader users get a
  navigable outline. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A))
- **Mandatory - Don't use "fake" headings:** Never use `<div>` or `<span>` elements to look like headings without
  standard `<h1>`–`<h6>` elements. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A))
- **Avoid nesting headings incorrectly:** Make sure that, if a sub-heading is visually less important than its parent
  heading, its heading level is lower in the heading hierarchy. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A))
- **Use one `<h1>` element per page:** Use the `<h1>` element for the page's main heading. Having more than one `<h1>`
  element on a page makes it difficult for screen reader users to identify the actual main heading. (Best Practice)
    - **Caveat:** If a page includes a modal dialog that is marked up using the `<dialog>` element, `role="dialog"`, or
      `role="alertdialog"`, it is fine to mark up its main heading using the `<h1>` element because the dialog is a new
      window that is separate from the page.
- **Avoid "skipped" heading levels:** Avoid jumping directly from (for example) `<h1>` → `<h4>` to avoid breaking the
  logical hierarchy. (Best Practice)
- **Avoid placing headings inside the `<summary>` element:** Some browsers still expose this element as a button, which
  removes all roles from its children including headings. If a heading must act as a disclosure trigger, use an
  accordion or a disclosure implemented with ARIA where the heading element wraps the button, rather than use the
  `<details>` and `<summary>` elements. (Best Practice)

### Lists

- **Use lists for repeated, contiguous content:** `<ul>`/`<ol>` give assistive tech a count of listitems up front and
  let users skip the entire list. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A))
- **Use the correct list element:** Use the `<ul>` element for unordered lists where the order of the items is **not**
  important (such as a list of related products), and use the `<ol>` element for ordered lists where the order of the
  content **is** important (such as a list of instructions). (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A))
- **Don't use lists for non-list content:** Do not use list markup to mark up separate paragraphs of text, as screen
  readers will announce list information when they encounter lists, therefore leading to a screen reader hearing
  potentially confusing and redundant information about the related content. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A))
- **Don't use lists for checkboxes and radio buttons:** When marked up correctly, screen readers will already announce
  the number of checkboxes or radio buttons, as well as the number of the currently focused checkbox / radio button in
  the set, even though there is no list markup. Additional list markup will lead to duplication. (1.3.1 Info and
  Relationships (Level A))

### Tables

- **Do use the correct table elements:** Use the `<table>` element to identify the table, the `<caption>` element to
  provide a title and accessible name for the description, the `<tr>` element to identify individual rows in the table,
  and the `<th>` and `<td>` elements to identify header and data cells respectively. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (
  Level A))
- **Do use the `scope` attribute on `<th>` elements:** The `scope` attribute indicates whether the `<th>` element
  represents a row header (`<th scope="row">`) or a column header (`<th scope="col">`). (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (
  Level A))
- **Mandatory - Don't use tables for layout:** Screen readers will announce redundant information about the layout,
  which may be confusing for screen reader users, while the use of tabular markup has an impact on the reading and
  keyboard focus order of content. Use CSS Grid/Flexbox for visual layouts instead. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level
  A))
- **Avoid overly-complex tables:** Spanned rows, spanned columns, nested tables, and expandable / collapsible rows can
  make sense visually and meet the related WCAG success criterion, but the overall structure can be disorienting and
  difficult to navigate for screen reader users. In such cases, break tables up into smaller tables that are easier and
  more efficient to navigate. (Best Practice)

### Skip links

- **Provide skip links** prior to repeated content like site headers with navigation or long/infinite lists, so that
  keyboard users can easily bypass them. (2.4.1 Bypass Blocks (Level A))
    - **Caveat:** Sometimes screen magnifiers do not follow the focus when a skip link’s target is not normally
      focusable.
      The recommended workaround is to make the target programmatically focusable, but not a part of the tab order,
      using `tabindex="-1"`.
      If the target contains focusable elements, this creates another usability issue as clicking within the target will
      always set the **sequential focus navigation start point** to the target rather than at a point between focusable
      elements.
      A solution that satisfies both user expectations is to make the first meaningful element within the intended
      target the actual target of the skip link with `tabindex="-1"`, for example a heading (
      `<h1 id="content" tabindex="-1">`).
      Beware that any content prior to such an element will be skipped, including other relevant content within the
      targeted section, and this creates usability gaps for other assistive tech users.
- **Avoid using skip links where they are not needed:** A set of pages whose only common element is a single link to the
  Home page does not need a skip link. (Best Practice)
- **Avoid overusing skip links:** A single skip link, or two skip links to cover the primary and secondary sets of
  common navigation links, is usually sufficient on a single page. Multiple unnecessary skip links add to the number
  of <kbd>Tab</kbd> stops to a page, which causes frustration for people who use the keyboard alone for navigation. (
  Best Practice)

```html
<!-- Good: Skip to main content -->
<a href="#content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>
<main id="content">...</main>
```

### Code Example: good use of landmarks, headings, lists, tables, and a skip link

```html
<!-- Good: Semantic landmarks, heading hierarchy, skip link -->
<header>
  <a href="#platform-dashboard" class="skip-link visually-hidden">Skip to content</a>
  <nav aria-label="Primary">
    <ul>
      <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
    </ul>
  </nav>
</header>
<main>
  <h1 id="platform-dashboard" tabindex="-1">Platform Dashboard</h1>
  <section>
    <h2>User Statistics</h2>
    <table>
      <caption>Monthly active users</caption>
      <thead>
        <tr>
          <th scope="col">Month</th>
          <th scope="col">Users</th>
        </tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr>
          <td>January</td>
          <td>12,000</td>
        </tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
    <h3>Notes</h3>
    <ul>
      <li>Results do not include users without active subscriptions</li>
      <li>Results are accurate as of 31 December 2025</li>
    </ul>
  </section>
</main>
```

## 2. Semantic HTML and ARIA

### Prefer native HTML

- **Prefer HTML elements and attributes to ARIA:** Avoid `<div role="button">` or `<a role="button">` and use `<button>`
  instead. Native HTML elements and attributes already have the correct role and behavior, including keyboard support,
  built-in by default. `<button>` already implies `role="button"`, `required` already implies `aria-required`, and no
  additional JavaScript is required to ensure the correct role and behavior is supported. (Best Practice)
    - **Caveat:** ARIA is required when the related feature is not available in HTML, for example there are no HTML
      elements explicitly intended for building a tabbed navigation widget, but ARIA includes appropriate role and state
      properties for this purpose.
- **Don't add redundant ARIA roles or properties:** Avoid `<ul role="list">`, `<nav role="navigation">`, and
  `<input required aria-required="true">`. (Best Practice)
    - **Caveat:** Safari removes list semantics from `<ul>`/`<ol>` outside `<nav>` when `list-style: none` or
      `display: flex`/`grid` is applied. In that case `role="list"` is required to restore them.
- **Don't apply interactive ARIA roles to structural HTML elements:** Use
  `<li><span role="button">Button in a list</span></li>`, not `<li role="button">Button in a list</li>`, to avoid
  breaking the container list semantics. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A))
    - **Caveat:** It is acceptable to apply ARIA roles to structural HTML elements that have similar semantics, for
      example a tree view: `<ul role="tree"><li role="treeitem">…</li>…</ul>`.

### ARIA roles and states

- **Match ARIA implementations to actual behavior:** When applying `role="tab"` to an element, it must then behave like
  a tab — including keyboard interactions. Many ARIA patterns can't be implemented in CSS alone and need JavaScript. (
  4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A))
- **Manage toggle states:** Utilize `aria-expanded` and `aria-pressed` to communicate toggle states for custom
  controls. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A))
- **Be deliberate about `disabled` vs `aria-disabled`:** `disabled` removes the element from the focus order entirely (
  and `tabindex="0"` won't bring it back), which is often wrong for toolbar buttons or links. `aria-disabled="true"`
  keeps the element focusable so users can land on it and learn it's disabled, but because it only communicates state to
  assistive technologies, you must also prevent activation (such as pointer clicks and keyboard triggers) in
  JavaScript. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A))
- **Mandatory - Don't hide interactive elements from screen readers:** Do not apply `aria-hidden="true"` to interactive
  elements that receive focus, or to their parent elements. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A))
- **Mandatory - Don't suppress the roles of interactive elements:** Applying `role="presentation"` or `role="none"` to
  an interactive element strips its semantics. The element will still be exposed to assistive technologies and announced
  by screen readers, but its role and any state information will not be, which results in confusion and potentially
  unexpected behavior. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A))
- **Don't assume custom elements have no ARIA:** Custom elements can attach ARIA via `ElementInternals`, which some
  automated test tools can't see — so the absence of `role`/`aria-*` attributes in markup doesn't prove the element has
  no semantics. Verify with the browser's accessibility-tree inspector. (Best Practice)

## 3. Accessible Names and Descriptions

Every interactive element and some landmarks need an accessible name, and many benefit from an accessible description.
Names are short and identify the element; descriptions add context.

### Naming mechanisms

- **Prefer native naming mechanisms:** `<label>` for form controls, `<caption>` for `<table>`, `<legend>` for
  `<fieldset>`, `<figcaption>` for `<figure>`. (Best Practice)
- **Explicitly associate `<label>` with its control via `for`/`id`:** As well as ensuring the control is appropriately
  labeled by the contents of the `<label>` element, this results in a larger target area for people to activate the
  label _or_ its related control to move focus to the control, which isn't globally supported with other forms of
  labeling (such as using the `aria-labelledby` attribute). Additionally, some assistive technologies, particularly
  voice recognition software, require the `for`/`id` relationship to be explicitly set, even if an equivalent
  accessibility-supported approach (such as nesting an `<input>` inside a `<label>`) is taken. (4.1.2 Name, Role,
  Value (Level A))
- **Prefer `aria-labelledby` over `aria-label` when a visible label exists:** This avoids duplication, improves
  maintainability, and translates better. (Best Practice)
- **Don't use `title` as a naming mechanism:** The value of this attribute is only displayed on mouse hover, and cannot
  be displayed or otherwise accessed using the keyboard in any browser. (Best Practice)
    - **Caveat:** `<iframe>` is an exception, as the `title` attribute is the standard way of providing an accessible
      name for this element.
- **Don't use `placeholder` as a naming mechanism:** While the value of this attribute is initially displayed inside an
  `<input>` or `<textarea>`, it disappears as soon as the user enters text into the field, meaning that there is no
  longer a visual cue as to what the field represents. The contrast between `placeholder` text and its background in
  most browsers is very low, and therefore is difficult for people to perceive. (3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (Level A))
- **Don't put `aria-label`/`aria-labelledby` on elements that shouldn't be named:** Examples include plain `<div>`,
  `<span>`, and other custom elements without a role. These attributes are only intended for providing accessible names
  for elements that have explicit or implicit widget (for example, button, link, and tab), landmark, image, or iframe
  roles. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A))
    - **Caveat:** Custom elements may have an implicit role set via `ElementInternals`, so the absence of a `role`
      attribute isn't conclusive.

### Choosing the name

- **Avoid inconsistent link text:** If multiple hyperlinks direct users to the same target page, make sure each link has
  the same accessible name, which should typically be the same as its visible link text. For example, if the target page
  for a link is `profile.html`, make sure that all links have an accessible name of "My Profile" **or** "Profile"; do
  not use "My Profile" in one instance, and "Profile" in the other. (Best Practice)
- **Disambiguate controls that look visually identical but which perform different actions by their accessible name:**
  For example, a page may include multiple "Edit" buttons, each of which triggers functionality to perform a different
  action, such as edit the user's name, edit the user's password, and edit the user's address. While it may be visually
  obvious from the surrounding content what the purpose of these buttons might be, screen reader users may only hear "
  Edit, button". Techniques to resolve this include the following: (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A))
    - **Use visually hidden text:** The text is included in the DOM but is visually hidden using CSS. For example
      `<button>Edit <span class="visually-hidden">first name</span></button>`. Refer to
      the [code example: visually hidden utility](#code-example-visually-hidden-utility) for the full CSS.
    - **Apply the `aria-label` attribute to the control:** The value of this attribute should then include the visible
      text as well as important contextual information, for example `<button aria-label="Edit name">Edit</button>`,
      `<button aria-label="Edit address">Edit</button>`, and so on.
    - **Use the `aria-labelledby` or `aria-describedby` attribute to associate the control with the content it relates
      to:** Chaining IDs in `aria-labelledby` appends the related text to the control's accessible name (for example,
      `<p id="firstName">First name</p> <button id="editFirstName" aria-labelledby="editFirstName firstName">Edit</button>`),
      whereas `aria-describedby` provides the context as an accessible description (
      `<p id="firstName">First name</p> <button aria-describedby="firstName">Edit</button>`).
- **Do include a control's visible text in its accessible name:** Any visible text used to label a control must be
  included exactly as written in the control's accessible name. The accessible name can include additional information
  before or after the visible text, but the visible text itself must not differ. For example, the accessible name for a
  link containing the link phrase "Read more" can be "Read more about [subject]", because the visible text is included
  without modification. However, the accessible name cannot be "Read some more about [subject]", because the term "some"
  appears between the words "Read" and "more", which is not reflected in the visible text. (2.5.3 Label in Name (Level
  A))
- **Don't reuse an accessible name across controls with different effects in the same view:** Make sure that each
  accessible name is disambiguated. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A))
    - **Caveat:** Having two separate buttons with the accessible name of "Close" in two separate dialog boxes is fine,
      because only one dialog box is reachable at a time; however, multiple "Edit" buttons for different effects in the
      same dialog box is not.
- **Don't reuse an accessible name across hyperlinks that point to different `href` targets:** For example, avoid
  `<a href="annualreport2025.html">Annual Report</a>` and `<a href="annualreport2026.html">Annual Report</a>`. Use
  `<a href="annualreport2025.html">Annual Report 2025</a>` and
  `<a href="annualreport2026.html">Annual Report 2026</a>` (or an equivalent technique for disambiguating controls)
  instead.
- **Don't pack descriptions, error messages, or instructions into the label:** Verbose labels confuse and frustrate
  people who use screen readers. Instead, use the `aria-describedby` attribute to programmatically associate any
  additional content with the field. For example:
  `<label for="yourComments">Your comments</label><p id="yourCommentsWarning">Please do not include any personal information in this field.</p><textarea id="yourComments" aria-describedby="yourCommentsWarning"></textarea>`.
  Screen readers will then announce the label first, followed by the control type, and only then announce additional
  information that a user can skip if they are already aware of it. (Best Practice)
- **Don't repeat state information already exposed by ARIA inside the label:** Examples include information exposed via
  the `aria-expanded`, `aria-checked`, `aria-selected`, `aria-pressed`, and similar attributes. This creates
  duplication, redundancy, and ambiguity. (Best Practice)
- **Don't include the role name in the label:** This will lead to duplication. For example,
  `<nav aria-label="Primary navigation">` will be read by screen readers as "Primary navigation, navigation". (Best
  Practice)

### Descriptions

- **Identify instructions, error messages, and any other important information explicitly related to a control as a
  description:** Examples of descriptions include: (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A))
    - A list of password requirements when creating an account
    - An error message related to a field in a previously submitted form
    - Additional instructions, such as "You must agree to the terms and conditions before you can submit the form"
- **Make sure the description is available to assistive technologies when the related element receives focus:** Take one
  of the following approaches (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)):
    - If the description is already visible on the page, programmatically associate it with the element using the
      `aria-describedby` attribute.
    - If the description is not visible on the page and is explicitly for screen reader users (in other words, when
      providing a visible description is not appropriate or useful), apply the `aria-description` attribute to the
      element and use it to provide an appropriate description.
- **Avoid including a description for every element:** if the primary label already provides sufficient information (
  such as "First name"), any additional description is likely to be redundant. (Best Practice)
    - **Caveat:** Inline error messages associated with controls, such as error messages below / above text fields, as
      well as secondary labels that should be announced when the element receives focus, are exceptions.
- **Avoid including information in the description that is already provided by attributes applied to the element:** For
  example, including "This is a required field" as a description for an `<input>` element that already includes the
  `required` attribute will lead to duplicate announcements. (Best Practice)
    - **Caveat:** `aria-invalid="true"` is an exception; many screen readers announce "invalid" when they reach an
      `<input>` that includes this attribute set to `true`, which indicates that the field is in error. However, it does
      not indicate what the error is. In such cases, a description (the actual human readable error message) is
      required. This attribute should only be applied and set to true when the error message is present.
- **Avoid including interactive elements in an `aria-describedby` target** unless the content of the element reads
  sensibly as a description on its own. For example: (Best Practice)
    - This is acceptable, as the entire text string makes sense when announced:
      `<p id="description">I understand the <a href="tandc.html">terms and conditions</a>.</p>`
    - This is not appropriate, as the description will be announced as "Please don't include personal information in
      this field. Learn more.", where "Learn more" will be announced out of its intended context:
      `<p id="description">Please don't include personal information in this field. <a href="…">Learn more</a></p>`.
      Instead, only include the plain text in the referenced description:
      `<p><span id="description">Please don't include personal information in this field.</span> <a href="…">Learn more</a></p>`.

### Code Example: Visually Hidden Utility

A `.visually-hidden` utility provides text for screen readers without rendering it visually. It's commonly used for skip
links, additional context on icon-only buttons, and supplementary labels.

```css
/* Hides content visually but keeps it in the accessibility tree.
   :focus-within / :active opt elements out — useful for skip links and
   any focusable content wrapped in this class. */
.visually-hidden:where(:not(:focus-within, :active)) {
  position: absolute !important;
  clip-path: inset(50%) !important;
  overflow: hidden !important;
  width: 1px !important;
  height: 1px !important;
  margin: -1px !important;
  padding: 0 !important;
  border: 0 !important;
  white-space: nowrap !important;
}
```

When the hidden content is focusable (skip links, focus-receiving wrappers), the `:focus-within`/`:active` exception
lets it become visible. Style the visible state per situation, e.g. a skip link to the main content typically wants
fixed positioning at the top-left of the viewport so the rest of the page doesn't shift.

## 4. Document Metadata and Language

### Language

- **Do declare the page's human language:** Always apply the `lang` attribute to the page's `<html>` element, and always
  set it to the primary human language of the page's content. For example, `<html lang="en">`. (3.1.1 Language of Page (
  Level A))
- **Do declare changes in the page's human language:** If there is a language change on the page, apply the `lang`
  attribute to the parent/container element for the affected content, and set the value of this attribute to the
  shortcode for the language of the affected content. For example:
  `<p>In Germany, you may be greeted by someone saying <span lang="de">Guten Morgen</span>.</p>`. (3.1.2 Language of
  Parts (Level AA))
- **Don't set the value of the `lang` attribute to a value that doesn't match the human language of the content:** This
  causes screen readers and other text-to-speech software to announce the content in a non-understandable manner. (3.1.1
  Language of Page (Level A), 3.1.2 Language of Parts (Level AA))

### Titles

- **Do include the `<title>` element in the `<head>` section for all pages:** This includes pages embedded into a
  document using an `<iframe>`. (2.4.2 Page Titled (Level A))
- **Provide unique page titles:** Every page should have its own title that unambiguously reflects the page's purpose or
  content. (2.4.2 Page Titled (Level A))
- **Front-load the page's `<title>` with unique content:** For example, `<title>Page Topic | Site Name</title>`. (Best
  Practice)
- **Update single-page application (SPA) titles during page transitions:** For example, if the page title is
  `<title>Contact Us</title>` when a contact form is displayed, update the title to
  `<title>Thank you for contacting us!</title>` when the form is successfully submitted. (2.4.2 Page Titled (Level A))
- **Don't include an empty `<title>` element in the `<head>` section of a page:** No matter how short or inconsequential
  a page appears, do not use `<title></title>`. Page titles appear in the browser tab, so pages are distinguishable when
  users have multiple tabs open, and are typically announced by screen readers when the page is opened. (2.4.2 Page
  Titled (Level A))
- **Avoid using the same title for multiple pages, or using ambiguous page titles:** In such cases, pages are
  indistinguishable without reviewing the actual page content itself. (2.4.2 Page Titled (Level A))

### Iframes

- **Do provide a descriptive `title` for `<iframe>` elements:** All `<iframe>` elements should include a `title`
  attribute set to a value that unambiguously describes the contents of the `<iframe>`. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level
  A))
- **Don't disable iframe scrolling** using `scrolling="no"` (deprecated) or `overflow: hidden` on iframes. Users who
  zoom in or enlarge text need to scroll to reach content that overflows. (1.4.4 Resize Text (Level AA), 1.4.10 Reflow (
  Level AA))

### Code Example: using the `<title>` and `<iframe>` elements

```html
<!-- Good: Distinct title and language declaration -->
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <title>Analytics Reports | Guidance Platform</title>
</head>
<body>
  <p>The motto is <span lang="la">"Carpe diem"</span>.</p>
  <iframe title="Interactive Sales Chart" src="/chart"></iframe>
</body>
</html>
```

## 5. Keyboard and Focus Management

### Tab order and focusability

- **Provide a logical tab order:** Make sure that the order in which elements receive focus follows an appropriate
  sequence. (2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A))
    - **Caveat:** In left-to-right reading languages, the tab order is logical when focus moves from top-to-bottom and
      left-to-right. However, in right-to-left reading languages, the tab order is logical when focus moves from
      top-to-bottom and right-to-left.
- **Use `tabindex` only when necessary:** Apply `tabindex="0"` to elements requiring focus where an appropriate
  interactive role has been applied but the element isn't focusable by default; for example,
  `<span role="button" tabindex="0">Print</span>` (2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A))
- **Manage focus correctly to and from updated content:** For example, if a dialog box appears on the page, make sure
  that focus immediately moves to the dialog box, is restricted to the contents of the dialog box, and (when dismissed)
  returns to the element that originally triggered the dialog box. (2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A))
- **Don't apply `tabindex="0"` to interactive elements that are already focusable by default:** Native elements like the
  `<button>`, `<a>` (only with the associated `href` attribute), and `<input>` elements are already keyboard focusable,
  and therefore do not require `tabindex="0"`. (2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A))
- **Don't apply `tabindex="0"` to static, non-interactive, and hidden elements:** Only elements that (when activated)
  perform a specific action should be included in a page's tab order. Static, non-interactive, and hidden elements (
  whether hidden temporarily or permanently) must not be focusable. (2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A))
- **Mandatory - Don't use positive `tabindex` values:** Never apply `tabindex="1"` (or any value > 0) to elements, as
  doing so imposes a tab order on the page that bears no resemblance to the intended or expected tab order. (2.4.3 Focus
  Order (Level A))

### Keyboard handlers

- **Attach <kbd>Enter</kbd>/<kbd>Space</kbd> handlers for custom simulated interactive elements:** When implementing a
  custom keyboard handler for button-like elements, <kbd>Enter</kbd> should be a `keydown` handler and <kbd>Space</kbd>
  should be a `keyup` handler (matching native `<button>` behavior where <kbd>Enter</kbd> repeats and <kbd>Space</kbd>
  triggers on release). (2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A))
- **Don't attach keyboard handlers to native interactive elements:** Native elements such as the `<button>`, `<input>`,
  and `<a>` (with the required `href` attribute) elements already support the <kbd>Enter</kbd> and (except for the `<a>`
  element) the <kbd>Space</kbd> keys by default, so adding these keyboard handlers is redundant. (Best Practice)
    - **Caveat:** if the `<a>` element is repurposed as a button through the inclusion of `role="button"`, a `keyup`
      handler is still required to support the <kbd>Space</kbd> key to match native `<button>` behavior.

#### Code Example: Keyboard handlers

```javascript
// Good: Keyboard handlers for complex custom widgets (e.g., Tree items, tabs).
// NOTE: This pattern applies ONLY to non-standard UI where no native HTML tag exists.
// Always prioritize native <button> or <input> elements for standard interactions.
// Elements MUST have the appropriate ARIA role (e.g., role="treeitem" or role="tab").
customWidget.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
  if (e.key === 'Enter') {
    toggleWidgetState();
  }
  if (e.key === ' ') {
    e.preventDefault(); // Prevent page scrolling on Spacebar keydown
  }
});

customWidget.addEventListener('keyup', (e) => {
  if (e.key === ' ') {
    toggleWidgetState();
  }
});

function toggleWidgetState() {
  // E.g., Manage toggle/expanded states for custom controls
  const isExpanded = customWidget.getAttribute('aria-expanded') === 'true';
  customWidget.setAttribute('aria-expanded', !isExpanded);
}
```

### Focus indicators

- **Use `:focus-visible` when styling focus indicators:** When defining custom focus indicators, always style the
  `:focus-visible` state (not `:focus`) explicitly. (Best Practice)
- **Prefer browser native focus indicators over custom focus indicators:** Leave focus indication to the browser unless
  custom focus styling is needed to meet contrast or design requirements. (Best Practice)
- **Mandatory - Don't disable browser native focus indicators without providing a replacement custom focus indicator:**
  When using `outline: none;` to suppress the browser native focus indicator, provide an equivalent custom focus
  indicator that has a contrast ratio of at least `3:1` against adjacent content (2.4.7 Focus Visible (Level AA), 1.4.11
  Non-text Contrast (Level AA)).
- **Prefer `outline` over other properties for focus rings:** If `box-shadow` must be relied on for focus rings, provide
  an `outline`-based fallback for High Contrast Mode using the `forced-colors` media query. (Best Practice)
- **Pair custom focus outlines with `outline-offset`:** This visually separates the ring from the element. (Best
  Practice)

#### Code Example: Custom focus indication

```css
/* Good: High contrast focus border */
:where(a:any-link, button):focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #ff0055;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}
```

### Target sizes

- **Do size interactive elements to have a target of at least 24x24 CSS pixels:** Enforce the target size of elements
  using `min-block-size` / `min-inline-size` or through padding rather than `width` / `height` so that content grows the
  target but not shrink it. (2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (Level AA))
    - **Caveat:** Interactive elements _may_ have a target of less than 24x24 CSS pixels _as long as_ they are
      positioned in such a way that if a 24 CSS pixel diameter circle is centered on the bounding box of each element,
      the circles do not intersect nearby targets or circles for other targets that are less than 24x24 CSS pixels.
- **Bump targets up on coarse pointers:** `@media (pointer: coarse) { … }`. (2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (Level AA))
- **Don't use `touch-action: none;` for custom gestures:** This disables page scrolling through the element. Scope to
  the axis you actually need - `pan-y` for horizontal swipes (the page still scrolls vertically), and `pan-x` for
  vertical swipes. Reserve `none` for elements where no native touch behavior makes sense, such as a drawing canvas. (
  2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A))

## 6. Alternate Text and Media

### Images

- **Mandatory - Apply the `alt` attribute to all `<img>` elements:** browsers replace the image with the value of this
  attribute for people who use screen readers. (1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A))
- **Do provide informative visual descriptions:** Describe the purpose of the image (for example, "Search", not "
  Magnifying glass"). (1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A))
- **Do apply `alt=""` to decorative visuals:** This prevents screen readers from announcing them. (1.1.1 Non-text
  Content (Level A))
- **Don't use clichéd prefixes:** Avoid terms like "Image of…" and "Picture of…". (Best Practice)
- **Don't use underscores in filenames:** Use dashes if the filename might be announced as fallback. (Best Practice)

#### Code Example: Providing a text description for `<img>` elements

```html
<!-- Decorative -->
<img src="divider.png" alt="">

<!-- Informative (Functional) -->
<a href="/search">
  <img src="glass.png" alt="Search the platform">
</a>
```

### Inline SVGs

- **Do apply `role="img"` to the `<svg>` element for non-decorative SVGs:** This is so that they are globally exposed as
  images. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A))
- **Do provide a text description for non-decorative SVGs:** Use one of the following techniques: (1.1.1 Non-text
  Content (Level A))
    - Include a nested `<title>` element as a child of the `<svg>` element that includes the text description. **or**
    - Apply the `aria-label` attribute to the `<svg>` element and set its value to an appropriate text description.
- **Do hide decorative SVGs from assistive technologies:** Apply `aria-hidden="true"` to decorative `<svg>` elements to
  prevent screen readers from announcing them. (1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A))

#### Code Example: Providing a text description for non-decorative SVGs using the `<title>` element

```html
<!-- Inline non-decorative SVG: example that uses the <title> element -->
<svg role="img" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
  <title>Home</title>
  <path d="M10 20v-6h4v6h5v-8h3L12 3 2 12h3v8z"/>
</svg>
```

#### Code Example: Providing a text description for non-decorative SVGs using the `aria-label` attribute

```html
<!-- Inline non-decorative SVG: example that uses the aria-label attribute -->
<svg role="img" viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-label="Home">
  <path d="M10 20v-6h4v6h5v-8h3L12 3 2 12h3v8z"/>
</svg>
```

#### Code Example: Identifying decorative SVGs

```html
<!-- Inline Decorative SVG (hide from assistive technologies) -->
<svg aria-hidden="true" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
  <path d="M10 20v-6h4v6h5v-8h3L12 3 2 12h3v8z"/>
</svg>
```

### Complex images and charts

- **Provide long descriptions for complex images:** Use `<figure>`/`<figcaption>` or `aria-describedby` for charts and
  infographics. (1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A))
- **Provide semantic data tables as alternatives:** Provide semantic data tables as accessible alternatives for charts
  and other complex visualizations. (1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A))

#### Code Example: Complex graph with figcaption

```html
<!-- Complex graph with figcaption -->
<figure>
  <img src="chart.png" alt="Sales growth graph 2024.">
  <figcaption>Sales grew 20% in Q3 due to new platform launch.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

### Audio and video

- **Mandatory - Provide a transcript for audio-only content and combined video & audio content:** The transcript should
  be verbatim, and include all of the dialogue as well as text descriptions of important non-speech sounds such as sound
  effects. (1.2.1 Audio-only and Video-only (Prerecorded) (Level A), 1.2.3 Audio Description or Media Alternative (
  Prerecorded) (Level AA))
- **Mandatory - Provide a text description or an audio track for video-only content:** Examples include text-based
  instructions for an animation on how to use a particular product, and a separate audio track that includes a
  description of the action in the video. (1.2.1 Audio-only and Video-only (Prerecorded) (Level A))
- **Mandatory - Provide synchronous captions for videos:** Supply WebVTT captions for audio tracks within video content.
  The captions should be verbatim and synchronous with the audio track, and include all of the dialogue as well as
  meaningful non-speech content such as sound effects and other important information conveyed within the soundtrack (
  for example, "Ominous music plays"). (1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded) (Level A))
    - **Caveat:** Captions are not required if the video is a decorative alternative for text that is already present
      and is clearly identified as such.
- **Do provide an audio description for videos:** Include an additional audio track within the video that augments the
  visual content displayed on-screen. The audio description should convey information about the scene that is not
  described or spoken in the main audio track, and should be conveyed during existing pauses in the dialogue. (1.2.3
  Audio Description or Media Alternative (Prerecorded) (Level A), 1.2.5 Audio Description (Prerecorded) (Level AA))

#### Code Example: Video and audio content with captions and transcript

```html
<!-- Video with Captions tracks -->
<video controls>
  <source src="intro.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  <track src="caps.vtt" kind="captions" srclang="en" label="English">
</video>

<!-- Audio with expandable transcript details -->
<audio controls src="podcast.mp3" aria-details="podcast-transcript"></audio>
<details id="podcast-transcript">
  <summary>View Transcript</summary>
  <div class="transcript-content">
    Welcome to the show...
  </div>
</details>
```

### CSS generated content

- **Alt text for CSS generated content:** Use the alternative text argument of `content` (e.g.
  `content: url(icon.svg) / "Save";`) and keep meaningful text in the DOM. See `accessible-generated-content` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "accessible-generated-content"`) for more details. (1.1.1 Non-text
  Content (Level A))

### Content Visibility Decision Matrix

| Intent                 | Visual | Screen Reader | Focusable            | Structural Pattern                                |
|:-----------------------|:-------|:--------------|:---------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|
| **Visible to all**     | Yes    | Yes           | Yes                  | Standard rendering                                |
| **Screen Reader only** | No     | Yes           | Yes (if interactive) | Visually hidden utility (e.g. `.visually-hidden`) |
| **Visual only**        | Yes    | No            | No                   | `aria-hidden="true"`                              |
| **Hidden for all**     | No     | No            | No                   | `hidden` attribute / `display: none`              |

**Heuristic Rule:** If an element can receive keyboard focus, it must not be hidden via `aria-hidden="true"`.

**Note:** only use screen reader only content as a last resort. If content is important, it should be visible for
everyone.

## 7. Forms and Input Controls

### Labels and hints

- **Mandatory - Provide a label for all form controls:** Do not rely on the currently selected input or value as a way
  of labeling the control. (3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (Level A))
- **Connect Labels Programmatically:** Use `<label for="id">` linked to `<input id="id">`. (1.3.1 Info and
  Relationships (Level A))
- **Don't use placeholders as primary labels:** Placeholders are not persistent labels. Only use placeholders to provide
  brief hints, such as an example of an appropriate input. (3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (Level A))
- **Link hints to inputs via `aria-describedby`:** Associate help text with inputs, and place the hint above the input
  so autocomplete popovers don't cover it during editing. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A))

#### Code Example: A labeled form control with a hint for passwords

```html
<!-- Good: Semantic forms with hints for passwords -->
<form>
  <label for="pwd">Password:</label>
  <span id="pwd-hint">Must contain at least 8 characters.</span>
  <input id="pwd" type="password" aria-describedby="pwd-hint" autocomplete="current-password" required>
</form>
```

### Input assistance and validation

- **Mandatory - Use the `autocomplete` attribute:** Apply the `autocomplete` attribute to `<input>`, `<textarea>`, and
  `<select>` elements that explicitly collect personal information about the user, and set it to the correct value (for
  example `"email"` or `"given-name"`). (1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose (Level AA))
- **Provide form validation constraints:** Use `required` (or `aria-required="true"` only when `required` isn't
  applicable) to signal mandatory inputs. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A))
- **Don't trigger context shifts on focus changes:** Avoid auto-submitting forms or jumping pages on focus change events
  alone. (3.2.1 On Focus (Level A), 3.2.2 On Input (Level A))

## 8. Live Regions

Live regions let assistive tech announce content updates that aren't tied to navigation or focus changes. They're easy
to misuse — too many regions, or noisy ones, quickly become spam for screen-reader users.

### Live Region Urgency Table

| Urgency      | Visual Analogue | `aria-live` Value               | Behavioral Impact                           | Example                        |
|:-------------|:----------------|:--------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------|
| **Critical** | Modal / Alert   | `assertive` (or `role="alert"`) | Interrupts immediately, clears speech queue | Session timeout, API failure   |
| **Standard** | Toast / Banner  | `polite`                        | Announces at next graceful break            | Search results, "Saved" status |
| **Passive**  | Silent text     | `off`                           | Only if user navigates to it                | Live character count           |

**Heuristic Rule:** Use `assertive` only for critical, time-sensitive updates that require immediate attention or
prevent safe continuation (e.g., data loss, session timeouts, or network drops).

### When to announce live regions

- **Announce dynamic errors via live regions:** Use `aria-live` or shift focus to error lists (4.1.3 Status Messages (
  Level AA)).
- **Don't use live regions for interstitial states** like "Loading…" or "Updating…" unless they're meaningfully
  informative — they usually just create noise. Use the HTML `<progress>` element or the ARIA `progressbar` role for
  this purpose instead. (Best Practice)

```html
<!-- Session Timeout Warning with controls -->
<div role="alert" class="timeout-warning">
  Your session will expire in 2 minutes.
  <button type="button" onclick="extendSession()">Extend Session</button>
</div>
```

### Managing announcements

- **Centralize live regions for non-visible announcements:** A single `polite` region and a single `assertive` region
  per page (with whatever `aria-atomic` configuration you need) keeps announcements consistent and easier to maintain.
  Many frameworks ship their own announcer abstraction — use it. (Best Practice)
- **Debounce frequently-changing regions:** If a region can update many times per second (e.g. a combobox's result count
  as the user types), debounce so users aren't spammed. (Best Practice)
- **Delay slightly when other announcements may collide:** When the user is typing or focus is being managed, a small
  delay before announcing keeps live-region updates from overlapping other speech. (Best Practice)
- **Don't add live-region updates to inert DOM:** When dialogs open or sections become `inert`, queued or debounced
  messages will be unannounced — or announced from DOM the user can't reach. Coordinate live-region updates with
  dialog/inert state changes. (4.1.3 Status Messages (Level AA))

See `color` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "color"`) for accessible color (contrast requirements,
light and dark color schemes, Forced Colors Mode, etc).

See `typography` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "typography"`) for readable typography.

## 12. Modals and Native Dialogs

Modern browsers provide native solutions for creating modal dialogs which avoid the need for focus traps, managing the
accessibility of outside content, ensuring the content is on top, and dimming the background content — all of which are
error prone and require heavy JavaScript event tracking to maintain.

### Native `<dialog>`

- **Use the native `<dialog>` element:** Invoke the dialog using the `.showModal()` method to open it in a modal state.
  When in a modal state, the browser sets outside content as inert (i.e. the outside content is hidden from the
  accessibility tree and cannot be interacted with nor be focused). (1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence (Level A), 2.4.3 Focus
  Order (Level A), 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A))
    - **Note:** it is still possible to navigate to the browser chrome when using the `<dialog>` element.
- **Don't implement focus traps for native modal dialogs:** When a `<dialog>` element is opened in a modal state,
  browsers set outside content as inert which is sufficient for ensuring only the dialog’s content can be focused. (Best
  Practice)

#### Code Example: HTML & JavaScript: Native `<dialog>` with standard close events

```html
<!-- Dialog opens natively with showModal() and locks focus -->
<button id="open-btn">Open Dialog</button>

<dialog id="accessible-modal" aria-labelledby="title-id">
  <h2 id="title-id">Account Settings</h2>
  <p>Update your details here.</p>
  <button onclick="this.closest('dialog').close()">Close Dialog</button>
</dialog>

<script>
  document.getElementById('open-btn').addEventListener('click', () => {
    document.getElementById('accessible-modal').showModal();
  });
</script>
```

### Custom overlays

- **Use the `inert` attribute for custom overlays:** When `<dialog>` cannot be used (e.g., some non-modal overlays,
  framework constraints, or layouts where `<dialog>`'s top-layer/positioning behavior conflicts with the design), apply
  `inert` to outside content to ensure it cannot be interacted with by keyboard, pointer, or assistive technology. This
  requires structuring elements in such a way that the custom overlay is not a descendant of the element with `inert`
  set on it. (1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence (Level A), 2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A))
- **Apply `role="dialog"` to the custom overlay:** When applied to the element used as the container for the custom
  overlay, it ensures that it is exposed as a dialog box to assistive technologies. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A))
- **Move focus to the overlay:** Ensure keyboard and screen reader focus moves to the container for the overlay so that
  people using a screen reader and people using the keyboard alone can start navigating its contents. Don't leave focus
  in outside content. (1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence (Level A), 2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A))

## 13. Testing Validations

### Automated checks

- **Run Automated checks via axe-core or Lighthouse audits:** Catch missing alt texts or low contrasts (e.g., via
  Lighthouse in Chrome DevTools MCP).
- **Don't rely purely on scores:** A 100% score does not guarantee real usability.

### Manual testing

- **Validate Sequential Navigations using keyboards alone:** Using only keyboard shortcuts, such as <kbd>
  Tab</kbd> / <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>Tab</kbd>, arrow keys, <kbd>Enter</kbd>, <kbd>Space</kbd>, and <kbd>Esc</kbd>,
  confirm every interactive element is reachable and operable, and that focus never gets stuck.
- **Test on Screen Readers with calibrated browsers:** Rely on standard bindings (e.g., JAWS with Chrome, NVDA with
  Firefox, Narrator with Edge, VoiceOver with Safari on macOS and iOS, TalkBack with Chrome for Android).

# Accessible Error Announcement

## The Problem

Standard HTML5 validation provides visual feedback (via `:invalid` or `:user-invalid`), but it doesn't automatically
synchronize with accessibility attributes like `aria-invalid`.

If you use standard `:invalid` styling, screen readers might announce "Invalid entry" the moment a user tabs into a
required field that is currently empty. This creates a disruptive experience for users using assistive technologies, as
the error is announced before interaction has occurred.

## The Solution

We want the *programmatic* state (`aria-invalid="true"`) to be applied **at the exact same moment** the *visual* state (
`:user-invalid`) applies. Since `:user-invalid` relies on the browser's internal "user-interacted" flag, we can use
JavaScript to check that this selector matches during standard interaction events.

Set `aria-invalid="false"` until `:user-invalid` matches, rather than leaving the attribute unset. Firefox and Safari
expose an empty `required` field as invalid from page load, so an unset attribute still causes the premature "invalid
entry" announcement there.

### Implementation Strategy

1. **Visual Layer**: Use CSS `:user-invalid` to show borders/icons.
2. **Accessibility Layer**: Use `aria-invalid`, and list the error message in `aria-describedby` while the field is
   invalid, to communicate state to Assistive Technology (AT). Announce an error that appears when the user leaves a
   field through one polite live region for the page.
3. **Bridge Visual & Accessibility Layer**: Create a lightweight JavaScript utility that listens for `blur`, `change`,
   `input` and `invalid` events, checks if the element matches `:user-invalid`, and updates the ARIA attributes
   accordingly.
4. **Focus on Submit**: Screen readers announce a field's error when focus reaches the field, so after a failed submit,
   move focus to the first invalid field, or to an error summary (a heading followed by a link to each invalid field) on
   a long form. Native validation moves focus to the first invalid field for you; if the form uses `novalidate`, move it
   in your submit handler.

## Implementation Guide

### 1. HTML Structure

Link your input to its error message by setting the input's `data-error` attribute to the error message's `id`. The
script in section 3 lists that `id` in `aria-describedby` only while the field is invalid. Don't reference the error
from `aria-describedby` in the markup: the error element is always in the page, and text that `aria-describedby`
references is announced even when it's hidden, so the error would be read out before the user has interacted.

```html
<form>
  <div class="field">
    <label for="email">Email</label>
    <input 
      type="email" 
      id="email" 
      required 
      data-error="email-error"
    >
    <span id="email-error" class="error-msg">
      Please enter a valid email address.
    </span>
  </div>
</form>
```

### 2. CSS

Control the visibility of the error message using the native pseudo-class `:user-invalid`.

```css
.error-msg {
  display: none;
  color: #d93025;
}

/* Show error message when input is user-invalid */
input:user-invalid ~ .error-msg {
  display: block;
}

/* Optional: Visual cues on the input itself */
input:user-invalid {
  border-color: #d93025;
}
```

### 3. JavaScript

Since there is no "UserInvalidChanged" event, hook into standard form events to check the state.

Native `:user-invalid` does not automatically sync with ARIA attributes. Add the following JavaScript to keep
`aria-invalid` in sync with the visual state:

* Set `aria-invalid="false"` until `:user-invalid` matches, rather than leaving it unset. Firefox and Safari expose an
  empty `required` field as invalid from page load, and Chromium doesn't expose an empty `required` field as invalid
  after interaction unless `aria-invalid="true"` is set.
* Link each field to its error message by setting the field's `data-error` attribute to the error message's `id` (
  `data-error="email-error"` for `<div id="email-error">`), and let the script list that `id` in `aria-describedby` only
  while the field is invalid. Don't reference the error from `aria-describedby` in the markup: the error element is
  always in the page, and text that `aria-describedby` references is announced even when it's hidden.
* Announce an error that appears when the user leaves or changes a field through one polite live region for the page, a
  moment later so it doesn't talk over the next field. Don't make each error message a live region: a live region that
  is shown, rather than changed, isn't announced reliably. After a failed submit, move focus to the first invalid field
  so that its error is announced instead.

```javascript
// List the field's error message (the id in data-error) in aria-describedby only while
// it's shown: text that aria-describedby references is announced even when it's hidden.
const linkError = (el, shown) => {
  const errorId = el.dataset.error;
  if (!errorId) return;
  const ids = (el.getAttribute('aria-describedby') || '').split(/\s+/).filter((id) => id && id !== errorId);
  if (shown) ids.push(errorId);
  if (ids.length) el.setAttribute('aria-describedby', ids.join(' '));
  else el.removeAttribute('aria-describedby');
};

// One polite live region for the page announces an error that appears when the user
// leaves or changes a field. Run this once the form is in the page.
const announcer = document.createElement('div');
announcer.setAttribute('aria-live', 'polite');
announcer.classList.add('visually-hidden');
document.body.append(announcer);
let announceTimer;
let announcedField;

// Text as a screen reader reads it: icons' text alternatives in, aria-hidden text out.
const spokenText = (node) => {
  const copy = node.cloneNode(true);
  copy.querySelectorAll('[aria-hidden="true"]').forEach((n) => n.remove());
  copy.querySelectorAll('[role="img"][aria-label]').forEach((n) => n.replaceWith(`${n.getAttribute('aria-label')}: `));
  return copy.textContent.replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim();
};
const announceError = (el) => {
  const error = document.getElementById(el.dataset.error);
  if (!error) return;
  const label = el.labels?.[0] ? `${spokenText(el.labels[0])}: ` : '';
  clearTimeout(announceTimer);
  announcer.textContent = '';
  announcedField = el;
  // Wait until the screen reader has announced the field that receives focus next.
  announceTimer = setTimeout(() => { announcer.textContent = label + spokenText(error); }, 500);
};

// Sync aria-invalid with the CSS :user-invalid state. Only form fields are synced, and
// an aria-invalid="true" that this script didn't set (for example from a server check)
// is left alone.
const flagged = new WeakSet();
// Fields whose current error has been announced, or read out by focus after a failed
// submit. A field can become invalid while the user types, so this is tracked separately.
const announced = new WeakSet();
const syncAria = (el, announce = false) => {
  if (!el.matches?.('input, select, textarea')) return;
  const invalid = el.matches(':user-invalid');
  if (invalid) {
    if (announce && !announced.has(el)) {
      announceError(el);
      announced.add(el);
    }
    el.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');
    linkError(el, true);
    flagged.add(el);
  } else if (flagged.has(el) || el.getAttribute('aria-invalid') !== 'true') {
    el.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'false');
    linkError(el, false);
    flagged.delete(el);
    announced.delete(el);
    // Clear a fixed field's announcement so it isn't found later when reading the page.
    if (announcedField === el) {
      clearTimeout(announceTimer);
      announcer.textContent = '';
    }
  }
};

// Start every field at aria-invalid="false".
document.querySelectorAll('input, select, textarea').forEach((el) => syncAria(el));

// Update on blur (to show and announce an error) and input (to clear it)
document.addEventListener('blur', (e) => syncAria(e.target, true), true);
document.addEventListener('input', (e) => {
  if (e.target.hasAttribute('aria-invalid')) syncAria(e.target);
});

// Checkboxes, radio buttons and other controls that commit on 'change' can become
// :user-invalid without losing focus, so update on change too.
document.addEventListener('change', (e) => syncAria(e.target, true), true);

// A failed submit fires 'invalid' on each failing field, including required fields the
// user never touched, so update those too. 'invalid' doesn't bubble. Focus moving to the
// first invalid field announces its error, so these aren't announced.
document.addEventListener('invalid', (e) => {
  announced.add(e.target);
  syncAria(e.target);
}, true);

// Reset clears :user-invalid after the 'reset' event, so update each field afterwards.
document.addEventListener('reset', (e) => {
  setTimeout(() => [...e.target.elements].forEach((el) => syncAria(el)));
}, true);
```

Hide the live region with the `.visually-hidden` utility:

```css
/* Hides content visually but keeps it in the accessibility tree */
.visually-hidden:where(:not(:focus-within, :active)) {
  position: absolute !important;
  clip-path: inset(50%) !important;
  overflow: hidden !important;
  width: 1px !important;
  height: 1px !important;
  margin: -1px !important;
  padding: 0 !important;
  border: 0 !important;
  white-space: nowrap !important;
}
```

## Fallbacking & Browser Support

### Fallbacks & browser support for :user-valid and :user-invalid

Baseline status for :user-valid and :user-invalid: Widely available. It's been Baseline since 2023-11-02.
Supported by: Chrome 119 (Oct 2023), Edge 119 (Nov 2023), Firefox 88 (Apr 2021), and Safari 16.5 (May 2023).

### CSS for Fallback

```css
/* Applies to every field that can be invalid (input, select, textarea). :is() keeps the
   rule working where :user-invalid isn't supported: in a plain selector list, one
   unsupported selector drops the whole rule. */
:is(:user-invalid, .user-invalid-fallback) {
  border-color: #d93025;
  background-color: #fce8e6;
}

:is(:user-invalid, .user-invalid-fallback) + .error-msg {
  display: block;
}
```

### JavaScript Fallback

Use a reusable utility that tracks interaction state using a `WeakMap`. This avoids polluting the DOM with "dirty"
classes or data attributes.

```javascript
const UserInvalidFallback = (() => {
  const dirtyState = new WeakMap();

  const updateState = (input) => {
    // validity.valid gives the current state without firing an 'invalid' event, as checkValidity() does.
    const isValid = input.validity.valid;

    // Update both visual and ARIA state
    input.classList.toggle('user-invalid-fallback', !isValid);
    input.classList.toggle('user-valid-fallback', isValid);

    input.setAttribute('aria-invalid', isValid ? 'false' : 'true');
    linkError(input, !isValid);
  };

  // List the error message (the id in data-error) in aria-describedby only while it's
  // shown: text that aria-describedby references is announced even when it's hidden.
  const linkError = (input, shown) => {
    const errorId = input.dataset.error;
    if (!errorId) return;
    const ids = (input.getAttribute('aria-describedby') || '').split(/\s+/).filter((id) => id && id !== errorId);
    if (shown) ids.push(errorId);
    if (ids.length) input.setAttribute('aria-describedby', ids.join(' '));
    else input.removeAttribute('aria-describedby');
  };

  const handleEvent = (event) => {
    const input = event.target;

    if (event.type === 'reset') {
      const controls = input.elements || [];
      for (const control of controls) {
        dirtyState.delete(control);
        control.classList.remove('user-invalid-fallback');
        control.classList.remove('user-valid-fallback');
        if (control.matches('input, select, textarea')) control.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'false');
        if (control.dataset?.error) linkError(control, false);
      }
      return;
    }

    if (!input.checkValidity) return;

    // A submit attempt counts as interaction: the browser fires 'invalid' on each failing
    // field, including required fields the user never touched, so flag them all.
    if (event.type === 'invalid') {
      dirtyState.set(input, { hasInteracted: true, hasBlurred: true });
      updateState(input);
      return;
    }

    if (event.type === 'input' || event.type === 'change') {
      const state = dirtyState.get(input) || { hasInteracted: false, hasBlurred: false };
      state.hasInteracted = true;
      dirtyState.set(input, state);
      if (state.hasBlurred) {
        updateState(input);
      }
    } else if (event.type === 'blur') {
      const state = dirtyState.get(input) || { hasInteracted: false, hasBlurred: false };
      state.hasBlurred = true;
      dirtyState.set(input, state);
      if (state.hasInteracted) {
        updateState(input);
      }
    }
  };

  const init = (root = document) => {
    if (CSS.supports('selector(:user-invalid)')) return;

    // Firefox and Safari expose an empty required field as invalid from page load.
    root.querySelectorAll('input, select, textarea').forEach((el) => {
      if (!el.hasAttribute('aria-invalid')) el.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'false');
    });

    root.addEventListener('blur', handleEvent, true); // Capture phase
    root.addEventListener('input', handleEvent);
    root.addEventListener('change', handleEvent);
    root.addEventListener('invalid', handleEvent, true); // invalid doesn't bubble
    root.addEventListener('reset', handleEvent, true); // Capture resets
  };

  return { init };
})();

// Initialize for a specific form
const form = document.querySelector('#demo-form');
UserInvalidFallback.init(form);
```

# Accessible generated content

- **DON'T** use `content` to convey meaningful text (labels, state, instructions) — keep that in the DOM (WCAG F87). The
  alt text argument is harm reduction for cases where decoration accidentally carries meaning, not a license.
- Use the alternative text argument of `content` to provide alt text for screen readers. E.g.
  `content: url(cloud.svg) / "Save";`
- Use `content: "text" / "";` to prevent purely decorative text from being announced to screen readers.
- **DON'T** use an empty alt text argument for images — they're already presentational by default. E.g. this is wrong:
  `content: url(cloud.svg) / "";`.
- **DON'T** use the alt text argument to describe emojis unless the description differs from the official emoji name.
  E.g. don't do `content: "🎉" / "celebration";`, but `content: "🎉" / "Yay!";` is fine.

**ONLY** use the alt text argument when the text is different than the primary value and is not already present in the
DOM. I.e. this is wrong:

HTML:

```html
<button class="save">Save</button>
```

CSS:

```css
button.save::before {
  content: url(cloud.svg) / "Save";
}
```

A screen reader would read it out as "Save save".

## Fallback strategies

Baseline status for Alt text for generated content: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2024-07-09.
Supported by: Chrome 77 (Sep 2019), Edge 79 (Jan 2020), Firefox 128 (Jul 2024), and Safari 17.4 (Mar 2024).

If your Baseline target includes browsers that do not support the `/` alternative text syntax, precede the declaration
with a single-value `content` fallback so unsupported browsers do not drop the entire declaration as invalid CSS:

```css
.more-link::after {
  /* Fallback: render the glyph in browsers without `/` support
     (screen readers there will still announce it) */
  content: " →";
  content: " →" / "";
}
```

For non-empty alternative text (`content: url(...) / "..."`), a single-value `content: url(...)` fallback keeps the
image visible in older browsers but drops its alt text. If that label is required in older browsers, put it in the DOM
instead (e.g., via a visually hidden `<span>` or `aria-label`) and use a plain `content: url(...)` declaration without
`/`.

# Respect Operating System Text Scale

## Overview

Users with visual impairments often configure text scaling at the operating system level (such as Dynamic Type on iOS or
Font Size scaling on Android/ChromeOS). By default, mobile browsers ignore these OS-level accessibility settings to
prevent legacy, fixed-pixel websites from breaking visually.

Instead of keeping your page static or relying on custom, fragile JavaScript layout calculations, opt into native
operating system text scaling using the `<meta name="text-scale">` tag. When active, the browser dynamically scales the
root font size (`1rem`) to match the user's OS preference, allowing all relative (`rem`/`em`) font sizes, layouts, and
spacing to scale automatically and gracefully.

## Implementation

### 1. Opt Into OS Text Scaling

Place the `<meta name="text-scale">` element inside your document's `<head>`. This signals to supporting browsers that
your layout is modern, adaptive, and safe to scale:

```html
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8" />
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width" />
  
  <!-- Opt this page into OS-level dynamic type and accessibility text scaling -->
  <meta name="text-scale" content="scale" />
  
  <title>Adaptive Accessibility Layout</title>
</head>
```

### 2. Use Relative Typography & Spacing

Define font sizes using relative units (`rem` or `em`) rather than fixed pixels (`px`). Use unitless values for line
heights so they scale proportionally with each element's computed font size.

Use relative units for margins and padding where the spacing is coupled to text size or must adapt as text is scaled.
Spacing that is independent of text may use fixed units when appropriate, provided that scaling does not cause text
clipping, overlap, loss of content, or an unusable layout:

```css
body {
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  /* Inherits the root font-size, which scales automatically with the OS setting */
  line-height: 1.5;      /* Unitless so it scales proportionally with computed font-size */
  padding: 1.5rem;       /* Scales proportionally to prevent dense crowding at larger scales */
}

h1 {
  font-size: 2.25rem;    /* Scales proportionally to the root base */
  margin-bottom: 1rem;
}
```

Set the base text size on `body` only when the design needs a size different from the inherited browser default;
otherwise, let it inherit. Set sizes on specific elements, such as headings, with relative units such as `rem` or `em`.
Use `rem` for a size relative to the root font size, and `em` when the size should depend on the parent element's font
size. Do not set a custom font size on `:root` or `html`.

#### Fluid Typography

Fluid typography MAY use viewport-relative units such as `vw`, provided that font sizes also include a font-relative
component such as `rem` or `em`. For more fluid-scaling techniques, including container query units and `clamp()`, see
`fluid-scaling` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "fluid-scaling"`).

Avoid sizing text exclusively with viewport units:

```css
/* ❌ DO NOT DO THIS: The font size does not respond fully to user text scaling */
.heading {
  font-size: 5vw;
}
```

Instead, combine a font-relative value with viewport-relative scaling and use relative minimum and maximum bounds:

```css
.heading {
  font-size: clamp(2rem, 1.25rem + 2vw, 4rem);
}
```

Test that text can be resized to at least 200% of its default size without loss of content or functionality. For fluid
typography, a useful rule of thumb is to keep the maximum font size no more than 2.5 times the minimum. Also test reflow
at a 320 CSS-pixel viewport width (equivalent to 400% zoom from a 1280 CSS-pixel-wide viewport); content MUST remain
available without two-dimensional scrolling, except where essential.

### 3. Use Scalable Responsive Breakpoints

Responsive breakpoints MUST NOT assume that text will remain at its default size. Where a breakpoint is intended to
respond to available space for text, prefer content-driven layouts, container queries, or `em`-based media queries
rather than fixed pixel thresholds.

Test responsive layouts with operating system text scaling and browser zoom enabled. Text MUST remain readable and
content MUST remain visible without overlap, clipping, or horizontal scrolling.

### 4. Ensure Content Wrapping & Flexible Heights

When text scales up, elements require more vertical and horizontal space to prevent truncation or overlap. To keep your
components robust, design your layouts to expand dynamically around the content rather than forcing rigid coordinates:

* **Allow Text Containers to Grow**: Text-containing components and containers MUST be able to grow to accommodate
  scaled text. Avoid fixed `height` or `block-size` values and restrictive `max-height` or `max-block-size` values that
  can cause clipping or overflow. Prefer content-driven sizing; use `min-height` or `min-block-size` only when a minimum
  size is needed.
* **Allow Natural Wrapping**: Do not restrict inline-axis text wrapping with `white-space: nowrap` on blocks that
  contain sentences. Let text reflow to new lines naturally.
* **Employ Flexible Flexbox & Grid wrapping (Optional Example)**: For multi-column card galleries, use reflowing columns
  like `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 16rem), 1fr))` so items stack vertically if their relative width thresholds
  are crossed:

```css
/* Card container using min-height to ensure expansion and auto-fit to reflow if needed */
.card {
  padding: 1.5rem;
  border: 1px solid #ccc;
  border-radius: 8px;
  /* Use min-height so the box expands vertically when the font is enlarged */
  min-height: 10rem;
}
```

### 5. DO NOT Override the Root Font Size

When opting in via the `<meta name="text-scale" content="scale">` element, **DO NOT** explicitly set the root
`font-size` in your stylesheet. This includes declarations on either `:root` or `html`, and applies to absolute units,
relative units, and calculated values.

For example, do not override the root font size with a fixed value:

```css
/* ❌ DO NOT DO THIS: This can prevent the browser from applying text scaling */
html {
  font-size: 16px;
}
```

Do not combine the `<meta name="text-scale" content="scale">` opt-in with `env(preferred-text-scale)` to apply operating
system text scaling manually. The browser applies the scale through the meta opt-in, so using both can result in
double-scaling:

```css
/* ❌ DO NOT DO THIS: The meta opt-in already applies the operating system text scale */
:root {
  font-size: calc(1rem * env(preferred-text-scale));
}
```

Leave the root font size to the browser. The browser handles the operating system text scale automatically and applies
it to content sized relative to the root font size.

## Fallback Strategies

Browser support for <meta name="text-scale">: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 146 (Mar 2026) and Edge 146 (Mar 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.

On browsers where `<meta name="text-scale" content="scale">` is unsupported, the layout degrades gracefully. The page
will display the layout at the browser's standard default base font size (typically 16px), and the user can still
utilize standard manual page zoom or pinch-to-zoom options.

# Language Detection

The **Language Detector API** is a client-side web API designed to identify the language of a given text string. By
performing detection locally in the browser, it enhances user privacy and reduces the need for heavy external libraries
or costly server-side calls.

## Key Use Cases

- **Translation Prep:** Identifying the source language before sending text to a translator.
- **Safety & Filtering:** Loading specific models for tasks like toxicity detection.
- **Accessibility:** Labeling content with the correct `lang` attribute for screen readers.
- **UI Localization:** Adjusting application interfaces based on the user's input language.

## Hardware & System Requirements

- **OS:** Windows 10/11, macOS 13+, Linux, or Chromebook Plus.
- **Storage:** 22 GB free space (model is removed if space drops below 10 GB).
- **RAM/CPU:** 16 GB RAM and 4+ CPU cores.
- **VRAM:** 4 GB+ if using a GPU.

## Implementation Guide

### 1. Model Management & User Activation

Check model availability before attempting to instantiate the detector or trigger download.

**MANDATORY:** Instantiating the language detector or triggering a model download with `LanguageDetector.create()` *
*MUST** be initiated by a user gesture (such as a button click) to prevent a `NotAllowedError` when the model is in a
`downloadable` or `downloading` state.

```javascript
// Check if the model is available or downloadable
const availability = await LanguageDetector.availability();

if (availability !== 'unavailable') {
  button.addEventListener('click', async () => {
    const detector = await LanguageDetector.create({
      monitor(m) {
        m.addEventListener('downloadprogress', (e) => {
          console.log(`Downloaded ${e.loaded * 100}%`);
        });
      },
    });
  });
}
```

### 2. Running Detection

The API returns a ranked list of potential languages with a confidence score between `0.0` and `1.0`.

```javascript
const someUserText = 'Hallo und herzlich willkommen!';
const results = await detector.detect(someUserText);

for (const result of results) {
  // result.detectedLanguage (e.g., 'de')
  // result.confidence (e.g., 0.999)
  console.log(result.detectedLanguage, result.confidence);
}
```

Avoid using the detector on very short phrases or single words, as accuracy drops significantly.

## Security and Environment

- **Iframes:** Cross-origin iframes require an explicit Permissions Policy to access the API.

  ```html
  <iframe
    src="https://cross-origin.example.com/"
    allow="language-detector"
  ></iframe>
  ```

- **Web Workers:** The API is **not** currently available in Web Workers due to Permission Policy complexities.
- **Privacy:** No data is sent to Google or third parties during the detection process.

## Fallback Strategy

Browser support for Language detector: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 138 (Jun 2025) and Edge 148 (May 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.

Before use, check if the `LanguageDetector` object is available in the global scope:

```javascript
if ('LanguageDetector' in self) {
  // The Language Detector API is supported.
} else {
  // Execute fallback strategy
}
```

If the `LanguageDetector` API is unsupported or availability checks return `'unavailable'`, you must gracefully fall
back:

1. **Remote API Fallback**: Redirect the detection request to a server endpoint or a cloud API (such as the Vertex AI
   Gemini API) to identify the language.
2. **Graceful Degradation**: Disable language detection elements/buttons and inform the user that client-side detection
   is currently unsupported in this browser, preventing any unhandled exceptions or crashes.
