# Single-line text overflow

Text that has to stay on one line (tab and chip labels, table cells, sidebar items, file names, media titles) is often
longer than its space, especially with user content and translations.

Keep the full text in the DOM and only adapt how it renders: the full text is the accessible name, and what
find-in-page, copy, and search see.

This guide does not cover use cases where wrapping is an acceptable option.

There are two components to handling single-line text overflow:

1. How to display the truncated text
2. How can users find out what the full text is

## How to display truncated text

Truncation is visual only. Screen readers announce the full text, find-in-page matches it, and copying copies it. This
is why the string must never be cut in script.

### 1. Truncate with an ellipsis (at the end or middle)

```css
.label {
  white-space: nowrap;
  overflow: hidden;
  text-overflow: ellipsis;
}
```

- Use `overflow: hidden`, not `clip`. Both render the ellipsis, but only `hidden` makes the element a scroll container,
  which the fade, the scroll reveal, and the CSS detection of truncation below depend on.
- In flex/grid: Let the containing flex or grid item shrink. Items refuse to shrink below their content by default (
  `min-inline-size: auto`). When the truncated element is the item itself, `overflow: hidden` already allows it; when it
  is a descendant (such as a label inside a button), set `min-inline-size: 0` on the item.
- In tables, set `table-layout: fixed` and an inline size on the table. With automatic layout, cells grow to fit their
  text instead of truncating it.
- An element's own `overflow: hidden` does not clip its own focus outline, so buttons and links can truncate their text
  directly. Outlines are clipped by an ancestor that clips overflow, such as a scrolling row of items; give those items
  an inset outline (`outline-offset: -2px`).

#### Keeping the end visible

Wrap the part that may truncate, such as everything before the file extension or the last few characters, and leave the
end as plain text after it. The split is in the markup (or done once in script when rendering), never by cutting
characters out.

```html
<!-- No whitespace before the extension, or it renders as a space -->
<span class="filename"><span>quarterly-report-final-v2</span>.pdf</span>
```

```css
.filename {
  display: flex;
  white-space: nowrap;
}

/* The trailing text is an anonymous flex item, which never shrinks below its content */
.filename > span {
  overflow: hidden;
  text-overflow: ellipsis;
}
```

### 2. Fade out the end

Use a mask that fades the end of the text. Only fade when the text overflows, or text that fits fades for no reason. An
element with `overflow: hidden` is a scroll container, so its scroll timeline is only active when its content overflows.
An animation on that timeline applies exactly when the text is truncated:

```css
/* --truncated is the flag the animation sets, registered so it does not inherit into nested elements.
   --fade-size is the configured size, registered so it can transition. */
@property --truncated {
  syntax: "<integer>";
  inherits: false;
  initial-value: 0;
}

@property --fade-size {
  syntax: "<length>";
  inherits: false;
  initial-value: 0px;
}

.label {
  white-space: nowrap;
  overflow: hidden;
  /* Example value: how much of the text fades */
  --fade-size: 2rem;
  /* Gradient directions and positions are physical, so flip them for right-to-left text */
  --fade-dir: right;
  --fade-pos: 100%;
  /* An opaque layer that is not clipped to the box, minus a band at the end.
     Masking only the band keeps everything else visible, including a focus outline outside the box.
     The band is --fade-size while truncated, 0 otherwise. */
  mask:
    linear-gradient(black, black) no-clip subtract,
    linear-gradient(to var(--fade-dir), transparent, black) var(--fade-pos) 0 / calc(var(--truncated) * var(--fade-size)) 100% no-repeat no-clip;
  /* Sets the flag only while the text overflows: with no overflow the timeline is inactive and the animation has no effect */
  animation: truncated linear both;
  animation-timeline: scroll(self inline);

  &:dir(rtl) {
    --fade-dir: left;
    --fade-pos: 0;
  }
}

@keyframes truncated {
  from, to {
    --truncated: 1;
  }
}
```

Keep the keyframes to the flag and derive the band from it. The reveal below transitions `--fade-size`, and a keyframe
that set the band or the mask directly would not follow that transition in every browser.

DO NOT use a single gradient as the mask. A mask is clipped to the border box by default, so it also hides the element's
focus outline, which is outside the box.

### 3. Replace with a predefined shorter version

Put both versions in the markup and switch them with a container query on the cell or item. The short version is
presentational: hide it from assistive technology and from selection, and hide the long version visually rather than
with `display: none`, so the full text stays the accessible name and what copy and find-in-page see.

```html
<!-- The wrapper is the container: size containment has no effect on table cells themselves -->
<td><div class="day"><span class="long">Saturday</span><span class="short" aria-hidden="true">Sat</span></div></td>
```

```css
.day {
  container-type: inline-size;
}

.short {
  display: none;
  user-select: none;
}

/* Example threshold: relative units resolve against the container's own font */
@container (inline-size < 6em) {
  /* Visually hidden, but still in the accessibility tree */
  .long {
    position: absolute;
    inline-size: 1px;
    block-size: 1px;
    overflow: hidden;
    clip-path: inset(50%);
    white-space: nowrap;
  }

  .short {
    display: inline;
  }
}
```

## Reveal full text on demand

Reveal on `:hover` and `:focus-visible` of the interactive element, never on hover alone. Move the text only when
`prefers-reduced-motion` is `no-preference`; otherwise leave the ellipsis.

Hover and focus reveal nothing on touch. Give the full text another route: the selected item shows it untruncated (a
selected tab is never shrunk), a row opens a detail view, or the text is also shown in full elsewhere.

Choose by whether the element may grow:

1. **Scroll the text inside its box** when nothing else may move: grids, tables, tab strips, dense lists. The element
   keeps its size.
2. **Expand the element** when it may grow to its text, such as a chip or a tag with a `min-inline-size` and
   `max-inline-size`. Siblings shift to make room, so do not use it in grids or tables, where it breaks alignment.
3. **Use a tooltip** when it would add information beyond the label, or when the full text can be exceedingly long (
   methods 1 and 2 are less tolerant of extreme variance)

### 1. Scroll the text inside its box

Move the text by the difference between the element's width and its own: a percentage margin resolves against the
element, a percentage translate against the text itself. The element's own scroll timeline flags truncation in a custom
property, and a style query on it limits the motion to truncated text, so text that fits stays put. The inner `span` is
the only extra markup: it becomes the box that moves. The same class works on non-interactive elements such as list
items, where hover still reveals.

```html
<a class="label" href="…"><span>Meeting notes from Tuesday afternoon</span></a>
```

```css
.label {
  display: block;
  white-space: nowrap;
  overflow: hidden;
  text-overflow: ellipsis;
  /* Active only while the text overflows */
  animation: truncated linear both;
  animation-timeline: scroll(self inline);
}

/* The same flag as the fade, registered there so it does not inherit */
@keyframes truncated {
  from, to {
    --truncated: 1;
  }
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  /* Outside the query: a container cannot query itself */
  .label:is(:hover, :focus-visible) {
    text-overflow: clip;
  }

  @container style(--truncated: 1) {
    .label:is(:hover, :focus-visible) > span {
      /* Needs its own box to be moved. It stays inline otherwise, so the ellipsis renders. */
      display: inline-block;
      /* Forward by the element's width, then back by the text's own width */
      margin-inline-start: 100%;
      /* 1px short, so the text still overflows and the timeline stays active */
      translate: calc(1px - 100%);
      /* Example values. Set only here: when the pointer leaves, the text snaps back behind the ellipsis */
      transition: margin-inline-start 2s ease-in, translate 2s ease-in;
    }

    /* The overflow is on the left, so the text moves right */
    .label:is(:hover, :focus-visible):dir(rtl) > span {
      translate: calc(100% - 1px);
    }
  }
}
```

The duration is fixed, so longer text scrolls faster. CSS cannot measure the text, so if a constant speed matters, set a
`--scroll-width` custom property from script to the hidden width (`scrollWidth - clientWidth`, as a number) in the
`ResizeObserver` from the detection section below, and derive the duration from it, for both the scroll and the fade:

```css
/* Example speed: 10ms per hidden pixel. Without script, assumes 200px. */
transition-duration: calc(var(--scroll-width, 200) * 10ms);
```

Use a timing function that starts slowly and accelerates, such as `ease-in`: a pointer that only passes over barely
moves the text, and the end, which is what the user is waiting for, arrives quickly.

With a fade instead of an ellipsis, the text would scroll under the fade and its end would stay unreadable. Shrink the
fade in step with the scroll, so it is gone when the end arrives:

```css
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .label:is(:hover, :focus-visible) {
    --fade-size: 0px;
    /* Same duration and easing as the scroll. Set only here, so the fade is back as soon as the text snaps back. */
    transition: --fade-size 2s ease-in;
  }
}
```

### 2. Expand the element

Let the element grow to its text, and transition the growth. Set `interpolate-size: allow-keywords` so the transition
can interpolate to `max-content`.

```css
.chip {
  /* Example values */
  min-inline-size: 6rem;
  max-inline-size: 12rem;
  interpolate-size: allow-keywords;

  & > span {
    display: block;
    white-space: nowrap;
    overflow: hidden;
    text-overflow: ellipsis;
  }

  &:is(:hover, :focus-visible) {
    max-inline-size: var(--expanded-max-inline-size, max-content);
  }

  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
    transition: max-inline-size .3s;
  }
}
```

### 3. Use a tooltip

A tooltip is exposed as the element's description, while the label stays its name.
If the tooltip only repeats the label, hide it from assistive technology (`aria-hidden="true"`), or screen readers
announce the text twice.
If it adds information, leave it exposed: name and description are announced as different things. If it also repeats the
label, hide that part of the tooltip (`aria-hidden="true"` on it), so the description holds only the addition.
DO NOT rely on `title` alone: it is unreachable from the keyboard and on touch.
See `interest-triggered-tooltips` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "interest-triggered-tooltips"`) for
tooltips.

## Detecting whether the text is truncated

No property reports truncation. Derive it from overflow: the element is truncated when it can scroll toward its inline
end. `text-overflow` only changes painting, so this holds with an ellipsis too.

- **In CSS**, use a scroll-driven animation on the element's own inline scroll timeline, as in the fade above: it is
  active only while the text overflows. Declarations in the keyframes apply to the element itself. For descendants and
  pseudo-elements, set a custom property in the keyframes and read it with a style query. For example, to hint that
  hovering reveals more:

  ```css
  /* Registered so the flag does not inherit into nested truncated elements */
  @property --truncated {
    syntax: "<integer>";
    inherits: false;
    initial-value: 0;
  }

  .label {
    animation: truncated linear both;
    animation-timeline: scroll(self inline);
  }

  @keyframes truncated {
    from, to {
      --truncated: 1;
    }
  }

  @container style(--truncated: 1) {
    .label > span {
      text-decoration: underline dotted;
    }
  }
  ```

  The element's `animation` carries the detection: add any other animation to that list, since declaring `animation`
  again replaces it.
  DO NOT use a scroll-state query (`scrollable`) for this: the spec excludes `overflow: hidden` containers, so a browser
  that matches today may stop.

- **In script**, when the result drives something CSS cannot (adding a tooltip, setting an attribute), compare
  `scrollWidth` to `clientWidth` in a `ResizeObserver`. Run the check again when the text changes: `ResizeObserver`
  reacts only to size changes.

  ```js
  const observer = new ResizeObserver(entries => {
    for (const { target } of entries) {
      target.classList.toggle('truncated', target.scrollWidth > target.clientWidth);
    }
  });
  observer.observe(label);
  ```

## Fallback strategies

### Fallbacks & browser support for scroll-driven animations

Baseline status for Scroll-driven animations: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2026-10-27.
Supported by: Chrome 115 (Jul 2023), Edge 115 (Jul 2023), Firefox 159 (Oct 2026), and Safari 26 (Sep 2025).

Without scroll-driven animations the fade never shows, the hint never shows, and the scroll reveal never starts: the
text is clipped with no indication. If your Baseline target does not support them, toggle a class from script: a
`ResizeObserver` compares `scrollWidth` to `clientWidth`, and the class sets the same flag as the keyframes. Run the
check again when the text changes: `ResizeObserver` reacts only to size changes.

```js
if (!CSS.supports('animation-timeline', 'scroll()')) {
  const observer = new ResizeObserver(entries => {
    for (const { target } of entries) {
      target.classList.toggle('truncated', target.scrollWidth > target.clientWidth);
    }
  });

  for (const label of document.querySelectorAll('.label')) {
    observer.observe(label);
  }
}
```

```css
/* Same as the keyframes */
.label.truncated {
  --truncated: 1;
}
```

### Fallbacks & browser support for style queries

Baseline status for Container style queries: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2026-05-19.
Supported by: Chrome 111 (Mar 2023), Edge 111 (Mar 2023), Firefox 151 (May 2026), and Safari 18 (Sep 2024).

Without style queries the fade still works, since it is on the element itself, but the hint and the scroll reveal never
apply. Gate them on the class from the scroll-driven animations fallback above instead, and set that class without the
`CSS.supports` guard: at-rules cannot be feature-detected.

```css
/* Same as the style queries */
.label.truncated > span {
  text-decoration: underline dotted;
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .label.truncated:is(:hover, :focus-visible) > span {
    display: inline-block;
    margin-inline-start: 100%;
    translate: calc(1px - 100%);
    transition: margin-inline-start 2s ease-in, translate 2s ease-in;
  }
}
```

### Fallbacks & browser support for `interpolate-size`

Browser support for interpolate-size: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 129 (Sep 2024) and Edge 129 (Sep 2024).
Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.

Without it, `max-content` cannot be interpolated and the element expands instantly. Transition to a length instead: one
a little wider than the longest text. The growth stops as soon as the text fits, so a value far above it cuts the
visible transition short.

```css
.chip {
  @supports not (interpolate-size: allow-keywords) {
    --expanded-max-inline-size: 20rem;
  }
}
```

### Fallbacks & browser support for container queries

Baseline status for Container queries (size): Widely available. It's been Baseline since 2023-02-14.
Supported by: Chrome 105 (Sep 2022), Edge 105 (Sep 2022), Firefox 110 (Feb 2023), and Safari 16 (Sep 2022).

Container queries and their units are widely available. No fallback is needed.

### Fallbacks & browser support for masks

Baseline status for Masks: Widely available. It's been Baseline since 2023-12-07.
Supported by: Chrome 120 (Dec 2023), Edge 120 (Dec 2023), Firefox 53 (Apr 2017), and Safari 15.4 (Mar 2022).

Masks, including `mask-composite` and `mask-clip: no-clip`, are widely available. No fallback is needed.

# State-Aware Sticky Headers

Sticky headers are a common UI pattern, but they often need to change their appearance when they become "stuck" to
maintain readability or save space. Traditional solutions required JavaScript scroll listeners, which can cause
performance issues. Modern CSS allows you to handle this natively using **Scroll State Queries**.

## Implementation Steps

### 1. Create the Sticky Container

You need a container that will act as the sticky element and the container for the scroll state query.

```html
<!-- Wrap in a section to define the containment area for the sticky element -->
<div class="section">
  <div class="sticky-container">
    <div class="sticky-header">
      Section Header
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="content">
    <!-- Content goes here -->
  </div>
</div>
```

### 2. Apply CSS for Sticky Behavior and Container Type

Set `container-type: scroll-state` on the `position: sticky` element, not on its scrollable ancestor. Always specify a
`container-name`, since these queries may be nested and unnamed containers will collide. You can also combine it with
size queries, e.g., `container-type: scroll-state inline-size`.

```css
.sticky-container {
  position: sticky;
  top: 0;
  /* MANDATORY: Always specify a container name to avoid collisions if CQs are nested */
  container-type: scroll-state;
  container-name: section-header;
  z-index: 10;
}

.sticky-header {
  /* Base styles for the header */
  background: #f0f0f0;
  padding: 20px;
  transition: background-color 0.3s, box-shadow 0.3s;
}
```

**Important:** The scroll state is queried by **descendants** of the scroll-state container. The styles in the
`@container` query will not apply to the `.sticky-container` itself, but to its children (like `.sticky-header`). You
cannot style the container element itself with its own scroll-state query.

Add `scroll-padding-top` to the scrollport and set the value to be equal or greater than the sticky element's height.
This approach should ensure that when controls receive focus, they'll be consistently visible below the sticky content,
adhering to WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), which requires that focused components are not fully obscured.

```css
html {
  /* Accounts for the height of the header */
  scroll-padding-top: var(--header-height); 
}
```

### 3. Target the Stuck State

Use the `@container scroll-state(...)` query to apply styles when the header is stuck.

```css
/* Apply styles when the named container is stuck at the top */
@container section-header scroll-state(stuck: top) {
  .sticky-header {
    background: #0056b3;
    color: white;
    box-shadow: 0 4px 6px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.15);
  }
}
```

**Tip:** You can also use logical properties like `stuck: block-start` or `stuck: inline-start` to better support
internationalization (i18n) and right-to-left (RTL) layouts by querying flow-relative edges rather than physical ones.

### Notes on Dimension Changes

Without scroll anchoring disabled, changing layout-affecting properties (height, padding, font-size) when stuck can
cause visual flickering. Scroll anchoring on the in-flow content below the sticky element adjusts the scroll offset to
compensate for the layout change, which pushes the element back out of its stuck position and triggers an oscillation.

Disable scroll anchoring on the parent of the sticky element to avoid this:

```css
.section {
  overflow-anchor: none;
}
```

Apply `overflow-anchor: none` to the direct parent of the `position: sticky` element, not to `:root` or `body`, which
would disable scroll anchoring for the entire page. With this in place, you can freely change any property in the stuck
state, including box-model properties and transforms.

DO NOT: Rely on `overflow-anchor: none` for elements stuck to the **bottom**. Scroll anchoring only compensates for
layout shifts above the current scroll position, so it has no effect on bottom-stuck elements. Avoid changing box-model
properties in the stuck state for bottom-stuck headers.

### Fallback strategies

Browser support for Container scroll-state queries: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 144 (Jan 2026) and Edge 144 (Jan 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.

Scroll state queries are a progressive enhancement. In browsers that do not support `container-type: scroll-state`, the
header will still stick to the top (due to `position: sticky`), but it will not visually transform. For most use cases,
this is the recommended approach.

If stickiness is not essential, but `position: sticky` without different styling would be a worse experience than no
stickiness at all, you can wrap the `position: sticky` and related declaration in an `@supports` query as well:

```css
.sticky-container {
  @supports (container-type: scroll-state) {
	  position: sticky;
	  top: 0;
	  container-type: scroll-state;
	  container-name: section-header;
	  z-index: 10;
	}
}
```

**Tip:** If your "stuck" styling requires a different background color for readability, consider setting your layout up
so that the default styling works everywhere (Progressive Enhancement). If you must use a fallback, you can gate the
`position: sticky` behaviour itself inside an `@supports (container-type: scroll-state)` query.

If the visual transformation is absolutely critical to the design (e.g., the stuck state introduces a background or
compaction without which the content is unreadable), you can implement a robust JavaScript fallback using
`IntersectionObserver`. You must duplicate your CSS styles under an `.is-stuck` class. The following generic polyfill
checks `getComputedStyle` to traverse up and find the correct scroll container (defaulting to the viewport), matching
the behavior of `@container scroll-state(stuck: top)`:

```javascript
function getScrollParent(node) {
  if (node == null || node === document.body || node === document.documentElement) {
    return null; // default to viewport
  }
  if (node.scrollHeight > node.clientHeight || node.scrollWidth > node.clientWidth) {
    const overflow = getComputedStyle(node).overflow;
    if (overflow !== 'visible' && overflow !== 'clip') {
      return node;
    }
  }
  return getScrollParent(node.parentNode);
}

document.querySelectorAll('.sticky-container').forEach(container => {
  const root = getScrollParent(container);
  
  const topOffset = parseFloat(getComputedStyle(container).top) || 0;
  
  const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
    ([e]) => {
      // Toggle the fallback class on the sticky header container
      e.target.classList.toggle('is-stuck', e.intersectionRatio < 1);
    },
    { 
      root: root,
      threshold: [1],
      rootMargin: `-${topOffset + 1}px 0px 0px 0px` 
    }
  );
  
  observer.observe(container);
});
```

*Note: This generic IntersectionObserver pattern can also be used as a polyfill for the `scroll-state(scrollable)`
query.*

# Viewport-Aware Dropdowns

A revealed action panel or popover button group is a useful pattern for users to access additional functionality while
taking up minimal space. This overlay pattern comes with layout complexity, as the panel must remain tethered to a
trigger element while adapting to viewport constraints. Traditionally, this required complex JavaScript libraries (like
Popper.js or Floating UI) to calculate positions and handle collisions.

CSS Anchor Positioning provides a declarative, performance-optimized way to handle these relationships entirely in CSS,
allowing browsers to manage the positioning and overflow logic natively.

> [!NOTE]
> This guide demonstrates anchor-positioning and popover mechanics — it does not prescribe a specific accessible UI
> pattern. The trigger and panel below are shown as a plain **button-revealing-a-button-group**. If you need a true ARIA
> menu (`role="menu"` with arrow-key navigation), a combobox, a disclosure widget, or any other named pattern, layer that
> pattern's full semantics and keyboard contract on top of the positioning techniques shown here.

### 1. Define the Button and Panel Relationship

The first step is to create a trigger button that opens the overlay container using the Popover API.

**MANDATORY Accessibility Distinction:** This pattern explicitly models a **button group revealed inside a popover**
rather than a true ARIA menu. Do not apply `role="menu"` or `role="menuitem"` unless you fully implement the
corresponding keyboard navigation contract (such as handling spatial arrow-key navigation between items). For the same
reason, do not add `aria-haspopup` to the trigger — its value (`menu`, `listbox`, `tree`, `grid`, or the legacy `true`)
is a promise that the target exposes a matching role, which this pattern does not.

```html
<button popovertarget="action-panel">
  Open Actions
</button>
<!-- Use the Popover API (`popover="auto"`) for the overlay to ensure it is placed in the top layer and handled accessibly by the browser. -->
<div id="action-panel" popover="auto" class="panel">
  <button class="action-item" type="button">Edit</button>
</div>
```

This creates an *implicit* anchor association between the button and the panel, so that the panel can be positioned
relative to the button natively without needing `anchor-name` on the button or `position-anchor` on the panel.

### 2. Positioning with `position-area`

Instead of manual `top`/`left` offsets, use `position-area` to place the target on a 3x3 grid relative to the anchor.

```css
.panel {
  /* 
     Position the panel below the anchor (block-end), 
     aligned to the start of the anchor and spanning to its end (span-inline-end).
  */
  position-area: block-end span-inline-end;
  
  /* Reset insets to allow the grid to take control */
  inset: auto;
}
```

Prefer logical keywords (`span-inline-end`, `block-start`) over physical ones (`left`, `top`) to support RTL and
different writing modes automatically.

**MANDATORY**: Do not mix physical and logical keywords in `position-area`.

### 3. Implement Edge-Resilience (Fallbacks)

To prevent the panel from being cut off at the edge of the screen, define "try tactics" that the browser should attempt
if the default position overflows.

```css
.panel {
  /* 
     If the panel overflows the bottom, flip it to the top (flip-block).
     If it overflows the inline edges, flip it horizontally (flip-inline).
     If it overflows both (e.g., in a corner), flip on both axes (flip-block flip-inline).
  */
  position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline, flip-block flip-inline;
}
```

If your dropdown or flyout includes a directional arrow or border that needs to change style depending on which fallback
position was chosen, see `position-aware-tooltips` (via
`npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "position-aware-tooltips"`). For declarative invocation of dialogs and
popovers without JavaScript, see `declarative-dialog-popover-control` (via
`npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "declarative-dialog-popover-control"`).

## Fallback strategies

### Fallbacks & browser support for Popover

Baseline status for Popover: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-01-27.
Supported by: Chrome 116 (Aug 2023), Edge 116 (Aug 2023), Firefox 125 (Apr 2024), Safari 17 (Sep 2023), and Safari iOS
18.3 (Jan 2025).

The Popover API is mostly **progressive enhancement**, but its defining behaviors — top-layer promotion, light-dismiss,
and `popovertarget` invocation — have no CSS-only equivalent. Older browsers need a polyfill, or a manual fallback if
you would rather not ship one.

**Polyfill:** To support the `popover` attribute in older browsers, conditionally load [
`@oddbird/popover-polyfill`](https://github.com/oddbird/popover-polyfill). **MANDATORY:** Feature detect by checking for
the `popover` property on `HTMLElement.prototype`, and load the polyfill **only** when native support is missing — do
NOT load it unconditionally.

With a bundler or import map:

```js
// MANDATORY: Feature detect 'popover' on HTMLElement.prototype.
if (!Object.hasOwn(HTMLElement.prototype, "popover")) {
  import("@oddbird/popover-polyfill");
}
```

If not using a package manager, import from a CDN, e.g.
`"https://unpkg.com/@oddbird/popover-polyfill@latest/dist/popover.min.js"`.

Caveats when using the polyfill:

- Do NOT use the `popover` IDL attribute for any code that may run before the polyfill is fully loaded. It will not be
  mirrored as an attribute, the popover will not be picked up by the polyfill, and the property will be shadowing the
  accessor the polyfill adds forever. Use `setAttribute()`/`removeAttribute()` instead.
- **Styling caveat:** The polyfill cannot define the real `:popover-open` pseudo-class, so it applies a
  `.\:popover-open` class instead. **MANDATORY:** Combine the two with `:is()` or `:where()`, otherwise browsers that
  lack `:popover-open` discard the entire rule:

```css
[popover]:is(:popover-open, .\:popover-open) {
  display: block;
}
```

### Fallbacks & browser support for Anchor positioning

Browser support for Anchor positioning: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 157 (Nov 2026), Edge 157 (Nov 2026), and Safari 27 (Sep 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox.

Without CSS Anchor Positioning, tethered elements such as `[popover]` overlays fall back to their default user-agent
placement (centered in the viewport for popovers). Depending on whether spatial tethering is required for your use case,
either conditionally load the polyfill or gate your positioning rules with `@supports`.

#### Option 1: Polyfill (`@oddbird/css-anchor-positioning`)

When the positioned element must stay spatially tethered to its trigger in unsupported browsers, conditionally load the
`@oddbird/css-anchor-positioning` package.

**MANDATORY:** Feature-detect support via `CSS.supports("anchor-name: --a")` (or
`"anchorName" in CSSStyleDeclaration.prototype`), and load the polyfill **only** when native support is missing — do NOT
load it unconditionally.

With a bundler or import map:

```js
// MANDATORY: Feature-detect anchor positioning support before loading the polyfill.
if (!CSS.supports("anchor-name: --a")) {
  import("@oddbird/css-anchor-positioning");
}
```

Without a bundler, import from a CDN inside a `<script type="module">`:

```html
<!-- MANDATORY: Conditionally install the anchor positioning polyfill -->
<script type="module">
  if (!CSS.supports("anchor-name: --a")) {
    import("https://unpkg.com/@oddbird/css-anchor-positioning");
  }
</script>
```

**Polyfill caveats:**

- **No implicit anchors:** The polyfill does not support implicit anchor associations (such as those created by
  `popovertarget`, `commandfor`, `interestfor`, or `showPopover({ source })`). You **MUST** set a unique explicit
  `anchor-name` on each trigger and a matching `position-anchor` on the positioned element.
- **No `position-area` with `position-try-fallbacks`:** `position-area` with `position-try-fallbacks` is not supported
  by the polyfill. When using the polyfill on elements needing fallbacks, position elements using `anchor()` functions
  on inset properties (`top`, `left`, `right`, `bottom`) with `inset: auto` instead of `position-area`.
- **Do not wrap polyfilled rules in `@supports`:** Browsers without native anchor positioning evaluate
  `@supports (position-area: ...)` and `@supports (anchor-name: --a)` to `false` and discard the block before the
  polyfill can process it.

```css
.trigger {
  /* MANDATORY: Each trigger and positioned element pair must share a unique anchor name. */
  anchor-name: --my-trigger;
}

[popover].anchored-overlay {
  position-anchor: --my-trigger;
  /* MANDATORY: Use anchor() on inset properties rather than position-area when using the polyfill on elements needing position-try-fallbacks. */
  inset: auto;
  top: anchor(bottom);
  left: anchor(left);
  margin: 0;
}
```

#### Option 2: Progressive enhancement with `@supports` (no polyfill)

If you do not ship the polyfill, **DO NOT** set `inset: auto` or `margin: 0` unconditionally on a `[popover]` element
that relies on `position-area` or `anchor()`. In browsers without anchor positioning, `inset: auto` overrides the
user-agent centering (`inset: 0; margin: auto`) while `position-area` is ignored, leaving the popover stranded at
`(0, 0)` or overlapping its trigger.

Instead, gate `inset: auto` and `margin: 0` inside `@supports` for the specific positioning feature used (for example,
`@supports (position-area: block-end)` or `@supports (top: anchor(bottom))`) so unsupported browsers retain the default
centered popover placement, or provide a matching `@supports not (...)` fallback layout (such as a fixed bottom sheet):

```css
@supports (position-area: block-end) {
  [popover].anchored-overlay {
    inset: auto;
    margin: 0;
    position-area: block-end span-inline-end;
    position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline, flip-block flip-inline;
  }
}

@supports not (position-area: block-end) {
  /* Optional: override default popover centering with a fixed bottom bar */
  [popover].anchored-overlay {
    position: fixed;
    inset: auto 0 0 0;
    width: auto;
    margin: 0;
  }
}
```

================================================
# Two-Dimensional Panning

When a user scrolls a two-dimensional scroll container, browsers typically apply a scroll axis-locking heuristic (also
known as "railing"). If a gesture begins with significantly more movement along one axis than the perpendicular axis,
the browser locks the scroll to that single horizontal or vertical axis and ignores perpendicular deltas—often for the
remainder of the gesture.

While axis-locking prevents accidental sideways drift in one-dimensional reading flows, it creates friction on
two-dimensional panning surfaces such as interactive maps, zoomed images, infinite canvases, node graphs, and large data
grids. Because the lock persists across the gesture, it affects any panning that involves two directions—whether both
axes are panned simultaneously (diagonal panning) or one after the other within a single gesture (such as curved,
circular, or L-shaped paths). The CSS `scroll-axis-lock` property disables this heuristic directly on a native scroll
container, allowing unrestricted two-dimensional panning while preserving compositor-thread scrolling, momentum physics,
native scrollbars, and keyboard navigation.

## Implementation

### 1. Disable axis-locking and contain overscroll on the two-dimensional scroll container

Apply `scroll-axis-lock: none` directly to the element that establishes the two-dimensional scroll container (
`overflow: auto` or `overflow: scroll`). While a 2D scroll container can already update scroll deltas along both axes
under the default `auto` value, `auto` allows the browser's railing heuristic to kick in when a gesture starts
predominantly along one axis. Setting `scroll-axis-lock: none` prevents that railing from engaging across touchscreens,
trackpads, and mouse wheels.

Pair `scroll-axis-lock: none` with `overscroll-behavior: none` (or `overscroll-behavior: contain`) on the scroll
container so that reaching an edge does not chain scrolling to the parent page or trigger accidental browser overscroll
navigations (such as horizontal back/forward swipe navigation or pull-to-refresh).

### 2. Preserve keyboard focusability and accessibility

Because a 2D panning surface often lacks focusable child controls (for example, a map or zoomed image), ensure keyboard
users can focus the container and pan it with the Arrow keys by adding `tabindex="0"`, an appropriate `role` and
accessible label, and a visible `:focus-visible` indicator.

## Example Code

```html
<!-- Make the 2D scroll container keyboard-focusable and labeled so keyboard
     users can focus the viewport and pan in all directions with Arrow keys. -->
<div class="pan-viewport" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Interactive canvas">
  <div class="pan-surface">
    <!-- 2D overflowing content (map tiles, zoomed image, canvas nodes, or grid) -->
  </div>
</div>
```

```css
.pan-viewport {
  /* Example viewport dimensions; adjust to fit your layout. */
  inline-size: 100%;
  block-size: 500px;

  /* MANDATORY: Establish a scroll container that can overflow on both axes. */
  overflow: auto;

  /* MANDATORY: Prevent browser scroll axis-locking ("railing") from kicking in
     so 2D gestures never get locked to a single axis. */
  scroll-axis-lock: none;

  /* Contain scrolling and prevent accidental swipe navigations at edges
     (use `none` or `contain`). */
  overscroll-behavior: none;
}

/* Provide a clear focus indicator when keyboard users focus the viewport. */
.pan-viewport:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #005fcc;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

.pan-surface {
  /* Example surface dimensions larger than .pan-viewport in both axes. */
  inline-size: 3000px;
  block-size: 3000px;
}
```

## Best Practices & Constraints

- **Apply it to the scroll container itself, not an ancestor wrapper**: `scroll-axis-lock` is not inherited, so setting
  it on a wrapper has no effect on descendant scroll containers.
- **Contain overscroll and prevent accidental navigations**: Add `overscroll-behavior: none` or
  `overscroll-behavior: contain` to the 2D scroll container so panning into a boundary does not chain to the parent page
  or trigger browser back/forward swipe navigation and pull-to-refresh gestures.
- **Nested one-dimensional panels keep railing automatically**: Because `scroll-axis-lock` does not inherit, a sidebar
  or inspector panel nested inside `.pan-viewport` retains the default `scroll-axis-lock: auto` behavior.
- **Keep `auto` on standard vertical feeds, articles, and one-dimensional lists**: Axis-locking prevents unintentional
  perpendicular drift in unidirectional content.
- **Do not set `touch-action` unconditionally**: `touch-action` controls whether the browser handles touch gestures at
  all (and has no effect on trackpad or wheel input), so restricting it disables native compositor touch scrolling. Only
  apply it inside `@supports not (scroll-axis-lock: none)` when implementing the JavaScript pointer fallback, and use
  `touch-action: pinch-zoom` rather than `none`, so users can still pinch-zoom (WCAG 1.4.4 Resize Text).
- **Pan with `scrollLeft` / `scrollTop`, never CSS `transform`**: Translating the surface with `transform` stops the
  element from functioning as a scroll container—breaking native scrollbars, boundary clamping, keyboard Arrow-key
  scrolling, `scroll` events, `IntersectionObserver`, and scroll-driven animations.

## Fallback strategies

Browser support for scroll-axis-lock: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 153 (Sep 2026).
Unsupported in: Edge, Firefox, and Safari.

Choose between **progressive enhancement** and a **JavaScript fallback** based on your application's requirements:

### Option 1: Progressive Enhancement (No JavaScript)

Use progressive enhancement when preserving native compositor-thread touch scrolling and inertial fling momentum is more
important than eliminating axis-locking in unsupported browsers:

- **Supporting browsers**: The browser prevents its axis-locking ("railing") heuristic from kicking in on the 2D scroll
  container during scroll gestures.
- **Unsupported browsers**: Browsers that do not recognize `scroll-axis-lock: none` safely ignore the declaration and
  keep their default `auto` 2D scrolling behavior—scrolling across both axes natively, while still railing gestures that
  begin predominantly along a single axis.

### Option 2: JavaScript Fallback (`wheel` + `pointermove` with `scrollLeft`/`scrollTop`)

If unrestricted two-dimensional panning across all browsers is required, use `@supports not (scroll-axis-lock: none)`
and `CSS.supports('scroll-axis-lock', 'none')` to conditionally intercept `wheel` and pointer drag gestures.

Because `wheel` (`e.deltaX`, `e.deltaY`) and `pointermove` (`e.clientX`, `e.clientY`) expose raw, unlocked 2D deltas
before the browser's scrolling engine applies axis-locking, you can apply those deltas directly to `scrollLeft` and
`scrollTop`:

- **Why `scrollLeft`/`scrollTop` instead of CSS `transform`**: Updating `scrollLeft` and `scrollTop` keeps the element
  as a true scroll container. The browser automatically clamps scroll positions to `[0, scrollWidth - clientWidth]` and
  `[0, scrollHeight - clientHeight]`, native scrollbars stay synchronized, keyboard Arrow-key scrolling continues to
  work, and `scroll` events and `IntersectionObserver` fire normally.
- **Trade-offs**: Intercepting `wheel` with `{ passive: false }` moves scrolling onto the main thread, and setting
  `touch-action: pinch-zoom` on touchscreens hands panning to the script, which loses native inertial fling momentum
  after `pointerup`. `pinch-zoom` keeps pinch-to-zoom working, which `touch-action: none` would also disable.

```css
/* Only disable native touch panning when scroll-axis-lock is unsupported
   and the JavaScript pointer fallback below is active. pinch-zoom keeps
   pinch-to-zoom working. */
@supports not (scroll-axis-lock: none) {
  .pan-viewport {
    touch-action: pinch-zoom;
  }
}
```

```javascript
// Only attach the main-thread gesture fallback when native support is missing
if (!CSS.supports('scroll-axis-lock', 'none')) {
  const viewport = document.querySelector('.pan-viewport');
  let lastPointer = null;

  // 1. Trackpad and mouse wheel fallback
  viewport.addEventListener(
    'wheel',
    (e) => {
      if (e.ctrlKey) return; // Ctrl+wheel and trackpad pinch zoom the page
      e.preventDefault();
      viewport.scrollLeft += e.deltaX;
      viewport.scrollTop += e.deltaY;
    },
    { passive: false },
  );

  // 2. Touch and pointer drag fallback
  viewport.addEventListener('pointerdown', (e) => {
    // Ignore non-primary buttons and clicks on native scrollbars
    const rect = viewport.getBoundingClientRect();
    if (
      !e.isPrimary ||
      e.button !== 0 ||
      e.clientX - rect.left - viewport.clientLeft >= viewport.clientWidth ||
      e.clientY - rect.top - viewport.clientTop >= viewport.clientHeight
    ) {
      return;
    }
    lastPointer = { x: e.clientX, y: e.clientY };
    viewport.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);
  });

  viewport.addEventListener('pointermove', (e) => {
    if (!lastPointer) return;
    viewport.scrollLeft -= e.clientX - lastPointer.x;
    viewport.scrollTop -= e.clientY - lastPointer.y;
    lastPointer = { x: e.clientX, y: e.clientY };
  });

  const endPointerPan = () => {
    lastPointer = null;
  };
  viewport.addEventListener('pointerup', endPointerPan);
  viewport.addEventListener('pointercancel', endPointerPan);
}
```

# Anchor Positioning Tab Underline

In a tab menu, provide a visual indicator showing users which tab is active by underlining the active tab item. With
anchor positioning, you can create a smooth animation between the positions of the underline as the active tab changes.
This does not work when changing the active tab loads a new web page.

You can also use this effect to add an animated dot to indicate the active tab in a vertical tab bar.

Create the underline using a `::before` pseudo-element on the `<ul>` that contains the `<li>` elements. **Using a
pseudo-element is the preferred approach as it keeps the DOM clean and avoids adding extra elements for purely
decorative effects.**

```css
ul::before {
  /* Use a pseudo-element on the container to represent the animated indicator */
  content: '';
}
```

Make the active list item an anchor by adding the `anchor-name` property, which has a value that starts with `--`.

```css
li.active {
  /* Make a unique anchor-name for the active element. */
  anchor-name: --active;
}
```

Tether the underline to the active item anchor with a `position-anchor` that matches the `anchor-name` on the anchor,
and making it `position: absolute`.

```css
ul::before {
  /* Tether the underline to the active element. */
  position: absolute;
  position-anchor: --active;
}
```

Position the underline relative to the anchor using the inset properties and `anchor()` functions.

```css
ul::before {
  /* DO NOT use position-area, which can not be transitioned. */
  /* Use calc() to offset the top slightly */
  inset-block-start: calc(anchor(bottom) + .1lh);
  inset-inline-start: anchor(left);
  inset-inline-end: anchor(right);
}
```

Draw the underline with a border. DO NOT use a background or `box-shadow`: forced colors mode removes both, leaving no
indicator.

```css
ul::before {
  /* Apply your project's styles for the indicator */
  border-block-end: .25lh solid red;
}
```

Finally, add a transition on the `inset` properties.

```css
ul::before {
  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
    /* MANDATORY: The transition must be wrapped in a prefers-reduced-motion media query to respect user preferences. */
    transition: inset .2s;
  }
}
```

This is only a visual indicator, and must not be a replacement for setting the appropriate `aria-current="page"` or
`aria-selected` aria values.

```html
<!-- MANDATORY: Provide explicit assistive technology state alongside the visual tab underline -->
<nav aria-label="Primary">
  <ul>
    <li class="active">
      <a href="/home" aria-current="page">Home</a>
    </li>
    <li>
      <a href="/about">About</a>
    </li>
  </ul>
</nav>
```

## Fallback strategies

Browser support for Anchor positioning: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 157 (Nov 2026), Edge 157 (Nov 2026), and Safari 27 (Sep 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox.

If anchor positioning is not supported in the browser, use a `border-bottom` to add an underline. It will not be
animated.

```css
ul li.active {
  @supports not (position-anchor: auto) {
    /* Choose a color appropriate to the app theme. */
    border-bottom: .25lh var(--primary) solid;
  }
}
```

# Animate Element Entry and Exit

In the past, CSS transitions could not animate elements when they were first added to the DOM or when their `display`
property changed from `none`. The `@starting-style` at-rule and `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` provide a
declarative way to create smooth entry and exit animations.

## Implementation

### 1. Animating `display: none` Toggles

To animate an element when toggling its visibility via an attribute (e.g., `hidden` with `display: none`):

1. **Define the visible state**: Set the final property values (e.g., `opacity: 1`) on the base class.
2. **Define the entry starting state**: Use `@starting-style` to specify the values to transition *from* when the
   element becomes visible.
3. **Enable discrete transitions**: Include `display` in the `transition` property and use
   `transition-behavior: allow-discrete`.
4. **Define the exit state**: Set the target values in the `hidden` attribute.

```css
.card {
  display: block;
  opacity: 1;
  translate: 0;
  transition:
    display,
    opacity ease-out,
    translate ease-out;
  transition-duration: 0.4s;
  /* Separate after transition so the shorthand doesn't reset it or fail in older browsers */
  transition-behavior: allow-discrete;
}

/* Entry animation: transition FROM these values when first rendered */
@starting-style {
  .card {
    opacity: 0;
    translate: 0 -20px;
  }
}

/* Exit animation: transition TO these values when hidden */
.card[hidden] {
  display: none;
  opacity: 0;
  translate: 0 -20px;
}

/* Respect user preference for reduced motion */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .card {
    /* Disable movement and shorten duration for a simple fade */
    translate: none;
    transition-duration: 0.1s;
  }

  @starting-style {
    .card {
      translate: none;
    }
  }

  .card[hidden] {
    translate: none;
  }
}
```

### 2. Animating DOM Insertion and Removal

For elements added via `appendChild()` or removed via `remove()`:

- **Entry**: Use `@starting-style` as shown above. The browser will automatically detect the style change from "nothing"
  to the element's initial styles and trigger the transition from the `@starting-style` values.
- **Removal**: Since `element.remove()` is instantaneous and doesn't trigger a CSS transition on its own, you must
  trigger the exit transition first and wait for it to finish before removing the node from the DOM.

```javascript
// 1. Trigger exit transition
element.hidden = true;

// 2. Wait for all active transitions/animations to finish,
//    with a failsafe timeout in case an animation never ends (e.g. for looping animations)
const animations = element.getAnimations();
if (animations.length > 0) {
  await Promise.race([
    // Promise.allSettled ensures we wait even if some animations fail
    Promise.allSettled(animations.map(a => a.finished)),
    new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 2000))
  ]);
}

// 3. Finally remove the node from the DOM
element.remove();
```

## Constraints & Accessibility

- **MANDATORY**: Use `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` when transitioning `display`. Without it, the element will
  instantly disappear during exit.
- **DO NOT** use `allow-discrete` in the `transition` shorthand — it will make older browsers ignore the entire
  `transition` declaration. Except in use cases where that is desirable, use a separate
  `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` declaration.
- **MANDATORY**: Use `@starting-style` for entry animations. Browsers skip transitions on an element's first style
  update (initial render or `display: none` change) unless this is provided.
- **DO**: Include `overlay` in the `transition` list if animating top-layer elements like `<dialog>` or `popover` to
  ensure they stay in the top layer during the exit animation.
- **DO**: Respect user preferences for reduced motion using the `prefers-reduced-motion` media query.
- **DO NOT**: Rely on `@starting-style` for exit animations; it only defines the *starting* point for an entry
  transition. Exit animations are defined by the transition to the hidden state.

## Fallback strategies

Baseline status for @starting-style: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2024-08-06.
Supported by: Chrome 117 (Sep 2023), Edge 117 (Sep 2023), Firefox 129 (Aug 2024), and Safari 17.5 (May 2024).

### Fallbacks & browser support for transition-behavior

Baseline status for transition-behavior: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2024-08-06.
Supported by: Chrome 117 (Sep 2023), Edge 117 (Sep 2023), Firefox 129 (Aug 2024), and Safari 17.4 (Mar 2024).

Browser support for the css.properties.transition-behavior.transitionable_display capability: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 117 (Sep 2023), Edge 117 (Sep 2023), and Safari 18 (Sep 2024).
Unsupported in: Firefox.

Firefox 129+ parses `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` (`CSS.supports('transition-behavior', 'allow-discrete')`
returns `true`) without actually transitioning the `display` property (Firefox bug 1882408), causing elements to
disappear immediately on exit.

To reliably detect discrete `display` transition support, probe whether a temporary element's computed `display` remains
visible when transitioned to `none` rather than relying solely on
`CSS.supports('transition-behavior', 'allow-discrete')`:

```javascript
let supportsDisplayTransition;
function canTransitionDisplay() {
  if (supportsDisplayTransition !== undefined) return supportsDisplayTransition;
  if (!window.CSS?.supports?.('transition-behavior', 'allow-discrete') || !document.body) {
    return false;
  }
  const probe = document.createElement('div');
  // The shorthand is intentional here: browsers that don't parse allow-discrete
  // drop the whole declaration, so display: none applies instantly and the probe
  // correctly returns false. !important guards against global reduced-motion
  // resets like `* { transition: none !important }`.
  probe.style.cssText = 'transition: display 1s allow-discrete !important; display: block;';
  document.body.appendChild(probe);
  getComputedStyle(probe).display;
  probe.style.display = 'none';
  supportsDisplayTransition = getComputedStyle(probe).display === 'block';
  probe.remove();
  return supportsDisplayTransition;
}
```

### Exit fallback when discrete `display` transitions are unsupported

Entry animations using `@starting-style` work across all modern browsers without JavaScript. When discrete `display`
transitions are unsupported (`!canTransitionDisplay()`), setting `hidden` applies `display: none` immediately and skips
the exit animation (both when hiding and before `element.remove()`). Separate the visual exit state (`[data-closing]`)
from `display: none` (`[hidden]`) so `opacity` and `translate` finish animating before hiding or removing the element.
Replace the `.card[hidden]` rules from step 1 (including the `prefers-reduced-motion` override) with:

```css
.card:where([hidden], [data-closing]) {
  opacity: 0;
  translate: 0 -20px;
}

.card[hidden] {
  display: none;
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .card:where([hidden], [data-closing]) {
    translate: none;
  }
}
```

```javascript
async function hideElement(el) {
  if (canTransitionDisplay()) {
    el.hidden = true;
  } else {
    el.setAttribute('data-closing', '');
  }

  const animations = el.getAnimations();
  if (animations.length > 0) {
    await Promise.race([
      Promise.allSettled(animations.map((a) => a.finished)),
      new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 2000)),
    ]);
  }

  // Skipped if showElement() cancelled the close mid-animation.
  if (el.hasAttribute('data-closing')) {
    el.removeAttribute('data-closing');
    el.hidden = true;
  }
}

function showElement(el) {
  el.removeAttribute('data-closing');
  el.hidden = false;
}

async function removeElement(el) {
  await hideElement(el);
  el.remove();
}
```

# Animate Elements To and From Top Layer

Elements that render in the "top layer" (like `<dialog>`, elements with the `popover` attribute, or tooltips) have
historically been difficult to animate because they toggle between `display: none` and a visible state. Modern CSS
provides `@starting-style`, `transition-behavior: allow-discrete`, and the `overlay` property to enable smooth entry and
exit transitions for these elements. Note that native CSS nesting is used in the examples below.

## Implementation

### 1. Enable Discrete Transitions

To animate the `display` property, you must set `transition-behavior: allow-discrete`. This allows the element to remain
visible during its exit transition. If using the `transition` shorthand, place `transition-behavior: allow-discrete`
afterward so the shorthand does not reset it.

### 2. The `overlay` Property

When an element moves in or out of the top layer, it must transition the `overlay` property. This ensures the element
stays in the top layer for the duration of the animation, preventing it from being clipped by other elements or the
viewport prematurely.

### 3. Entry Animations with `@starting-style`

Use the `@starting-style` at-rule to define the styles an element should transition *from* when it is first rendered or
its `display` changes from `none`.

### 4. Animating the Backdrop

The `::backdrop` pseudo-element can be animated similarly by applying transitions to its own properties.

## Example

```css
/* 1. Define the visible (open) state */
dialog[open],
[popover]:popover-open {
  opacity: 1;

  /* 2. Define the starting state for entry (must come after open state) */
  @starting-style {
    opacity: 0;
  }

  /* Scale only for users who haven't asked for reduced motion (see 5) */
  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
    transform: scale(1);

    @starting-style {
      transform: scale(0.9);
    }
  }
}

/* 3. Define the base (closed/exit) state and transitions */
dialog,
[popover] {
  opacity: 0;

  /* MANDATORY: transition display and overlay for top-layer elements */
  transition-property: opacity, transform, display, overlay;
  transition-duration: 0.3s;
  transition-timing-function: ease-out;
  /* Separate after transition so a shorthand doesn't reset it or fail in older browsers */
  transition-behavior: allow-discrete;

  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
    transform: scale(0.9);
  }
}

/* 4. Animate the backdrop */
dialog::backdrop,
[popover]::backdrop {
  background-color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0);
  transition-property: background-color, display, overlay;
  transition-duration: 0.3s;
  transition-timing-function: ease-out;
  /* Separate after transition so a shorthand doesn't reset it or fail in older browsers */
  transition-behavior: allow-discrete;
}

dialog[open]::backdrop,
[popover]:popover-open::backdrop {
  background-color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5);

  @starting-style {
    background-color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0);
  }
}

/* 5. Respect user preference for reduced motion: the scale above only applies
   with no-preference, so this only shortens the fade */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  dialog,
  [popover] {
    transition-duration: 0.1s;
  }
}
```

## Constraints & Accessibility

- **MANDATORY**: Include `overlay` in your `transition` list for any element moving into or out of the top layer.
- **MANDATORY**: Use `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` when transitioning `display` and `overlay`.
- **DO NOT**: Use `allow-discrete` in the `transition` shorthand — it will make older browsers ignore the entire
  `transition` declaration. Except in use cases where that is desirable, use a separate
  `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` declaration.
- **MANDATORY**: Respect user preferences for reduced motion by applying transforms only inside
  `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)` and shortening the transition duration inside
  `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`, so users who prefer reduced motion get a short fade.
- **DO**: Place the `@starting-style` block inside or after the "open" state selector to ensure proper cascading.
- **DO NOT**: Use `@starting-style` for exit animations; exit animations are defined by the transition to the base (
  closed) state.

## Fallback strategies

Baseline status for @starting-style: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2024-08-06.
Supported by: Chrome 117 (Sep 2023), Edge 117 (Sep 2023), Firefox 129 (Aug 2024), and Safari 17.5 (May 2024).

Browser support for overlay: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 117 (Sep 2023) and Edge 117 (Sep 2023).
Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.

### Fallbacks & browser support for transition-behavior

Baseline status for transition-behavior: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2024-08-06.
Supported by: Chrome 117 (Sep 2023), Edge 117 (Sep 2023), Firefox 129 (Aug 2024), and Safari 17.4 (Mar 2024).

Browser support for the css.properties.transition-behavior.transitionable_display capability: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 117 (Sep 2023), Edge 117 (Sep 2023), and Safari 18 (Sep 2024).
Unsupported in: Firefox.

Firefox 129+ parses `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` (`CSS.supports('transition-behavior', 'allow-discrete')`
returns `true`) without actually transitioning the `display` property (Firefox bug 1882408), causing elements to
disappear immediately on exit.

To reliably detect discrete `display` transition support, probe whether a temporary element's computed `display` remains
visible when transitioned to `none` rather than relying solely on
`CSS.supports('transition-behavior', 'allow-discrete')`:

```javascript
let supportsDisplayTransition;
function canTransitionDisplay() {
  if (supportsDisplayTransition !== undefined) return supportsDisplayTransition;
  if (!window.CSS?.supports?.('transition-behavior', 'allow-discrete') || !document.body) {
    return false;
  }
  const probe = document.createElement('div');
  // The shorthand is intentional here: browsers that don't parse allow-discrete
  // drop the whole declaration, so display: none applies instantly and the probe
  // correctly returns false. !important guards against global reduced-motion
  // resets like `* { transition: none !important }`.
  probe.style.cssText = 'transition: display 1s allow-discrete !important; display: block;';
  document.body.appendChild(probe);
  getComputedStyle(probe).display;
  probe.style.display = 'none';
  supportsDisplayTransition = getComputedStyle(probe).display === 'block';
  probe.remove();
  return supportsDisplayTransition;
}
```

### Top-layer exit fallback

Entry animations work in pure CSS across all browsers that support `@starting-style`—no `.is-opening` class is needed
because entry transitions do not depend on `overlay` or discrete `display` transitions.

Exit animations require both `overlay` and discrete `display` transition support. When either is unsupported (such as in
Firefox and Safari), wrap the open-state selectors in `:is()` and append `:where(:not([data-closing]))` (nesting
`&::backdrop` and `@starting-style`) so setting `data-closing` triggers the exit transition while the element remains in
the top layer, then wait for `getAnimations()` to settle before calling `.close()` or `.hidePopover()`:

```css
:is(dialog[open], [popover]:popover-open):where(:not([data-closing])) {
  opacity: 1;

  @starting-style {
    opacity: 0;
  }

  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
    transform: scale(1);

    @starting-style {
      transform: scale(0.9);
    }
  }

  &::backdrop {
    background-color: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.5);

    @starting-style {
      background-color: transparent;
    }
  }
}
```

```javascript
// Evaluate lazily: canTransitionDisplay() needs document.body, so a top-level
// const would be permanently false if this script runs in <head>.
function supportsTopLayerExit() {
  return window.CSS?.supports?.('overlay', 'auto') && canTransitionDisplay();
}

async function closeTopLayer(element) {
  if (!supportsTopLayerExit()) {
    element.setAttribute('data-closing', '');
    const animations = element.getAnimations({ subtree: true });
    if (animations.length > 0) {
      await Promise.race([
        Promise.allSettled(animations.map((a) => a.finished)),
        new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 2000)),
      ]);
    }
    if (!element.hasAttribute('data-closing')) return;
    element.removeAttribute('data-closing');
  }

  element.close();
  // Or for popover:
  // element.hidePopover();
}

// Route native close requests (Esc, closedby light dismiss) through the same
// helper so they animate too, instead of closing instantly.
dialog.addEventListener('cancel', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  closeTopLayer(dialog);
});
```

Popover light dismiss and `popovertarget` toggles cannot be intercepted (`beforetoggle` is only cancelable when
opening), so in browsers that need the fallback those exits are instant. Provide an explicit close control that calls
`closeTopLayer()` if the exit animation matters.

### Fallbacks & browser support for Popover

Baseline status for Popover: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-01-27.
Supported by: Chrome 116 (Aug 2023), Edge 116 (Aug 2023), Firefox 125 (Apr 2024), Safari 17 (Sep 2023), and Safari iOS
18.3 (Jan 2025).

The Popover API is mostly **progressive enhancement**, but its defining behaviors — top-layer promotion, light-dismiss,
and `popovertarget` invocation — have no CSS-only equivalent. Older browsers need a polyfill, or a manual fallback if
you would rather not ship one.

**Polyfill:** To support the `popover` attribute in older browsers, conditionally load [
`@oddbird/popover-polyfill`](https://github.com/oddbird/popover-polyfill). **MANDATORY:** Feature detect by checking for
the `popover` property on `HTMLElement.prototype`, and load the polyfill **only** when native support is missing — do
NOT load it unconditionally.

With a bundler or import map:

```js
// MANDATORY: Feature detect 'popover' on HTMLElement.prototype.
if (!Object.hasOwn(HTMLElement.prototype, "popover")) {
  import("@oddbird/popover-polyfill");
}
```

If not using a package manager, import from a CDN, e.g.
`"https://unpkg.com/@oddbird/popover-polyfill@latest/dist/popover.min.js"`.

Caveats when using the polyfill:

- Do NOT use the `popover` IDL attribute for any code that may run before the polyfill is fully loaded. It will not be
  mirrored as an attribute, the popover will not be picked up by the polyfill, and the property will be shadowing the
  accessor the polyfill adds forever. Use `setAttribute()`/`removeAttribute()` instead.
- **Styling caveat:** The polyfill cannot define the real `:popover-open` pseudo-class, so it applies a
  `.\:popover-open` class instead. **MANDATORY:** Combine the two with `:is()` or `:where()`, otherwise browsers that
  lack `:popover-open` discard the entire rule:

```css
[popover]:is(:popover-open, .\:popover-open) {
  display: block;
}
```

# Carousel Snap Highlights

Scroll-state container queries allow you to style elements based on their current scroll state, such as whether an
element is "stuck" (via sticky positioning) or "snapped" (via scroll snapping). This enables carousel or gallery
experiences where the active item can be visually distinguished without relying on JavaScript intersection observers or
scroll event listeners.

### Core implementation

To highlight snapped items, you must establish a scroll-snap container, define the snap targets as scroll-state
containers, and then query that state to style descendants.

#### 1. Establish the scroll snap container

The parent container must have `scroll-snap-type` enabled.

```html
<div class="carousel">
  <div class="carousel-item">
    <div class="card">Product 1 content</div>
  </div>
  <div class="carousel-item">
    <div class="card">Product 2 content</div>
  </div>
</div>
```

```css
.carousel {
  display: flex;
  overflow-x: auto;
  /* MANDATORY: Enable scroll snapping on the container */
  scroll-snap-type: x mandatory;
}
```

#### 2. Define snap targets as scroll-state containers

Each item in the carousel that should be tracked for snapping must be declared as a `scroll-state` container.

```css
.carousel-item {
  /* Define where the item snaps within the container */
  scroll-snap-align: center;
  
  /* MANDATORY: Establish this element as a scroll-state query container */
  container-type: scroll-state;
}
```

#### 3. Query the `snapped` state

Because container queries style **descendants**, you must apply the highlight styles to an element *inside* the snap
target. Because the scroll container is set to overflow on the x axis, use the `scroll-state(snapped: x)` query.

**MANDATORY**: Wrap the styles in ` @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)` to only show the effect to users who
have not requested reduced motion. Depending on your use case, you may retain portions of the effect, but in this case,
the cards flash from white to blue in a way that may cause problems for some users, so we disable it completely.

```css
/* Specify transition outside of queries so that it is applied regardless of state.  */
.card {
  transition:
    scale 0.4s cubic-bezier(0.25, 0.8, 0.25, 1),
    background-color 0.4s,
    color 0.4s,
    box-shadow 0.4s;
}
/* 
Only show the effect for users not requesting reduced motion. Disable completely, including the color change, as it causes a flash that may be problematic.
*/
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  /* Style the content when its parent .carousel-item is snapped on the x axis */
  @container scroll-state(snapped: x) {
    .card {
      background: #007bff;
      color: white;
      scale: 1.15;
      box-shadow: 0 10px 25px rgba(0, 123, 255, 0.3);
    }
  }
}

/* MANDATORY Copy-Paste Safety: Disable highlight scaling/flashing for motion sensitive users */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .card {
    transition: none !important;
    scale: 1 !important;
  }
}
```

The `snapped` descriptor can query specific axes: `x`, `y`, `inline`, `block`, or `both`.

### Accessibility

* **DON'T** use `scroll-state` as a way to have people select an option.
* **AVOID**: using `scroll-state` with interactive elements.

Visual highlights for snapped items can improve the UX, but the snapped item is not exposed to the accessibility tree.
Therefore, snapping an item must not be used as a way of selecting content, and as a result, the visual theme applied to
a snapped item must not convey that the element is active or focused. A sufficiently contrasting keyboard focus ring (
with a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent colors) should be distinct from the `snapped` highlight. If the
snapped item is interactive, you must use other standard accessibility practices to make it accessible.

Snapping occurs due to scrolling, which does not move keyboard focus. However, if focus moves to an element inside the
scroll container, this may cause the scroll container to move, causing a change in the snapped item, which may or may
not be the focused item. This will likely be a source of confusion for users and is why including interactive elements
in the container is discouraged.

> [!NOTE]
> This pattern does not represent a traditional carousel component in which slides typically automatically change, in a
> way that doesn't allow people to pause or stop the transition, or accurately communicate the visible information to
> people using screen readers. If the intended use case is a carousel that only presents a single slide at any time, then
> do not use this technique, as it lacks the accessibility information required for such a component. Instead, opt for a
> tab-like implementation, ensuring that the carousel can be operated using a keyboard alone, that the carousel can be
> paused or stopped, and that the semantic information including the name, role, and state, is accurately conveyed to
> people using screen readers. Making carousel components accessible to everyone is highly nuanced and context-dependent;
> be sure to refer to established accessibility standards and perform thorough user testing for production environments.

For content in the container that is not currently highlighted, ensure that this content is not inadvertently made
difficult to perceive. For example, don't make the non-highlighted items in a gallery greyscale with a low opacity, only
receiving adequate contrast once scroll snapped and highlighted. The content must always have sufficient contrast, in
order for it to be perceivable, and to allow people to understand that there is more content that they can navigate to.

Finally, to ensure consistent operability across different browsers and assistive technology combinations, ensure that
the scrollable container can receive focus (by applying `tabindex="0"`), and has an accessible name that describes the
content, along with an appropriate role (such as `role="region"`).

```html
<div class="carousel-snap" role="region" aria-label="Highlights" tabindex="0">
  …
</div>
```

## Fallback strategies

Browser support for Container scroll-state queries: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 144 (Jan 2026) and Edge 144 (Jan 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.

For browsers that do not support scroll-state queries, you should provide a functional base experience where all items
are legible, even without the "active" highlight.

#### Feature detection

You can use `@supports` to provide enhancements only to supported browsers:

```css
@supports (container-type: scroll-state) {
  /* Enhancement styles here */
}
```

#### JavaScript fallback

If the highlight is critical for the user experience, use `IntersectionObserver` to determine the snapped item. Adjust
the observed area to a thin slice in the center of the carousel by providing a `rootMargin` with a negative inline
value. For example, to consider an element to be intersecting if it is in the center 2% of the carousel, set the
`rootMargin` to `"0px -49%"`.

```javascript
// Optional: detect support and apply a JS-based fallback
if (!CSS.supports('container-type', 'scroll-state')) {
  const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
    entries.forEach(entry => {
      // Toggle a class based on intersection
      entry.target.classList.toggle('is-snapped', entry.isIntersecting);
    });
  }, {
    root: document.querySelector(".carousel"),
    // Carousel item intersects if any part of the carousel item is in the middle 2% of the carousel.
    rootMargin: "0px -49%"
  });

  document.querySelectorAll('.carousel-item').forEach(item => {
    observer.observe(item);
  });
}
```
