# Accordion

Build accordions from a set of adjacent `details` elements.

If the accordion is a distinct section of the page, group its items in an element with an accessible name, such as a
`section` labeled by the group heading.

```html
<section class="accordion" aria-labelledby="faq-heading">
	<h2 id="faq-heading">Frequently Asked Questions</h2>
	<details>
		<summary>Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet?</summary>
		<!-- answer 1 -->
	</details>
	<details>
		<summary>Consectetur adipiscing elit?</summary>
		<!-- answer 2 -->
	</details>
</section>
```

**Warning:** Do not put headings inside `summary`. JAWS and TalkBack expose `summary` as a button and drop any heading
inside it, so their users cannot move between items by heading.
If each item needs its own heading, build a custom accordion instead (see below).

Accessibility notes:

- Do not wrap every small accordion in a landmark or `region`; that adds navigation noise for screen reader users.
- Do not add arrow key navigation, roving `tabindex`, or `Home`/`End` handling.
  Accordion contents are often long enough to need scrolling, and arrow keys on a focused trigger are how keyboard users
  scroll.
- If a heading for the entire accordion is not desirable, use an `aria-label` on the container element to provide an
  accessible name for the group.

## Exclusive accordions

An exclusive accordion only allows one item to be open at a time.

To make an accordion exclusive, add the same `name` to each `details` element that should be part of the exclusive
group.
Ensure that `name` is not used elsewhere on the page unless it is intended to be part of the same exclusive accordion
group.

```html
<section class="accordion" aria-labelledby="faq-heading">
	<h2 id="faq-heading">Frequently Asked Questions</h2>
	<details name="faq-question">
		<summary>Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet?</summary>
		<!-- answer 1 -->
	</details>
	<details name="faq-question">
		<summary>Consectetur adipiscing elit?</summary>
		<!-- answer 2 -->
	</details>
</section>
```

Avoid exclusive accordions, as they can produce suboptimal user experience:

- Sometimes users want to reference between the contents of multiple items, which exclusive accordions prevent.
- They also can cause content to shift out of the user’s view which can cause significant problems for those using
  screen magnifiers.

### Keeping one item always open

To require that one item is always open, stop the open item’s `summary` from closing it and expose it as disabled.
Opening another item still closes it through `name`. This compounds the downsides above, since users can never reclaim
the space, so only use it when the layout depends on an item being open.

```html
<section class="accordion always-open" aria-labelledby="plans-heading">
	<h2 id="plans-heading">Plans</h2>
	<details name="plan" open>
		<!-- Mirrors the open state; the script keeps it in sync -->
		<summary aria-disabled="true">Basic</summary>
		<!-- Basic plan -->
	</details>
	<details name="plan">
		<summary>Pro</summary>
		<!-- Pro plan -->
	</details>
</section>
```

```javascript
// Enter and Space on a summary also dispatch click, so this covers keyboard too
document.addEventListener("click", event => {
	if (event.target.closest(".accordion.always-open details[open] > summary")) event.preventDefault();
});

// toggle does not bubble, hence capture
document.addEventListener("toggle", event => {
	if (!event.target.matches(".accordion.always-open details")) return;
	event.target.querySelector(":scope > summary").setAttribute("aria-disabled", event.target.open);
}, { capture: true });
```

Keep the disabled `summary` focusable so focus is not lost when the item a user just opened becomes disabled, but
exclude it from hover and pointer styles so it does not look clickable:

```css
/* :where() keeps the guard from raising specificity */
summary:where(:not([aria-disabled="true"])) {
	cursor: pointer;

	&:hover {
		background: var(--color-hover);
	}
}
```

## Optional: Expand/Collapse All button

For non-exclusive accordions, a single button that expands or collapses every item can improve user experience.
Give it `aria-expanded` and keep it in sync with the items, so screen readers announce the change (VoiceOver does not
reliably announce a label change on its own).
Mark it expanded only once every item is open; in a mixed state it reads "Expand all" and pressing it opens everything.

```html
<section class="accordion" id="support-accordion" aria-labelledby="support">
	<h2 id="support">Support</h2>
	<button type="button" commandfor="support-accordion" command="--toggle-all" aria-expanded="false">
		<span class="expand">Expand all</span>
		<span class="collapse">Collapse all</span>
	</button>
	<!-- Accordion items -->
</section>
```

```css
/* Show the label for the action the button will perform */
[command="--toggle-all"][aria-expanded="true"] .expand,
[command="--toggle-all"][aria-expanded="false"] .collapse {
	display: none;
}
```

```javascript
document.addEventListener("command", event => {
	if (event.command !== "--toggle-all") return;
	const expand = event.source.getAttribute("aria-expanded") !== "true";

	// Command events fire on the commandfor target
	for (const details of event.target.querySelectorAll(":scope > details")) {
		details.open = expand;
	}
}, { capture: true }); // Command events do not bubble, hence capture

// Items also open and close individually, so derive the button state from them
document.addEventListener("toggle", event => {
	if (!event.target.matches(".accordion > details")) return;
	const accordion = event.target.parentElement;
	const button = accordion.querySelector(':scope > [command="--toggle-all"]');
	if (!button) return;

	const items = accordion.querySelectorAll(":scope > details");
	button.setAttribute("aria-expanded", Array.prototype.every.call(items, details => details.open));
}, { capture: true }); // toggle does not bubble, hence capture
```

Separate buttons are also possible and improve discoverability, at the cost of _feedback_: there are states where one of
the buttons will produce no visible result, and disabling it accessibly introduces challenges and increases complexity.

## Styling

The disclosed content lives in the `::details-content` pseudo-element. While closed it is hidden with
`content-visibility: hidden`, not `display: none`, which is what keeps it findable and lets its size animate. Style the
item on `details`, the trigger on `summary`, and the content on `details::details-content`.

### Customizing the marker

`summary` renders as a list item, so its disclosure triangle is a `::marker`. Remove it with `list-style: none` and draw
your own with `::before`, which unlike `::marker` can be sized, positioned, and animated.
Render the icon as a mask so it follows the text color, and rotate it for the closed state so one icon serves both
states and both writing directions.
See `icons` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "icons"`) for more details on including and customizing
icons via CSS.

Prefer keeping the marker directly next to the label text, not pushed to the opposite edge of the summary, especially
for accordions that can get wide.
A marker far from its label makes it harder for users to associate with the correct label, and falls outside the field
of view of users with low vision or screen magnification.
Right before the label text is preferable to right after, as it facilitates vertical scanning.

```css
summary {
	/* Removes the default triangle */
	list-style: none;
	display: flex;
	align-items: center;
	gap: 0.5ch;

	&::before {
		content: "";
		inline-size: 1em;
		block-size: 1em;
		flex-shrink: 0;
		background-color: currentColor;
		/* Example chevron pointing down, the open state; any single-color SVG works */
		mask: url("icons/chevron-down.svg") no-repeat center / contain;
		/* Closed: point toward the inline end */
		rotate: -90deg;
	}

	&:dir(rtl)::before {
		rotate: 90deg;
	}

	/* Rotate rather than swap icons, so the change can animate */
	details[open] > &::before {
		rotate: 0deg;
	}

	@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
		&::before {
			transition: rotate 0.2s;
		}
	}
}
```

### Slide up/down animation

To animate opening and closing, transition `block-size` between `0` and its intrinsic size, and transition
`content-visibility` discretely so the content stays rendered until the collapse finishes.

```css
details::details-content {
	/* Lets block-size transition to and from its intrinsic auto size */
	interpolate-size: allow-keywords;
	overflow: clip;
	/* Keeps layout containment constant across states; otherwise content-visibility toggling it
	   makes the transition jitter when the content has outward margins (e.g. a nested p) */
	contain: layout;
}

details:not([open])::details-content {
	block-size: 0;
}

/* Only animate for users who have not asked for reduced motion */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
	details::details-content {
		transition: block-size, content-visibility, display;
		/* Example duration; match the surrounding motion design */
		transition-duration: 0.3s;
		transition-timing-function: ease-in-out;
		/* Defers content-visibility: hidden until the collapse ends */
		transition-behavior: allow-discrete;
	}
}
```

See `animate-to-intrinsic-sizes` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "animate-to-intrinsic-sizes"`) for
more details.

## Excluding a `details` element’s contents from find-in-page

If it’s undesirable for a `details` element’s contents to be included in what’s matched with the browser’s find-in-page
feature, hide the closed contents with `display: none`. To keep the slide animation, set the collapsed size in
`@starting-style`. See `animate-element-entry-exit` (via
`npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "animate-element-entry-exit"`) for more details.

```css
.accordion.unsearchable > details {
	/* Excludes the contents from find-in-page */
	&:not([open])::details-content {
		display: none;
	}

	/* Where the opening transition starts from, since display: none has no size */
	&[open]::details-content {
		@starting-style {
			block-size: 0;
		}
	}
}
```

## Custom accordion

Use a custom accordion only when each item is a section of the page that needs its own heading, such as a FAQ or a long
reference page where screen reader users move between items by heading.
It costs JavaScript for every behavior, including exclusivity, so prefer `details` everywhere else.

Place the `button` inside the heading so the heading keeps its semantics, and put the content element immediately after
the heading.
Hide the content with `hidden="until-found"` so it stays findable, or with plain `hidden` to exclude it from
find-in-page.
`aria-controls` on the trigger is optional; screen readers gain nothing from it.

```html
<section class="accordion" aria-labelledby="faq-heading">
	<h2 id="faq-heading">Frequently Asked Questions</h2>
	<h3>
		<button type="button" commandfor="answer-1" command="--toggle" aria-expanded="false">How do I reset my password?</button>
	</h3>
	<div id="answer-1" hidden="until-found"><!-- Answer --></div>
</section>
```

```javascript
document.addEventListener("command", event => {
	if (event.command !== "--toggle") return;
	const content = event.target;

	content.hidden = content.hidden ? false : "until-found";
	event.source.setAttribute("aria-expanded", !content.hidden);
}, { capture: true }); // Command events do not bubble, hence capture

// Find-in-page reveals the content directly, so mirror that into the trigger
document.addEventListener("beforematch", event => {
	document.querySelector(`[commandfor="${CSS.escape(event.target.id)}"]`)?.setAttribute("aria-expanded", "true");
});
```

To make it exclusive, hide the other items' content and reset their triggers in both handlers, since find-in-page can
also open an item.
See `custom-button-actions` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "custom-button-actions"`) for more details
on custom commands and `search-hidden-content` (via
`npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "search-hidden-content"`) for `hidden="until-found"`.

## Fallback strategies

### Mutually exclusive `details`

Baseline status for Mutually exclusive <details> elements: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2024-09-03.
Supported by: Chrome 120 (Dec 2023), Edge 120 (Dec 2023), Firefox 130 (Sep 2024), and Safari 17.2 (Dec 2023).

In browsers that don't support `name` on `details`, several items stay open, which is still a working (non-exclusive)
accordion.
If the exclusivity is crucial to the user experience, you can implement a fallback. It also keeps always-open accordions
working, since the open item still closes when another opens:

```javascript
// Only needed where the name attribute is unsupported
if (!Object.hasOwn(HTMLDetailsElement.prototype, "name")) {
	document.addEventListener("toggle", event => {
		const details = event.target;
		if (!(details instanceof HTMLDetailsElement) || !details.open || !details.hasAttribute("name")) return;

		const name = CSS.escape(details.getAttribute("name"));
		for (const other of document.querySelectorAll(`details[name="${name}"]`)) {
			if (other !== details) other.open = false;
		}
	}, { capture: true }); // toggle does not bubble, hence capture
}
```

### Expand all and Collapse all

Baseline status for Invoker commands: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-12-12.
Supported by: Chrome 135 (Apr 2025), Edge 135 (Apr 2025), Firefox 144 (Oct 2025), and Safari 26.2 (Dec 2025).

If your Baseline target does not support invoker commands, the button does nothing. Feature-detect with
`Object.hasOwn(HTMLButtonElement.prototype, "commandForElement")` and fall back to a `click` listener that runs the same
loop. See `custom-button-actions` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "custom-button-actions"`) for more
details.

### Open and close animation

Baseline status for ::details-content: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-09-16.
Supported by: Chrome 131 (Nov 2024), Edge 131 (Nov 2024), Firefox 143 (Sep 2025), and Safari 18.4 (Mar 2025).

Browser support for interpolate-size: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 129 (Sep 2024) and Edge 129 (Sep 2024).
Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.

Baseline status for transition-behavior: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2024-08-06.
Supported by: Chrome 117 (Sep 2023), Edge 117 (Sep 2023), Firefox 129 (Aug 2024), and Safari 17.4 (Mar 2024).

The animation is a progressive enhancement and needs no fallback. Without `interpolate-size`, items open and close
instantly. Without `transition-behavior`, the content hides at the start of the collapse and the height animates empty,
while opening still animates.

### Custom accordion

Browser support for hidden="until-found": Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 102 (May 2022), Edge 102 (May 2022), and Firefox 148 (Feb 2026).
Unsupported in: Safari.

Where `until-found` is unsupported, the attribute behaves as plain `hidden`: the content is hidden but not findable, and
the accordion still works.

# Build an application menu bar

An application menu bar (File, Edit, View, Help) is a row of menus that behaves as one widget: one `Tab` stop,
`ArrowLeft` and `ArrowRight` move between menus, focusing a menu title shows its menu, and once one menu is open,
pointing at another title switches to it. Use it for an application command bar.

Do not use it for site navigation (a short list of links users `Tab` through) or for a few unrelated menu buttons in a
toolbar or page header. Those are standalone menus: each trigger is its own `Tab` stop, looks like a separate button,
and has none of the bar behavior below.

Each menu in the bar is a complete popup menu: invoker-triggered popover, nested focusgroup, submenus, separators,
checkable items, positioning, pointer handling, and fallbacks. Build them as described in `menu` (via
`npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "menu"`); this guide covers only what the bar adds on top of each menu.

## Structure

* Put `role="menubar"` with an `aria-label` on the container of the top-level triggers, never on a popover. Each
  top-level trigger is a direct child of the menubar, immediately followed by its popover.
* Each top-level trigger has an accessible name that describes its purpose, and has a `role="menuitem"` attribute.
* Style the bar as one continuous strip with no gaps or borders between triggers. Visually separate buttons signal one
  `Tab` stop each; a continuous bar signals one widget.
* Give the trigger with `aria-expanded="true"` a visible active style so users can tell which menu is open or previewed.

```html
<div role="menubar" aria-label="Document commands">
  <!-- Only the active trigger is tabbable; the script moves tabindex with ArrowLeft and ArrowRight. -->
  <button id="file-trigger" type="button" aria-haspopup="menu" aria-expanded="false"
    commandfor="file-menu" command="toggle-popover" role="menuitem">File</button>
  <div id="file-menu" popover="auto">
    <div focusgroup="menu nomemory" aria-labelledby="file-trigger">
      <!-- Items and submenus as in the menu guide -->
    </div>
  </div>

  <button id="edit-trigger" type="button" aria-haspopup="menu" aria-expanded="false"
    commandfor="edit-menu" command="toggle-popover" tabindex="-1">Edit</button>
  <div id="edit-menu" popover="auto">
    <div focusgroup="menu nomemory" aria-labelledby="edit-trigger">
      <!-- … -->
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
```

## Keyboard and focus

The menu guide's keyboard model applies inside every menu. The bar adds, on top of it:

* **One tab stop.** `Tab` enters at the first top-level trigger. `ArrowLeft` and `ArrowRight` move between top-level
  triggers and wrap at either end. `Home` and `End` on a trigger enter its menu at the first or last item.
    * **Note: which trigger `Tab` returns to.** The APG allows either the first trigger or the last one used. The guide
      specifies the first, but moving the tab stop with `ArrowLeft` and `ArrowRight` means that after keyboard
      navigation `Shift`+`Tab` returns to the last trigger reached. Pointer use does not move it, so the same sequence
      can land on a different trigger. Either behavior is acceptable; pick one and keep it consistent.
* **Preview.** Focusing a top-level trigger shows its menu and sets `aria-expanded="true"`. Focus stays on the trigger,
  and no item is focused. Blurring the trigger closes a preview-only menu.
* **Enter and Space on a preview.** They close the preview and keep focus on the trigger. The native `toggle-popover`
  action handles this, so the script must not intercept these keys.
* **ArrowDown on a preview.** Converts it to an open menu and focuses the first item.
* **ArrowLeft or ArrowRight in an open top-level menu.** Closes it and previews the adjacent menu with focus on its
  trigger, wrapping at either end. `ArrowDown` then enters it. Left and Right never land inside a menu.
* **ArrowRight on a submenu item without a child submenu.** Closes the hierarchy and previews the next top-level menu
  while focus stays on its trigger. `ArrowDown` then enters it.
* **Pointer over another top-level trigger while a menu is open.** Closes it and previews the hovered one, focusing its
  trigger without a ring. Nothing open: hover does nothing.
* **Tab.** Leaves the bar from a trigger or from inside any menu, closing every open menu.

## Implementing the bar

1. **Roving tabindex.** Set `tabindex="0"` on the first top-level trigger and `-1` on the rest. When `ArrowLeft` or
   `ArrowRight` moves to another trigger, move the `0` with it. Do not put the triggers in a focusgroup: the bar needs
   preview on focus and menu switching, which focusgroup does not provide.
2. **Preview on focus.** A top-level trigger's `focus` handler calls `menu.showPopover({ source: trigger })` so the menu
   anchors to it. Ignore focus returning from inside the trigger's own menu, or from another window (flag on window
   `blur`, cleared a tick after window `focus`, or app-switching reopens the last menu). Hide a previewed menu on `blur`
   unless focus moved into it.
3. **Moving between menus.** One function closes every open top-level menu, moves the tabindex, and focuses the target
   trigger; preview on focus does the rest. Call it from `ArrowLeft`/`ArrowRight` on a trigger, from the same keys
   inside an open top-level menu, and from `ArrowRight` on a submenu item with no child submenu.

```js
// Direct children only: submenu triggers live inside the bar's nested popovers.
const rootTriggers = [...document.querySelectorAll('[role="menubar"] > [commandfor]')];

// Left/Right always land on the adjacent trigger as a preview, never inside its menu, as in
// native menubars. ArrowDown then enters.
function moveToRootTrigger(from, direction) {
  const next = rootTriggers[(rootTriggers.indexOf(from) + direction + rootTriggers.length) % rootTriggers.length];
  rootTriggers.forEach(trigger => { trigger.tabIndex = trigger === next ? 0 : -1; });
  rootTriggers.map(menuFor).filter(isOpen).forEach(menu => menu.hidePopover());
  next.focus({ preventScroll: true }); // Focusing the trigger previews its menu.
}
```

4. **Hover switches open menus.** On `pointerenter` of a top-level trigger while another top-level menu is open: hide
   it, focus the hovered trigger without a ring (`focus({ focusVisible: false })`), and preview on focus previews it.
   Nothing open: do nothing. Keep `:hover` on top-level triggers: with nothing open it is plain button feedback, with a
   menu open the hover switches menus and focus follows.
5. **Entering from a trigger.** `ArrowDown` on a previewed trigger focuses the first item; on a closed trigger it marks
   the menu to be entered and calls `trigger.click()`, so the invoker stays the only open path. `Home` and `End` preview
   the menu if needed, then focus its first or last enabled item.
6. **Outside focus.** The `document` `focusin` listener that closes every menu must treat the menubar as inside the menu
   system, or `Tab` landing on a trigger closes the menu it just previewed.
7. **Instant switching.** Native menubars switch between open menus without animation. If menus animate, disable the
   transition while another menu in the bar is already open:

```css
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  /* Switching between open menubar menus is instant, as in native menubars. */
  [role="menubar"]:has(> [popover]:popover-open) > [popover] {
    transition: none;
  }
}
```

## Verify before finishing

An instruction cannot guarantee behavior, so test the result. Open the page and check each of these with the real
keyboard and mouse; fix and re-test any that fail. Check the menus themselves against the menu guide's list.

* **One tab stop.** `Tab` lands on the first trigger once and previews its menu; `Shift`+`Tab` from the page content
  returns to the bar once, not to every trigger.
* **Arrow keys.** `ArrowRight` and `ArrowLeft` on a trigger preview the adjacent menu, wrapping, without focusing an
  item; `ArrowDown` enters; inside an open menu, `ArrowRight` and `ArrowLeft` switch to the adjacent menu as a preview.
* **Hover.** With File open, pointing at Edit switches to it instantly; with nothing open, pointing at a trigger does
  nothing.
* **Window focus.** Switching to another window and back does not reopen the last menu.
* **Leaving.** `Tab` from a trigger or from inside a menu closes everything and leaves the bar.

## Fallback strategies

The bar itself is roving tabindex, focus handling, and `showPopover()`, all widely supported script. Beyond the menus,
the bar only adds the `[role="menubar"]:has(> [popover]:popover-open)` rule that disables the transition while
switching; without `:has()`, switching animates like a plain open.

The menus in the bar use focusgroup, popovers, invoker commands, anchor positioning, and `:has()`. Their fallbacks
follow.

### Fallbacks & browser support for focusgroup

Browser support for focusgroup: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 150 (Jun 2026) and Edge 150 (Jul 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.

Keep `focusgroup="menu nomemory"` in the markup. If `'focusGroup' in HTMLElement.prototype` is false, install Up, Down,
Home, and End, set `role="menu"` on each menu container, and `role="menuitem"` on buttons with no role; leave checkable
items, `<hr>`, and `role="group"` alone. Never install it when native focusgroup is present. Submenu preview, open, and
close are author script either way.

```js
if (!('focusGroup' in HTMLElement.prototype)) {
  document.querySelectorAll('[focusgroup~="menu"]').forEach(group => {
    group.setAttribute('role', 'menu');
    group.querySelectorAll('button:not([role])').forEach(item => {
      item.setAttribute('role', 'menuitem');
    });
    group.addEventListener('keydown', event => {
      if (!['ArrowDown', 'ArrowUp', 'Home', 'End'].includes(event.key)) return;
      // Own items only: a nested submenu has its own focusgroup, a role="group" wrapper does not.
      const items = [...group.querySelectorAll('button')]
        .filter(item => item.closest('[focusgroup]') === group)
        .filter(item => !item.disabled && item.getAttribute('aria-disabled') !== 'true');
      const current = items.indexOf(document.activeElement);
      if (current < 0) return;
      const next = event.key === 'Home' ? 0 : event.key === 'End' ? items.length - 1 :
        (current + (event.key === 'ArrowUp' ? -1 : 1) + items.length) % items.length;
      event.preventDefault();
      event.stopImmediatePropagation();
      items[next].focus({ preventScroll: true });
    }, true);
  });
}
```

### Fallbacks & browser support for Popover

Baseline status for Popover: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-01-27.
Supported by: Chrome 116 (Aug 2023), Edge 116 (Aug 2023), Firefox 125 (Apr 2024), Safari 17 (Sep 2023), and Safari iOS
18.3 (Jan 2025).

The Popover API is mostly **progressive enhancement**, but its defining behaviors — top-layer promotion, light-dismiss,
and `popovertarget` invocation — have no CSS-only equivalent. Older browsers need a polyfill, or a manual fallback if
you would rather not ship one.

**Polyfill:** To support the `popover` attribute in older browsers, conditionally load [
`@oddbird/popover-polyfill`](https://github.com/oddbird/popover-polyfill). **MANDATORY:** Feature detect by checking for
the `popover` property on `HTMLElement.prototype`, and load the polyfill **only** when native support is missing — do
NOT load it unconditionally.

With a bundler or import map:

```js
// MANDATORY: Feature detect 'popover' on HTMLElement.prototype.
if (!Object.hasOwn(HTMLElement.prototype, "popover")) {
  import("@oddbird/popover-polyfill");
}
```

If not using a package manager, import from a CDN, e.g.
`"https://unpkg.com/@oddbird/popover-polyfill@latest/dist/popover.min.js"`.

Caveats when using the polyfill:

- Do NOT use the `popover` IDL attribute for any code that may run before the polyfill is fully loaded. It will not be
  mirrored as an attribute, the popover will not be picked up by the polyfill, and the property will be shadowing the
  accessor the polyfill adds forever. Use `setAttribute()`/`removeAttribute()` instead.
- **Styling caveat:** The polyfill cannot define the real `:popover-open` pseudo-class, so it applies a
  `.\:popover-open` class instead. **MANDATORY:** Combine the two with `:is()` or `:where()`, otherwise browsers that
  lack `:popover-open` discard the entire rule:

```css
[popover]:is(:popover-open, .\:popover-open) {
  display: block;
}
```

### Fallbacks & browser support for Anchor positioning

Browser support for Anchor positioning: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 157 (Nov 2026), Edge 157 (Nov 2026), and Safari 27 (Sep 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox.

Without CSS Anchor Positioning, a popover falls back to the UA's centered viewport placement. Never ship that for a
menu: it detaches the menu from its trigger, and a centered submenu covers its parent. Gate the anchored rules behind
`@supports (position-area: block-end)` and position the menu from script when it fails:

* Place the menu below its trigger (top level) or beside it (submenu), flipping to the other side and clamping to the
  viewport when it would overflow.
* Run it in the `toggle` handler when the menu opens, and apply the result as `left` and `top` on the menu. Use
  `position: fixed` with `inset: auto` and `margin: 0` so the coordinates are viewport-relative.
* Keep these overrides inside `@supports not (position-area: block-end)`, so browsers with anchor positioning are
  unaffected.

Baseline status for the api.HTMLElement.showPopover.options_source_parameter.implicit_anchor_reference capability: Newly
available. It's been Baseline since 2026-01-13.
Supported by: Chrome 137 (May 2025), Edge 137 (May 2025), Firefox 147 (Jan 2026), and Safari 26 (Sep 2025).

If targeting earlier implementations where `showPopover({ source })` does not establish an implicit anchor (no `source`
on `ToggleEvent.prototype`), give each trigger a unique `anchor-name` and each menu a matching `position-anchor` from
script, instead of writing per-menu CSS rules.

For browsers without anchor positioning at all, see `viewport-aware-dropdowns` (via
`npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "viewport-aware-dropdowns"`) for the polyfill route.

### Fallbacks & browser support for Invoker commands

Baseline status for Invoker commands: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-12-12.
Supported by: Chrome 135 (Apr 2025), Edge 135 (Apr 2025), Firefox 144 (Oct 2025), and Safari 26.2 (Dec 2025).

Without invokers, `command="toggle-popover"` does nothing, so script must toggle the menu.

* Feature-detect the interface, not an instance: `'commandForElement' in HTMLButtonElement.prototype`.
* On each trigger `click`, call `preventDefault()` so a browser with invokers cannot toggle twice.
* If the menu is open, close it with `closeAndRestore(menu)`. Otherwise call `menu.showPopover({ source: trigger })`.
* Mark the menu in `enterOnOpen` unless the click came from the pressed trigger (`pointerTrigger`), so only keyboard
  opens enter the menu.
* `Enter` and `Space` still work because they generate a click on buttons.

### Fallbacks & browser support for `:has()`

Baseline status for :has(): Widely available. It's been Baseline since 2023-12-19.
Supported by: Chrome 105 (Sep 2022), Edge 105 (Sep 2022), Firefox 121 (Dec 2023), and Safari 15.4 (Mar 2022).

If targeting browsers without `:has()`, add a class to each menu popover instead of selecting
`[popover]:has(> [focusgroup~="menu"])`.

### Fallbacks & browser support for `sign()`

Baseline status for abs() and sign(): Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-06-26.
Supported by: Chrome 138 (Jun 2025), Edge 138 (Jun 2025), Firefox 118 (Sep 2023), and Safari 15.4 (Mar 2022).

If your Baseline target lacks `sign()`, skip `--bridge-side` and pick the edge and the apex nudge with `clamp()`: a
large multiplier pushes `--pointer-x` past either bound, so the result is one end or the other.

```css
@supports not (width: calc(sign(1px) * 1px)) {
  [data-bridge]::before {
    --bridge-edge: clamp(100vw, 50% + var(--pointer-x) * 1e6, 100% - 100vw);
    --bridge-apex: calc(100vw + var(--pointer-x) + clamp(-1 * var(--bridge-slack), var(--pointer-x) * 1e6, var(--bridge-slack)));
  }
}
```

# Build breadcrumbs

Breadcrumbs show where the user is in a site hierarchy and link to each ancestor page.

This is not for switching between views of the same page (tabs) or for site-wide navigation (a navbar).

## 1. Semantics

- Wrap the trail in `<nav aria-label="Breadcrumbs">` containing an ordered list (`<ol>`) of `<li>` items, each holding
  an `<a>`. Order conveys hierarchy, so use `ol`, not `ul`.
- Give each `<nav>` a unique label if a page has several landmarks (e.g. "Breadcrumbs").
- Mark the current page, the last item, as a link with `aria-current="page"`. Keep it a link (not plain text) so the
  trail structure stays consistent.
- Dividers are decorative. Do not put them in the markup as text. Generate them in CSS with an empty alt so they stay
  out of the accessibility tree:

```css
/* The empty alt text after the slash hides the divider from screen readers; li + li skips the first item */
.breadcrumb > ol > li + li::before { content: "/" / ""; }
```

- A styled character (`/`, `›`, `>`) generated as above is the simplest divider. For an icon divider such as a chevron,
  render it the way the codebase renders icons and keep it decorative; see `icons` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "icons"`).

## 2. Styling

- Lay out with `display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; align-items: center; gap` on the `<ol>`; reset list styles.
- Whatever the visual style, the trail must read as a path: each step visibly follows the previous one through a
  separator (slash or chevron) or an arrow or slant shape. Plain links with a separator are the default and the safest
  choice.
- **DO NOT** drop the separator in chip-like styles. Pills, tags and a segmented bar without one look like tabs or
  filters (items on the same level), not a hierarchy. Plain text with no divider is also weak, since order is then the
  only cue; avoid it.
- Choose a visual variant:
    - **Plain (slash or chevron):** use when the trail should stay visually quiet. Underline links at rest, or at least
      on hover and focus, so they never rely on color alone.
    - **Bar:** one bordered, segmented container with `overflow: clip`; use when segments need large, clear touch
      targets. Keep a separator in each segment after the first. A bar must not wrap: when its segments no longer fit on
      one row, stack it in a column in a container query set just above the bar's natural width (measure it and round
      up, so it stacks only when it would not fit), with compact rows (smaller block padding), separated by a 1px
      `border-block-start` and the chevron turned to point down and use a fixed `border-radius` for a joined pill, since
      `999px` becomes an oval once it grows tall. For a joined pill, round the container (`border-radius: 999px`) and
      separate segments with a 1px `border-inline-start` and no gap. Give the current page's `<li>` the same background
      as its link, so the chevron outside the link does not sit on the bar's background. Round the container, not the
      individual links, so the clip handles the end caps, and give the end links the same end radius so an inset focus
      ring follows the rounded ends instead of being cut off.
    - **Pills / tags:** use rounded or shaped links when the trail is a prominent control, with a separator between
      them. Show backgrounds only on hover for tags.
- Style the current page distinctly (weight, color) and non-current links with a hover state.
- Custom palettes must meet WCAG AA contrast (4.5:1 for text) for links, hover, and the current page against their
  actual backgrounds (e.g. dark red on light gray). Keep a non-color cue on the current page, such as font weight.
- Provide a clear `:focus-visible` outline that has a contrast of at least `3:1` with the background color. For shaped
  or clipped segments use a negative `outline-offset` or a background/color change, since outlines get clipped.
- Lift the focused link above its neighbors (`position: relative; z-index: 1` on `a:focus-visible`). Neighbors that
  overlap it (shaped segments) are painted later and cover an outside ring.
- In `forced-colors: active`, restore borders and an underline on `[aria-current="page"]` since backgrounds are removed.
  An icon divider drawn as a masked background also needs `forced-color-adjust: none` and a system color such as
  `CanvasText`, since forced colors replaces the background.

### Shaped segments

Pick the simplest technique that produces the shape, and use **one** shape per trail. The snippets are alternatives, not
meant to be combined.

- Selectors are illustrative; use your own hook (`.breadcrumb` here). Scope to `> ol > li > a`.
- Make the slant or point size responsive with `clamp()` and container units (`cqi`).
- Pair state colors with the shape: hover and current-page styles must use background or text color, not border color.
  Keep the focus style visually distinct from hover.
- Use a negative `outline-offset` for focus, since outside outlines are covered by neighbors.

#### Overlapping segments

Overlapping segments communicate hierarchy even without a separator. Pull each segment under the previous one with a
negative inline margin, and stack them in reverse source order so each earlier segment sits above the next.
`sibling-index()` and `sibling-count()` make this possible without per-item rules:

```css
.breadcrumb > ol > li { position: relative; z-index: calc(sibling-count() - sibling-index()); }
/* The focused segment sits above every other segment (the li is the stacking context, so lift it, not the link) */
.breadcrumb > ol > li:has(> a:focus-visible) { z-index: calc(sibling-count() + 1); }
```

#### Simple irregular shapes (`corner-shape`)

Prefer `corner-shape: bevel` with an irregular `border-radius` for parallelograms and arrows. It has better browser
support than `border-shape` and keeps normal border flexibility (per-side widths, colors and styles), whereas
`border-shape` needs explicit inner and outer shapes or is limited to a uniform stroke. Use logical corner properties so
RTL mirrors automatically; no `:dir(rtl)` rule is needed.

Slant (`/`): bevel the start-start and end-end corners with a horizontal radius of the slant and a vertical radius of
100%.

Arrow (`>`): bevel both end corners with a horizontal radius of the point and a vertical radius of 50%. Overlap the next
segment so the tip of each segment covers the flat start edge of the next.

```css
.breadcrumb { --slant: clamp(.4rem, 2cqi, .75rem); }
.breadcrumb > ol, .breadcrumb > ol > li { gap: 0; }
.breadcrumb > ol > li > a {
  display: block;
  corner-shape: bevel;
  /* Extra inline padding equal to the slant keeps text out of the angled corners */
  padding: .55rem calc(var(--slant) + .8rem);
}
/* The shape shows direction, so drop the separator */
.breadcrumb > ol > li + li::before { content: none; }

/* SLANT ONLY: leans like "/" in LTR and "\" in RTL */
.breadcrumb > ol > li > a {
  border-start-start-radius: var(--slant) 100%;
  border-end-end-radius: var(--slant) 100%;
}
/* Overlap by the slant, minus a small visible gap (example .25rem), so the angled edges run parallel */
.breadcrumb > ol > li + li { margin-inline-start: calc(.25rem - var(--slant)); }

/* ARROW ONLY: tip on the end side; a contrasting segment border separates the overlapped edges */
.breadcrumb > ol > li > a {
  border-start-end-radius: var(--slant) 50%;
  border-end-end-radius: var(--slant) 50%;
}
.breadcrumb > ol > li + li { margin-inline-start: calc(var(--slant) * -1); }
```

#### Fully irregular shapes (`border-shape`)

Use `border-shape` only for shapes `corner-shape` cannot make, such as a notched arrow with a concave leading edge.
Define the polygon in a custom property (`--shape`) and apply it with `border-shape` so borders and focus outlines
follow the shape. Polygons are physically directional and logical properties don't flip `polygon()` coordinates, so each
shape needs an explicit `:dir(rtl)` mirror.

```css
/* The first item drops the inner notch vertex so its leading edge stays flat */
.breadcrumb > ol > li > a {
  --shape: polygon(0 0, calc(100% - var(--point)) 0, 100% 50%, calc(100% - var(--point)) 100%, 0 100%, var(--point) 50%);
  padding: .55rem calc(var(--point) + .8rem);
  border-shape: var(--shape);
}
.breadcrumb > ol > li:first-child > a {
  --shape: polygon(0 0, calc(100% - var(--point)) 0, 100% 50%, calc(100% - var(--point)) 100%, 0 100%);
}
/* Overlap by slightly less than --point so the notch and tip interlock */
.breadcrumb > ol > li + li { margin-inline-start: calc(.25rem - var(--point)); }
/* RTL mirror: swap 0 with 100% and calc(100% - var(--point)) with var(--point) in each x coordinate */
.breadcrumb:dir(rtl) > ol > li > a {
  --shape: polygon(100% 0, var(--point) 0, 0 50%, var(--point) 100%, 100% 100%, calc(100% - var(--point)) 50%);
}
.breadcrumb:dir(rtl) > ol > li:first-child > a {
  --shape: polygon(100% 0, var(--point) 0, 0 50%, var(--point) 100%, 100% 100%);
}
```

## 3. Optional UX enhancements

These are optional. Implement them only when the trail needs them, and choose the implementation yourself.

- **Sibling menus:** when ancestors have meaningful siblings (e.g. docs sections), let an ancestor expose its siblings
  in a menu. Keep the ancestor link navigating and put the toggle in a separate button, never inside the `<a>`. For menu
  mechanics, see `menu` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "menu"`).
- **Long trails:** collapse the middle of a trail with more than 3 items on narrow containers instead of letting it
  wrap, keeping the first item and the last two. Put the hidden links in a popup opened from a "…" button, and keep the
  full trail when script is unavailable.
- **Long labels:** keep every item on one line and never truncate the current page. See `single-line-overflow` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "single-line-overflow"`) for techniques for truncating ancestor labels and
  revealing the full label on demand without UX friction.

## Fallback strategy

### `corner-shape`

Browser support for corner-shape: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 139 (Aug 2025) and Edge 139 (Aug 2025).
Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.

- Rounded corners are not an acceptable fallback for slants and arrows. Keep plain bordered rectangular segments with a
  separator (`li + li::before`) as the base style, and put everything from the shape snippets that makes the shape (
  `corner-shape`, the radii, the padding, the overlap margins and `content: none` on the separator) inside
  `@supports (corner-shape: bevel)`, so unshaped segments neither overlap nor lose their separator.

### `sibling-index()` and `sibling-count()`

Baseline status for sibling-count() and sibling-index(): Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2026-08-18.
Supported by: Chrome 138 (Jun 2025), Edge 138 (Jun 2025), Firefox 154 (Aug 2026), and Safari 26.2 (Dec 2025).

- Without support, later segments paint on top: slants are unaffected, but arrow tips are hidden. Put the stacking rules
  in `@supports (z-index: sibling-index())`, and gate the arrow shape on both `corner-shape` and `sibling-index()` so it
  stays plain with a separator otherwise:

```css
@supports (corner-shape: bevel) and (z-index: sibling-index()) {
  /* Arrow-only shape, overlap and stacking rules from above */
}
```

### `border-shape`

Browser support for border-shape: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 147 (Apr 2026) and Edge 147 (Apr 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.

- Use `clip-path: var(--shape)` with the same polygon as the base style, and enhance inside
  `@supports (border-shape: polygon(0 0, 100% 0, 100% 100%))` by setting `clip-path: none` and applying `border-shape`.
- `clip-path` clips borders and outlines, so under the fallback use a color/background change plus negative
  `outline-offset` for focus instead of an outside outline.
- `clip-path` also cuts the slanted sides off a border, and `forced-colors: active` removes the background that draws
  the shape, so a clipped segment loses its outline. Under forced colors, drop the clip and use plain bordered segments
  with a text separator so the trail still reads as a path:

```css
@media (forced-colors: active) {
  /* Only without border-shape: with it, the border follows the shape and needs no change */
  @supports not (border-shape: polygon(0 0, 100% 0, 100% 100%)) {
    .breadcrumb > ol > li > a { clip-path: none; border: 2px solid LinkText; }
    .breadcrumb > ol > li + li { margin-inline-start: 0; } /* undo the shape overlap */
    .breadcrumb > ol > li + li::before { content: "›" / ""; } /* the shape no longer shows direction */
  }
}
```

- The trail remains fully functional; only borders and outlines differ.

# Build a Card

## Overview

A card groups one related piece of content or one choice. It is a visual pattern, not a fixed semantic or interaction
model, so preserve the content's meaning and use the native interaction that matches its purpose.

## Guidelines

Choose semantics for the content and its interaction separately:

- use `<article>` as the card root, whether or not it links to a destination;
- use a native link for navigation. When the whole card is one destination, a single link may wrap the `<article>` only
  if the card contains no other interactive elements (`a`, `button`, `input`, `select`, `textarea`);
- keep links and buttons for independent actions as separate native controls;
- use a radio button or checkbox with an associated `<label>`, or an `option` in a native `<select>`, when the card is a
  choice.

Keep media, title, supporting content, and actions in meaningful source order; don't use CSS `order` to contradict it (
see `css-layout` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "css-layout"`)).

## Implementation

Keep the markup minimal and let CSS selectors recognize each region, so simple cards stay simple and richer cards stay
possible. A card has up to four regions, in this source order, and any of them can be omitted. Regions are direct
children of the card, not grouped in wrapper elements such as `.card__body`, which prevents placing and styling regions
by selector. A region with a single element is that element itself, not wrapped: a lone paragraph is the `<p>`. Use a
wrapper only when a region holds multiple elements.

- **Media**: an `<img>`, `<picture>`, `<video>`, or `<svg>` as the first child. Add a `.media` class only to arbitrary
  hero content that is not one of those elements, and never wrap a plain `<img>` in a `.media` element.
- **Header**: a heading on its own. Use `<hgroup>` only when the heading has a subtitle or tagline, and `<header>` when
  the region carries more than a title, such as a byline or badge. When the card has a primary destination, the link
  goes inside the heading.
- **Content**: a single `<p>`, `<ul>`, or `<dl>` stands on its own. When the content is several elements, such as
  multiple paragraphs or a paragraph plus a list, group them in one `<div>` so the region is a single grid item.
- **Footer**: a `<footer>` holding independent actions as native links and buttons. A "read more" link may share the
  heading link's URL, but give it a descriptive accessible name that starts with the visible text, using visually hidden
  text (for example, `Read more<span> about poached eggs</span>`), because identical "read more" links are ambiguous in
  a screen reader's link list. Don't add other footer links that repeat the heading's URL.

The simplest card is an `<article>` containing a heading and a paragraph. Choose the link and action pattern that
matches the card's behavior; see [Interaction models](#interaction-models).

For card images or video that should fill a fixed-ratio area, set `aspect-ratio` and `object-fit: cover` on the `<img>`
or `<video>` itself, so it fills the area without distortion (cropping may occur). Use a `.media` container's
`aspect-ratio` only for other hero content. Otherwise, preserve the media's intrinsic ratio. Give informative images an
appropriate text alternative; use `alt=""` for decorative images.

### Adapt to available space

Base the layout on the card's available space, not the viewport. To adapt the card's descendants (media, text, actions),
make the card the size container (`container-type: inline-size`) and write `@container` rules against its children.
Avoid sizing from the grid or list parent: the card's actual width can depend on column count, gaps and so on, making
parent-based breakpoints are noisy.

In a narrow container, stack the regions in source order. In a wide container, place the media in a side column beside
the other regions, but only for cards that have media: scope those rules with `:has()` on the media child (for example
`.card:has(> img)`) so the column definitions and `grid-column` placements never apply to a card without media. A card
without media stays single-column at every width, and must not reserve an empty media column.

### Align cards in a grid

When cards in a row should share the heights of their regions, use `subgrid`: make each card span four shared row
tracks (media, header, content, footer) and place regions by element selector, treating everything that is not media, a
heading, or a `<footer>` as content. A card that omits a region leaves its track empty, so the remaining regions still
line up with neighboring cards. Each track holds one grid item, so wrap the content region in a `<div>` only when it has
more than one element and cards share tracks. Cards that are not aligned with siblings need neither wrapper nor subgrid.

## Interaction models

### Content cards

Use an `<article>` as the card root. Keep links and buttons as separate native controls.

### Single-destination cards

When the whole card is one destination and has no independent actions, use one native link. The link can wrap the
`<article>`. Do not nest other links, buttons, or form controls inside the link, and keep any "read more" text a plain
`<p>` or `<span>`. Because the link's accessible name is all of the card's text, keep the content short; if the card has
a lot of text or other actions, use the stretched-link pattern below so only the heading is the link:

```html
<a href="/recipes/poached-eggs">
  <article class="card">
    <h3>Poached eggs</h3>
    <p>Two poached eggs served on toasted sourdough.</p>
  </article>
</a>
```

### Clickable cards with independent actions

If clicking the card triggers an action rather than navigating, use a `<button>` instead of a link.

When a content card links to a primary destination, also contains other interactive elements, and needs to be clickable
as a whole:

- Use a single opt-in, on the primary link itself: put `.card-link` on exactly one link per card (the heading link).
  Footer and other links never get it, or each would stretch its own overlay and the last one would capture the whole
  card.
- Link its title and stretch the pointer hit area across the card with `::after`

```css
.card:has(a.card-link) {
	position: relative;
}

.card a.card-link::after {
	content: "";
	position: absolute;
	inset: 0;
}
```

- Elevate interactive elements with `position: relative; z-index: 1` so they remain operable. Target types of elements (
  e.g. `a, button`) rather than requiring opt-in via classes.
- Do NOT apply `z-index` to entire containers as that would make them capture pointer events that don't produce any
  action.

```css
.card:has(a.card-link) {
	/* Keep other interactive elements above the overlay */
	a:not(.card-link), button, input, x-button {
	    position: relative;
	    z-index: 1;
	}
}
```

- Style the card itself on hover/focus, rather than the stretched link:

```css
.card {
	a.card-link {
		&:focus-visible {
			outline: none; /* Draw it on the card instead */
		}
	}
	
	&:has(a.card-link:focus-visible) {
		/* Focus ring */
	}

	&:has(a.card-link:hover) {
		/* Hover styles */
	}
}

```

### Choice cards

For cards that represent predefined choices, use `<label class="card">` with a checkbox or radio as a direct child.

Style the selected card with `:has(:checked)`. Never change layout-affecting properties such as `border-width`,
`padding`, or `font-weight` on selection, because the card and its neighbors jump; draw the emphasis with `outline`,
`box-shadow`, or a transparent border that only changes color:

```css
.card {
  border: 2px solid transparent;

  &:has(> :checked) {
    border-color: var(--accent);
  }
}
```

The visible checkbox or radio is itself a non-color indicator of selection, so the color change alone is sufficient. If
the control is visually hidden (keep it focusable and in the accessibility tree, never `display: none`), add a non-color
indicator that does not affect layout, such as a check icon or a thicker `outline`.

When choices belong in a dropdown picker whose options are laid out as cards, use a native `<select>` with
`appearance: base-select` and style `::picker(select)` and `<option>` elements rather than replacing the select with
`<div>` cards; see `custom-select-picker-layouts` (via
`npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "custom-select-picker-layouts"`) for more details and fallbacks.

# Build a carousel

Build a carousel for a finite set of related items. Use native scrolling and CSS scroll snap as the foundation; add HTML
previous/next and marker controls, with a small script for wiring them and for status updates. This keeps content and
basic scrolling usable without JavaScript.

## Structure and accessibility

- Use a named `region` with `aria-roledescription="carousel"` when the carousel is a meaningful page section. Give each
  slide `role="group"`, `aria-roledescription="slide"`, and an `aria-label` that includes its position (for example,
  `aria-label="2 of 4"`). Write the labels in the markup, localized with the rest of the page; if slides change at
  runtime, regenerate them from the same localized strings. The position is the slide's place in the original sequence,
  not its current visual position. Keep slide content available to assistive technology.
- Give every control a clear accessible name: use a native `<button>` with a text or `aria-label` name, not an unlabeled
  chevron.
- Announce the current slide in a visually hidden polite status region after scrolling settles. Update it whenever the
  visible slide changes, whether through the buttons, the markers, or direct scrolling, so assistive technology receives
  feedback.
- Ensure that where possible all interactive elements have a target size of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, as these
  provide a way to quickly navigate to each individual slide. This can be achieved by providing undersized elements with
  enough spacing so that a 24px circle centered on it does not overlap neighboring targets. To do this, make the target
  itself a little larger than the visible shape with padding, a pseudo-element, or a thin transparent border (with
  `background-clip: padding-box` so the fill stays on the visible shape), and leave the rest of the spacing to a gap. Do
  not rely on wide gaps alone, and do not make the invisible area so large that clicks well away from a control activate
  it. This adheres to the requirements in WCAG 2.5.8 Target Size.
- Ensure that all controls have sufficient contrast, with non-text elements requiring a contrast ratio of at least 3:1
  between the non-text content and adjacent colors, in order to adhere to WCAG 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast.
- Ensure that when a previous/next control becomes disabled, causing focus to be lost, that focus is redirected
  elsewhere, such as the opposite control (e.g. move focus to "Next" if previous becomes disabled and has focus, or move
  focus to "Previous" if next becomes disabled and has focus).
- The active slide's control must not communicate that it is active through color alone, in order to adhere to WCAG
  1.4.1 Use of Color. There must be another visual affordance, such as an outline, or use of a larger height/width, to
  convey that the control is active.

## Scrolling and controls

- Make the track natively scrollable and snap slides on its scrolling axis. For horizontal carousels, arrange slides in
  a row and use the inline axis; for vertical carousels, use a column and the block axis.
- Set `overscroll-behavior` to `contain` on the track's scrolling axis (`overscroll-behavior-x` for horizontal,
  `overscroll-behavior-y` for vertical). A scroll that reaches an end of the track then stays on the carousel instead of
  scrolling the page or starting a back or forward swipe, which makes repeated swipes at the ends smoother. Do not use
  the `overscroll-behavior` shorthand: it also contains the other axis, which can stop the page from scrolling while the
  pointer is over the carousel.
- Use HTML `<button>` elements for previous/next controls and one marker button per slide for direct navigation, in
  every browser. Do not use `::scroll-button()` or `::scroll-marker` for now.

- Keep controls visible, operable, and clearly focused with `:focus-visible`. Loop previous/next controls continuously
  from the last slide to the first and back by default when there are at least three slides (see Looping); disable them
  at the ends only when finite navigation is requested. Preserve native keyboard behavior; do not intercept keys from
  links, form fields, or buttons. Add custom key handling only for a defined interaction need, and avoid overriding
  nested controls.

## Related patterns

- For styling the active slide itself, see `carousel-snap-highlights` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "carousel-snap-highlights"`).
- For a continuous progress indicator instead of discrete markers, see `scroll-progress-indicator` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "scroll-progress-indicator"`).
- For scroll-driven slide effects, see `carousel-slide-effects` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "carousel-slide-effects"`).
- For synchronizing other UI with snap events, see `scroll-snap-state-sync` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "scroll-snap-state-sync"`).

## Example: horizontal carousel

This example uses full-width horizontal slides. Adapt the slide sizing for a peek layout or use the block axis for a
vertical carousel. Give each marker a name that identifies its destination. The CSS below is split by concern, and only
the parts that are easy to get wrong are shown; everything else is described in prose. Adapt dimensions, spacing, and
colors to the design.

```html
<section class="carousel" aria-roledescription="carousel" aria-label="Featured products">
  <div class="carousel-controls">
    <button type="button" data-direction="previous">Previous slide</button>
    <button type="button" data-direction="next">Next slide</button>
  </div>

  <div class="carousel-track" tabindex="0" role="group" aria-label="Slides">
    <div role="group" aria-roledescription="slide" aria-label="1 of 3"
        data-marker-name="Go to slide 1">
      <h3>Product one</h3>
    </div>
    <div role="group" aria-roledescription="slide" aria-label="2 of 3"
        data-marker-name="Go to slide 2">
      <h3>Product two</h3>
    </div>
    <div role="group" aria-roledescription="slide" aria-label="3 of 3"
        data-marker-name="Go to slide 3">
      <h3>Product three</h3>
    </div>
  </div>

  <p class="visually-hidden" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p>

  <nav class="carousel-markers" aria-label="Choose a slide"></nav>
</section>
```

### Track and snapping

The track is a flex row that scrolls on the inline axis and snaps to slides. Each slide fills the track and snaps to
center.

```css
.carousel-track {
  display: flex;
  gap: 1rem; /* example value */
  overflow-x: auto;
  /* mandatory so the track always rests on a slide, which the settled-scroll status relies on */
  scroll-snap-type: x mandatory;
  /* keep a scroll that reaches either end on the carousel; only the scrolling axis, so the page still scrolls the other way */
  overscroll-behavior-x: contain;
}

.carousel-track > * {
  flex: 0 0 100%; /* one slide per view; use a smaller basis for a peek layout */
  scroll-snap-align: center;
}
```

### Controls

Position the Previous and Next buttons over the track's start and end edges (a `position: absolute` container with a
`z-index` so slides don't cover them, and `pointer-events: none` on the container with `pointer-events: auto` on the
buttons so the track stays scrollable between them). Build the marker buttons from the slides' `data-marker-name`
values, and style the active one with `[aria-current="true"]`.

```css
.carousel-markers button[aria-current="true"] {
  background: #0a5; /* example color; any clear contrast with the other markers works */
}
```

### Supporting styles

Write these to fit the design:

- Style the markers as dots in a centered flex row with a gap, using the pointer cursor.
- Show a clear `:focus-visible` outline on the control and marker buttons.
- Set `touch-action: manipulation` on the track and the control buttons, so quick taps on them do not trigger double-tap
  zoom on touch devices.
- Keep the status region visually hidden without removing it from the accessibility tree.
- Enable `scroll-behavior: smooth` on the track only inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)`.

## Fallback strategies

The controls are plain HTML, so the fallbacks below only cover the platform features that the script and CSS rely on.
Scrolling and snap behavior remain native, and small amounts of script add the controls' behavior and status updates.

### Scrolling and completion

Baseline status for scroll-behavior: Widely available. It's been Baseline since 2022-03-14.
Supported by: Chrome 61 (Sep 2017), Edge 79 (Jan 2020), Firefox 36 (Feb 2015), and Safari 15.4 (Mar 2022).

Smooth scrolling is optional. The example enables it only when reduced motion is not requested.

Browser support for overscroll-behavior: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 144 (Jan 2026), Edge 144 (Jan 2026), and Firefox 150 (Apr 2026).
Unsupported in: Safari.

Containing overscroll is a progressive enhancement and needs no fallback. Without support, a scroll that reaches an end
of the track can scroll the page or start a swipe navigation, and the carousel still works.

Baseline status for scrollend: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-12-12.
Supported by: Chrome 114 (May 2023), Edge 114 (Jun 2023), Firefox 109 (Jan 2023), and Safari 26.2 (Dec 2025).

If `scrollend` is unavailable, use a debounced `scroll` listener to run the settled-scroll handler. Run the initial
marker, button, and parking sync once on load, leaving the polite status region empty until user-initiated scrolling
settles so page load is not interrupted.

Browser support for Scroll snap events: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 129 (Sep 2024) and Edge 129 (Sep 2024).
Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.

The carousel does not depend on snap events. If they are unavailable, use settled-scroll tracking for status; use
`scrollsnapchange` only when other UI must follow the browser-selected snap target.

### Scroll snap

Baseline status for Scroll snap: Widely available. It's been Baseline since 2020-01-15.
Supported by: Chrome 69 (Sep 2018), Edge 79 (Jan 2020), Firefox 68 (Jul 2019), and Safari 11 (Sep 2017).

The track remains natively scrollable with touch, pointer, and keyboard input. JavaScript adds the controls' behavior
and announcements without replacing basic scrolling. Place the script in a `<script type="module">` element so it runs
after the document has been parsed.

### Looping

Baseline status for sibling-count() and sibling-index(): Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2026-08-18.
Supported by: Chrome 138 (Jun 2025), Edge 138 (Jun 2025), Firefox 154 (Aug 2026), and Safari 26.2 (Dec 2025).

If `sibling-count()` is unsupported, the script supplies the number of slides instead, so the carousel still loops. Set
a `--children-count` custom property on the track only when `CSS.supports("order: sibling-count()")` is false, and read
the count in CSS as `var(--children-count, sibling-count())` instead of `sibling-count()`.
Browsers with support never get the property, so they keep counting natively.
Do not wrap the parking rules in `@supports`.

```css
.carousel-track > :first-child {
  /* --children-count is only set where sibling-count() is unsupported */
  order: clamp(0, var(--current) - (var(--children-count, sibling-count()) - 3), 1);
}
```

```js
if (!CSS.supports("order: sibling-count()")) {
  track.style.setProperty("--children-count", track.children.length);
}
```

If content is not static, update the property when slides are added or removed (e.g. via a `MutationObserver`).

### Scroll-driven effects

Baseline status for Scroll-driven animations: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2026-10-27.
Supported by: Chrome 115 (Jul 2023), Edge 115 (Jul 2023), Firefox 159 (Oct 2026), and Safari 26 (Sep 2025).

Treat slide effects as optional enhancements and keep them inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)`. The
carousel's navigation and current-slide feedback must not depend on them.

## Controls and status updates

Update the active marker as the track scrolls (throttled to one update per animation frame) so the dots keep pace with
the visible slide, and run announcements and button state after scrolling settles. Measure only the carousel's scrolling
axis.

Write a small script that adapts to your markup and covers these requirements:

- **Wire the HTML controls.** On a Previous or Next click, find the current slide from the track's scroll position along
  its scrolling axis, then scroll the track to the adjacent slide's snap position in visual order (which differs from
  DOM order when looping), for example with `track.scrollBy()` using that slide's offset from the track's center. Do not
  scroll by a fixed viewport width, keep a separate index that can drift from the real scroll position, or use
  `scrollIntoView()` without limiting it to the track, which can scroll the page. Create one named marker button per
  slide that scrolls the track to that slide. Keep the Previous and Next buttons before the track in DOM order.
- **Track the current slide** along the carousel's scrolling axis, for horizontal or vertical layouts.
- **Update the active marker live.** From a `scroll` listener throttled with `requestAnimationFrame`, compute the
  nearest slide and set the active marker's `aria-current="true"` immediately, and also set it from the pending target
  the moment a marker or Previous/Next button is clicked, so the dots change when the user decides instead of after the
  slide moves. Skip the write when the current slide is unchanged, and skip the listener entirely while a click or key
  press has a pending target, because recomputing every frame during a scripted smooth scroll makes Safari stutter.
- **Update the rest after scrolling settles**, from a single handler driven by the settled scroll position: update the
  buttons' disabled state (and slide parking when looping), and announce "Slide N of M" in the status region only when
  the settled slide changes from the previously settled slide (keeping initial load and compensating park scrolls
  silent). Controls only initiate scrolling; they never update state directly.
- **Settle on `scrollend`**, with a debounced `scroll` listener only where `scrollend` is unsupported. Do not run two
  settle handlers, and do not reorder or re-scroll the track (such as when parking a slide) while a scroll is still in
  flight, because that cancels it. The one exception is a marker click when looping, whose own scroll replaces the one
  in flight (see Looping).
- **Resolve clicks from a pending target.** Make rapid previous/next clicks build on the slide already being scrolled
  to, not on the nearest slide, and clear the target when scrolling settles. Ignore a `scrollend` that arrives after the
  next scroll has started, because acting on it (such as parking) cancels that scroll. Also ignore a settle at the exact
  scroll position where a scroll to another slide was just requested: it belongs to an earlier scroll (such as a
  compensating one), and the requested scroll has yet to move.
- **Respect reduced motion** for any smooth scrolling.

## Looping (continuous navigation)

Loop previous and next navigation from the last slide to the first and back by keeping the track endless instead of
disabling controls at the ends (unless the carousel has fewer than three slides or finite navigation is requested). Do
not clone slides or move them in the DOM, which conflicts with frameworks and duplicates content for assistive
technology. Instead, park an end slide beside the current one with CSS `order`, and only when the carousel is at or one
step from that end. Parking one step early puts the neighbor in place before scrolling reaches an end, so the previous
and next buttons never disable mid-scroll. The track then always has a neighbor on both sides, and keyboard scrolling,
touch, and snapping all keep working. Only the first and last slides ever get `order`. Because parking starts one step
before an end, a short carousel can have an end slide parked at every position (with 4 slides, always; with 3, both ends
at the middle slide). DOM order applies unchanged only at positions that are more than one step from both ends, which
needs 5 or more slides.

- Keep a `--current` custom property on the track: the zero-based index of the current slide. Do not give it a default
  in CSS: while it is undefined, `order` falls back to 0, so no slide is parked and the carousel starts on the first
  slide without JavaScript. The script sets it on load. Park the last slide before the first (`order: -1`) when
  `--current` is `0` or `1`, and park the first slide after the last (`order: 1`) when `--current` is the last or
  second-to-last index. Set `order` only on the first and last slides (`:first-child` and `:last-child`), not on every
  slide. `sibling-count()` is needed to find the last indexes. The formulas below are the part that is easy to get
  wrong.
- When scrolling settles, update `--current` from the scroll position. If the parking changes, measure the current
  slide's offset along the scrolling axis before and after, then instantly scroll by the difference in the same task so
  the change is invisible. Turn scroll snapping off (`scroll-snap-type: none`) around the reorder and the compensating
  scroll and restore it afterward, because some browsers otherwise re-snap to another slide and keep scrolling. Also
  lock overflow on the scrolling axis (`overflow-x: hidden`, or `overflow-y: hidden` for vertical) for the same step and
  restore it two animation frames later: Safari on iOS otherwise paints the reordered layout for a frame before the
  compensating scroll lands, which flickers. Restoring it immediately breaks looping, so keep the delay. This also
  applies when a parked slide is released after the user leaves an end slide.
- Markers must scroll in sequence order. A parked end slide sits on the opposite side of the track from its place in the
  sequence, so a direct scroll to it goes the short way round (from the first slide, the last slide's marker would
  scroll backward one step). On a marker click for any slide other than the current one, set `--current` to `initial` on
  the track before scrolling, so every slide is back in DOM order for the trip. Do it in the same measured, compensated
  step as parking, but without the overflow lock: Safari does not start the scroll that follows on a locked track. The
  settle handler then sets `--current` again, which re-parks. Do not do this for previous/next navigation, which must
  reach the parked slide to wrap. While the slides are in DOM order, an end slide has no neighbor to wrap to, so a
  Previous or Next click made during the trip cannot be followed yet. Hold it and replay it when scrolling settles and
  the slides are parked again, and skip the overflow lock for that parking step too, for the same reason.
- Looping needs at least three slides. Because the compensation is measured, slides may differ in size.
- The previous/next controls and the status calculation must work from visual order, not DOM sibling order. Per-slide
  labels ("2 of 4") and the status region use each slide's original index, which does not change when slides are parked.
  Do not renumber slides when `--current` changes.
- Keep `scroll-behavior: smooth` inside `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference` for user navigation; only the
  compensating scroll is instant.

```css
/* The first slide parks after the last while --current is the last or second-to-last index. */
.carousel-track > :first-child {
  order: clamp(0, var(--current) - (sibling-count() - 3), 1);
}

/* The last slide parks before the first while --current is 0 or 1. */
.carousel-track > :last-child {
  order: calc(-1 * clamp(0, 2 - var(--current), 1));
}
```

Parking only changes visual order, so the DOM order stays as the reading and focus order, and no slide is inert or
aria-hidden.

# Styling Checkboxes

Use semantic, accessible HTML with each checkbox associated with its label, either by nesting the `<input>` inside the
`<label>` or by matching the label’s `for` attribute to the input’s `id`.

Modern CSS provides two approaches to styling checkboxes: customize the native appearance with `accent-color`, or
override the default presentation with `appearance: none` on the `<input type="checkbox">` element.

## Native customization with `accent-color`

For simple, brand-consistent styling that retains native rendering, keyboard behavior, validation, and operating-system
focus indicators, use `accent-color`.

```css
.checkbox-native {
  accent-color: #1a73e8;

  /* Sizing is controlled via relative units */
  inline-size: 1.25em;
  aspect-ratio: 1;
  margin: 0;
  cursor: pointer;
}
```

## Fully custom styling with `appearance: none`

Use `appearance: none` when the design requires control over the checkbox’s
shape, size, states, or indicators. This removes the native visual styling while
leaving the `<input>` as the interactive target.

Set explicit relative sizes for `--checkbox-size` and `--checkbox-icon-size` because `appearance: none` removes the
browser’s default dimensions. Keep the icon smaller than the checkbox to provide space for its border and visual
padding.

```css
/* Reusable SVG assets */
:root {
  --icon-check: url("data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' viewBox='0 0 24 24' fill='none' stroke='black' stroke-width='3.5' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-linejoin='round'><polyline points='20 6 9 17 4 12'></polyline></svg>");
  --icon-dash: url("data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' viewBox='0 0 24 24' fill='none' stroke='black' stroke-width='4.5' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-linejoin='round'><line x1='5' y1='12' x2='19' y2='12'></line></svg>");
}

/* Custom checkbox */
.checkbox-custom {
  --checkbox-size: 1.25em;
  --checkbox-icon-size: 0.7em;

  appearance: none;
  display: inline-grid;
  place-content: center;
  inline-size: var(--checkbox-size);
  aspect-ratio: 1;
  margin: 0;
  border: 2px solid currentColor;
  cursor: pointer;

  &::before {
    content: "";
    inline-size: var(--checkbox-icon-size);
    aspect-ratio: 1;
    background-color: currentColor;
    mask: var(--checkbox-icon) no-repeat center / contain;
    scale: 0;

    @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
      transition: scale 150ms ease;
    }

    @media (forced-colors: active) {
      background-color: CanvasText;
    }
  }

  &:checked {
    --checkbox-icon: var(--icon-check);
  }

  &:indeterminate {
    --checkbox-icon: var(--icon-dash);
  }

  &:is(:checked, :indeterminate)::before {
    scale: 1;
  }

  &:focus-visible {
    outline: 2px solid currentColor;
    outline-offset: 2px;
  }

  &:disabled {
    cursor: not-allowed;
    opacity: 0.5;
  }
}
```

## The indeterminate state

The indeterminate state cannot be set via an HTML attribute; set the `indeterminate` DOM property in JavaScript (
`checkbox.indeterminate = true`) and ensure the `:indeterminate` pseudo-class is visually distinct from both `:checked`
and unchecked states:

* **Native (`accent-color`):** Automatically styled by the browser using the element's `accent-color` (no extra
  `:indeterminate` CSS rule needed).
* **Custom (`appearance: none`):** Swap `--checkbox-icon` to `var(--icon-dash)` on `.checkbox-custom:indeterminate` as
  shown above.

```js
const selectAll = document.querySelector("#select-all");
selectAll.indeterminate = true;
```

## Accessibility and interaction

- **DO** use `:focus-visible` rather than `:focus` to style focus indicators on custom checkboxes so a distinct outline
  appears for keyboard navigation without showing on pointer clicks.
- **DO NOT** use `outline: none` or hide focus indicators on checkboxes.
- **DO** ensure the contrast of focus indicators has a contrast of at least `3:1` with the background color
- **DO** ensure the color for the checked and indeterminate state has a contrast of at least `3:1` with the background
  color
- **DO** ensure the checkbox or its wrapping `<label>` provides an interactive hit target of at least `44px x 44px`
  while keeping the visual checkbox box sized in relative units:
  ```css
  label {
    display: inline-flex;
    align-items: center;
    gap: 0.65rem;
    min-block-size: 44px;
    cursor: pointer;
  }
  ```
- **DO** provide a `:disabled` style variant that lowers opacity and sets `cursor: not-allowed` to convey inactive
  states clearly.

### Issues to be aware of when using accent-color

Browser rendering of `accent-color` varies.
For indicators generally painted over an accent color background, such as checkbox marks and radio-button dots, browsers
may apply different treatments:

- **Chromium** and **Firefox** generally select a contrasting indicator color.
- **Safari** may instead preserve a white indicator in light mode or a black indicator in dark mode, while modifying the
  accent color behind it. This adjustment does not always provide sufficient contrast for every supplied color, so test
  important combinations in Safari, including both light and dark color schemes. Do not assume that Safari will
  automatically choose whichever indicator color provides the best contrast.

## Fallback strategies

### Fallbacks & browser support for accent-color

Browser support for accent-color: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 93 (Aug 2021), Edge 93 (Sep 2021), Firefox 92 (Sep 2021), and Safari 26.2 (Dec 2025).

The `accent-color` property is progressive enhancement.
Browsers that do not support this property will ignore it and use their default UI colors.

### CSS Masks

Baseline status for Masks: Widely available. It's been Baseline since 2023-12-07.
Supported by: Chrome 120 (Dec 2023), Edge 120 (Dec 2023), Firefox 53 (Apr 2017), and Safari 15.4 (Mar 2022).
