# Copy button

Build a button that copies the text of another element (code block, inline value, read-only field) or the current
selection. Declare the target with Invoker Commands (`command` + `commandfor`) instead of per-button JavaScript wiring,
and write with the Async Clipboard API.

## Implementation

### 1. Markup

```html
<!-- Custom commands MUST start with "--". commandfor is the id of the element whose text is copied. -->
<span class="copy"> <!-- positioning context for the bubble -->
  <!-- aria-label names the content being copied; several bare "Copy" buttons are indistinguishable to screen readers -->
  <button type="button" class="copy-button" command="--copy" commandfor="snippet" aria-label="Copy CSS code">
    <!-- Decorative icon, rendered however the codebase renders icons -->
    <span class="icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
  </button>
  <!-- The confirmation bubble IS the live region. Keep it empty until a copy, and outside the button:
       a button's children are presentational, so a live region inside one is not reliably announced -->
  <span class="tip" role="status"></span>
</span>
<pre><code id="snippet">…</code></pre>
```

- Use `type="button"` so the button never submits a form.
- Size the button at least 24×24 CSS px with `min-inline-size`/`min-block-size` (not `inline-size`/`block-size`), so
  content can grow the target but never shrink it.
- Name an icon-only button with `aria-label`. If the button shows visible text, that text is the name; do not add an
  `aria-label` that differs from it.
- Render the icon with whatever the codebase uses for icons (see `icons` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "icons"`)) and mark it decorative; the button's accessible name comes from
  `aria-label`, not the icon.

### 2. Copying logic

Put the copy logic in one function so the native and fallback paths share it.

```js
let selectedText = ''; // set by the optional selection popover (step 3)

async function copy(button, target, command = '--copy') {
  // Form controls expose text via .value; innerText (unlike textContent) keeps rendered line breaks
  const text = command === '--copy-selection'
    ? selectedText
    : target.matches('input, textarea') ? target.value : target.innerText.trim();
  if (!text) return;
  try {
    await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text);
    report(button, true); // see Feedback below
  } catch {
    report(button, false); // clipboard access can be denied: show the failure too, not only announce it
  }
}

// `command` events do not bubble: listen in the capture phase on document.
// event.source is the clicked button; event.target is the commandfor element.
document.addEventListener('command', (event) => {
  if (event.command.startsWith('--copy')) copy(event.source, event.target, event.command);
}, true);
```

- **One element for sighted and screen reader users:** `report()` sets `data-copied` (or `data-failed`) on the button
  and writes the message into the bubble, which is both the visible feedback and the live region. Sighted and screen
  reader users then get the same message for both outcomes. Keep messages short ("Copied", "Copy failed").
- **Show and hide the bubble with `opacity`,** not `display: none` or `visibility: hidden`, which take it out of the
  accessibility tree so the text is not announced.
- **Clean up:** after a short timeout, remove the state attributes and clear the bubble's text, so no stale "Copied" is
  left for screen reader browse mode.
- **Not color alone:** swap the icon (copy to check) on success and use the bubble text for both outcomes.
- **Repeat clicks:** clear the pending timeout and restart the animation instead of stacking timers. DO NOT disable the
  button while showing feedback: copying is idempotent, and disabling drops keyboard focus, announces a misleading
  unavailable state, and blocks retrying after a failure.
- **Reduced motion:** under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, replace icon and bubble animations with an opacity fade.

```js
const timers = new WeakMap();

function report(button, ok) {
  const tip = button.nextElementSibling; // the role="status" bubble
  clearTimeout(timers.get(button));
  button.removeAttribute('data-copied');
  button.removeAttribute('data-failed');
  const message = ok ? 'Copied' : 'Copy failed';
  tip.textContent = '';
  void button.offsetWidth; // restart the CSS animation
  button.setAttribute(ok ? 'data-copied' : 'data-failed', '');
  requestAnimationFrame(() => (tip.textContent = message));
  timers.set(button, setTimeout(() => { // 2000ms is an example value
    button.removeAttribute('data-copied');
    button.removeAttribute('data-failed');
    tip.textContent = '';
  }, 2000));
}
```

### 3. Copy the current selection (optional)

Add this only for long prose where users want a floating button on selection. Skip it for code blocks, inline values,
and fields.

- Use a `popover="manual"` element (not light-dismissed, so the selection survives) containing a button with
  `command="--copy-selection" commandfor="<container id>"`.
- Show it on `selectionchange` (debounced; wait for `pointerup` while dragging) only when the selection is non-collapsed
  and inside the container. A triple-click ends at the start of the next element, so do not require the end node to be
  inside: clip the range's end to the container and accept it when the clipped text equals the selected text. Copy and
  position from the clipped range, using its `getBoundingClientRect()`: centered on the inline axis and above the
  selection on the block axis, so it never covers selected text. Only enable the popover when
  `matchMedia('(pointer: fine)').matches`: touch browsers already offer Copy in their native selection menu, which the
  popover would duplicate and collide with.
- Assign the selected text to `selectedText` when showing the popover; `copy()` reads that saved string for
  `--copy-selection`; interacting with the button can collapse the live selection.
- Call `preventDefault()` on the popover's `pointerdown` to keep the selection. This also stops the button from taking
  focus on click or tap, so `:focus-within` cannot tell you that a press is in progress. Set a flag on the popover's
  `pointerdown` and, while it is set, do not hide the popover even if the selection collapses (some touch browsers clear
  it anyway). Clear the flag and re-check when the copy feedback ends (and on `pointercancel`). Otherwise, hide it on
  `Escape`, and when the selection collapses unless keyboard focus is inside the popover (re-check when focus leaves
  it).
- DO NOT hide the popover when the copy feedback timeout ends: a keyboard user's focus is on its button, and hiding it
  drops focus to the page, so the next `Tab` starts from the top. If `Escape` hides it while focus is inside, first move
  focus to the container: set `tabindex="-1"` on it just before the move and remove it on `blur`. Do not leave it in the
  markup, because a focusable container makes `Tab` skip the copy button in Firefox after a click in the text.

### 4. Repeated copyable elements (optional)

When a page repeats copyable elements (code blocks, list rows, token or ID cells), a visible button on each one adds
noise. Keep the button hidden until the element is hovered, reveal it for keyboard users too, and never make it
hover-only.

```css
/* Touch devices (no hover): the button stays visible, so keep it in flow where it cannot cover content */
.copyable { display: flex; align-items: start; gap: .5rem; }
.copyable .copy { flex: none; order: 1; }

/* Only hide where hover exists; the overlay is then revealed on demand */
@media (hover: hover) {
  .copyable { display: block; position: relative; }
  .copyable .copy { position: absolute; inset-block-start: .5rem; inset-inline-end: .5rem; } /* .copy is the bubble's positioning context, so move it, not the button */
  .copyable .copy-button { opacity: 0; transition: opacity .15s; }
  .copyable:hover .copy-button,
  .copyable:focus-within .copy-button,
  .copyable .copy-button:focus-visible,
  .copyable .copy-button[data-copied],
  .copyable .copy-button[data-failed] { opacity: 1; }
}
```

- Hide with `opacity` only. `display: none` and `visibility: hidden` remove the button from the tab order, so keyboard
  users could never reach it.
- Reveal on `:focus-within` of the container, as well as `:hover`, so the button shows when focus is on it or on
  focusable content in the block (such as a scrollable `<pre tabindex="0">`).
- Keep it visible on `(hover: none)` devices, where there is no hover to reveal it. Lay it out in flow beside the
  content there so it never covers it.
- Keep it visible while feedback shows (`data-copied` / `data-failed`), so the state does not vanish when the pointer
  leaves.
- Keep the button's 24×24 px minimum size and its accessible name; a hidden-by-opacity button is still announced by
  screen readers.
- DO NOT add `aria-hidden`, `inert` or `hidden` to the button to "hide" it, and do not toggle them on hover. Screen
  reader users (VoiceOver included) must be able to reach it with no hover, and focus moving onto it (including a screen
  reader cursor that moves focus) is what makes it visible.
- Add `padding-inline-end` on the `<pre>` so the button clears the code at rest. On a horizontally scrolling `<pre>`,
  that padding is only reached at the end of the scroll range, so long lines can pass under the button while scrolling.
  Give the button a mostly opaque background and a visible border so it stays legible over code, rather than reserving a
  permanent margin that narrows the code area on small screens.

## Fallbacks and browser support

### Invoker Commands

Baseline status for Invoker commands: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-12-12.
Supported by: Chrome 135 (Apr 2025), Edge 135 (Apr 2025), Firefox 144 (Oct 2025), and Safari 26.2 (Dec 2025).

If your Baseline target does not include Invoker Commands, keep the same markup and add a click listener that calls the
same `copy()` function. This is a short, robust fallback (progressive enhancement of the same experience):

```js
// Detect on the interface, not an instance
if (!('CommandEvent' in window)) {
  // Resolve the target from commandfor, as the browser does for command events
  document.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
    const button = event.target.closest('button[command^="--copy"]');
    if (!button) return;
    const target = document.getElementById(button.getAttribute('commandfor'));
    if (target) copy(button, target, button.getAttribute('command')); // a missing target would throw inside copy()
  });
}
```

Register only one of the two paths so a click never copies twice.

### Async Clipboard

Baseline status for the api.Clipboard.writeText capability: Widely available. It's been Baseline since 2020-03-24.
Supported by: Chrome 66 (Apr 2018), Edge 79 (Jan 2020), Firefox 63 (Oct 2018), Safari 13.1 (Mar 2020), and Safari iOS
13.4 (Mar 2020).

`navigator.clipboard` is only available in secure contexts (`https:` or `localhost`), and the write is rejected when
permission is denied. `copy()` already covers both: a missing `navigator.clipboard` throws inside the `try`, so the
failure message is shown and announced. Serve the page over HTTPS: that is the real fix.

Only as a last resort, when you cannot control the protocol of the host page (for example a component embedded on
third-party sites), fall back to the deprecated `document.execCommand('copy')` so copying still works for the user. It
must run synchronously inside the user's click handler, so use it only when `navigator.clipboard` is missing or the
write rejects:

```js
function legacyCopy(text) {
  const field = Object.assign(document.createElement('textarea'), { value: text });
  field.setAttribute('readonly', '');
  field.style.cssText = 'position:fixed;inset-block-start:0;opacity:0';
  document.body.append(field);
  field.select();
  try { return document.execCommand('copy'); } finally { field.remove(); }
}

// In copy(), replace the plain write with:
try {
  await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text);
} catch {
  if (!legacyCopy(text)) throw new Error('Copy failed'); // reaches the existing failure path
}
```

Only the optional selection button (step 3) uses Popover.

### Fallbacks & browser support for Popover

Baseline status for Popover: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-01-27.
Supported by: Chrome 116 (Aug 2023), Edge 116 (Aug 2023), Firefox 125 (Apr 2024), Safari 17 (Sep 2023), and Safari iOS
18.3 (Jan 2025).

The Popover API is mostly **progressive enhancement**, but its defining behaviors — top-layer promotion, light-dismiss,
and `popovertarget` invocation — have no CSS-only equivalent. Older browsers need a polyfill, or a manual fallback if
you would rather not ship one.

**Polyfill:** To support the `popover` attribute in older browsers, conditionally load [
`@oddbird/popover-polyfill`](https://github.com/oddbird/popover-polyfill). **MANDATORY:** Feature detect by checking for
the `popover` property on `HTMLElement.prototype`, and load the polyfill **only** when native support is missing — do
NOT load it unconditionally.

With a bundler or import map:

```js
// MANDATORY: Feature detect 'popover' on HTMLElement.prototype.
if (!Object.hasOwn(HTMLElement.prototype, "popover")) {
  import("@oddbird/popover-polyfill");
}
```

If not using a package manager, import from a CDN, e.g.
`"https://unpkg.com/@oddbird/popover-polyfill@latest/dist/popover.min.js"`.

Caveats when using the polyfill:

- Do NOT use the `popover` IDL attribute for any code that may run before the polyfill is fully loaded. It will not be
  mirrored as an attribute, the popover will not be picked up by the polyfill, and the property will be shadowing the
  accessor the polyfill adds forever. Use `setAttribute()`/`removeAttribute()` instead.
- **Styling caveat:** The polyfill cannot define the real `:popover-open` pseudo-class, so it applies a
  `.\:popover-open` class instead. **MANDATORY:** Combine the two with `:is()` or `:where()`, otherwise browsers that
  lack `:popover-open` discard the entire rule:

```css
[popover]:is(:popover-open, .\:popover-open) {
  display: block;
}
```

### Repeated announcements (VoiceOver)

VoiceOver skips a message identical to the previous one from the same region, even if the region was emptied in between.
Track the last message in a variable (not by reading the bubble, which is cleared) and, when a message repeats, append a
no-break space (`\u00A0`) so it differs. It is not read aloud. One page-wide value is the simplest way to track it: a
message from another button's bubble gets the space too, which is harmless. Do not use `ariaNotify()` for this.

```js
let lastMessage = '';

// In report(), replace `const message` with `let message`, then:
if (message === lastMessage) message += '\u00A0'; // differs from the last one, so it is announced
lastMessage = message;
```

# Dark mode toggles

A dark mode toggle lets users override the system color scheme for one site.
The override is applied by updating `<meta name="color-scheme">`: `light dark` means "follow the system preference",
`light` or `dark` pin an explicit scheme.
Colors (`light-dark()`), system colors, and native UI all key off the CSS `color-scheme` property, so the toggle works
by keeping that property in sync with the `<meta>` (see [Reflect the override in CSS](#reflect-the-override-in-css)).

## Persistent toggle, settings control, or no toggle at all?

Most sites do not need a persistent color scheme toggle in the site UI (header, nav, footer, etc.).
Follow the system preference by default and, if a manual override is needed at all, put the control in a separate
settings surface: a settings page, panel, or overlay.

Pinning a scheme against the OS is a legitimate but rare intent, and rare intents belong behind progressive disclosure,
not in a control that is visible at all times.

Persistent toggles are mostly found on developer-facing or developer-adjacent (e.g. for designers) sites, where
switching schemes is a far more frequent task than it is for the average web user.
Do NOT add one just because it is a common pattern on developer sites: the developer's interest in this control is not
representative of typical users.

## Implementation

First, follow all steps in `dark-mode` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "dark-mode"`) to support both
schemes, defaulting to the system preference.

### Data model

The data model for the dark mode toggle typically includes three states:

1. System (no stored value): The UI follows the system color scheme. Ideally this should be the default.
2. Light (stored as `"light"`): The UI uses the light theme regardless of the system color scheme.
3. Dark (stored as `"dark"`): The UI uses the dark theme regardless of the system color scheme.

This state is usually stored in `localStorage` and reflected in a `<meta name="color-scheme">` element in the document
head.

### Reflect the override in CSS

The `<meta>` is only a *presentational hint*: any `color-scheme` declaration in author CSS overrides it.
Since `dark-mode` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "dark-mode"`) sets `color-scheme: light dark` on
`:root`, updating the `<meta>` alone is a **no-op** — CSS wins.
Map the `<meta>` back to the property so the cascade follows it:

```css
:root {
  color-scheme: light dark;

  &:has(> head > meta[name="color-scheme"][content="dark"]) {
    color-scheme: dark;
  }
  &:has(> head > meta[name="color-scheme"][content="light"]) {
    color-scheme: light;
  }
}
```

**DO NOT** hardcode `color-scheme: light` or `color-scheme: dark` as the root default; the base declaration MUST stay
`light dark`.
CSS MUST NOT depend on JS: if JS never runs, the `<meta>` stays `light dark` and the site follows the system
preference — nothing breaks.

### Persistence and FOUC prevention

Persist the override in `localStorage`; remove the entry when returning to the system default.

To avoid a flash of the wrong scheme, apply the stored value in an inline script (NOT `type=module`, NOT `defer`) placed
immediately after the `<meta>` element:

```html
<meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">
<script>
document.querySelector('meta[name="color-scheme"]').content = localStorage.getItem("color-scheme") ?? "light dark";
</script>
```

- This inline script exists **only** for FOUC prevention. Keep it as small as possible; additional JS for handling color
  scheme toggling can load later.
- In rare cases `localStorage` access can throw (e.g. site data blocked), but since this script does nothing else, the
  only side effect would be a console error. Wrap in `try .. catch` if this matters. Ensure the theme is still applied
  to the page, even if it cannot be persisted.
- The override can change from another tab: handle `window`'s `storage` event to stay in sync.
- **DO NOT** use `matchMedia()` to remove the stored value when the system preference changes to match it.
  Many users' OS switches schemes automatically based on time of day; removing the stored value whenever the two happen
  to coincide would make it impossible to pin a scheme at all.

### Branching for HTML and non-color values

Colors need no extra work: once the `<meta>` is mapped to `color-scheme` (above), `light-dark()` follows the override.
This section is about adapting other values (e.g. `font-weight`, media sources, etc.).

When the page simply follows the system preference, `(prefers-color-scheme: dark)` can be used for branching, including
in `<picture>` or `<video>` sources.
Overriding the color scheme adds an additional complication: the system preference is no longer the source of truth, and
for APIs that only accept media queries there is no direct alternative.

Do NOT rely exclusively on JS-applied classes like `.dark` for branching, as they will be incorrect if JS doesn't load
and the OS default is dark.

You can combine the media query with a `:root:has(> head > meta[name="color-scheme"][content="dark"])` (or `light`)
selector to branch.
See `selector-atrule-combinations` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "selector-atrule-combinations"`) for
details on how to implement this elegantly.

The control's own options are non-color branches too: include both states in the markup (icon plus visually hidden
action text, e.g. "Switch to dark theme") and hide the inactive one via these selectors.
`display: none` also removes the redundant option from the AT so the control needs no JS to stay current when the system
preference changes.

For in-HTML media, the only way right now is to include both versions as separate elements and toggle visibility
appropriately.
Hiding `<source>` elements with `display: none` does not work.

## User Interface

### Two or three states?

In all cases, the UI MUST support reverting or setting the color scheme to system.

Prefer displaying two states in space-constrained toggles, such as persistent toggles in the site chrome (header, nav,
footer, etc.) where space is limited and tweaking settings is usually orthogonal to the user goal.

A color scheme control in a separate settings surface (page, panel, or overlay) is a different scenario and MAY expose
all three states explicitly ("Light", "Dark", "System"): there, the user is already making deliberate decisions about
future behavior, and there is room to explain the options.

Three explicit states are also warranted if the site implements context-aware schemes (e.g. a dimmer light mode when the
OS is dark), since "Light" and "System (currently light)" then genuinely differ.

### Two-state toggles

When such a control is used, it tends to be a temporary comfort adjustment ("it's too bright right now"), rather than
ensuring the current state is preserved long-term.
Therefore, for two-state toggles, it is sufficient to display two out of three settings: system (so that the setting can
be reverted) and the current opposite of system, stored as its current literal value.

The only two states should be:

1. **System default** — no stored value, `<meta>` content `light dark`. Displayed as its current resolved value (e.g. a
   sun icon when light).
2. **Override** — stored literally as `light` or `dark`.

Essentially, it is a tri-state control (`light dark`, `light`, `dark`) where the explicit state matching the current
system preference is unreachable.

When the user toggles:

1. Target scheme = the opposite of the currently *rendered* scheme (stored value if any, else system preference). The
   user intent is "select the opposite of what I see right now", NOT "select the inverse of the system default".
2. If the target differs from the current system preference, store it literally.
3. If the target matches the current system preference, the user is undoing their adjustment: remove the stored value.
   DO NOT store it — that would invisibly pin the scheme against future system changes.
4. Set the `<meta>` content to the stored value, or `light dark` if none.

IMPORTANT: Divergence must be checked only at storage time, never retroactively: a stored value that the system
preference later changes to match MUST be kept.
Many users' OS switches schemes automatically based on time of day; removing the stored value whenever the two happen to
coincide would make it impossible to pin a scheme at all.

Example scenario, starting with the OS set to light:

1. The user toggles. Dark differs from the system preference, so `dark` is stored; the site turns dark.
2. The OS setting changes to dark. The site stays dark (the stored value now matches the system preference, but is
   kept).
3. The OS setting changes back to light. The site stays dark.
4. The user toggles. The target (light) matches the system preference, so the stored value is removed and the site
   follows the system again.

### Three-state toggles

When there is more space and users are already in the mindset of setting long-term preferences, a tri-state control can
provide more clarity.
In this case, the data model cleanly maps to the three UI options: system, light, and dark.

To reduce cognitive load, the "system" option should also display what the current system setting is, for example via:

- Icon, e.g. a sun icon at the bottom right of the system icon
- Text, e.g. "System (Currently light)"

# Dialog

## Overview

Use the native `<dialog>` element for modal and non-modal dialogs. It provides the accessibility semantics, focus
handling, top-layer rendering and `Esc` handling that custom overlays have to rebuild by hand.

## Choose the overlay type

Pick the first rule that matches. If unsure, use Rule 1.

### Rule 1: The overlay interrupts the user and blocks the page (default)

Use for confirmations, forms, sign-in, destructive actions, and any "modal", "dialog", "lightbox" or "popup" request
that does not say otherwise.

Use `<dialog>` opened as a modal, declaratively with `command="show-modal"` (see `declarative-dialog-popover-control` (
via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "declarative-dialog-popover-control"`)) or from script with
`showModal()`.

```html
<button type="button" command="show-modal" commandfor="confirm">Delete</button>

<!-- MANDATORY: no role="dialog" or aria-modal; the native modal already provides them -->
<dialog id="confirm" aria-labelledby="confirm-title">
  <h2 id="confirm-title">Delete this item?</h2>
  <form method="dialog">
    <button value="cancel" autofocus>Cancel</button>
    <button value="delete">Delete</button>
  </form>
</dialog>
```

The browser provides: inert page, focus containment, top layer, `::backdrop`, `Esc` and back-gesture dismissal, and
focus return to the invoker.

- **DON'T** add `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal`, a focus trap, `inert` toggling or an `Esc` handler.
- **DON'T** open it with `show()` or the `open` attribute.
- **DO** stop the page scrolling behind it with the CSS below. See `prevent-page-scroll-under-modal-dialog` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "prevent-page-scroll-under-modal-dialog"`) for the details.
- **DON'T** lock scrolling with `overflow: hidden` or `position: fixed` on `html` or `body`.

```css
/* MANDATORY (both rules): without them, scrolling over the backdrop or inside the dialog scrolls the page behind it */
dialog:modal {
  overscroll-behavior: contain; /* stops scroll gestures in the dialog chaining to the page */
}
dialog::backdrop {
  overflow: hidden; /* ::backdrop is not a scroll container by default, so it would ignore overscroll-behavior */
  overscroll-behavior: contain;
}
```

Not for menus or tooltips: see Rule 3.

### Rule 2: The user keeps working in the page while the panel is open

Use for find bars, inspectors, palettes and compose panes that are still dialogs semantically.

Use `<dialog popover>` for a top-layer panel with popover dismissal (`auto` light-dismisses, `manual` does not). Use
`dialog.show()` only when the panel must not be in the top layer.

```html
<button type="button" popovertarget="find">Find</button>
<dialog id="find" popover="manual" aria-labelledby="find-title">
  <h2 id="find-title">Find</h2>
  <input type="search" aria-label="Search">
  <button type="button" popovertarget="find" popovertargetaction="hide">Close</button>
</dialog>
```

The page stays interactive and is not made inert.

- **DO** include a visible close button.
- **DON'T** use `showModal()`, which blocks the page.

Not for blocking confirmations: see Rule 1.

### Rule 3: The overlay is not a dialog

Use for menus, dropdowns, tooltips, hovercards and toasts.

Use a semantic element with the `popover` attribute, not `<dialog>`.

```html
<button type="button" popovertarget="menu">Actions</button>
<ul id="menu" popover>
  <li><a href="/rename">Rename</a></li>
</ul>
```

## Choose how it can be dismissed

The default depends on how the dialog is opened. If `closedby` is absent or invalid, `showModal()` behaves as
`closerequest` and any other way of opening behaves as `none`.

- **Esc and back gesture only (modal default):** set nothing, or `closedby="closerequest"`.
- **Also click outside to close:** use `closedby="any"`.
- **Only the developer closes it (for example a form with unsaved changes):** use `closedby="none"` and add a
  confirmation path. See Closing below.

## Guidelines

### Accessible name and initial focus

- **DO** name every dialog with `aria-labelledby` pointing at its heading, or `aria-label` when there is no visible
  title.
- **DO** put `autofocus` on the primary control or first field.
- **DO** put `autofocus` on the safe action (such as Cancel or Keep) in a destructive confirmation.
- **DON'T** write code to return focus on close. The browser returns it to the invoker.

### Opening

- **DO** open declaratively with `command="show-modal"` and `commandfor` on a `<button>`. See
  `declarative-dialog-popover-control` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "declarative-dialog-popover-control"`).
- **DO** use `dialog.showModal()` when opening from script.

### Closing

- **DO** close with `<form method="dialog">` buttons or `command="close"`.
- **DO** choose `closedby` deliberately: `any` (light dismiss and `Esc`), `closerequest` (`Esc` only, the modal default)
  or `none` (developer-controlled close only).
- **DO** use `command="request-close"` or `requestClose()` for Cancel buttons that must honor unsaved-changes logic.
  They fire `cancel` first and ignore `closedby`.
- **DO** treat `closedby` as progressive enhancement. `Esc` and the mobile back gesture already close modals without it.

### Hooking into close

- **DO** read `dialog.returnValue` in a `close` listener to learn which button was used, then reset it with
  `dialog.returnValue = ''`. `Esc` and other close requests set no value, and browsers differ on whether they clear the
  previous one, so without the reset a stale value can leak. Treat `''` as "dismissed without choosing".
- **DO** use `cancel` to intercept `Esc` and `request-close`, but do not rely on `preventDefault()` for repeated `Esc`
  presses without user activation.
- **DO** use `closedby="none"` with an explicit confirmation step for dirty forms.
- **DO** tell the user why the dialog stayed open when `cancel` is prevented: show a visible message and reference it
  with `aria-describedby` from the control that receives focus (such as Discard), so a screen reader reads it when focus
  moves. Without it, focus moving to a new button announces only that button's name.
- **DON'T** let the confirmation move controls under the pointer. Reserve the message's space (hide it with
  `visibility`, not `display` or `hidden`) and add the destructive button where existing buttons do not move (for
  example first in a right-aligned row), so a second click at the same spot cannot discard the user's changes.

### Non-modal dialogs

- **DO** use `<dialog popover>` (`auto` or `manual`) for a top-layer panel, and `dialog.show()` when you do not want the
  top layer.
- **DO** include a visible close button in every non-modal dialog.

### Backdrop and styling

- **DO** style `::backdrop` and use `dialog:modal` to target modal-only styles.
- **DO** leave animation to `animate-to-from-top-layer` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "animate-to-from-top-layer"`), dragging to `drag` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "drag"`), and reparenting to `persistent-top-layer-ui` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "persistent-top-layer-ui"`).
- **DON'T** set `display` on `dialog` unconditionally. It overrides the closed state. Scope it with `dialog[open]`.

### Accessibility

- **DON'T** add `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal`, a manual focus trap or `inert` toggling to a native modal.
- **DO** use a native `<button>` with an accessible name for close controls.
- **DO** use one consistent heading level for dialog titles.

## Fallback strategies

### `closedby` (`dialog-closedby`)

Browser support for <dialog closedby>: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 134 (Mar 2025), Edge 134 (Mar 2025), and Firefox 141 (Jul 2025).
Unsupported in: Safari.

Without `closedby`, a modal still closes with `Esc` and the back gesture; only click-outside is lost, so this is
graceful degradation. `closedby="none"` is ignored the same way: `Esc` fires `cancel` and then closes the dialog. Keep
the unsaved-changes guard in a `cancel` handler, not in `closedby="none"` alone, so it also protects where `closedby` is
missing. If your Baseline target requires light dismiss, add this where `closedby` is missing:

```js
if (!('closedBy' in HTMLDialogElement.prototype)) {
  // Test the pointer position, not event.target: the <dialog> is also the target for its own
  // padding and the gaps between its children, so a target check would close on those clicks
  const outside = (e, dialog) => {
    const r = dialog.getBoundingClientRect();
    return e.clientX < r.left || e.clientX > r.right || e.clientY < r.top || e.clientY > r.bottom;
  };
  for (const dialog of document.querySelectorAll('dialog[closedby="any"]')) {
    let pressedOutside = false;
    dialog.addEventListener('pointerdown', (e) => { pressedOutside = outside(e, dialog); });
    // Require the press and the release outside, so a text-selection drag that ends on the backdrop does not dismiss
    dialog.addEventListener('pointerup', (e) => { if (pressedOutside && outside(e, dialog)) dialog.close(); });
  }
}
```

### `overscroll-behavior`

Browser support for overscroll-behavior: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 144 (Jan 2026), Edge 144 (Jan 2026), and Firefox 150 (Apr 2026).
Unsupported in: Safari.

Treat scroll containment as progressive enhancement. Do not feature-detect it: `@supports` reports the property as
supported even where non-scrollable containers ignore it. Where it is not enforced, the dialog still contains scroll
whenever its own content overflows, and `showModal()` still makes the page inert. Do not fall back to `overflow: hidden`
or `position: fixed` on `html` or `body`, which removes the root scrollbar and shifts the layout.

### Invoker Commands (`command` / `commandfor`)

Baseline status for Invoker commands: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-12-12.
Supported by: Chrome 135 (Apr 2025), Edge 135 (Apr 2025), Firefox 144 (Oct 2025), and Safari 26.2 (Dec 2025).

If your Baseline target does not include Invoker Commands, keep the same markup and conditionally load the polyfill (the
same experience, as progressive enhancement). Detect on the interface and never load it unconditionally:

```js
// MANDATORY: feature detect on HTMLButtonElement.prototype and load only when native support is missing
if (!('commandForElement' in HTMLButtonElement.prototype)) {
  import('invokers-polyfill'); // npm install invokers-polyfill
}
```

Only Rules 2 and 3 use Popover.

### Fallbacks & browser support for Popover

Baseline status for Popover: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-01-27.
Supported by: Chrome 116 (Aug 2023), Edge 116 (Aug 2023), Firefox 125 (Apr 2024), Safari 17 (Sep 2023), and Safari iOS
18.3 (Jan 2025).

The Popover API is mostly **progressive enhancement**, but its defining behaviors — top-layer promotion, light-dismiss,
and `popovertarget` invocation — have no CSS-only equivalent. Older browsers need a polyfill, or a manual fallback if
you would rather not ship one.

**Polyfill:** To support the `popover` attribute in older browsers, conditionally load [
`@oddbird/popover-polyfill`](https://github.com/oddbird/popover-polyfill). **MANDATORY:** Feature detect by checking for
the `popover` property on `HTMLElement.prototype`, and load the polyfill **only** when native support is missing — do
NOT load it unconditionally.

With a bundler or import map:

```js
// MANDATORY: Feature detect 'popover' on HTMLElement.prototype.
if (!Object.hasOwn(HTMLElement.prototype, "popover")) {
  import("@oddbird/popover-polyfill");
}
```

If not using a package manager, import from a CDN, e.g.
`"https://unpkg.com/@oddbird/popover-polyfill@latest/dist/popover.min.js"`.

Caveats when using the polyfill:

- Do NOT use the `popover` IDL attribute for any code that may run before the polyfill is fully loaded. It will not be
  mirrored as an attribute, the popover will not be picked up by the polyfill, and the property will be shadowing the
  accessor the polyfill adds forever. Use `setAttribute()`/`removeAttribute()` instead.
- **Styling caveat:** The polyfill cannot define the real `:popover-open` pseudo-class, so it applies a
  `.\:popover-open` class instead. **MANDATORY:** Combine the two with `:is()` or `:where()`, otherwise browsers that
  lack `:popover-open` discard the entire rule:

```css
[popover]:is(:popover-open, .\:popover-open) {
  display: block;
}
```

# Build an interactive hovercard

Hovercards provide an interactive preview of content when a user expresses interest in a link (via hover or focus). This
is shown to users before they navigate, and either provides the user with the content they need or helps verify that the
link will contain the content they are looking for.

If you need plain-text, non-interactive tooltips rather than structured link previews, see
`interest-triggered-tooltips` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "interest-triggered-tooltips"`).

## 1. Triggering the hovercard

Use the **Interest Invokers** API to trigger the hovercard. This ensures the card appears on both hover and focus.

- Add the `popover="hint"` attribute to your card container. Use `hint` to avoid closing unrelated popover menus that
  may be open.
- Add the `interestfor` attribute to the trigger link, pointing to the card's `id`.

```html
<a href="/article" interestfor="article-preview">Article title</a>

<!-- The `id` must match the `interestfor` value on the trigger. -->
<div id="article-preview" popover="hint" class="hovercard">
  <h2>The buzz on hummingbirds</h2>
  <p class="byline">By Delphi Aguilar</p>
  <div>
    <img src="bird.jpg" alt="A vibrant hummingbird">
    <p>Brief summary of the article...</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

You do not need to include an additional link to the content inside of the hovercard, as it is redundant to the
triggering link.

### Accessibility

`interestfor` is specified to wire hint popovers (`popover="hint"`) for assistive technology itself, based on what the
target contains. A **plain hint** (text and images only) becomes the trigger's accessible description, or its name if it
has none. A **rich hint** (headings, links, or other interactive content) gets a minimum role of `tooltip`, the trigger
gets `aria-expanded` and an `aria-details` relation while the hint is open, and the open hint comes right after the
trigger in the tab order so keyboard users can reach its content.

Browsers and screen readers do not yet expose this consistently, so add explicit ARIA as well:

- **Hint that repeats the trigger's accessible name** (e.g. an icon-only button with `aria-label="Bold"` and a "Bold"
  tooltip): add nothing. A description identical to the name would be read twice.
- **Hint on a trigger with no visible label of its own** (e.g. an icon-only button without `aria-label`):
  `aria-labelledby` on the trigger pointing at the hint, so the hint becomes the name.
- **Hint whose trigger also opens it on activation** (a toggletip, or any button whose only job is the hint: give it
  `popovertarget` with `popovertargetaction="show"`): `role="tooltip"` on the hint and `aria-expanded` on the trigger,
  kept in sync with the popover's `toggle` event. A description read right after "button" suggests further actions and
  muddles the role; the expanded state tells the user there is content to reveal and whether it is open, and pressing
  the button delivers it. Place the hint right after the trigger in the DOM so reading keys reach its content once it is
  open.
- **Hint whose trigger does something else on activation** (a link, a button with its own action): `role="tooltip"` on
  the hint and `aria-describedby` on the trigger, never `aria-expanded`. A trigger announced as "collapsed" suggests
  `Enter` would expand it, but `Enter` navigates or acts. The hint must be something the user can afford to miss: a
  hovercard previews the destination, a tooltip on an action button describes the action.
- **DO NOT** attach a hint that opens on activation to a control that already uses `aria-expanded` for something else (
  for example, a menu button). Give that hint its own trigger instead.
- **DO NOT** move focus into the target when interest is shown (no `autofocus`, no `focus()` in an `interest` listener).
  Interest is triggered by hover or focus alone, so moving focus would fail WCAG 3.2.1 (On Focus).

Not every screen reader reads descriptions when moving through the page (NVDA skips them in browse mode by design), so a
hint exposed as a description must only carry content the user can afford to miss. Link previews and tooltips on action
controls qualify; anything the user needs belongs in a toggletip or inline.

Wire this with a short script instead of hand-authoring the attributes, so the markup stays declarative and the same
rules apply to every hint. The script should:

1. Run in every browser, before loading the `interestfor` polyfill, once the DOM is parsed, and expose a function that
   can be called again for content inserted later. Scanning upfront is required: a browse-mode screen reader user needs
   the attributes in place before any interaction, so wiring them lazily on `focus` or `interest` is too late, and so is
   waiting for the polyfill, which wires its ARIA only on `load` and adds no `role="tooltip"` to plain hints.
2. For every `[interestfor]` trigger whose target has `popover="hint"`, normalize whitespace and compare the hint text
   with the trigger's accessible name (`aria-labelledby` targets, else `aria-label`, else text content including image
   `alt`, else `title`). Equal: do nothing. Otherwise set `role="tooltip"` on the hint if it has no role.
3. When the trigger has no name, point `aria-labelledby` at the hint unless it already has one. Otherwise, if the
   trigger also opens the hint on activation (a `popovertarget` or `commandfor` naming the hint), set `aria-expanded` to
   the popover's current state (`:popover-open`) unless it already has `aria-expanded`, and remember which triggers the
   script owns; if not, point `aria-describedby` at the hint unless it already has one.
4. Keep `aria-expanded` in sync from the popover's `toggle` event in every browser with a single capturing listener on
   `document`, updating every trigger with a matching `interestfor` that the script owns (the `interestfor` polyfill
   does not sync `aria-expanded` on plain-text hints or when a toggletip is opened via `popovertarget`).

Things that are easy to get wrong:

- `toggle` does not bubble. A bubbling listener on `document` never fires; use the capture phase (or a listener per
  popover).
- Sync `aria-expanded` from `toggle`, not from `interest`/`loseinterest`. The popover is the source of truth: it can be
  closed by `Escape`, light dismiss, or another invoker, and several triggers can share one hint.
- A hidden popover is a valid `aria-describedby` or `aria-labelledby` target. Do not force the hint open or duplicate
  its text to make it "visible".
- Do not add `aria-haspopup` or a live region to any hint.
- Do not override author ARIA: an existing `aria-describedby`, `aria-labelledby`, or `aria-expanded` on the trigger
  wins.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Only use hovercards to provide supplemental information (e.g. a preview of information that can otherwise be obtained
> by clicking on the link), never information that is not available in any other way.

## 2. Positioning with Anchor Positioning

Position the hovercard relative to its trigger using **CSS Anchor Positioning**. When using `interestfor`, the trigger
becomes an implicit anchor for the popover.

```css
[popover].hovercard {
  /* Position the card below the trigger, aligned with its inline-start edge
     and spanning toward the inline-end, flipping if it overflows the viewport. */
  position-area: block-end span-inline-end;
  position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline, flip-block flip-inline;
}
```

## 3. Animating entry and exit

By default, interest is shown and lost for keyboard and mouse users with a delay of half a second. This prevents the
targeted popover from opening while tabbing through a page or moving your mouse around, and from closing while moving
your mouse from the trigger to the popover. To adjust the timing, use the `interest-delay` CSS property.

```css
[interestfor]{
  /* Shorthand for interest-delay-start and interest-delay-end */
  interest-delay: 0.2s 0.1s;
}
```

If users are likely to move through multiple triggers in quick succession, set the initial delay to `0s` if an
interest-triggered popover is already open. To prevent performance issues with `:has()`, select a nearby container with
a small number of child nodes, and target the triggers as directly as possible.

```css
.container:has( > li > a:interest-source) [interestfor] {
  interest-delay-start: 0s;
}
```

Use `@starting-style` to define the entry animation and `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` (along with `display` and
`overlay`) to animate the exit from the top layer, gating the transitions behind
`@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)`. Declare `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` as a separate property
after `transition` rather than inside the `transition` shorthand so older browsers do not ignore the entire `transition`
declaration.

```css
[popover].hovercard {
  opacity: 0;
  transform-origin: top;
}

[popover].hovercard:popover-open {
  opacity: 1;
  transform: translateY(0) scale(1);
}

@starting-style {
  [popover].hovercard:popover-open {
    opacity: 0;
    transform: translateY(-10px) scale(0.95);
  }
}

/* MANDATORY: Respect user preference for reduced motion by selectively applying transitions. */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  [popover].hovercard {
    transition:
      opacity,
      transform,
      display,
      overlay;
    transition-duration: 0.4s;
    /* Separate after transition so the shorthand doesn't reset it or fail in older browsers */
    transition-behavior: allow-discrete;
  }
}
```

## 4. OPTIONAL: Seamlessly morphing to the next page

You can optionally use **Cross-Document View Transitions** to create a seamless "morph" animation between the hovercard
and the destination page. See `consistent-cross-document-transitions` (via
`npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "consistent-cross-document-transitions"`) for guidance on implementation.

By assigning matching `view-transition-name` values to elements in the hovercard and their counterparts on the next
page, the browser will animate them across the navigation. You can name multiple elements (e.g. titles, images, bylines)
to create a complex, multi-element morphing effect. Assign the `view-transition-name` to elements on the open popover
using `:popover-open`, to avoid creating duplicate `view-transition-name`s or requiring link-specific
`view-transition-name`s.

```css
/* Opt-in to cross-document transitions on both pages */
@view-transition {
  navigation: auto;
}

/* Don't show transitions when loading this page */
::view-transition-group(*) {
  animation-duration: 0s;
}

/* Assign names ONLY when the popover is open to ensure only the correct elements are selected. */
[popover]:popover-open {
  view-transition-name: --hovercard;
  view-transition-class: morph;

  h2 {
    view-transition-name: --title;
    view-transition-class: morph;
  }

  img {
    view-transition-name: --image;
    view-transition-class: morph;
  }
}
```

**MANDATORY:** To ensure the transition is stable and doesn't flicker, the destination page should use
`blocking="render"` and `<link rel="expect">` to wait for critical content to be parsed before rendering the first
frame.

```html
<!-- On the destination page: -->
<head>
  <!-- Block rendering until the hero image and title are parsed,
       ensuring the view transition snapshot is taken at the right time. -->
  <link rel="expect" href="#main-content" blocking="render">
</head>
<body>
  <main id="main-content">
    <h1>The buzz on hummingbirds</h1>
    <img src="bird.jpg">
  </main>
</body>
```

```css
/* On the destination page: */
main {
  view-transition-name: --hovercard;
  view-transition-class: morph;
}
h1 {
  view-transition-name: --title;
  view-transition-class: morph;
}
img {
  view-transition-name: --image;
  view-transition-class: morph;
}

/* By default no transition */
::view-transition-group(*) {
  animation-duration: 0s;
}
/* Short transition for morphing elements */
::view-transition-group(.morph) {
  animation-duration: 0.4s;
}
/* Disable transition if no `old` view */
::view-transition-new(.morph):only-child {
  animation-duration: 0s;
}
```

## Fallback strategies

Because the trigger is a standard `<a href="...">` link, browsers without support can still navigate on click if you
choose to treat the hovercard as a progressive enhancement. When cross-browser hovercard support is required,
conditionally load polyfills as needed.

### Fallbacks & browser support for Popover

Baseline status for Popover: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-01-27.
Supported by: Chrome 116 (Aug 2023), Edge 116 (Aug 2023), Firefox 125 (Apr 2024), Safari 17 (Sep 2023), and Safari iOS
18.3 (Jan 2025).

The Popover API is mostly **progressive enhancement**, but its defining behaviors — top-layer promotion, light-dismiss,
and `popovertarget` invocation — have no CSS-only equivalent. Older browsers need a polyfill, or a manual fallback if
you would rather not ship one.

**Polyfill:** To support the `popover` attribute in older browsers, conditionally load [
`@oddbird/popover-polyfill`](https://github.com/oddbird/popover-polyfill). **MANDATORY:** Feature detect by checking for
the `popover` property on `HTMLElement.prototype`, and load the polyfill **only** when native support is missing — do
NOT load it unconditionally.

With a bundler or import map:

```js
// MANDATORY: Feature detect 'popover' on HTMLElement.prototype.
if (!Object.hasOwn(HTMLElement.prototype, "popover")) {
  import("@oddbird/popover-polyfill");
}
```

If not using a package manager, import from a CDN, e.g.
`"https://unpkg.com/@oddbird/popover-polyfill@latest/dist/popover.min.js"`.

Caveats when using the polyfill:

- Do NOT use the `popover` IDL attribute for any code that may run before the polyfill is fully loaded. It will not be
  mirrored as an attribute, the popover will not be picked up by the polyfill, and the property will be shadowing the
  accessor the polyfill adds forever. Use `setAttribute()`/`removeAttribute()` instead.
- **Styling caveat:** The polyfill cannot define the real `:popover-open` pseudo-class, so it applies a
  `.\:popover-open` class instead. **MANDATORY:** Combine the two with `:is()` or `:where()`, otherwise browsers that
  lack `:popover-open` discard the entire rule:

```css
[popover]:is(:popover-open, .\:popover-open) {
  display: block;
}
```

### Fallbacks & browser support for `popover="hint"`

Browser support for popover="hint": Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 151 (Jul 2026), Edge 151 (Jul 2026), and Firefox 153 (Jul 2026).
Unsupported in: Safari.

The `@oddbird/popover-polyfill` package does not polyfill `popover="hint"` in browsers that already support native
`popover` (`auto` and `manual`). In those browsers, the unrecognized `"hint"` value defaults to `popover="manual"` (the
HTML invalid value default), so a hovercard opened via keyboard focus may remain open if a second hovercard is opened
via pointer hover unless explicitly dismissed on loss of interest by the invoker.

### Fallbacks & browser support for Interest invokers

Browser support for Interest invokers: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 149 (Jun 2026) and Edge 149 (Jun 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.

Interest invokers must be conditionally polyfilled using the `interestfor` polyfill package from NPM. Prefer bundling
the polyfill over using the CDN.

**MANDATORY:** Feature detect by checking for the `interestForElement` property on `HTMLButtonElement.prototype`, and
load the polyfill **only** when native support is missing.

```html
<script type="module">
  if (!("interestForElement" in HTMLButtonElement.prototype)) {
    // CDN link only used for example, prefer bundling.
    await import("https://unpkg.com/interestfor@latest");
  }
</script>
```

### CSS Polyfill Caveats

When using the polyfill, the CSS API changes slightly to account for the lack of native pseudo-class and property
support:

- **Pseudo-classes:** The polyfill cannot define real `:interest-source` and `:interest-target` pseudo-classes, so it
  applies `.interest-source` and `.interest-target` classes instead. **MANDATORY:** Combine them with `:is()` to support
  both native and polyfilled states.

```css
/* Styles to apply when the effect is being previewed */
:is(:interest-source, .interest-source) { /* ... */ }
:is(:interest-target, .interest-target) { /* ... */ }
```

- **CSS Properties:** For `interest-delay`, `interest-delay-start`, and `interest-delay-end`, the polyfill requires
  using CSS variables as it cannot read the custom properties directly in all browsers.

```css
/* Adjust the start and end delay for interest invokers */
[interestfor] {
  --interest-delay-start: 0.2s;
  interest-delay-start: var(--interest-delay-start);
  --interest-delay-end: 0.1s;
  interest-delay-end: var(--interest-delay-end);
}
```

Set the initial delay to `0s` if an interest-triggered popover is already open and users are likely to move through
multiple triggers in quick succession.

```css
.container:has([interestfor]:is(:interest-source, .interest-source)) [interestfor] {
  --interest-delay-start: 0s;
}
```

### Fallbacks & browser support for Anchor positioning

Browser support for Anchor positioning: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 157 (Nov 2026), Edge 157 (Nov 2026), and Safari 27 (Sep 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox.

Without CSS Anchor Positioning, tethered elements such as `[popover]` overlays fall back to their default user-agent
placement (centered in the viewport for popovers). Depending on whether spatial tethering is required for your use case,
either conditionally load the polyfill or gate your positioning rules with `@supports`.

#### Option 1: Polyfill (`@oddbird/css-anchor-positioning`)

When the positioned element must stay spatially tethered to its trigger in unsupported browsers, conditionally load the
`@oddbird/css-anchor-positioning` package.

**MANDATORY:** Feature-detect support via `CSS.supports("anchor-name: --a")` (or
`"anchorName" in CSSStyleDeclaration.prototype`), and load the polyfill **only** when native support is missing — do NOT
load it unconditionally.

With a bundler or import map:

```js
// MANDATORY: Feature-detect anchor positioning support before loading the polyfill.
if (!CSS.supports("anchor-name: --a")) {
  import("@oddbird/css-anchor-positioning");
}
```

Without a bundler, import from a CDN inside a `<script type="module">`:

```html
<!-- MANDATORY: Conditionally install the anchor positioning polyfill -->
<script type="module">
  if (!CSS.supports("anchor-name: --a")) {
    import("https://unpkg.com/@oddbird/css-anchor-positioning");
  }
</script>
```

**Polyfill caveats:**

- **No implicit anchors:** The polyfill does not support implicit anchor associations (such as those created by
  `popovertarget`, `commandfor`, `interestfor`, or `showPopover({ source })`). You **MUST** set a unique explicit
  `anchor-name` on each trigger and a matching `position-anchor` on the positioned element.
- **No `position-area` with `position-try-fallbacks`:** `position-area` with `position-try-fallbacks` is not supported
  by the polyfill. When using the polyfill on elements needing fallbacks, position elements using `anchor()` functions
  on inset properties (`top`, `left`, `right`, `bottom`) with `inset: auto` instead of `position-area`.
- **Do not wrap polyfilled rules in `@supports`:** Browsers without native anchor positioning evaluate
  `@supports (position-area: ...)` and `@supports (anchor-name: --a)` to `false` and discard the block before the
  polyfill can process it.

```css
.trigger {
  /* MANDATORY: Each trigger and positioned element pair must share a unique anchor name. */
  anchor-name: --my-trigger;
}

[popover].anchored-overlay {
  position-anchor: --my-trigger;
  /* MANDATORY: Use anchor() on inset properties rather than position-area when using the polyfill on elements needing position-try-fallbacks. */
  inset: auto;
  top: anchor(bottom);
  left: anchor(left);
  margin: 0;
}
```

#### Option 2: Progressive enhancement with `@supports` (no polyfill)

If you do not ship the polyfill, **DO NOT** set `inset: auto` or `margin: 0` unconditionally on a `[popover]` element
that relies on `position-area` or `anchor()`. In browsers without anchor positioning, `inset: auto` overrides the
user-agent centering (`inset: 0; margin: auto`) while `position-area` is ignored, leaving the popover stranded at
`(0, 0)` or overlapping its trigger.

Instead, gate `inset: auto` and `margin: 0` inside `@supports` for the specific positioning feature used (for example,
`@supports (position-area: block-end)` or `@supports (top: anchor(bottom))`) so unsupported browsers retain the default
centered popover placement, or provide a matching `@supports not (...)` fallback layout (such as a fixed bottom sheet):

```css
@supports (position-area: block-end) {
  [popover].anchored-overlay {
    inset: auto;
    margin: 0;
    position-area: block-end span-inline-end;
    position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline, flip-block flip-inline;
  }
}

@supports not (position-area: block-end) {
  /* Optional: override default popover centering with a fixed bottom bar */
  [popover].anchored-overlay {
    position: fixed;
    inset: auto 0 0 0;
    width: auto;
    margin: 0;
  }
}
```

### Fallbacks & browser support for Cross-document view transitions

Browser support for Cross-document view transitions: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 126 (Jun 2024), Edge 126 (Jun 2024), and Safari 18.2 (Dec 2024).
Unsupported in: Firefox.

Cross-document view transitions are a progressive enhancement. In browsers that do not support
`@view-transition { navigation: auto; }`, the rule (along with `blocking="render"` and `<link rel="expect">` on the
destination page) degrades gracefully and clicking the link performs a standard page navigation without the morph
animation.
