# Creating Persistent App Tours

Onboarding tours require overlays that persist while users interact with the highlighted features. Unlike auto popovers,
manual popovers do not close when the user clicks elsewhere on the page. Combining `popover="manual"` with CSS Anchor
Positioning allows you to create non-modal, tethered tour steps. This pattern is used to introduce new/updated content.
There is no explicit relationship between the popovers themselves, so dismissing the first popover doesn't assume that
the user needs to immediately move to the second popover to learn about the related feature - they can find out about it
when they navigate to that section of the page.

## Recommended Implementation

### HTML

```html
<div id="feature-target">Highlight this feature</div>

<dialog id="tour-step" popover="manual" aria-labelledby="tour-title">
  <!-- Assume an <h1> precedes this element in the full document outline -->
  <h2 id="tour-title">Start a review</h2>
  <p>Begin the process by starting a review of the submitted document.</p>
  <button popovertarget="tour-step" popovertargetaction="hide">Got it</button>
</dialog>
```

### CSS

```css
#feature-target {
  anchor-name: --feature-target;
}

#tour-step {
  popover: manual;
  position-anchor: --feature-target;
  position-area: right center;
  inset: auto;
  margin: 1rem;
  padding: 1rem;
  border: 1px solid blue;
  border-radius: 0.5rem;
  background: aliceblue;
}
```

### JavaScript

```javascript
const tourStep = document.getElementById('tour-step');
tourStep.showPopover();

// At this point, as this is an initial onboarding tour popover, set the rest of the document to be inert. Ensure that the onboarding modal popover is not a child of this element, otherwise it too will be rendered inert and therefore inaccessible.
// Ensure that inert is removed once the initial onboarding tour has finished
const main = document.querySelector("main");
main.inert = true;

// MANDATORY: Programmatically route focus into the non-modal popover so keyboard/assistive technology users immediately perceive the new context
tourStep.querySelector('button').focus();
```

## Implementation Guidelines

* **MANDATORY:** Use `popover="manual"` to prevent the tour step from closing accidentally during user interaction.
* **MANDATORY:** Mark the container with `role="dialog"` and link its heading via `aria-labelledby`.
* **MANDATORY:** Shift programmatic focus inside the popover immediately after opening to prevent focus abandonment.
* **DO** use CSS Anchor Positioning to tether the tour step to the specific feature being explained.
* **DO** provide an explicit "Close" or "Next" button within the popover that uses `popovertargetaction="hide"`.

## Accessibility considerations

Popovers should provide sufficient context around the features they're introducing, to be understood independently. *
*DON'T** make the content in a popover heavily reliant on content outside of it to be understood. For example: "New
feature. Click here", relies heavily on visual information that people may not have, or may not be able to access (
particularly if the content outside the popover is `inert`). Instead, something like: "New chat functionality. Start a
chat to review items with fellow members", is much easier to understand when read in isolation. Tour popovers should
begin with a heading, so that as to provide context to the content in the popover, as well as to provide an easy way for
people using screen readers to navigate to them, when used in a non-modal way.

Focus must not be moved to these popovers on page load. This is to both prevent confusion from hijacking focus. It's
likely that when navigating to the page, the person using the functionality may have a goal for they want to complete,
therefore, tours for new features should be treated as supplemental information and not distract the user.

In keeping this information supplemental, the popover should be positioned in the DOM immediately before the
functionality/control it relates to. This will help people using screen readers to easily identify the relationship
between the popover and related content when reading through the page. When the popover is dismissed, focus should move
to the related control/functionality.

Content in popovers must scale in size and remain visible when resizing text up to 200% to adhere to WCAG 1.4.4 Resize
Text (Level AA). Content in popovers must remain visible when adjusting text styling and spacing with CSS to adhere to
1.4.12 Text Spacing (Level AA). Content in popovers must remain visible, or can be accessed still, when using a viewport
sized to 320 by 256 CSS pixels to adhere to 1.4.10 Reflow (Level AA).

Use of non-modal popovers may result in controls being obscured when they receive focus, which would result in a fail
against WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (Level AA), as focused items cannot be completely obscured. While there
may not be generic guidance to completely mitigate against this issue, consider strategies that adjust the position of
the tooltip or its presence. This includes ensuring that tooltips do not obscure interactive elements as they receive
focus via keyboard. If the tooltip is likely to obscure an interactive element when it receives focus, either change the
position of the tooltip to prevent focus being obscured, or dismiss the tooltip if it is no longer relevant to the user.

## Fallback strategies

### Fallbacks & browser support for Popover

Baseline status for Popover: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-01-27.
Supported by: Chrome 116 (Aug 2023), Edge 116 (Aug 2023), Firefox 125 (Apr 2024), Safari 17 (Sep 2023), and Safari iOS
18.3 (Jan 2025).

The Popover API is mostly **progressive enhancement**, but its defining behaviors — top-layer promotion, light-dismiss,
and `popovertarget` invocation — have no CSS-only equivalent. Older browsers need a polyfill, or a manual fallback if
you would rather not ship one.

**Polyfill:** To support the `popover` attribute in older browsers, conditionally load [
`@oddbird/popover-polyfill`](https://github.com/oddbird/popover-polyfill). **MANDATORY:** Feature detect by checking for
the `popover` property on `HTMLElement.prototype`, and load the polyfill **only** when native support is missing — do
NOT load it unconditionally.

With a bundler or import map:

```js
// MANDATORY: Feature detect 'popover' on HTMLElement.prototype.
if (!Object.hasOwn(HTMLElement.prototype, "popover")) {
  import("@oddbird/popover-polyfill");
}
```

If not using a package manager, import from a CDN, e.g.
`"https://unpkg.com/@oddbird/popover-polyfill@latest/dist/popover.min.js"`.

Caveats when using the polyfill:

- Do NOT use the `popover` IDL attribute for any code that may run before the polyfill is fully loaded. It will not be
  mirrored as an attribute, the popover will not be picked up by the polyfill, and the property will be shadowing the
  accessor the polyfill adds forever. Use `setAttribute()`/`removeAttribute()` instead.
- **Styling caveat:** The polyfill cannot define the real `:popover-open` pseudo-class, so it applies a
  `.\:popover-open` class instead. **MANDATORY:** Combine the two with `:is()` or `:where()`, otherwise browsers that
  lack `:popover-open` discard the entire rule:

```css
[popover]:is(:popover-open, .\:popover-open) {
  display: block;
}
```

### Fallbacks & browser support for Anchor positioning

Browser support for Anchor positioning: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 157 (Nov 2026), Edge 157 (Nov 2026), and Safari 27 (Sep 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox.

Without CSS Anchor Positioning, tethered elements such as `[popover]` overlays fall back to their default user-agent
placement (centered in the viewport for popovers). Depending on whether spatial tethering is required for your use case,
either conditionally load the polyfill or gate your positioning rules with `@supports`.

#### Option 1: Polyfill (`@oddbird/css-anchor-positioning`)

When the positioned element must stay spatially tethered to its trigger in unsupported browsers, conditionally load the
`@oddbird/css-anchor-positioning` package.

**MANDATORY:** Feature-detect support via `CSS.supports("anchor-name: --a")` (or
`"anchorName" in CSSStyleDeclaration.prototype`), and load the polyfill **only** when native support is missing — do NOT
load it unconditionally.

With a bundler or import map:

```js
// MANDATORY: Feature-detect anchor positioning support before loading the polyfill.
if (!CSS.supports("anchor-name: --a")) {
  import("@oddbird/css-anchor-positioning");
}
```

Without a bundler, import from a CDN inside a `<script type="module">`:

```html
<!-- MANDATORY: Conditionally install the anchor positioning polyfill -->
<script type="module">
  if (!CSS.supports("anchor-name: --a")) {
    import("https://unpkg.com/@oddbird/css-anchor-positioning");
  }
</script>
```

**Polyfill caveats:**

- **No implicit anchors:** The polyfill does not support implicit anchor associations (such as those created by
  `popovertarget`, `commandfor`, `interestfor`, or `showPopover({ source })`). You **MUST** set a unique explicit
  `anchor-name` on each trigger and a matching `position-anchor` on the positioned element.
- **No `position-area` with `position-try-fallbacks`:** `position-area` with `position-try-fallbacks` is not supported
  by the polyfill. When using the polyfill on elements needing fallbacks, position elements using `anchor()` functions
  on inset properties (`top`, `left`, `right`, `bottom`) with `inset: auto` instead of `position-area`.
- **Do not wrap polyfilled rules in `@supports`:** Browsers without native anchor positioning evaluate
  `@supports (position-area: ...)` and `@supports (anchor-name: --a)` to `false` and discard the block before the
  polyfill can process it.

```css
.trigger {
  /* MANDATORY: Each trigger and positioned element pair must share a unique anchor name. */
  anchor-name: --my-trigger;
}

[popover].anchored-overlay {
  position-anchor: --my-trigger;
  /* MANDATORY: Use anchor() on inset properties rather than position-area when using the polyfill on elements needing position-try-fallbacks. */
  inset: auto;
  top: anchor(bottom);
  left: anchor(left);
  margin: 0;
}
```

#### Option 2: Progressive enhancement with `@supports` (no polyfill)

If you do not ship the polyfill, **DO NOT** set `inset: auto` or `margin: 0` unconditionally on a `[popover]` element
that relies on `position-area` or `anchor()`. In browsers without anchor positioning, `inset: auto` overrides the
user-agent centering (`inset: 0; margin: auto`) while `position-area` is ignored, leaving the popover stranded at
`(0, 0)` or overlapping its trigger.

Instead, gate `inset: auto` and `margin: 0` inside `@supports` for the specific positioning feature used (for example,
`@supports (position-area: block-end)` or `@supports (top: anchor(bottom))`) so unsupported browsers retain the default
centered popover placement, or provide a matching `@supports not (...)` fallback layout (such as a fixed bottom sheet):

```css
@supports (position-area: block-end) {
  [popover].anchored-overlay {
    inset: auto;
    margin: 0;
    position-area: block-end span-inline-end;
    position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline, flip-block flip-inline;
  }
}

@supports not (position-area: block-end) {
  /* Optional: override default popover centering with a fixed bottom bar */
  [popover].anchored-overlay {
    position: fixed;
    inset: auto 0 0 0;
    width: auto;
    margin: 0;
  }
}
```

# Creating Toast Notifications

Toast notifications are transient status messages. Unlike menus, they should not close when a user interacts with other
parts of the page. The popover="manual" state is ideal because it lacks "light-dismiss" behavior and allows multiple
notifications to coexist.

## When to use

Toast notifications must be used to provide non-critical, supplemental information about the results of an interaction,
or an event (e.g. an email has been received). An example may include confirming that a form submission was successful.
Notifications that require immediate attention should instead use an alternative component. Examples include inline
banners, dialogs or modal dialogs. These examples surface information in a way that is easier to identify for everyone.
Toasts should be used sparingly, as making them accessible to everyone means addressing complex considerations, and is
the reason why some companies have opted to no longer use them, and instead, utilize the alternative aforementioned
components.

## Implementation guidelines

Prefer persistent toast notifications that remain present until they are dismissed, except for frequent, low importance
events, where the friction persistence creates outweighs the value of the information provided. In those cases, do
evaluate whether toasts actually add to the user experience in general — in some cases it may be preferable to not have
them at all. If using a pattern that does dismiss toasts after a short period of time, check whether focus is on a
control in the toast before dismissal. If the user is focused on a control inside the toast, pause dismissal until focus
has left the toast.

* **MANDATORY:** Use popover="manual" so the notification stays visible until explicitly closed or timed out by a
  script.
* **MANDATORY:** Ensure that the information in the toast can be identified by other means, so that if it is part of a
  pattern that disappears after a short period of time, people can still identify the information without the toast
  being present.
* **DO** use a container to manage the stacking of multiple toasts. Since popovers in the Top Layer ignore parent
  z-index, you must position them individually or within a common layout group.
* **DO** add toast notifications consistently to the same container in the page, so that people using assistive
  technologies can consistently locate them.
* **DO** make the container a region, with an accessible name, so that it can be easily identified using a screen
  reader. For example: `<div role="region" aria-label="Notifications"></div>`.
* **DO** use `ariaNotify()` to announce the content present in toasts that are displayed. This ensures that people using
  screen readers, who cannot see the screen, are aware of the presence of toast messages
* **DO** ensure that only the toast's visible text is announced as part of the `ariaNotify()` and not the names of any
  controls. If actions are available in the toast (aside from a close control), append "Actions available" to the end of
  the announcement.
* **DO** provide an explicit "Close" button within the toast using popovertargetaction="hide".
* **DO** ensure that a toast's dismiss button is keyboard-focusable (without automatically stealing focus when the toast
  appears), so keyboard users can navigate to the toast region and dismiss notifications.
* **DO** manage focus when a user manually dismisses a currently focused toast: move focus to the next remaining toast
  in the stack, or—if no toasts remain—return focus to the user's prior focus location (or the control that triggered
  the toast).
* **DO** declare `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` as a separate property after `transition` (rather than inside the
  `transition` shorthand) to animate entry and exit from the Top Layer without older browsers ignoring the `transition`
  declaration.
* **DO** provide a non-animated version using the `prefers-reduced-motion` media query
* **DO** ensure that toast messages scale in size, and that all toast content remains visible when resizing text up to
  200% to adhere to WCAG 1.4.4 Resize Text (Level AA)
* **DO** ensure that all toast content remains visible when adjusting text styling and spacing with CSS to adhere to
  1.4.12 Text Spacing (Level AA)
* **DO** ensure that all toast content remains visible, or can be accessed still, when using a viewport sized to 320 by
  256 CSS pixels to adhere to 1.4.10 Reflow (Level AA)

* **DON'T** surface toasts in scenarios where focus redirection may be used at the same time. The focus redirection may
  cancel out the toast announcements, resulting in people missing information.
* **DON'T** use toasts in modal dialogs. Content outside of the dialog will be inert and unavailable to assistive
  technologies. Placing the toast in a modal dialog, separate from the existing toast container makes it difficult to
  locate, and may lead to people not being able to locate it.
* **DON'T** surface toast notifications in the background while a modal dialog is open. It's likely the notification
  will be missed. Instead, suppress the notification until the modal dialog is dismissed.
* **DON'T** include controls in toast notifications that perform actions not already permanently available outside the
  toast notifications. Controls in toasts should be used sparingly, and only provided as a shortcut for actions already
  available via the UI.

## Optional: Usability & accessibility improvements

* **Surface previous toasts**: Provide a way for people to access a list of past toast messages. This can help people
  who may encounter difficulty in remembering what the toast informed them, or reduce anxiety for people who
  inadvertently dismissed a toast message.
* **Customize toast notifications**: Provide a way for people to customize which toast notifications are provided. This
  can help to ensure that information provided to people is relevant, reducing distractions and confusion.
* **Use an alternative way to communicate toasts are present**: It is recommended that there are multiple ways to
  communicate that a toast has been made visible. An example of this may be a brief sound effect (which could be turned
  off). This will help people using screen magnification software, who may otherwise find it difficult to identify that
  toasts are present.

## Fallback strategies

### Fallbacks & browser support for Popover

Baseline status for Popover: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-01-27.
Supported by: Chrome 116 (Aug 2023), Edge 116 (Aug 2023), Firefox 125 (Apr 2024), Safari 17 (Sep 2023), and Safari iOS
18.3 (Jan 2025).

### Fallbacks & browser support for ariaNotify()

Baseline status for ariaNotify(): Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2026-09-14.
Supported by: Chrome 141 (Sep 2025), Edge 141 (Oct 2025), Firefox 150 (Apr 2026), and Safari 27 (Sep 2026).

Baseline status for ariaNotify(): Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2026-09-14.
Supported by: Chrome 141 (Sep 2025), Edge 141 (Oct 2025), Firefox 150 (Apr 2026), and Safari 27 (Sep 2026).

Use an ARIA live region, ensuring that the container is present in the page on load, and then add the messages to the
live region container when relevant.

```html
<!-- Pre-populated hidden live region container -->
<div id="notification" aria-live="assertive"></div>
```

This content will be present in the DOM, and can be read by a screen reader after the message has been announced.
Therefore, in order to provide context to this region, when the live region has content, add in text immediately before
the container to provide context to the announcement. This will help people understand the purpose of the content if
they identify it when reading the page.

```html
<p class="inclusively-hidden">Screen reader announcements</p>
<!-- Pre-populated hidden live region container -->
<div id="notification" aria-live="assertive">
  Dynamic announcement injected into the existing container.
</div>
```

### Fallbacks & browser support for Anchor positioning

Supported by: Chrome 157 (Nov 2026), Edge 157 (Nov 2026), and Safari 27 (Sep 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox.

```css
  [popover].anchored-overlay {
    position: fixed;
    inset: auto 0 0 0;
    width: auto;
    margin: 0;
  }
}
```

#### sibling-index()

* **Guidance:** If sibling-index() is not supported, use the `+` operator to add margin manually. I.e.
  `popover + popover { margin-top: 1rem }`

#### transition-behavior

* **Guidance:** If transition-behavior is not supported, use JavaScript to add animation via classes as the toast
  element transitions in and out.

# Progress ring

A progress ring (or circular progress bar) provides visual feedback on the status of a task. Unlike a linear progress
bar, its circular shape is ideal for dashboards, card components, or anywhere space is constrained.

This guide implements a progress ring by:

- Using the native `<progress>` element as the semantic foundation to ensure the component is accessible to screen
  readers and keyboard users out-of-the-box.
- Styling the component with `conic-gradient()` and `mask-image`, allowing for a fully responsive and themeable ring
  without the complexity of SVG path manipulation.
- Leveraging CSS Custom Properties and `@property` to enable smooth, GPU-accelerated transitions of the progress fill.

This approach is preferred over SVG-only solutions because it uses the semantic `<progress>` element rather than ARIA,
and more easily integrates with existing layout, design systems and typography.

See the `spinner` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "spinner"`) for handling indeterminate loading
states.

## Implementation

### 1. Markup

Use a wrapper to hold both the visual ring and the optional center content. The `<progress>` element remains the
semantic source of truth. Use a utility class to visually hide the native progress bar while keeping it accessible.

```html
<div class="progress-ring-wrapper">
  <progress value="75" max="100" aria-label="Task progress" class="progress-ring"></progress>
  <!-- Optional: Content to display in the center. Hidden from assistive
       technologies because it repeats the value of the <progress> element. -->
  <div class="progress-ring-content" aria-hidden="true">
    75%
  </div>
</div>
```

Hide the center content from assistive technologies with `aria-hidden="true"`. The `<progress>` element already exposes
its value, so screen readers would otherwise announce it twice.

If the center content shows the value in another form, such as "3 of 5 files" or a percentage, set the same text in
`aria-valuetext` on the `<progress>` element whenever you update it, otherwise screen readers only get the number.

### 2. Styles

#### Hiding Native UI

To style the `<progress>` element as a progress ring, first hide the default browser styling for progress bars.

```css
/* Hide native bars */
progress.progress-ring::-webkit-progress-bar {
  display: none;
  background: none;
}
progress.progress-ring::-webkit-progress-value {
  display: none;
  background: none;
}
progress.progress-ring::-moz-progress-bar {
  display: none;
  background: none;
}
progress.progress-ring::slider-fill {
  display: none;
  background: none;
}
```

#### Container and Ring

The wrapper provides the positioning context. The `<progress>` element handles the visual gradient. Forced colors mode
removes background gradients, so in `@media (forced-colors: active)`, opt the ring out with `forced-color-adjust: none`
and draw it with system colors, or the ring disappears.

```css
.progress-ring-wrapper {
  position: relative;
  display: grid;
  place-items: center;
}

progress.progress-ring {
  --size: 150px;
  --thickness: 16px;
  --track-color: #f1f5f9;
  --fill-color: #3b82f6;
  --value: attr(value type(<number>));
  width: var(--size);
  height: var(--size);

  transition: --value 0.4s cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1);
  border-radius: 50%;

  background: conic-gradient(
    var(--fill-color) calc(var(--value) * 1%),
    var(--track-color) 0
  );

  /* MANDATORY: Clip the background to the border-area. */
  background-clip: border-area;
  border: var(--thickness) solid transparent;
  background-origin: border-box;

  @media (forced-colors: active) {
    /* Keeps the gradient, which forced colors mode removes, and draws it in system colors */
    forced-color-adjust: none;
    --fill-color: CanvasText;
    --track-color: Canvas;
  }
}

.progress-ring-content {
  /* Positioned in the center of the wrapper */
  position: absolute;
}
```

You can also use a `radial-gradient` to make rounded end caps.

#### Enable smooth transitions with `@property`

To animate the progress ring smoothly when the value changes, register `--value` as a numeric custom property.

Users with motion sensitivities may find the transition between values disorienting. Respect the
`prefers-reduced-motion` media query by having a 0 second (immediate) duration by default, and setting a longer time for
users with no preference.

```css
@property --value {
  syntax: '<number>';
  inherits: true;
  initial-value: 0;
}

progress.progress-ring {
  transition: --value 0s ease-in-out;
  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
    transition-duration: 0.4s;
  }
}

```

### 3. Progress Updates

Update the `value` attribute on the `<progress>` element and the text content of `.progress-ring-content` (if displaying
a percentage) whenever the value changes.

### 4. Optional Success State

You can use the CSS attribute selector to automatically update the ring's appearance (e.g., changing the color to green)
when the task reaches completion.

```css
/* Change the fill color to green when the progress reaches 100% */
progress.progress-ring[value="100"] {
  --fill-color: #10b981;
}
```

## Fallback strategies

Do not add a fallback value inside the `<progress>` element. It is not used by assistive technology and ignored by all
modern browsers.

#### Animation fallback

Baseline status for Registered custom properties: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2024-07-09.
Supported by: Chrome 85 (Aug 2020), Edge 85 (Aug 2020), Firefox 128 (Jul 2024), and Safari 16.4 (Mar 2023).

If `@property` is not supported, the ring will jump to the new value instantly instead of transitioning smoothly. In
most cases this is fine, and does not break any functionality.

If the transition is absolutely necessary, you can check for `@property` support and use a `requestAnimationFrame()`
loop to interpolate `--value` in older browsers.

Browser support for background-clip: border-area: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 150 (Jun 2026), Edge 150 (Jul 2026), and Safari 18.2 (Dec 2024).
Unsupported in: Firefox.

For browsers that don't yet support `background-clip: border-area`, fall back to a `mask-image` to hollow out the center
of the `<progress>` element.

```css
@supports not (background-clip: border-area) {
  mask-image: radial-gradient(
    transparent calc(50% - var(--thickness)),
    black calc(50% - var(--thickness) + 0.5px)
  );
  border: 0;
}
```

Browser support for attr(): Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 133 (Feb 2025), Edge 133 (Feb 2025), and Firefox 155 (Sep 2026).
Unsupported in: Safari.

For browsers that don't support the `attr()` CSS function for any property, use a `MutationObserver` to automatically
sync the `value` attribute to the `--value` custom property.

```js
if (!CSS.supports("width: attr(value type(<number>))")) {
  const observer = new MutationObserver(() => {
    progress.style.setProperty("--value", progress.getAttribute("value"));
  });
  observer.observe(progress, {
    attributes: true,
    attributeFilter: ["value"],
  });
}
```

# Build a Styled Progress Bar

The `<progress>` element is the semantic way to represent the completion progress of a task, like downloading or
uploading information or completing part of a multi-step process. Using the native element helps with accessibility, as
screen readers have an implicit `role="progressbar"` and can announce values.

This guide implements a fully styled horizontal progress bar with style customizations.

## Progress bar or progress ring?

- If space is constrained or a square aspect ratio is preferable, consider using a circular progress bar (progress
  ring): `progress-ring` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "progress-ring"`)
- Prefer spinners for most indeterminate progress scenarios (`spinner` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "spinner"`)). Use indeterminate progress bars when the indeterminate state
  is temporary and will soon be replaced by a determinate progress bar (e.g. waiting for metadata around an upload
  before a progress % can be shown)

## Markup

1. **Use a native `<progress>` element**: It provides built-in accessibility and platform-consistent behavior.
2. Use `max` if a scale different from the default 0-1 scale is needed.
3. For a specific progress value, set a `value` attribute. Omit `value` for an indeterminate state (e.g. before more
   concrete feedback starts).
4. Use `<label for="...">`, `aria-labelledby`, or `aria-label` to associate the progress element with a label.

## What type of customization is needed?

For limited styling, these properties are sufficient:

- `accent-color` to change the color of the progress bar
- `width` / `inline-size` to change the width of the progress bar
- `height`/`block-size` applies inconsistently — test first
- `writing-mode: vertical-lr` for vertical bars.
- Effects that apply after painting: `opacity`, `filter`, `clip-path`, masks, transforms, `box-shadow`, etc.

If limited styling suffices, skip the next section.

WARNING: Certain properties (e.g. `border-radius`, `background`, `border`) will silently disable the default progress
bar styling. If you need styling beyond the properties above, you must implement fully custom styling as described in
the next section. Do NOT apply more extensive styling "just in case it works".

## Fully custom styling

### 1. Basic setup

- MANDATORY: Use `appearance: none` to enable custom styling.
- Reset UA borders with `border: 0 solid`
- To clip the active bar to the element’s border-radius, use `overflow: clip` OR apply the same `border-radius` to the
  bar. Do NOT use `border-radius: inherit` on the bar, which depends on the specific structure of elements in the shadow
  DOM.

```css
progress {
  /* Reset default browser styles */
  appearance: none;
  border: 0 solid;
  /* Clip bar to element’s border-radius  */
  overflow: clip;
}
```

### 2. Styling

- Style the track on the `progress` element itself.
- Use the appropriate browser-targeted pseudo-element to target the progress bar itself: `::-webkit-progress-value` for
  WebKit/Blink and `::-moz-progress-bar` for Firefox.
- MANDATORY: Do NOT group `-webkit-` and `-moz-` pseudo-elements in the same rule. The rule will be deemed invalid and
  will be ignored. `:is()` and `:where()` do not help here, as they don't support pseudo-elements.
- Each browser-targeted pseudo-element should appear exactly once. State-specific customizations (such as the
  indeterminate segment size and animation) should be routed through custom properties set on the `progress` element
  itself.
- Optional: Transition `inline-size` on the fill so determinate value changes animate instead of jumping. Firefox sizes
  the fill in layout and ignores it, which is harmless.

```css
progress {
  --progress-bar-radius: 1e5px;
  border-radius: var(--progress-bar-radius);
  /* Apply color for custom progress track (background) */
  background: var(--progress-bar-track, var(--color-neutral-90));
  /* Subtle depth on the empty part of the track */
  box-shadow: inset 0 1px 2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.1);
}

/* Let <progress> styling show through */
progress::-webkit-progress-bar {
  background: transparent;
}

/* Webkit, Chrome */
progress::-webkit-progress-value {
  background: var(--progress-bar-fill, var(--accent-color));
  border-radius: var(--progress-bar-radius);
  transition: inline-size 0.3s;
}

/* Firefox */
progress::-moz-progress-bar {
  background: var(--progress-bar-fill, var(--accent-color));
  border-radius: var(--progress-bar-radius);
  transition: inline-size 0.3s;
}
```

### 3. Indeterminate state styling

**Add a custom animation for the indeterminate state:** Turn the fill pseudo-element into a short segment and slide it
along the track.

- Style the fill itself; do NOT recreate it as a background on `progress`.
- The indeterminate fill exists only through its animation: the keyframes set its length with a real `inline-size` (this
  beats Chromium's UA inline `inline-size`) and moves it with `translate`. Do NOT use `scale` for the length; it
  distorts any pattern painted on the fill.
- `translate` percentages resolve against the fill's own width, so express positions in track units instead: make
  `progress` an inline-size container and use `cqi` in the keyframes. Include `margin-right: auto` in `from, to` so
  Chromium lays the fill out at the physical left in RTL too.
- Use transforms, not margins, to move the fill.
    - Transforms keep the animation in the compositor (unless `inline-size` is also being animated)
    - Margins break in RTL, for two separate reasons:
        - Firefox positions the indeterminate fill using only its physical left margin, so `margin-inline-start` has no
          effect in RTL and the fill never moves.
        - In Chromium and WebKit, which lay the fill out as a normal block, once a margin pushes the fill past the end
          of the track the margins add up to more than the track. Standard CSS resolves that by ignoring `margin-left`
          in RTL, so the segment jumps to the edge instead of sliding off it.
    - `translate` is applied after layout, so neither problem applies.
- To mirror the motion in RTL (as Chrome's native bar does), reverse the animation under `:dir(rtl)`:

```css
progress:dir(rtl) {
  --progress-bar-indeterminate-animation: progress-bar-indeterminate var(--progress-bar-indeterminate-animation-duration) infinite linear reverse;
}
```

- Define the public `--progress-bar-indeterminate-*` properties on `progress` (their name already scopes them to the
  state) so consumers can override them without knowing about `:indeterminate`.
- To vary the segment length (e.g. the leading edge races ahead and the trailing edge catches up), set
  `--progress-bar-indeterminate-animation` to two concurrent animations: one whose keyframes animate `translate` in
  `cqi` (position) and one whose keyframes animate `inline-size` (length), so each gets its own keyframes and easing. Do
  NOT try to shape both edges in a single keyframe list; per-keyframe `animation-timing-function` applies to every
  property in that keyframe.
- `--progress-bar-animation` applies in both states and can be used for effects such as a determinate shimmer.
  `revert-rule` is used to only override when it is set, to maximize composability.
- Never disable the indeterminate animation (`animation: none` leaves a zero-width fill in Chromium). For reduced
  motion, slow it down instead.

```css
progress {
  /* Lets the fill position itself in track units (cqi) */
  container-type: inline-size;
  /* Segment length relative to the track */
  --progress-bar-indeterminate-size: 30%;
  --progress-bar-indeterminate-animation-duration: 1.5s;

  /* Respect prefers-reduced-motion */
  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
    --progress-bar-indeterminate-animation-duration: 10s;
  }
}

progress:indeterminate {
  --progress-bar-animation: var(
      --progress-bar-indeterminate-animation,
      progress-bar-indeterminate var(--progress-bar-indeterminate-animation-duration) infinite linear
    );
}

/* Add to the existing pseudo-element rules */
progress::-webkit-progress-value {
  animation: var(--progress-bar-animation, revert-rule);
}

progress::-moz-progress-bar {
  animation: var(--progress-bar-animation, revert-rule);
}

/* Physical: left to right regardless of direction (reverse under :dir(rtl) to mirror). */
@keyframes progress-bar-indeterminate {
  from, to {
    inline-size: var(--progress-bar-indeterminate-size);
    /* Pin to the physical left; Chromium would otherwise lay the fill out at the inline start */
    margin-right: auto;
  }
  from { translate: -100%; } /* Own width: fully outside the left edge */
  to { translate: 100cqi; }  /* Track width: fully outside the right edge */
}
```

### Additional Accessibility Considerations

In addition to the guidelines mentioned above:

* **Announce completion without stealing focus**: Do not set `tabindex` or call `.focus()` on `<progress>`, as it is
  non-interactive and moving focus to it disrupts keyboard users. To announce when a background task finishes, update a
  polite status element (`role="status"` or `aria-live="polite"`).
* **Do not add fallback text inside `<progress>`**: Text inside `<progress>` is ignored by modern browsers and is not
  used by assistive technologies.
* Avoid `aria-busy` + `aria-describedby` on an unlabeled generic `<div>`. `aria-busy` has inconsistent screen reader
  support, and `aria-describedby` on an unnamed `<div>` without a role is ignored by assistive technologies. If a
  region's content is not ready while loading, hide it with `hidden` or `aria-hidden="true"`.
* **DO** ensure proper contrast between the progress bar and track when adding custom styles.
* **Consider alternatives to represent indeterminate state**: Indeterminate progress bar animations displayed in
  parallel to other content can be considered distracting for some users.

## Fallback strategies

### Fallbacks & browser support for accent-color

Browser support for accent-color: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 93 (Aug 2021), Edge 93 (Sep 2021), Firefox 92 (Sep 2021), and Safari 26.2 (Dec 2025).

The `accent-color` property is progressive enhancement.
Browsers that do not support this property will ignore it and use their default UI colors.

If `accent-color` is not supported and styling the progress bar is required, use the customized styling method to apply
preferred styling to the progress bar.

### Fallbacks & browser support for `revert-rule`

Baseline status for revert-rule: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2026-09-14.
Supported by: Chrome 148 (May 2026), Edge 148 (May 2026), Firefox 150 (Apr 2026), and Safari 27 (Sep 2026).

If `revert-rule` is not supported, `animation: var(--progress-bar-animation, revert-rule)` falls back to
`animation-name: revert-rule` with a `0s` duration when `--progress-bar-animation` is unset, which is a harmless no-op
when no `@keyframes revert-rule` exists.

# Build a Scrollspy Navigation

A scrollspy navigation is a common UI pattern that automatically highlights the navigation link corresponding to the
section of the page currently in the viewport. This provides users with a clear sense of where they are in a long
document as they scroll.

This pattern is common in two scenarios:

- **Single-page websites**: Where the primary site navigation links to different sections of a single page rather than
  separate URLs.
- **Long-form content**: Where a table of contents or sidebar navigation tracks the user's progress through an article,
  guide, or documentation.

## How to implement

Traditionally, the scrollspy pattern required JavaScript and the `IntersectionObserver` API. Modern CSS provides a
native way to achieve this using the `scroll-target-group` property and the `:target-current` pseudo-class.

1. **Ensure Navigation Links use Fragment Identifiers**: Your navigation must consist of anchor links (`<a>`) that point
   to sections on the same page using fragment identifiers (e.g., `<a href="#section-1">`) that match the `id` of your
   content sections.
2. **Enable Scroll Target Grouping**: Apply the `scroll-target-group: auto` property to the container of your navigation
   links. This tells the browser to treat these links as markers that track their respective targets.
3. **Style the Active Link**: Use the `:target-current` pseudo-class on your navigation links to apply styles when their
   target section is visible in the scroll container.
4. **Semantic State**: Use a script to update `aria-current="true"` on the active link when scrolling stops to ensure
   the state is correctly communicated to assistive technologies.

## Example code

This example highlights the active link in a fixed navigation menu as the user scrolls through sections.

```css

/* MANDATORY: The container of markers must have scroll-target-group: auto */
nav {
  /* Enables automatic tracking of fragment links */
  scroll-target-group: auto;
}
/* MANDATORY: Use :target-current to style the link whose target is in view. */
nav a:target-current {
  color: var(--accent, #007bff);
  border-bottom-color: var(--accent, #007bff);
}
```

```html
<nav>
  <a href="#intro">Introduction</a>
  <a href="#features">Features</a>
  <a href="#pricing">Pricing</a>
</nav>

<main>
  <!-- MANDATORY: Each section must have a unique ID matching a link fragment in the <nav> and tabindex="-1" so it can receive focus. -->
  <section id="intro" tabindex="-1">
    <h2>Introduction</h2>
    <!-- content -->
  </section>
  <section id="features" tabindex="-1">
    <h2>Features</h2>
    <!-- content -->
  </section>
  <section id="pricing" tabindex="-1">
    <h2>Pricing</h2>
    <!-- content -->
  </section>
</main>

<script type="module">
  if (CSS.supports('scroll-target-group: auto')) {
    const syncAriaCurrent = () => {
      const currentLink = document.querySelector('nav a:target-current');
      document.querySelectorAll('nav a').forEach(link => {
        link.setAttribute('aria-current', link === currentLink ? 'true' : 'false');
      });
    };
    // Update the aria on initial page load. Ensure the DOM content is loaded, either by using `<script type="module">` or an event listener for `DOMContentLoaded`.
    syncAriaCurrent();
    // Update the aria after scroll ends
    document.addEventListener('scrollend', syncAriaCurrent);
  }
</script>
```

## Accessibility considerations

To ensure that people can navigate the scrollable region after selecting an anchor element, apply the corresponding
element with a `tabindex="-1"` attribute. This will allow the element to receive focus, and allow people using a
keyboard to scroll the container, or easily navigate from that content.

```html
<li><a href="#section-2">Section 2</a></li>
…
<!-- Adding a tabindex="-1" attribute to the section target will mean that it can receive focus after being navigated to -->
<section id="section-2" tabindex="-1">
  <h2>Section 2</h2>
</section>
```

To ensure consistent operability across different browsers and assistive technology combinations, if the scrollable
container is not the `<body>` element, ensure that it can receive focus (by applying `tabindex="0"`), and has an
accessible name that describes the content, along with an appropriate role (such as `role="region"`), if it does not
already have an implicit role (which elements like `<main>` do).

## Best Practices

- **DO** use `scroll-target-group: auto` on a dedicated container for navigation links: This ensures the browser knows
  which links should be tracked.
- **DO** ensure targets have unique `id` attributes matching the links' `href` attributes.
- **DO** provide enough vertical space for sections: `scroll-target-group` most clearly identifies the visible target
  when sections are large enough that only one or two are visible at a time.
- **MANDATORY**: For accessibility, the visual state must be mirrored with `aria-current`. While `:target-current`
  handles the visual aspect, this is not exposed to screen readers.
- **AVOID** relying solely on color for the active state: Include other visual cues like font weight, an underline, or
  an indicator dot, or ensure there is sufficient contrast between the colors to ensure the difference is accessible to
  users with color vision deficiencies.

## Fallback strategies

Browser support for scroll-target-group: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 140 (Sep 2025) and Edge 140 (Sep 2025).
Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.

For browsers that do not support `scroll-target-group`, you should use a fallback based on the `IntersectionObserver`
API.

```html
<script>
  // Feature detection for scroll-target-group
  const supportsScrollTargetGroup = CSS.supports('scroll-target-group: auto');

  if (!supportsScrollTargetGroup) {
    const navLinks = document.querySelectorAll('nav a');
    const sections = document.querySelectorAll('main section');

    const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
      entries.forEach(entry => {
        if (entry.isIntersecting) {
          const id = entry.target.getAttribute('id');
          navLinks.forEach(link => {
            const isActive = link.getAttribute('href') === `#${id}`;
            // Use the escaped colon class for consistent styling
            link.classList.toggle('target-current', isActive);
            link.setAttribute('aria-current', isActive);
          });
        }
      });
    }, { rootMargin: '-50% 0px -50% 0px', threshold: 0 });

    sections.forEach(section => observer.observe(section));
  }
</script>

<style>
  /* Fallback style if :target-current is not supported.
     Use :is() to combine the native pseudo-class with a fallback class for older browsers. DO NOT use `nav a:target-current, nav a.target-current, as the unrecognized pseudoselector invalidates the entire rule in older browsers. */
  nav a:is(:target-current, .target-current) {
    color: var(--accent, #007bff);
    border-bottom-color: var(--accent, #007bff);
    font-weight: bold;
  }
</style>
```

# Loading spinner

A loading spinner (or activity indicator) informs users that a process is underway when the exact duration is unknown.
Unlike a progress ring, a spinner is "indeterminate" and typically uses animation to signal activity.

This guide implements a spinner by:

- Using the native `<progress>` element as the semantic foundation. By omitting the `value` attribute, the browser
  treats it as an indeterminate progress bar, ensuring correct announcement by assistive technologies.
- Styling the component with `conic-gradient()` to create a visual "trail" and `background-clip: border-area` to hollow
  out the center into a ring.
- Animating the spinner efficiently using CSS transforms and respecting `prefers-reduced-motion` to ensure a comfortable
  experience for all users.

See `progress-ring` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "progress-ring"`) for handling determinate tasks
with a known duration.

## Implementation

### 1. Markup

Use the native `<progress>` element as both the semantic source of truth and the visual component. Without a `value`
attribute, it is implicitly indeterminate.

```html
<progress aria-label="Loading" class="loading-spinner"></progress>
```

### 2. Styles

#### Hiding Native UI

To style the `<progress>` element as a spinner, first hide the default browser styling for indeterminate progress bars.

```css
/* Hide native bars */
progress.loading-spinner:indeterminate::-webkit-progress-bar {
  display: none;
  background: none;
}
progress.loading-spinner:indeterminate::-webkit-progress-value {
  display: none;
  background: none;
}
progress.loading-spinner:indeterminate::-moz-progress-bar {
  display: none;
  background: none;
}
progress.loading-spinner:indeterminate::slider-fill {
  display: none;
  background: none;
}
```

#### Spinner Ring and Trail

The spinner uses a `conic-gradient` to create a visual trail. Forced colors mode removes background gradients, so in
`@media (forced-colors: active)`, opt the spinner out with `forced-color-adjust: none` and draw it with system colors,
or the spinner disappears.

```css
@property --arc-start {
  syntax: "<angle>";
  inherits: false;
  initial-value: 0deg;
}
@property --arc-end {
  syntax: "<angle>";
  inherits: false;
  initial-value: 0deg;
}
/* Use a custom property to conditionally include the dash animation */
@property --progress-dash-animation {
  syntax: "*";
  inherits: false;
  initial-value: , progress-dash 3s ease-in-out infinite;
}

progress.loading-spinner:indeterminate {
  --_from: calc(90deg + var(--arc-start, 0deg));
  --_to: calc(90deg + var(--arc-end, 158deg));
  --size: 40px;
  --thickness: 2px;
  --spinner-color: #2563eb;
  --track-color: #e2e5e7;
  --spinner-duration: 1.5s;
  --_used-spinner-duration: var(--spinner-duration);
  --spinner-timing: linear;

  position: relative;
  width: var(--size);
  height: var(--size);
  border-radius: 50%;
  appearance: none;

  /* Create the fading trail with dynamic angles */
  background: conic-gradient(
      from var(--_from),
      var(--spinner-color) calc(var(--_to) - var(--_from)),
      transparent 0
    )
    var(--track-color);

  @supports (background-clip: border-area) {
    background-clip: border-area;
    border: var(--thickness) solid transparent;
    background-origin: border-box;
  }

  /* ... fallback for background-clip: border-area ... */

  @media (forced-colors: active) {
    /* Keeps the gradient, which forced colors mode removes, and draws it in system colors */
    forced-color-adjust: none;
    --spinner-color: CanvasText;
    --track-color: Canvas;
  }

  /* The dash animation is only included if @property is supported */
  animation:
    progress-spin var(--_used-spinner-duration) linear infinite
    var(--progress-dash-animation, );
}

@keyframes progress-spin {
  to {
    rotate: 1turn;
  }
}

@keyframes progress-dash {
  from {
    --arc-start: 0deg;
    --arc-end: 3deg;
  }
  50% {
    --arc-start: 100deg;
    --arc-end: 358deg;
  }
  to {
    --arc-start: 360deg;
    --arc-end: 363deg;
  }
}
```

#### Respecting Motion Preferences

Users with motion sensitivities may find fast-spinning elements disorienting. Always respect the
`prefers-reduced-motion` media query. Set the internal `--_used-spinner-duration` property to override the user's
`--spinner-duration` value, using the same selector as the spinner rule so that the override applies, and drop the dash
animation so that only a slow rotation remains.

```css
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  progress.loading-spinner:indeterminate {
    /* Slow down the animation significantly rather than stopping it entirely,
       so the user still knows that the process is active. */
    --_used-spinner-duration: 6s;
    /* Drops the dash animation, so the arc keeps a fixed length */
    --progress-dash-animation: ;
    --arc-end: 158deg;
  }
}
```

## Fallback strategies

Baseline status for Registered custom properties: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2024-07-09.
Supported by: Chrome 85 (Aug 2020), Edge 85 (Aug 2020), Firefox 128 (Jul 2024), and Safari 16.4 (Mar 2023).

If `@property` is supported, the dash animation is automatically included via the `--progress-dash-animation` property's
`initial-value`. In browsers without `@property` support, the property registration is ignored, and the animation falls
back to a simple rotation. No JavaScript is required for this fallback.

Browser support for background-clip: border-area: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 150 (Jun 2026), Edge 150 (Jul 2026), and Safari 18.2 (Dec 2024).
Unsupported in: Firefox.

For browsers that don't yet support `background-clip: border-area`, fall back to a `mask-image` to hollow out the
center.

```css
/* Fallback: use mask-image to create the ring */
@supports not (background-clip: border-area) {
  --clip-boundary: calc(100% - var(--thickness));
  mask-image: radial-gradient(
    farthest-side,
    transparent var(--clip-boundary),
    black var(--clip-boundary)
  );
  border: 0;
}
```
