# Build a toolbar

A toolbar groups related controls (formatting, alignment, view options) into one composite widget with a **single tab
stop**. Users `Tab` into it once, move between controls with the arrow keys, and `Tab` out. Use it only for controls
that act on something else (an editor, preview, canvas). For site navigation, see `navbar` (via
`npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "navbar"`); for a dropdown or context menu of commands without a persistent
row of controls, see `menu` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "menu"`).

## Structure and semantics

MANDATORY: Put `role="toolbar"` and an `aria-label` on the container. Wrap related controls in `role="group"` with their
own `aria-label`, and divide groups with `role="separator"` and `aria-orientation="vertical"`. If a wrapped separator
would sit alone at a row end, hide it visually with `opacity: 0`, not `display: none` or `visibility: hidden`, which
also remove it from the accessibility tree. Optionally add `aria-controls` pointing at the element the toolbar acts on;
it is only worth adding when the toolbar controls one specific element.

* Use real `<button type="button">` elements.
* Icon-only buttons need an `aria-label`; tooltips do not replace it. Render decorative icons with
  `<svg aria-hidden="true">` and `currentColor`, or with a CSS `mask`, `background-color: currentColor`, and
  `forced-color-adjust: none` so forced-colors mode does not strip the fill. For a reusable CSS icon token system, see
  `icons` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "icons"`).
* Toggle buttons (bold, italic) use `aria-pressed="true|false"`. Do not change their label when toggled.
* A mutually exclusive set (left/center/right) uses `aria-pressed` on each button, with script keeping exactly one
  `true`.
* Action buttons (copy, undo, save) run once and have no on/off state, so DO NOT add `aria-pressed` to them. Mark
  `aria-pressed` only on buttons that stay on or off.
* Disable with `aria-disabled="true"` rather than `disabled` so the control stays focusable and reachable by arrow keys.
  Ignore clicks while it is set.

```html
<div role="toolbar" focusgroup="toolbar wrap" aria-label="Text formatting" aria-controls="preview">
  <div role="group" aria-label="Style">
    <button type="button" aria-pressed="false" aria-label="Bold" title="Bold"></button>
  </div>
  <span role="separator" aria-orientation="vertical"></span>
  <!-- Overflow trigger: the last item in the toolbar -->
  <button type="button" aria-label="More actions" aria-haspopup="menu" aria-expanded="false"
    popovertarget="more-menu" title="More actions"></button>
</div>
```

## Action buttons and feedback

Toggles show their result through `aria-pressed`. An action has no state to show, so a screen reader user gets no
confirmation unless you provide it. When the result is not otherwise visible or announced (copy, save), write a short
message to a live region outside the toolbar. If the action changes content that is already announced or focused, skip
the message.

```html
<!-- Always present in the DOM so the announcement is reliable; keep it outside the toolbar -->
<p role="status"></p>
```

```js
// Report the outcome, including failure; clipboard access can be denied
try {
  await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text);
  status.textContent = "Text copied";
} catch {
  status.textContent = "Copy failed";
}
```

## Keyboard navigation

MANDATORY: Only one item is in the tab order at a time. Put `focusgroup="toolbar wrap"` on the `role="toolbar"`
container: the browser provides the roving tab stop, arrow-key movement across all groups (wrapping at the ends,
reversed in RTL), `Home`/`End`, and focus restoration after a click. Do not add a second roving-tabindex system
alongside it. Where `focusgroup` is unsupported, install the fallback in "Fallbacks" below.

## Vertical toolbar

Choose a vertical toolbar when controls stack along a side edge (a tool palette or zoom controls beside a canvas);
otherwise use a horizontal one. Everything above applies except:

* Set `aria-orientation="vertical"` on the toolbar and use `focusgroup="toolbar wrap block"` so `ArrowDown`/`ArrowUp`
  move between items.
* Lay items out in a column (`flex-direction: column`, no wrapping).
* A separator between stacked items is horizontal: use `aria-orientation="horizontal"` (the separator default) there,
  not `vertical`.
* Tooltips open beside the button (`position-area: inline-end`), not below it; see Tooltips below.

## Visible states

* Size each button at least 24×24 CSS px using `min-inline-size`/`min-block-size` (not `inline-size`/`block-size`), so
  content can grow the target but never shrink it. Enlarge it under `@media (pointer: coarse)`. Values like `2.5rem` and
  `3rem` are examples.

* Keep a clear `:focus-visible` outline with an offset; never remove it.
* Style toggled state from the ARIA attribute (`[aria-pressed="true"]`), not a separate class, so visual and accessible
  state cannot diverge.
* Show the toggled state by changing the button background; if the contrast between the button background and the
  adjacent background color is less than 3:1 in each supported color scheme, provide an additional visual cue such as an
  outline or inset shadow around the background that meets the 3:1 threshold. For more information, see `color` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "color"`).
* Under `forced-colors: active`, use system colors (`ButtonText`, `Highlight`).
* Draw separators and tooltip boxes with a border (a `transparent` one is fine), not `background` alone, which forced
  colors replaces with the page color.
* Wrap hover styles in `@media (hover: hover)` and transitions in `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)`.

## Tooltips for icon-only buttons

Give each icon-only button a `title` as the baseline tooltip. Only where both interest invokers and anchor positioning
are supported, upgrade it to an interest invoker with `popover="hint"`, which shows the tooltip without closing an open
menu popover. Elsewhere the native `title` tooltip stays.

MANDATORY: Position the hint on the axis the toolbar does not stack along: `position-area: block-end` (fallback
`flip-block`) for a horizontal toolbar, `position-area: inline-end` (fallback `flip-inline`) for a vertical one. A hint
placed along the stacking axis covers the next control and swallows its click, because the hint stays open while the
pointer is over it.

```html
<button type="button" aria-label="Bold" title="Bold">…</button>
```

```js
// Upgrade title tooltips only when interest invokers and anchor positioning both work
if ("interestForElement" in HTMLButtonElement.prototype && CSS.supports("position-area", "block-end")) {
  document.querySelectorAll('[role="toolbar"] button[title]').forEach((b, i) => {
    const tip = Object.assign(document.createElement("div"), { id: `tip-${i}`, textContent: b.title });
    tip.popover = "hint";
    b.setAttribute("interestfor", tip.id);
    b.removeAttribute("title"); // avoid a second, native tooltip
    document.body.append(tip); // keep open hint nodes out of role="group" / role="toolbar"
  });
}
```

`interestfor` is specified to wire hint popovers (`popover="hint"`) for assistive technology itself, based on what the
target contains. A **plain hint** (text and images only) becomes the trigger's accessible description, or its name if it
has none. A **rich hint** (headings, links, or other interactive content) gets a minimum role of `tooltip`, the trigger
gets `aria-expanded` and an `aria-details` relation while the hint is open, and the open hint comes right after the
trigger in the tab order so keyboard users can reach its content.

Browsers and screen readers do not yet expose this consistently, so add explicit ARIA as well:

- **Hint that repeats the trigger's accessible name** (e.g. an icon-only button with `aria-label="Bold"` and a "Bold"
  tooltip): add nothing. A description identical to the name would be read twice.
- **Hint on a trigger with no visible label of its own** (e.g. an icon-only button without `aria-label`):
  `aria-labelledby` on the trigger pointing at the hint, so the hint becomes the name.
- **Hint whose trigger also opens it on activation** (a toggletip, or any button whose only job is the hint: give it
  `popovertarget` with `popovertargetaction="show"`): `role="tooltip"` on the hint and `aria-expanded` on the trigger,
  kept in sync with the popover's `toggle` event. A description read right after "button" suggests further actions and
  muddles the role; the expanded state tells the user there is content to reveal and whether it is open, and pressing
  the button delivers it. Place the hint right after the trigger in the DOM so reading keys reach its content once it is
  open.
- **Hint whose trigger does something else on activation** (a link, a button with its own action): `role="tooltip"` on
  the hint and `aria-describedby` on the trigger, never `aria-expanded`. A trigger announced as "collapsed" suggests
  `Enter` would expand it, but `Enter` navigates or acts. The hint must be something the user can afford to miss: a
  hovercard previews the destination, a tooltip on an action button describes the action.
- **DO NOT** attach a hint that opens on activation to a control that already uses `aria-expanded` for something else (
  for example, a menu button). Give that hint its own trigger instead.
- **DO NOT** move focus into the target when interest is shown (no `autofocus`, no `focus()` in an `interest` listener).
  Interest is triggered by hover or focus alone, so moving focus would fail WCAG 3.2.1 (On Focus).

Not every screen reader reads descriptions when moving through the page (NVDA skips them in browse mode by design), so a
hint exposed as a description must only carry content the user can afford to miss. Link previews and tooltips on action
controls qualify; anything the user needs belongs in a toggletip or inline.

Wire this with a short script instead of hand-authoring the attributes, so the markup stays declarative and the same
rules apply to every hint. The script should:

1. Run in every browser, before loading the `interestfor` polyfill, once the DOM is parsed, and expose a function that
   can be called again for content inserted later. Scanning upfront is required: a browse-mode screen reader user needs
   the attributes in place before any interaction, so wiring them lazily on `focus` or `interest` is too late, and so is
   waiting for the polyfill, which wires its ARIA only on `load` and adds no `role="tooltip"` to plain hints.
2. For every `[interestfor]` trigger whose target has `popover="hint"`, normalize whitespace and compare the hint text
   with the trigger's accessible name (`aria-labelledby` targets, else `aria-label`, else text content including image
   `alt`, else `title`). Equal: do nothing. Otherwise set `role="tooltip"` on the hint if it has no role.
3. When the trigger has no name, point `aria-labelledby` at the hint unless it already has one. Otherwise, if the
   trigger also opens the hint on activation (a `popovertarget` or `commandfor` naming the hint), set `aria-expanded` to
   the popover's current state (`:popover-open`) unless it already has `aria-expanded`, and remember which triggers the
   script owns; if not, point `aria-describedby` at the hint unless it already has one.
4. Keep `aria-expanded` in sync from the popover's `toggle` event in every browser with a single capturing listener on
   `document`, updating every trigger with a matching `interestfor` that the script owns (the `interestfor` polyfill
   does not sync `aria-expanded` on plain-text hints or when a toggletip is opened via `popovertarget`).

Things that are easy to get wrong:

- `toggle` does not bubble. A bubbling listener on `document` never fires; use the capture phase (or a listener per
  popover).
- Sync `aria-expanded` from `toggle`, not from `interest`/`loseinterest`. The popover is the source of truth: it can be
  closed by `Escape`, light dismiss, or another invoker, and several triggers can share one hint.
- A hidden popover is a valid `aria-describedby` or `aria-labelledby` target. Do not force the hint open or duplicate
  its text to make it "visible".
- Do not add `aria-haspopup` or a live region to any hint.
- Do not override author ARIA: an existing `aria-describedby`, `aria-labelledby`, or `aria-expanded` on the trigger
  wins.

By default, interest is shown and lost for keyboard and mouse users with a delay of half a second. This prevents the
targeted popover from opening while tabbing through a page or moving your mouse around, and from closing while moving
your mouse from the trigger to the popover. To adjust the timing, use the `interest-delay` CSS property.

```css
[interestfor]{
  /* Shorthand for interest-delay-start and interest-delay-end */
  interest-delay: 0.2s 0.1s;
}
```

If users are likely to move through multiple triggers in quick succession, set the initial delay to `0s` if an
interest-triggered popover is already open. To prevent performance issues with `:has()`, select a nearby container with
a small number of child nodes, and target the triggers as directly as possible.

```css
.container:has( > li > a:interest-source) [interestfor] {
  interest-delay-start: 0s;
}
```

```css
[popover="hint"] {
  inset: auto;
  /* Anchor to the invoker; flip to the other side if there is no room */
  position-area: block-end;
  position-try-fallbacks: flip-block;
}
```

## Overflow menu for secondary actions (optional)

Two patterns fit a toolbar into a narrow space: an overflow menu, better on desktop, or a horizontally scrollable
toolbar with no scrollbar and scroll hints, better on mobile. For the scrollable pattern use
`overflow-x: auto; scrollbar-width: none; scroll-snap-type: x proximity`, and hint at hidden controls with edge fades (
`mask-image`) or a partly visible last item. Choose by input type (`@media (pointer: coarse)`) or container width.

Add a trailing "More actions" menu when the toolbar has secondary actions or must fit narrow containers; skip it if
every control is common and fits. If items must move into the menu dynamically as space runs out, build that overflow
behavior yourself.

* Make the trigger the last toolbar item (`aria-label="More actions"`, `aria-haspopup="menu"`, `aria-expanded="false"`,
  and `popovertarget` pointing at the menu popover) with the conventional three vertical dots icon (`⋮`). Open it only
  on activation—never preview on focus when arrowing across the toolbar.
* Anchor the `popover` container to its trigger (
  `inset: auto; position-area: block-end span-inline-start; position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline`) and nest
  `<div focusgroup="menu nomemory" aria-label="More actions">` inside it, adding `role="menu"`, `role="menuitem"`,
  `tabindex="-1"`, and `ArrowDown`/`ArrowUp`/`Home`/`End` only when `'focusGroup' in HTMLElement.prototype` is false.
  Sync `aria-expanded` and focus the first item on `toggle`, close the popover on `Tab` without trapping focus, and let
  `Space` on `role="menuitemcheckbox"` toggle `aria-checked` without closing. For nested submenus or radio groups, see
  `menu` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "menu"`).
* Announce the result of every menu activation in the toolbar's live region, such as `"Strikethrough on"` or
  `"Formatting cleared"`. When closing the menu returns focus to the trigger, delay the live-region write slightly—for
  example `500ms`—so the focus-change announcement does not preempt it.

## Fallback strategies

### Fallbacks & browser support for `focusgroup`

Browser support for focusgroup: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 150 (Jun 2026) and Edge 150 (Jul 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.

Keep `focusgroup` in the markup. Only if `'focusGroup' in HTMLElement.prototype` is false, load a roving-tabindex
fallback; never install it when native focusgroup is present. The fallback implements what focusgroup does natively:

* The active item has `tabindex="0"`; all others have `tabindex="-1"`. Initially the first item is active.
* On `focusin`, move `tabindex="0"` to the focused item so returning to the toolbar (including after a click) restores
  position.
* In a horizontal toolbar, `ArrowRight`/`ArrowLeft` move to the next/previous item across all groups and wrap at the
  ends. In RTL, reverse the directions. Do not wire `ArrowUp`/`ArrowDown`.
* In a vertical toolbar, `ArrowDown`/`ArrowUp` move to the next/previous item instead, and `ArrowLeft`/`ArrowRight` do
  nothing.
* `Home`/`End` move to the first/last item.
* Call `preventDefault()` only for keys the toolbar handles so `Tab` keeps working.

```js
if (!('focusGroup' in HTMLElement.prototype)) {
  // items = every toolbar control across all groups, in DOM order
  items.forEach((b, i) => (b.tabIndex = i ? -1 : 0));
  bar.addEventListener("focusin", ({ target }) => {
    if (items.includes(target)) items.forEach((b) => (b.tabIndex = b === target ? 0 : -1));
  });
  // Read direction and orientation at event time so runtime changes are honored
  const vertical = bar.getAttribute("aria-orientation") === "vertical";
  // Only horizontal toolbars flip with direction: RTL does not flip Up/Down
  const rtl = getComputedStyle(bar).direction === "rtl";
  const steps = vertical
    ? { ArrowDown: 1, ArrowUp: -1 }
    : { ArrowRight: rtl ? -1 : 1, ArrowLeft: rtl ? 1 : -1 };
  // keydown: look up steps[key] (or Home/End), move focus, preventDefault only for handled keys
}
```

### Fallbacks & browser support for Interest invokers

Browser support for Interest invokers: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 149 (Jun 2026) and Edge 149 (Jun 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.

Do not load an `interestfor` polyfill here: when native interest invokers or anchor positioning are missing, the upgrade
script is skipped and buttons keep their baseline `title` tooltip.

### Fallbacks & browser support for Popover

Baseline status for Popover: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-01-27.
Supported by: Chrome 116 (Aug 2023), Edge 116 (Aug 2023), Firefox 125 (Apr 2024), Safari 17 (Sep 2023), and Safari iOS
18.3 (Jan 2025).

The Popover API is mostly **progressive enhancement**, but its defining behaviors — top-layer promotion, light-dismiss,
and `popovertarget` invocation — have no CSS-only equivalent. Older browsers need a polyfill, or a manual fallback if
you would rather not ship one.

**Polyfill:** To support the `popover` attribute in older browsers, conditionally load [
`@oddbird/popover-polyfill`](https://github.com/oddbird/popover-polyfill). **MANDATORY:** Feature detect by checking for
the `popover` property on `HTMLElement.prototype`, and load the polyfill **only** when native support is missing — do
NOT load it unconditionally.

With a bundler or import map:

```js
// MANDATORY: Feature detect 'popover' on HTMLElement.prototype.
if (!Object.hasOwn(HTMLElement.prototype, "popover")) {
  import("@oddbird/popover-polyfill");
}
```

If not using a package manager, import from a CDN, e.g.
`"https://unpkg.com/@oddbird/popover-polyfill@latest/dist/popover.min.js"`.

Caveats when using the polyfill:

- Do NOT use the `popover` IDL attribute for any code that may run before the polyfill is fully loaded. It will not be
  mirrored as an attribute, the popover will not be picked up by the polyfill, and the property will be shadowing the
  accessor the polyfill adds forever. Use `setAttribute()`/`removeAttribute()` instead.
- **Styling caveat:** The polyfill cannot define the real `:popover-open` pseudo-class, so it applies a
  `.\:popover-open` class instead. **MANDATORY:** Combine the two with `:is()` or `:where()`, otherwise browsers that
  lack `:popover-open` discard the entire rule:

```css
[popover]:is(:popover-open, .\:popover-open) {
  display: block;
}
```

### Fallbacks & browser support for `popover="hint"`

Browser support for popover="hint": Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 151 (Jul 2026), Edge 151 (Jul 2026), and Firefox 153 (Jul 2026).
Unsupported in: Safari.

The popover polyfill does not add `popover="hint"`. Where `popover` exists without `hint`, two tooltips can stay open at
once (for example one opened by focus and one by hover). Treat this as graceful degradation: the upgrade only runs where
interest invokers are supported, and other browsers keep the native `title` tooltip.

### Fallbacks & browser support for Clipboard API

Baseline status for the api.Clipboard.writeText capability: Widely available. It's been Baseline since 2020-03-24.
Supported by: Chrome 66 (Apr 2018), Edge 79 (Jan 2020), Firefox 63 (Oct 2018), Safari 13.1 (Mar 2020), and Safari iOS
13.4 (Mar 2020).

Where the Clipboard API is unavailable, `navigator.clipboard` is undefined and the call throws, so the `catch` branch in
the feedback snippet reports the failure.

### Fallbacks & browser support for Anchor positioning

Browser support for Anchor positioning: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 157 (Nov 2026), Edge 157 (Nov 2026), and Safari 27 (Sep 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox.

Without anchor positioning, a popover is placed by the UA at the center of the viewport. Tooltips need no fallback: the
`title` upgrade above is skipped without anchor positioning. For the overflow menu, position it from script so it stays
attached to its trigger. Keep the CSS inside `@supports not (position-area: block-end)` so supporting browsers are
unaffected.

```css
@supports not (position-area: block-end) {
  #more-menu {
    /* Viewport coordinates are set from script when the menu opens */
    position: fixed;
    inset: auto;
    margin: 0;
  }
}
```

```js
// Only needed without anchor positioning; place the menu below its trigger
// and flip above it when it would overflow the viewport.
menu.addEventListener("toggle", ({ newState }) => {
  if (newState !== "open" || CSS.supports("position-area", "block-end")) return;
  const t = more.getBoundingClientRect();
  const m = menu.getBoundingClientRect();
  const below = t.bottom + m.height <= innerHeight;
  menu.style.top = `${below ? t.bottom : t.top - m.height}px`;
  // Right-align with the trigger, clamped to the viewport
  menu.style.left = `${Math.max(0, Math.min(t.right - m.width, innerWidth - m.width))}px`;
});
```

================================================
# Maximize content and reduce noise

Users come for the content. Keep the page frame small, move it out of the way while users read, and show secondary
content only when asked.

## Implementation

### Don't block or interrupt the user

- DO NOT open newsletter modals, interstitials, or full-screen promos when the page loads. Where possible, remove
  banners and unrelated content that compete with the main content.
- If a notice is legally required (for example, cookie consent), show it as a small, non-modal bar that covers well
  under 15% of the viewport, with a visible dismiss button labeled with text such as "Accept" or "Close".
- Match the interruption to the stakes: use a blocking dialog only for consequential actions, such as deleting an
  account, paying, or editing personal data. Use non-blocking messages for everything else.
- Don't move content while the user reads. Reserve space for images, ads, and embeds before they load (for example, with
  `width` and `height` attributes), don't insert content above what's on screen, and don't open popovers the user didn't
  ask for.

### Keep persistent bars compact

Keep every fixed or sticky bar under 12% of the viewport height. Use a single row, and don't stack several sticky bars (
announcement, header, and sub-navigation). Move extra items into a popover menu or drawer instead (see below).

### Hide persistent bars while the user scrolls down

Hide the top bar (the site header or navigation bar) while the user scrolls down and bring it back as soon as they
scroll up, so it's out of the way while reading but one flick away. A scroll-state container query tracks the scroll
direction in CSS, with no script. Hide bottom bars, such as a tab bar, the same way, sliding them down instead of up.

```css
/* The root scroller remembers the direction of the most recent scroll. */
html {
  container-type: scroll-state;
}
.top-bar {
  position: sticky;
  top: 0;
  z-index: 1; /* Example value: keeps positioned content from painting over the bar. */
}
/* Scrolling down: move the bar out of view. transform doesn't change layout, so content doesn't jump.
   (scrollable: top) shows the bar at the very top, even after jumps such as the Home key, which don't update "scrolled". */
@container scroll-state((scrolled: bottom) and (scrollable: top)) {
  .top-bar {
    transform: translateY(-100%);
  }
}
/* Keep the bar visible while it contains keyboard focus. */
.top-bar:focus-within {
  transform: none;
}
/* Example value: at least the bar's height, so in-page link targets don't land under the bar. */
:target {
  scroll-margin-top: 4rem;
}
```

Alternatively, shrink the bar to under 80% of its height as the user scrolls; see `shrinking-header-on-scroll` (via
`npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "shrinking-header-on-scroll"`).

### Put secondary UI in popovers and drawers

Use the `popover` attribute for menus, overflow actions, tooltips, hover cards, and onboarding tips instead of permanent
toolbars or custom JavaScript overlays. A button with `popovertarget` opens and closes the popover on click, <kbd>
Enter</kbd>, or <kbd>Space</kbd>. The default `popover="auto"` also closes it on <kbd>Esc</kbd> or a click outside.

```html
<button popovertarget="more-links">More</button>
<!-- Rendered in the top layer, so no z-index management is needed. -->
<nav id="more-links" popover aria-label="More links">
  <a href="/about">About</a>
  <a href="/contact">Contact</a>
</nav>
```

- Popovers open in the center of the screen by default. To place a popover next to its button, see
  `viewport-aware-dropdowns` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "viewport-aware-dropdowns"`).
- Buttons can also open popovers with `commandfor` and `command="toggle-popover"`; see
  `declarative-dialog-popover-control` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "declarative-dialog-popover-control"`).
- For larger sets of options, use an off-canvas drawer: a `popover` panel pinned to one side of the screen that slides
  in over the page (see `navigation-drawer` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "navigation-drawer"`) for
  swipe-to-close and animation). Show rows of related items as a horizontally scrolling carousel instead of a long
  stacked list.

### Collapse secondary content with `details`

Put long or rarely needed content (specs, FAQs, fine print) in a `details` element. It starts closed, and its `summary`
works with the keyboard and screen readers without JavaScript.

```html
<details>
  <summary>Shipping and returns</summary>
  <p>Free returns within 30 days.</p>
</details>
```

## Fallback strategies

### Scroll-state queries

Browser support for Container scroll-state queries: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 144 (Jan 2026) and Edge 144 (Jan 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.

Without scroll-state queries, the bar never hides, but it stays compact and usable. If your Baseline target includes
those browsers, add a small script so the bar hides there too. Browsers that support other scroll-state queries but not
`scrolled` also keep the bar visible.

```css
/* Don't hide the bar while it contains keyboard focus. */
.top-bar.is-hidden:not(:focus-within) {
  transform: translateY(-100%);
}
```

```js
// Runs only where scroll-state queries aren't supported. Run it after .top-bar is parsed (for example, in a module script).
if (!CSS.supports('container-type', 'scroll-state')) {
  const bar = document.querySelector('.top-bar');
  let lastY = scrollY;
  addEventListener('scroll', () => {
    // Clamp so rubber-band overscroll at the top or bottom doesn't flip the scroll direction.
    const y = Math.max(0, Math.min(scrollY, document.documentElement.scrollHeight - innerHeight));
    if (y === lastY) return;
    // Hide only after scrolling down past the bar's own height, so it doesn't flicker near the top.
    bar?.classList.toggle('is-hidden', y > lastY && y > bar.offsetHeight);
    lastY = y;
  }, { passive: true });
}
```

### Fallbacks & browser support for Popover

Baseline status for Popover: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-01-27.
Supported by: Chrome 116 (Aug 2023), Edge 116 (Aug 2023), Firefox 125 (Apr 2024), Safari 17 (Sep 2023), and Safari iOS
18.3 (Jan 2025).

The Popover API is mostly **progressive enhancement**, but its defining behaviors — top-layer promotion, light-dismiss,
and `popovertarget` invocation — have no CSS-only equivalent. Older browsers need a polyfill, or a manual fallback if
you would rather not ship one.

**Polyfill:** To support the `popover` attribute in older browsers, conditionally load [
`@oddbird/popover-polyfill`](https://github.com/oddbird/popover-polyfill). **MANDATORY:** Feature detect by checking for
the `popover` property on `HTMLElement.prototype`, and load the polyfill **only** when native support is missing — do
NOT load it unconditionally.

With a bundler or import map:

```js
// MANDATORY: Feature detect 'popover' on HTMLElement.prototype.
if (!Object.hasOwn(HTMLElement.prototype, "popover")) {
  import("@oddbird/popover-polyfill");
}
```

If not using a package manager, import from a CDN, e.g.
`"https://unpkg.com/@oddbird/popover-polyfill@latest/dist/popover.min.js"`.

Caveats when using the polyfill:

- Do NOT use the `popover` IDL attribute for any code that may run before the polyfill is fully loaded. It will not be
  mirrored as an attribute, the popover will not be picked up by the polyfill, and the property will be shadowing the
  accessor the polyfill adds forever. Use `setAttribute()`/`removeAttribute()` instead.
- **Styling caveat:** The polyfill cannot define the real `:popover-open` pseudo-class, so it applies a
  `.\:popover-open` class instead. **MANDATORY:** Combine the two with `:is()` or `:where()`, otherwise browsers that
  lack `:popover-open` discard the entire rule:

```css
[popover]:is(:popover-open, .\:popover-open) {
  display: block;
}
```

### Invoker commands

Baseline status for Invoker commands: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-12-12.
Supported by: Chrome 135 (Apr 2025), Edge 135 (Apr 2025), Firefox 144 (Oct 2025), and Safari 26.2 (Dec 2025).

Browsers without invoker commands ignore `commandfor`, so the button does nothing there. Prefer `popovertarget`, which
works wherever popovers do. If you use `commandfor`, dynamically import `invokers-polyfill` (through your bundler, or
from a CDN if you don't use one) only when `'commandForElement' in HTMLButtonElement.prototype` is false.

# Adapt to the form factor

The same interface runs on phones, laptops, and foldables, with touch, mouse, or keyboard. Size controls for the input,
let components adapt to their container, and keep text and controls clear of system UI.

For page-level responsive techniques (dynamic viewport units, aspect ratios, and fluid type), see `responsive-design` (
via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "responsive-design"`).

## Implementation

### Size targets for the input method

Make every control at least 24×24 CSS pixels (WCAG 2.5.8), and at least 44×44 on touch screens, where a fingertip is
less precise than a mouse pointer (WCAG 2.5.5). Links inside sentences are exempt. For checkboxes and radios, wrap the
input in its `<label>` and size the label. To keep small icons visually compact, extend their hit area with a
pseudo-element. Leave enough space around controls so extended hit areas do not overlap each other or reach past the
edge of the screen.

```css
:root { --target-size: 24px; }
@media (pointer: coarse) {
  :root { --target-size: 44px; }
}
:where(button, select, textarea, input:not([type="checkbox"], [type="radio"]), [role="button"], nav a, label:has(input[type="checkbox"], input[type="radio"])) {
  min-block-size: var(--target-size);
  min-inline-size: var(--target-size);
}
:where([role="button"], nav a, label:has(input[type="checkbox"], input[type="radio"])) { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; }
.icon-button { position: relative; }
.icon-button::after {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  inset: -10px;
}
```

### Let components respond to their container

Use container queries instead of viewport-width media queries for component layout, so a component adapts wherever it is
placed. Keep media queries for what a container can't know: the input device (such as `pointer: coarse` for touch
screens) and user settings (such as `prefers-color-scheme`).

```css
.product-list {
  /* Name containers so queries inside nested containers target the right ancestor. */
  container: products / inline-size;
}
/* A container query styles the container's descendants, never the container itself. */
@container products (inline-size > 40rem) {
  .product-card { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 10rem 1fr; }
}
```

DO NOT query `height` or `block-size` on an `inline-size` container: it measures only width. Use `container-type: size`
only on a container with a definite height.

- For more container query patterns, such as card layouts, see `size-aware-styling` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "size-aware-styling"`).
- To change a component's layout based on what child elements it contains (for example, switching a card to a
  side-by-side layout when it includes an image), see `content-based-styling` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "content-based-styling"`).

### Keep UI clear of notches and system bars

When drawing edge to edge with
`<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover">`, pad fixed and edge-anchored
UI by the safe-area insets.

```css
.bottom-bar {
  position: fixed;
  left: 0;
  right: 0;
  bottom: 0;
  padding-bottom: max(0.75rem, env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px));
  padding-left: max(0.75rem, env(safe-area-inset-left, 0px));
  padding-right: max(0.75rem, env(safe-area-inset-right, 0px));
}
```

Pad UI anchored to the top edge the same way with `safe-area-inset-top`.

Fixed bars cover the content that scrolls under them, so a focused element can end up hidden behind one. Set
`scroll-padding-bottom` (or `scroll-padding-top` for a top bar) on the scroll container to at least the bar's height,
including its safe-area padding, so the browser scrolls focused elements clear of the bar (WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not
Obscured (Minimum) requires a focused element to be at least partly visible).

```css
html {
  scroll-padding-bottom: calc(3.5rem + env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px));
}
```

### Balance headings and prettify body text

Apply `text-wrap: balance` to short headings (`h1, h2, h3`) and `text-wrap: pretty` to body text (`p, li`) to prevent
typographic orphans. For full text-wrapping rules, see `improve-text-layout-and-legibility` (via
`npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "improve-text-layout-and-legibility"`). DO NOT apply either property to `*`:
both incur layout overhead, and `balance` only helps short blocks of text.

### Label icon-only buttons

Give every icon-only button an accessible name using `aria-label`, an `<img alt>`, or visually hidden text, and hide
decorative icons with `aria-hidden="true"`. For more accessible naming patterns, see `accessibility` (via
`npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "accessibility"`).

### Keep content inside its box

Ensure text and controls are never clipped, squished to zero dimensions, or overflowing at any viewport width down to
320 CSS pixels (WCAG 1.4.10). Content that needs a two-dimensional layout to be understood, such as data tables, maps,
and diagrams, may scroll horizontally inside its own container while the page doesn't. Make that container
keyboard-scrollable with `tabindex="0"`, and give it `role="region"` and an accessible name. For making data tables
adapt to smaller viewports, see `responsive-table` (via
`npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "responsive-table"`).

```css
/* Media never overflows its column. */
img, video { max-inline-size: 100%; block-size: auto; }
/* Long words and URLs wrap instead of widening the page. */
body { overflow-wrap: break-word; }
/* Long URLs and code also wrap inside flex items and table cells. */
:where(a, code) { overflow-wrap: anywhere; }
/* Flex and grid items don't shrink below their content by default. Let non-control items shrink so controls keep their minimum size. */
:where(.toolbar > :not(button, input, select, textarea, a, [role="button"], label)) { min-inline-size: 0; }
.toolbar { display: flex; }
/* The target-size minimum lets controls in a crowded row shrink below their text, so let nav bars and toolbars that are already rows wrap. */
:where(nav, nav ul, .toolbar) { flex-wrap: wrap; }
```

- Use `min-block-size` instead of a fixed `height` on anything that contains text.
- Use `overflow-wrap: break-word` for text, and `anywhere` only on elements that hold long unbroken strings, such as
  links and code: `anywhere` also lets flex items and table cells shrink below their longest word, which breaks ordinary
  words mid-word.
- DO NOT truncate headings with `text-overflow: ellipsis`, and do not clip controls with `overflow: hidden` on their
  parents.
- DO NOT set `overflow-x: hidden` or `clip` on `html` or `body` to stop the page scrolling sideways: content past the
  edge is cut off and users can't scroll to it. Make the element that is too wide fit instead.
- To allow text and layouts to scale with operating system accessibility settings, see `respect-os-text-scale` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "respect-os-text-scale"`). To size form controls dynamically as users
  type, see `form-fields-automatically-fit-contents` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "form-fields-automatically-fit-contents"`).

## Fallback strategies

### Text wrapping

Baseline status for text-wrap: balance: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2024-05-13.
Supported by: Chrome 114 (May 2023), Edge 114 (Jun 2023), Firefox 121 (Dec 2023), and Safari 17.5 (May 2024).

Browser support for text-wrap: pretty: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 117 (Sep 2023), Edge 117 (Sep 2023), and Safari 26 (Sep 2025).
Unsupported in: Firefox.

Browsers without support ignore `text-wrap: balance` and `text-wrap: pretty` and wrap text normally. No fallback is
needed.

================================================
# Implement natural interactions

Interfaces feel natural when every input gets an immediate response, motion behaves like a physical object, content
follows the user's finger, and nothing depends on a mouse.

## Implementation

### Give every control hover, press, and focus feedback

```css
:where(button) {
  /* example durations */
  transition: box-shadow 150ms ease-out, scale 150ms ease-out;
}
button:hover { box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.2); }
a:hover { text-decoration-thickness: 2px; }
button:active { scale: 0.97; } /* example value */

:where(a, button, input, select, textarea, summary, [tabindex]):focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid CanvasText;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}
```

- Use `:focus-visible` so keyboard users always see a clear focus ring, without showing it on mouse clicks.
- DO NOT remove focus outlines (`outline: none` or `outline: 0`) without providing an equally visible replacement with
  at least a 3:1 contrast ratio against the page (WCAG 1.4.11). `CanvasText` is the text color for the page's
  `color-scheme`, so it contrasts with the default page background in light mode, in dark mode (with
  `color-scheme: light dark`), and in forced colors. If you set your own page background, pick a ring color with 3:1
  against it. `currentColor` fails when a button's text color matches the page.
- Make each interaction state look different, including combinations: hover, press, pressing while hovering, and
  keyboard focus. In the example, hover adds a shadow, press a scale, and focus an outline, so any combination shows
  each of its parts.

### Open disclosures from their trigger

Popovers and dropdowns should visibly open from the control that triggered them: scale out from the corner touching the
trigger, or slide out from its side. Menus and hovercards have their own open motion; follow `menu` (via
`npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "menu"`) and `hovercard` (via
`npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "hovercard"`). For other popovers, place the popover next to its trigger and
align `transform-origin` with the corner that touches it. To flip dropdowns at viewport edges, see
`viewport-aware-dropdowns` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "viewport-aware-dropdowns"`).

```css
.dropdown {
  /* popovertarget makes the trigger the popover's anchor. */
  position-area: bottom span-right;
  inset: auto;
  margin: 0;
  /* The corner touching the trigger; change it whenever the placement changes. */
  transform-origin: top left;
}
/* example durations */
.dropdown:is(:popover-open, .\:popover-open) { animation: fade-in 150ms ease-out both; }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .dropdown:is(:popover-open, .\:popover-open) {
    /* optional example spring curve, written inline */
    animation: grow 300ms linear(0, 0.45 15%, 1.08 35%, 0.97 55%, 1.01 75%, 1) both, fade-in 150ms ease-out both;
  }
}
@keyframes grow { from { scale: 0.9; } }
@keyframes fade-in { from { opacity: 0; } }
```

- Keep animations on the compositor (`transform`, its individual properties, and `opacity`) and respect reduced-motion
  preferences; see `motion` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "motion"`). This example animates the
  opening only; for exit transitions, see `animate-to-from-top-layer` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "animate-to-from-top-layer"`).
- Trigger popovers declaratively using `<button popovertarget="dropdown-id">` (see
  `declarative-dialog-popover-control` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "declarative-dialog-popover-control"`)) to get native click, keyboard, and
  dismiss behavior without JavaScript.
- For a springy open, use a `linear()` curve that overshoots slightly before settling (an output value above 1); see
  `physics-based-easing` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "physics-based-easing"`).

### Make horizontal scrollers swipeable

Any horizontally scrollable row of items, such as a carousel, gallery, or row of chips, should scroll natively and snap
to its items.

```css
.scroller {
  display: flex;
  gap: 1rem;
  overflow-x: auto;
  scroll-snap-type: x mandatory;
}
.scroller > * {
  flex: 0 0 85%; /* example item width */
  scroll-snap-align: start;
}
```

- Native overflow scrolling gives swiping its physics and momentum, and snapping makes each swipe come to rest on an
  item, with no touch listeners.
- If none of the scroller's items contains a link, button, or other focusable element, make the scroller itself
  focusable and labeled (`<div class="scroller" role="region" aria-label="Featured items" tabindex="0">`), so keyboard
  users can reach it and scroll it with the arrow keys. When items are focusable, tabbing to them already scrolls them
  into view.
- To highlight the item that snaps into place, see `carousel-snap-highlights` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "carousel-snap-highlights"`). To swipe a list item aside to reveal
  actions, see `swipe-to-reveal` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "swipe-to-reveal"`). For side menus
  that close when swiped away, see `navigation-drawer` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "navigation-drawer"`).
- For carousel controls such as previous and next buttons and scroll markers, see `carousel` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "carousel"`).

### Add motion blur to large, fast movements (optional)

For large, rapid translations (such as a full-screen sheet sliding into view), a subtle, temporary blur softens the
movement. `filter` doesn't run only on the compositor, so keep blur to large, brief movements, skip it for small
controls or slow transitions, and always guard it with a reduced-motion media query.

```css
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .sheet.is-open { animation: sheet-in 300ms ease-out both; } /* example duration */
}
@keyframes sheet-in {
  from { translate: 0 100%; filter: blur(6px); } /* example blur radius */
}
```

### Make every action reachable without a mouse

- Use `<button>` for actions and `<a>` with an `href` for navigation. Both receive keyboard focus and activate on <kbd>
  Enter</kbd>; buttons also activate on <kbd>Space</kbd>.
- Menus and dropdowns may open on hover, but never only on hover: they also open on click, tap, and keyboard activation,
  stay open while the pointer moves onto them, and close with <kbd>Esc</kbd> (WCAG 2.1.1, 1.4.13).
- Controls or details revealed in place on hover, such as card actions, must also appear on keyboard focus and be
  visible by default on devices without hover:

```css
.card .actions {
  opacity: 0;

  .card:hover &,
  .card:focus-within & { opacity: 1; }

  @media (hover: none) { opacity: 1; }
}
```

For tooltips and previews triggered on hover, focus, or long-press, see `interest-triggered-tooltips` (via
`npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "interest-triggered-tooltips"`) and `interest-triggered-action-previews` (
via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "interest-triggered-action-previews"`).

## Fallback strategies

### Fallbacks & browser support for Popover

Baseline status for Popover: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-01-27.
Supported by: Chrome 116 (Aug 2023), Edge 116 (Aug 2023), Firefox 125 (Apr 2024), Safari 17 (Sep 2023), and Safari iOS
18.3 (Jan 2025).

The Popover API is mostly **progressive enhancement**, but its defining behaviors — top-layer promotion, light-dismiss,
and `popovertarget` invocation — have no CSS-only equivalent. Older browsers need a polyfill, or a manual fallback if
you would rather not ship one.

**Polyfill:** To support the `popover` attribute in older browsers, conditionally load [
`@oddbird/popover-polyfill`](https://github.com/oddbird/popover-polyfill). **MANDATORY:** Feature detect by checking for
the `popover` property on `HTMLElement.prototype`, and load the polyfill **only** when native support is missing — do
NOT load it unconditionally.

With a bundler or import map:

```js
// MANDATORY: Feature detect 'popover' on HTMLElement.prototype.
if (!Object.hasOwn(HTMLElement.prototype, "popover")) {
  import("@oddbird/popover-polyfill");
}
```

If not using a package manager, import from a CDN, e.g.
`"https://unpkg.com/@oddbird/popover-polyfill@latest/dist/popover.min.js"`.

Caveats when using the polyfill:

- Do NOT use the `popover` IDL attribute for any code that may run before the polyfill is fully loaded. It will not be
  mirrored as an attribute, the popover will not be picked up by the polyfill, and the property will be shadowing the
  accessor the polyfill adds forever. Use `setAttribute()`/`removeAttribute()` instead.
- **Styling caveat:** The polyfill cannot define the real `:popover-open` pseudo-class, so it applies a
  `.\:popover-open` class instead. **MANDATORY:** Combine the two with `:is()` or `:where()`, otherwise browsers that
  lack `:popover-open` discard the entire rule:

```css
[popover]:is(:popover-open, .\:popover-open) {
  display: block;
}
```

### Anchor positioning

Baseline status for the html.elements.button.popovertarget.implicit_anchor_reference capability: Newly available. It's
been Baseline since 2026-01-13.
Supported by: Chrome 133 (Feb 2025), Edge 133 (Feb 2025), Firefox 147 (Jan 2026), and Safari 26 (Sep 2025).

Without support, `inset: auto` leaves the popover at the top-left corner of the viewport. When
`CSS.supports('position-area: bottom')` is false, set the popover's `top` and `left` from the trigger's
`getBoundingClientRect()` in a `beforetoggle` event listener.

### Linear easing

Baseline status for linear() easing: Widely available. It's been Baseline since 2023-12-11.
Supported by: Chrome 113 (May 2023), Edge 113 (May 2023), Firefox 112 (Apr 2023), and Safari 17.2 (Dec 2023).

Browsers without `linear()` drop the declaration that uses it, so precede it with one that uses a keyword such as
`ease-out`, as the fade-in above does. Write `linear()` inline, not through a custom property, or the earlier
declaration is discarded too.

# Adapt scrollbar to high-contrast preferences

Users who enable high-contrast modes in their operating system or browser expect UI elements (like scrollbars) to be
extremely legible, often relying on stark foreground-background separation rather than subtle grays or theme colors.

This guide provides instructions on how to use the `@media (prefers-contrast: more)` CSS media feature to enforce
high-contrast scrollbar styling.

## Enhance Legibility

When customizing scrollbars with `scrollbar-color` or custom variables, you can provide an explicit override for
high-contrast modes. This is especially helpful if your primary application theme uses lower-contrast scrollbars for
aesthetic reasons, although the default thumb still needs at least 3:1 contrast against the track (WCAG 1.4.11 Non-text
Contrast).

Use an `@media (prefers-contrast: more)` block to define dark, distinct colors for the thumb and track.

```css
/* Define default standard colors as variables */
.scroller {
  --scrollbar-thumb: #707070;
  --scrollbar-track: #f1f1f1;

  scrollbar-color: var(--scrollbar-thumb) var(--scrollbar-track);
}

/* Provide clear, high-contrast overrides */
@media (prefers-contrast: more) {
  .scroller {
    /* Use extremely distinct colors like solid black against white */
    --scrollbar-thumb: #000000;
    --scrollbar-track: #ffffff;
  }
}
```

### Issues to be aware of when using scrollbar-color

- Do NOT animate or transition `scrollbar-color`. A [WebKit bug](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=311752) causes
  the scrollbar to flicker every time `scrollbar-color` changes.
- Any computed `scrollbar-width` other than `auto` (`thin` or `none`) or computed `scrollbar-color` other than `auto` (
  including an inherited `scrollbar-color`) disables legacy `::-webkit-scrollbar` pseudo-elements on that element.
- With overlay scrollbars (such as the macOS default), `scrollbar-color` styles the thumb while scrolling, whereas the
  track may remain transparent. Ensure the thumb color has sufficient contrast against both the track color and the
  scrollable container's background rather than relying on the track to frame the thumb.

## Fallbacks & Browser Support

### Fallbacks & browser support for scrollbar-color

Baseline status for scrollbar-color: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-12-12.
Supported by: Chrome 121 (Jan 2024), Edge 121 (Jan 2024), Firefox 64 (Dec 2018), and Safari 26.2 (Dec 2025).

This feature is progressive enhancement and does not always require fallbacks.

If the styling is important and the user's Baseline target is "Baseline Widely Available" or earlier, you SHOULD include
the non-standard `::-webkit-scrollbar` pseudo-elements as fallbacks.

Place legacy fallbacks after the base rule inside an `@supports not (scrollbar-color: auto)` block to prevent conflicts
between standard properties and legacy WebKit selectors in browsers that support both natively. If you also set
`scrollbar-width: thin` on the scrollable container, reset `scrollbar-width: auto` on the same selector inside
`@supports not (scrollbar-color: auto)` so browsers that support `scrollbar-width` without `scrollbar-color` do not
suppress `::-webkit-scrollbar` styling.

If you are using custom properties to define colors, these will cascade to the legacy WebKit selectors automatically.
You do NOT need to duplicate them.

```css
/* Legacy fallback for WebKit/Blink browsers */
@supports not (scrollbar-color: auto) {
  .scroller {
    /* Reset scrollbar-width: thin (if set) so it does not disable
       ::-webkit-scrollbar in browsers without scrollbar-color */
    scrollbar-width: auto;
  }

  .scroller::-webkit-scrollbar {
    /* Must define a base size (e.g., 8px for thin or 12px for default) for custom colors to render in WebKit */
    width: 12px;
    height: 12px;
  }

  .scroller::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb {
    background: var(--scrollbar-thumb);
  }

  .scroller::-webkit-scrollbar-track {
    background: var(--scrollbar-track);
  }
}
```

# Apply WebGL shaders to HTML content

WebGL shaders provide powerful GPU-accelerated visual effects, enabling advanced capabilities like dynamic ripple
distortions, lighting models, color grading, and custom vertex transformations. The HTML-in-Canvas API allows developers
to apply WebGL textures to HTML content. This enables applying high-performance fragment and vertex shaders natively to
fully interactive UI components, such as buttons, input fields, and rich text, while retaining native accessibility,
text selection, and DOM event handling.

## How to implement

1. Check if HTML-in-Canvas is supported in the browser:

```js
if ('content' in HTMLCanvasElement.prototype) {
  // Use HTML in Canvas API
} else {
  // Use fallback strategy
}
```

2. Add the `content="drawable"` attribute to the `<canvas>` HTML element.
3. Place your HTML content inside the `<canvas>` element, and add the `drawable` attribute to every element that you
   draw. An element with `drawable` captures its subtree, except nested descendants that are also `drawable`.

```html
<canvas id="canvas" content="drawable">
  <div id="html-content" drawable></div>
</canvas>
```

4. Scale your canvas grid to match the device scale factor to prevent blurriness:

```js
const observer = new ResizeObserver(([entry]) => {
  const dpc = entry.devicePixelContentBoxSize;
  canvas.width = dpc
    ? dpc[0].inlineSize
    : Math.round(entry.contentRect.width * window.devicePixelRatio);
  canvas.height = dpc
    ? dpc[0].blockSize
    : Math.round(entry.contentRect.height * window.devicePixelRatio);
});

const supportsDevicePixelContentBox =
  typeof ResizeObserverEntry !== "undefined" &&
  "devicePixelContentBoxSize" in ResizeObserverEntry.prototype;
const options = supportsDevicePixelContentBox
  ? { box: "device-pixel-content-box" }
  : {};
observer.observe(canvas, options);
```

5. Pre-allocate the texture backing first using the `texImage2D` method. The snippets in this guide use a WebGL 2
   context (`canvas.getContext("webgl2")`).

Allocate texture storage first by calling `texImage2D()` with `null` instead of pixel data, which reserves GPU memory of
the given size and format without uploading any pixels. Follow these rules:

- Size the texture from `canvas.captureElementImage(element)`. Its `width` and `height` are in canvas grid (backing
  store) pixels, so round them up with `Math.ceil()`. `captureElementImage()` throws if the element has no paint record
  yet: call `requestPaint()`, and retry on the next `paint` event.
- Allocate level 0 only on the first upload, or when the size changes, because reallocating clears the texture. Use
  mutable storage: immutable `texStorage2D()` storage can't be resized when the element changes size.

```js
// Returns the element's size in canvas grid pixels, or null if the element
// has no paint record yet.
function getElementImageSize(canvas, element) {
  let elementImage;
  try {
    elementImage = canvas.captureElementImage(element);
  } catch (err) {
    canvas.requestPaint(); // No paint record yet: retry on the next paint event.
    return null;
  }
  const width = Math.ceil(elementImage.width);
  const height = Math.ceil(elementImage.height);
  elementImage.close();
  return width > 0 && height > 0 ? { width, height } : null;
}

// Binds the texture, and allocates its storage on the first upload, and when
// the element size changes. `state` stores the allocated size.
function allocateElementTexture(gl, texture, state, width, height) {
  gl.bindTexture(gl.TEXTURE_2D, texture);
  if (state.width === width && state.height === height) return;

  gl.texImage2D(
    gl.TEXTURE_2D,
    0,                // Mipmap level
    gl.RGBA8,         // Internal format: 8 bits per RGBA channel
    width,            // Size in canvas grid pixels
    height,
    0,                // Border: must be 0
    gl.RGBA,          // Format and type that match RGBA8
    gl.UNSIGNED_BYTE,
    null              // null reserves GPU memory without uploading pixels
  );
  gl.texParameteri(gl.TEXTURE_2D, gl.TEXTURE_MIN_FILTER, gl.LINEAR);
  state.width = width;
  state.height = height;
}

const texture = gl.createTexture();
const textureState = { width: 0, height: 0 };
```

6. Render the HTML content to the texture inside a `canvas.onpaint` event handler using the `texElementSubImage2D`
   method. Follow these rules:

- An element can only be uploaded after the canvas has painted it. Upload from the `paint` event, and call
  `canvas.requestPaint()` to request one.
- Pass `{ width, height }` in the config. It makes the copy fill the allocated texture regardless of how the canvas is
  scaled.
- Reallocate the texture if the size changed, as shown in step 5.

```js
// Uploads the element into the texture. Returns false if the element has no
// paint record yet. In that case, it's uploaded on the next paint event.
function uploadElementWebGL(gl, canvas, texture, element, state) {
  const size = getElementImageSize(canvas, element);
  if (!size) return false;
  const { width, height } = size;

  // Bind the texture, and reallocate it if the size changed (step 5).
  allocateElementTexture(gl, texture, state, width, height);
  gl.texElementSubImage2D(gl.TEXTURE_2D, 0, 0, 0, element, { width, height });
  return true;
}

canvas.onpaint = () => {
  try {
    uploadElementWebGL(gl, canvas, texture, uiElement, textureState);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('texElementSubImage2D copy failed:', err);
  }
};
```

When using a `requestAnimationFrame` loop to render the scene, call `canvas.requestPaint()` within the loop to ensure
that the HTML content is rendered to the canvas. `event.changedElements` lists the elements whose rendering changed.
Make sure you only re-upload the texture if there has been an update to the descendant HTML elements:

  ```js
  function render() {
    // Request to update the canvas
    canvas.requestPaint();
    requestAnimationFrame(render);
  }
  requestAnimationFrame(render);

  canvas.onpaint = (event) => {
    if (event.changedElements && event.changedElements.length > 0) {
      // Update the texture with uploadElementWebGL()
    }
    // Render the scene, and sync the element geometry as shown in step 7
  };
  ```

7. Sync the element geometry.

Compute a `DOMMatrix` that maps the element's border box, in CSS pixels, to the canvas, in CSS pixels. The browser needs
to map from the 3D coordinate space into the CSS coordinate space using a viewport transform. To facilitate this, do the
following:

- Normalize the HTML element. HTML elements are sized in pixels (for example, 200px wide). WebGL, however, usually
  treats objects as "unit squares", for example, ranging from -0.5 to 0.5. If you don't normalize, your 200px button
  will look 200 times larger. This step also flips the Y-axis, because in CSS, down is positive, but in WebGL, up is
  positive.
- Convert the WebGL MVP Matrix to a DOM Matrix.
- Map to the canvas viewport. This step is the "re-scaling" phase: it stretches that unit-space math back out to match
  the CSS pixel dimensions of your `<canvas>` element on the screen, and flips the Y-axis back.
- Calculate the final transform. Multiply the matrices in order: Viewport * MVP * Normalization. Combining them into one
  final transform produces a "map" that tells the browser exactly where that HTML element should sit to align with the
  3D drawing. The browser performs the perspective divide.

  ```js
  // Maps the element's border box (CSS pixels) to the canvas (CSS pixels), for a
  // quad that spans -0.5 to 0.5 in model space and is drawn with the `mvp` matrix.
  function computeCanvasTransform(canvas, element, mvp) {
    const width = element.offsetWidth;
    const height = element.offsetHeight;

    // 1. Normalize the HTML element (CSS pixels -> WebGL Model Space)
    const toGLModel = new DOMMatrix()
      // Scale pixels to 1 unit, flip Y (as in CSS it points down, and in WebGL it points up)
      .scale(1 / width, -1 / height, 1 / height)
      // Center the origin: (0,0) becomes (-width/2, -height/2) before scaling
      .translate(-width / 2, -height / 2);

    // 2. Convert WebGL MVP Matrix to DOM Matrix
    const mvpDOM = new DOMMatrix(Array.from(mvp));

    // 3. Map to the canvas viewport, in CSS pixels
    const clipToCanvasViewport = new DOMMatrix()
      // Move center (0,0) to center of canvas
      .translate(canvas.clientWidth / 2, canvas.clientHeight / 2)
      // Scale normalized clip (-1..1) to viewport size, and flip Y back
      .scale(canvas.clientWidth / 2, -canvas.clientHeight / 2, canvas.clientHeight / 2);

    // 4. Multiply: (Clip -> Pixels) * (MVP) * (pixels -> unit square)
    return clipToCanvasViewport.multiply(mvpDOM).multiply(toGLModel);
  }
  ```

Then pass the transform to `canvas.updateElementGeometry()` as `canvasTransform`. This moves the HTML element to sit
directly on top of its rendered pixels. This ensures that when a user clicks a button or selects text, they are actually
hitting the real HTML element. The browser also uses the transform for the element's accessibility bounds, for example,
for screen reader focus rings:

  ```js
  canvas.updateElementGeometry(targetHTMLElement, {
    canvasTransform: computeCanvasTransform(canvas, targetHTMLElement, htmlElementMVP),
  });
  ```

Use these options to control hit testing:

- Each `updateElementGeometry()` call moves the element to the top of the hit-testing order. Pass
  `{ preserveHitTestOrder: true }` to keep its position.
- Call `canvas.clearElementGeometry(element)` to remove an element from hit testing, for example, when you hide it.
- Pass `{ canvasClip }`, a `DOMRectInit` in the coordinate space of `canvasTransform`, to limit the hit-testable area,
  for example, when only part of the element is drawn.

## Example code

```html
<canvas id="canvas" content="drawable" style="width: 400px; height: 400px;">
  <div id="ui-element" drawable>
    <p>WebGL UI Element</p>
    <button>Action</button>
  </div>
</canvas>

<script>
  const canvas = document.getElementById("canvas");
  const gl = canvas.getContext("webgl2");
  const uiElement = document.getElementById("ui-element");

  // getElementImageSize() and allocateElementTexture() are defined in step 5.
  // uploadElementWebGL() is defined in step 6.
  // computeCanvasTransform() is defined in step 7.

  // Setup WebGL texture...
  const texture = gl.createTexture();
  gl.bindTexture(gl.TEXTURE_2D, texture);
  const textureState = { width: 0, height: 0 };

  canvas.onpaint = () => {
    // 1. Update texture with HTML content
    try {
      uploadElementWebGL(gl, canvas, texture, uiElement, textureState);
    } catch (err) {
      console.error('texElementSubImage2D copy failed:', err);
    }

    // ... Render your 3D scene here, calculating htmlElementMVP matrix ...

    // 2. Sync DOM position, hit testing, and accessibility bounds with 3D scene
    canvas.updateElementGeometry(uiElement, {
      canvasTransform: computeCanvasTransform(canvas, uiElement, htmlElementMVP),
    });
  };
</script>
```

## Best Practices

- **MANDATORY**: Check browser support for the HTML-in-Canvas API before using it.
- **MANDATORY**: Always add the `content="drawable"` attribute to the `<canvas>` element.
- **MANDATORY**: ALWAYS add the `drawable` attribute to the direct children of the canvas.
- **MANDATORY**: Add the `drawable` attribute to every element that you want to be able to draw independently from its
  parent elements.
- **MANDATORY**: Use an `onpaint` event handler to render the HTML content to the canvas.
- **MANDATORY**: Pre-allocate the texture buffer with `texImage2D()` once (when it's initialized or when the element
  size changes). Reallocate the texture only when the size changes, and set `TEXTURE_MIN_FILTER` to `LINEAR`.
- **MANDATORY**: Use the `texElementSubImage2D` method to render the HTML content to a texture that you pre-allocate
  with `texImage2D()`, sized from `captureElementImage()`.
- **MANDATORY**: Sync the geometry of the HTML element with the rendered content by calling
  `canvas.updateElementGeometry(element, { canvasTransform })`.
- **MANDATORY**: Use `ResizeObserver` to observe the screen size and update the canvas size to match device pixels.
- **DO NOT** embed cross-origin content in a canvas, as it is not supported.
- **DO NOT** initialize `ResizeObserver` within the `onpaint` event handler, as it may lead to memory leaks.

### Fallback strategies

Browser support for HTML-in-canvas: Limited availability.
Supported by: Chrome 157 (Nov 2026) and Edge 157 (Nov 2026).
Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.

The HTML-in-Canvas API is not currently supported in all modern browsers, thus a fallback strategy is typically
required.

However, given the improved performance benefits of this API, HTML-in-Canvas should be used if the browser supports it.

The fallback strategy depends on the use case. For example, for an interactive HTML content in canvas, if HTML-in-Canvas
is not supported, place the HTML content on top of the canvas using CSS.

### HTML-in-Canvas polyfill

Use the following polyfill script to mimic the HTML-in-Canvas API in browsers that do not support it.

1. Install or embed the library:

```
# Install
npm install three-html-render
```

```
# Embed
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three-html-render/dist/polyfill.js"></script>
```

2. Run the `installHtmlInCanvasPolyfill()` method to translate HTML-in-Canvas.

# Theming browser-generated UI

Most browser-generated UI can be customized to some extent using CSS.
Even if it requires modern features, it degrades gracefully in older browsers, and thus often does not require a
polyfill or fallback.

Before re-creating browser UI (form controls, scrollbars, selections, error messages, etc), first verify that:

1. the browser UI cannot be customized enough for your needs, even with modern CSS,
2. the desired customization is sufficiently critical to justify the tradeoffs of re-creating built-in UI — most notably
   losing accessible semantics, keyboard handling, IME, and AT integration that the native UI provides for free.

Example customizations that are possible:

- Use `::selection` to customize highlighted text colors.
- **DON'T** apply `user-select: none` to content text — breaks copy-paste, translation tools, and AT "read from here"
  gestures. Limit it to chrome (drag handles, toolbars, redundant button labels).
- Use `accent-color` to apply the page's accent color to any browser-generated UI.
- Use `color-scheme` to have browser UI adapt to light/dark mode.
- Use `scrollbar-color` to customize scrollbar colors — keep the thumb visibly distinct from the track (contrast ≥3:1)
- **DON'T** use the `scrollbar-width` with any value other than `auto`, unless another accessible option is provided to
  scroll content. Although `scrollbar-width: thin` does provide a thumb, the target size of the thumb will be too small
  for some users to operate.
- Use `:user-invalid` / `:user-valid` for validity styling, **not** `:invalid` / `:valid` — they only match after the
  user has interacted with the field, avoiding the hostile default of flagging required-empty fields as errors on page
  load. Exclude range sliders when targeting `input` broadly (e.g., `input:not(input[type="range"]):user-valid`) so
  adjusting a slider does not apply field validity borders or backgrounds to it.
- Buttons and text fields (including `<textarea>`) can generally be styled as normal elements.
- Use `font-size` to scale and other textual properties to control typography
- Use text color contrast between the foreground and background colors of at least 4.5:1 for regular size text or at
  least `3:1` for large-scale text (18 point or 14 point bold font size).
- Use a contrast between adjacent colors of at least `3:1` for non-text content.

### Styling textual fields (`<input>` & `<textarea>`)

For most styling purposes (e.g. colors, borders, backgrounds, typography, etc) treat these elements as normal text
containers.

- Use `:placeholder-shown` and `::placeholder` to style input placeholders.
- Use `field-sizing: content` to make text fields size to content.
- For `<textarea>` elements, use `resize: vertical` to disable horizontal resizing.
- Do not use `resize: none` on `<textarea>` elements to disable all resizing, without an alternative resizing mechanism,
  such as using `field-sizing: content;` or providing custom resize buttons.

### Multiple choice controls (select, radios, checkboxes)

- To select one among many options presented in a dropdown: Use a `<select>` + `appearance: base-select` +
  `::picker(select)`. For more info see `branded-select-styling` (via
  `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "branded-select-styling"`)
- Selecting one or more among multiple options laid out inline in the page: Use a `<input type=checkbox>` or
  `<input type=radio>` inside a `<label>` for each option. Style via `label:has(:checked)`.
- Style checkboxes, radios and switches via `appearance: none` + generated content (`::before`/`::after`) or background
  images to draw the checked state.

<!-- Customizable select listbox version currently buggy + this has much better browser support -->

### Non-textual `<input>`s (buttons, sliders, file inputs etc.)

- File inputs: Use `::file-selector-button` to style the button.
- Do not use `<input>` with a `type` of `button`, `submit` or `reset`. Use `<button>` instead and style it as a regular
  element.
- Sliders: Use `appearance: none` + thumb pseudo-elements (`::-webkit-slider-thumb`, `::-moz-range-thumb`, etc) and
  track pseudo-elements (`::-webkit-slider-runnable-track`, `::-moz-range-track`, etc) for more granular control.

================================================
# Color

## Accessible color

**Don't use color alone to indicate the presence of a user interface component or its state**: Use iconography and/or
shape to help differentiate. Do not denote success/errors ONLY with color. Use icons or text (WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color).

```html
<!-- Good: Denotes state without colors alone -->
<div class="error-msg">
  <span aria-hidden="true">❌</span>
  <span>The password entered was invalid.</span>
</div>
```

### Contrast

- **Minimum contrast standards**: Maintain 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (at least 24px, or at least
  18.66px bold) or icons (WCAG 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) for text, WCAG 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast for icons).
- **Ensure non-text contrast standards**: Maintain a minimum contrast ratio of 3:1 for user interface component
  boundaries and states (WCAG 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast).
    - This includes visual elements (borders, backgrounds, box-shadows, underlines) that form the boundary or indicate
      the presence of a UI component (e.g., input field borders).
    - This also includes visual elements indicating active states within a component (e.g., checkbox checkmarks, switch
      thumbs or custom focus indicators).
    - **Caveat**: Meeting 3:1 non-text contrast can challenge minimalistic designs. Soft gradients or subtle
      inset/outset shadows can soften visual boundaries while satisfying accessibility requirements.
- **Use `prefers-contrast` only when warranted**: Reach for `@media (prefers-contrast: more)` when the design uses
  low-contrast accents (e.g., subtle borders, muted secondary text) that need to be reinforced; most sites that already
  meet baseline contrast won't need it. It strengthens colors that already meet the minimums above; it doesn't fix a
  default that fails them, because it only reaches users who have turned on the setting.

### Light and dark color schemes

- **Support light and dark color schemes**: Honor `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` and pair it with the
  `color-scheme` CSS property so form controls, scrollbars, and other UA-rendered surfaces match.
  See `dark-mode` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "dark-mode"`) for more details.

### Forced Colors Mode

- **Support Forced Colors Mode**: In Forced Colors Mode (High Contrast on Windows), the browser overrides author colors
  with system keywords, removes `box-shadow`, `text-shadow`, and gradient backgrounds, and may also remove
  `border-image`. `url()` background images can't be relied on either: they may be removed, or kept in their own colors,
  which may not contrast with the system colors. Define system color fallbacks for color tokens using
  `@media (forced-colors: active)`.
- **Use `forced-color-adjust: none` only where color is essential information** (syntax highlighter, color picker
  swatch). **DON'T** use `forced-color-adjust: none` just to preserve aesthetics. Where the element contains text, set
  both its text and background colors to a pair that meets the minimums above, because a transparent background shows
  what is behind it, usually the user's system `Canvas` color, which can be light or dark.
- **Don't rely on `background-image`, `box-shadow`, or `border-image` to convey borders, separators, or state**: In
  forced colors they disappear or keep their own colors, which may not contrast with the system colors (and they often
  disappear in print too). If you must, ensure there's an alternative in forced colors mode, such as `outline` or
  `border` with system color keywords (`CanvasText`, `LinkText`, `ButtonText`, `Highlight`, `GrayText`, etc.).

## Generating tints

Before generating tints dynamically, check if you can use an existing, predefined, design token. This allows much more
designer control and ensures consistency.

If you need to generate lighter or darker colors dynamically:

- **DO NOT** just adjust the lightness channel in `oklch`/`oklab` or `lch`/`lab`, e.g.
  `oklab(from var(--primary) 0.9 a b)`. While that is theoretically the correct way, browsers do not yet implement gamut
  mapping, so the resulting color is unpredictable.
- You can use `color-mix()` to mix with white or black (default to `in oklab` unless you have a reason to use a
  different color space for mixing). This keeps the color safely in gamut, but tends to over-desaturate colors and
  produce washed out tints and shades. Never use `in oklch` when mixing with neutrals. `oklch` confers no benefit in
  that case and due to a Chromium bug (565837690) low-chroma colors (`chroma < 0.02`) are treated as having powerless
  hue that resolves to `0deg` (magenta-red) in Chromium, producing an unintended reddish or pink tint.
- You MAY combine lightness adjustment with any of the other methods (e.g.
  `color-mix(in oklab, oklch(from var(--primary) 0.9 c h), white 30%)`) for a balance between the two, but avoid going
  above 30% for the lightness adjustment.

# Complex Shapes

## Overview

To clip elements to complex, free-form shapes like brush strokes or organic textures, use CSS Masking (`mask-image`).
While `clip-path` is excellent for geometric shapes or vector paths, `mask-image` allows you to use images (like PNGs
with transparency) or SVGs to define the visible area of an element. This approach is more expressive because it
supports semi-transparency, allowing for soft edges and complex textures that are difficult or impossible to achieve
with `clip-path`.

## Implementation

To implement complex shapes using CSS masks:

### Using transparency from an image

You can use the transparency of an image as a mask, with opaque parts visible and transparent parts hidden. This can be
a PNG, SVG, or other image with transparency, or a generated image, like a CSS gradient.

```css
.shaped-element {
  /* MANDATORY: Use vendor prefix for wider support in older browsers */
  -webkit-mask-image: url('mask.svg');
  -webkit-mask-size: cover; /* Scale mask to cover element */
  -webkit-mask-repeat: no-repeat; /* Do not tile the mask */

  /* Standard property for modern browsers */
  mask-image: url('mask.svg');
  mask-size: cover;
  mask-repeat: no-repeat;
}
```

### Using an SVG element in HTML

You can also reference a `<mask>` element defined in an inline SVG in your page's HTML. Use
`maskContentUnits="objectBoundingBox"` to make the mask scale automatically with the size of the element. This tells the
browser to interpret all coordinates inside the mask as fractions from `0` to `1` (like `0.5` for 50%) instead of
absolute pixels.

> **Luminance vs. Alpha Masking**: By default, SVG masks use **luminance** (brightness) to determine opacity, where
> white reveals, black hides, and gray creates semi-transparency. If you want the mask to use the **alpha channel** (
> transparency) of your SVG shapes instead, you can specify `mask-type: alpha;` in your CSS or `mask-type="alpha"`
> directly on the SVG `<mask>` element.

```html
<!-- White areas reveal content, gray creates semi-transparency, black or transparent hides it -->
<svg width="0" height="0">
  <defs>
    <!-- objectBoundingBox scales mask coordinates (0 to 1) with the element's size -->
    <mask id="custom-shape" maskContentUnits="objectBoundingBox">
      <!-- Use white shapes to define fully opaque areas -->
      <circle cx="0.5" cy="0.5" r="0.5" fill="white" />
      <!-- Use gray shapes to define semi-transparent/faded areas -->
      <circle cx="0.5" cy="0.5" r="0.25" fill="gray" />
    </mask>
  </defs>
</svg>

<div class="masked-content">
  <!-- Content to be masked -->
</div>

<style>
.masked-content {
  /* Reference the SVG mask ID */
  -webkit-mask-image: url(#custom-shape);
  mask-image: url(#custom-shape);
}
</style>
```

### Fallback strategies

Baseline status for Masks: Widely available. It's been Baseline since 2023-12-07.
Supported by: Chrome 120 (Dec 2023), Edge 120 (Dec 2023), Firefox 53 (Apr 2017), and Safari 15.4 (Mar 2022).

If a browser does not support `mask-image` or the prefixed version:

- The element will not be clipped and will display as a normal rectangle.
- Ensure the content is still readable and the layout does not break without the mask (progressive enhancement).
- Optionally, use feature detection to provide a simpler fallback shape with `clip-path`.

```css
/* Fallback for browsers that do not support masking */
@supports (not (mask-image: url(x))) and (not (-webkit-mask-image: url(x))) {
  .shaped-element {
    /* Use a simple rounded rectangle as fallback */
    clip-path: inset(5% round 15px);
  }
}
```
